Nice, a county and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy. The inhabitants supply <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> ships; and carry on a great trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>.—Although the county of Nice be on this side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, geographers have always considered it as a province of Italy, since they have given to this beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Italy the river Var for a western limit, which is also the boundary of the county, and flows into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> distance from the capital. This province is partly covered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; and is bordered on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and the states of Genoa; on the south by the Mediterranean; on the west by the Var; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Dauphiny. Its length is about 20 leagues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which make about 36 English miles; its breadth is 10 leagues; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is about 129,000 souls. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Nice is the capital, and the seat of the senate, the bishopric, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. It has become, within these few years, a delightful abode, by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of strangers who assemble there in the winter, either to re-establish their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to enjoy the mildness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the country, where an unceasing verdure presents eternal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The town is situated on the sea shore, and is backed by a rock entirely insulated, on which was formerly a castle, much esteemed for its position; but it was destroyed in the year 1706 by Marechal Berwick, the garrison being too thin to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the works. There is a distinction between the old and the new town; this last is regular, the houses are well built, and the streets are wide. Its position is by the side of the sea, and it is terminated, on one side, by a charming terrace, which serves for a promenade. Any person may live peaceably in this province, without fear of being troubled on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, provided he conduct himself with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>. The town has three suburbs. 1st, That of St John, which conduces to Cimier, about three leagues north from Nice, &c. The promenades this way are very delightful, and may be enjoyed in a carriage. 2d, That of the Poudriere. That of the Croix de Marbre, or Marble <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>. This suburb is new; and the English almost all lodge in it, being very near the town. The houses are commodious, facing on one side the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> which leads to France, and on the other a fine garden, with a prospect of the sea. All the houses are separate from each other: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> hire them for the season, i.e. from October till May. Apartments may be had from 15 to 250 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">louis</a>. The proprietors <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> furnish linen, plate, &c. There are also in the town very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and commodious houses; as well as the new road, which is opened from the town to the port, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> that part of the rock which inclined toward the sea. The situation is delightful, and warmest in winter, being entirely covered from the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and quite open to the south. "The company is brilliant at Nice, and the amusements of the Carnival are, in proportion to the size of the town, as lively as in any of the great ones in France. There is always an Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> and masked <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, alternately; and the company play rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. "It is impossible to find a happier climate than Nice, both for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter. Reamur's thermometer, in 1781, never fell more than three degrees below the freezing point, and that only for two days; while at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> it fell ten: and in the course of the winter of 1785 it fell only two degrees; while at Geneva it fell 15. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May is rarely so fine in France as February at Nice. The summer is not so hot as might be expected. The thermometer never rises more than 24 degrees (86° Fahrenheit) above temperate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; and there is always an agreeable sea breeze from ten in the morning till sunset, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> breeze comes on. There are three chains of graduated mountains, the last of which confound their summits with the Alps; and to this triple rampart is owing the mild temperature so sensibly different from that of the neighbouring parts. "The cultivation of the ground is as rich as can be desired. There are alternately rows of corn and beans, separated by vines attached to different fruit-trees, the almond and the fig; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> being incessantly cultivated, and covered with trees, olive, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, pomegranate, laurel, and myrtle, causes the constant appearance of spring, and forms a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> with the summits of the Alps, in the background, covered with snow." Nice, an ancient town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, now called Nice, with a Greek archbishop's see. It is famous for the general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> assembled here in 325, which endeavoured to suppress the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>. It was formerly a large, populous, and well built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and even now is not inconsiderable. See Nice. Nicene Creed, was composed and established, as a proper summary of the Christian faith, by the council at Nice in 325, against the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>.—It is also called the Constantinopolitan creed, because it was confirmed, with some few alterations, by the council of Constantinople in 381. See Creed. Nicephorus Gregoras, a Greek historian, was born about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 13th century, and flourished in the 14th, under the emperors Andronicus, John Palaeologus, and John Cantacuzenus. He was a great favourite of the elder Andronicus, who made him librarian of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Constantinople, and sent him Nicephorus, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>. He accompanied this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> in his misfortunes, and assisted at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; after which he repaired to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the younger Andronicus, where he seems to have been well received; and it is certain that, by his influence over the Greeks, that church was prevailed on to refuse entering into any conference with the legates of Pope John XXII. But in the dispute which arose between Barlaam and Palamos, taking the part of the former, he maintained it zealously in the council that was held at Constantinople in 1351, for which he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there till the return of John Palaeologus, who released him; after which he held a disputation with Palamos, in the presence of that emperor. He compiled a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which in 11 books contains all that passed from 1204, when Constantinople was taken by the French, to the death of Andronicus Palaeologus the younger, in 1341.—The best edition of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is that of the Louvre, in Greek and Latin, in 1792. Nicephorus, Caliphus, a Greek historian, who flourished in the 14th century under the emperor Andronicus Palaeologus the elder, wrote an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history in 23 books; 18 of which are still extant, containing the transactions of the church from the birth of Christ to the death of the emperor Phocas in 610.—We have nothing else but the arguments of the other five books, from the commencement of the reign of the emperor Heraclius, to the end of that of Leo the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a>, who died in the year 911. Nicephorus dedicated his history to Andronicus Palaeologus the elder. It was translated into Latin by John Langius; and has gone through several editions, the best of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1630. Nicéron, John Francis, a French philosopher, was born at Paris in 1613. Having finished his academical studies, with a success which raised the greatest hopes of him, he entered into the order of the Minims, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in 1632; and, as is usual, he changed the name given him at his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> for that of Francis, the name of his paternal uncle, who was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">Minim</a>, or Franciscan. The inclination and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which he had for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> appeared early. He began to apply himself to that science in his philosophical studies, and devoted to it all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he could spare from his other employments, after he had completed his studies in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. All the branches of the mathematics, however, did not equally engage his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; he confined himself particularly to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, and only learned of the rest as much as was necessary for rendering him perfect in this. There remain still, in several houses wherein he dwelt, especially at Paris, some excellent performances, which discover his skill in this way, and which make us regret that a longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> did not suffer him to carry it to that perfection which he desired; since one cannot help being surprized that he proceeded so far as he did, in the midst of those occupations and travels by which he was forced from it, during the short space of time which he lived. He hath himself observed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his Thaumaturgus Opticus, that he went twice to Rome; and that, on his return home, he was appointed teacher of theology. He was afterwards chosen to accompany Father Francis de la Noue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> general of the order, in his visitation of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> throughout all France. But the eagerness of of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> put him upon making the best of all the moments he had to spare for books; and that wife economy furnished him with as much as satisfied him. Being taken sick at Aix in Provence, he died there Sept. 22. 1646, aged 33. He was an intimate acquaintance of Des Cartes. The following are his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works: 1. L'Interpretation des chiffres, ou règles pour bien entendre et expliquer facilement toutes sortes des chiffres simples, &c. 2. La <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> curieuse, ou magie artificielle des effets merveilleux de l'optique, catoptrique, et dioptrique. This is only an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> to the following work: 3. Thaumaturgus opticus; i.e., Admiranda opticae, catoptrices, et dioptrices, pars prima, &c. Two other parts were intended to complete the latter work, but were unfinished at his death.

NICERON

Pages 7-7

John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, so much celebrated on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Men illustrious in the Republic of Letters, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 11. 1685. He was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, who were in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute about 1540. He studied with success in the Mazarine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Paris, and afterwards at the college Du Plessis. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, resolving to forsake the world, he consulted one of his uncles, who belonged to the order of Barnabite Jesuits. This uncle examined him; and, not dissident of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, introduced him as a probationer to that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> at Paris. He was received there in 1702, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in 1703, and made his vows in 1704, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 19. After he had professed himself, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTARGIS">Montargis</a>, to go through a course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; thence he went to Loches in Touraine to teach those sciences. He received the priesthood at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a> in 1708. As he was not arrived at the age to assume this order, a dispensation, which his uncommon piety had merited, was obtained in his favour. The college of Montargis having recalled him, he was their professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> two years, and of philosophy four.—In spite of all these avocations, he was humbly attentive to every call and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, and to the instruction of his fellow creatures, many of whom heard him deliver out fit rules of conduct for them, not only from the pulpits of most of the churches within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, but even from those of Paris.—In 1716, his superiors invited him to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, that he might have an opportunity of following, with the more convenience, those studies for which he always had expressed the greatest inclination. He not only understood the ancient but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages; a circumstance of infinite advantage in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of those works which he has given to the public, and which he carried on with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> assiduity to the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened, after a short illness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 8. 1738, at the age of 53. His works are, 1. Le <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Felirifuge; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, a Dissertation to prove that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is the best remedy in fevers, and even in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, translated from the English of John Hancock minister of St Margaret's, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in 12mo. This little treatise made its appearance, amongst other pieces relating to this subject, in 1720; and was attended with a success which carried it through three editions; the last came out in 1730, in 2 vols. 12mo, entitled, A Treatise on Common Water; Paris, printed by Cavelier. 2. The Voyages of John Ovington to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the revolution in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Golconda, and some observations upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; Paris, 1725, 2 vols. 12mo. 3. The Conversion of England to Christianity, compared with its pretended Reformation, a work translated from the English; Paris 1729, 8vo. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, translated from the English of Mr Woodward, by M. Nogues, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in physic; with an answer to the objections of Dr Camerarius; containing also several letters written on the same subject, and a methodical distribution of fossils, translated from the English by Niceron; Paris, 1735, 4to. 5. Memoirs of Men Illustrious in the Republic of Letters, with a critical account of their works; Paris, 12mo. The first volume of this great work appeared in 1727; the others were given to the public in succession, as far as the 39th, which appeared in 1738. The 40th volume was published after the death of the author, in 1739.

NICETAS

Pages 7-7

Arhominater, a Greek historian of the 13th century, called Coniates, as being born at Chone, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Colossus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. He was employed in several considerable affairs at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Constantinople; and when that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken by the French in 1204, he withdrew, with a young girl taken from the enemy, to Nice in Bithynia, where he married his captive, and died in 1206. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, or Annals, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Alexius Comnenus in the year 1118, to that of Baldwin in 1205; of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we have a Latin translation by Jerome Wolfius, printed at Bafil in 1557; and it has been inserted in the body of the Byzantine Historians, printed in France at the Louvre.

NICHE

Pages 7-7

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a hollow sunk into a wall, for the commodious and agreeable placing of a statue. The word comes from the Italian nechia, "feast-shell;" in regard the statue is here enclosed in a shell, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps on account of the shell wherewith the tops of some of them are adorned.

NICHOLLS

Pages 7-9

Dr Frank, physician and anatomist, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1699. His father was a barrister at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and both his parents were of good families in Cornwall. After receiving the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at a private school in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where his docility and sweetness of temper endeared him equally to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and his school fellows, Frank was in a few years removed to Weyminster, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sojourner) of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, under the tuition of Mr John Haviland, on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 4. 1714. There he applied himself diligently to all the usual academical studies, but particularly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and polite literature. Nicholls literature, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> were most conspicuous in his subsequent lectures on physiology. After <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> a few books on anatomy, in order to perfect himself in the nomenclature of the animal parts then adopted, he engaged in dissections, and then devoted himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, perfectly free and unbiased by the opinions of others. On his being chosen reader of anatomy in that university, he employed his utmost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to elevate and illustrate a science which had there been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> depressed and neglected; and by quitting the beaten track of former lecturers, and minutely investigating the texture of every bowel, the nature and order of every vessel, &c. he gained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> reputation. He did not then reside at Oxford; but, when he had finished his lectures, used to repair to London, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his abode, where he had determined to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>. He had once an intention of fixing in Cornwall, and for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> practised there with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; but being soon tired of the fatigues attendant on that profession in the country, he returned to London, bringing back with him a great insight, acquired by diligent observation, into the nature of the miliary fever, which was attended with the most salutary effects in his subsequent practice at London. About this time he resolved to visit the continent, partly with a view of acquiring the knowledge of men, manners, and languages; but chiefly to acquaint himself with the opinions of foreign naturalists on his favourite study. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, by conversing freely with the learned, he soon recommended himself to their notice and esteem. Windlow's was the only good system of physiology at that time known in France, and Morgagni's and Santorini's of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which Dr Nicholls likewise soon after visited. On his return to England, he repeated his physiological lectures in London, which were much frequented, not only by students from both the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, but also by many surgeons, apothecaries, and others. Soon after, his new and successful treatment of the miliary fever, then very prevalent in the southern parts of England, added much to his reputation. In 1725, at a meeting of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, he gave his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on the nature of aneurysms, in which he differed from Dr Freind in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic. At the beginning of the year 1728, he was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society, to which he afterwards communicated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of an uncommon disorder (published in the Transactions), viz. a polypus, resembling a branch of the pulmonary vein (for which Tulpus has strangely mistaken it), coughed up by an asthmatic person. He also made observations (in the same volume of the Transactions) on a treatise by M. Helvetius of Paris, on the Lungs. Towards the end of the year 1729, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic at Oxford. At his return to London, he underwent an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and censors of the College of Physicians, previous to his being admitted a candidate, which every practitioner must be a year before he can apply to be chosen a fellow. Dr Nicholls was chosen into the college on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 26, 1732; and two years after, being chosen Gulstonian reader of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATHOLOGY">Pathology</a>, he made the structure of the heart, and the circulation of the blood, the subject of his lectures. In 1736, at the request of the president, he again read the Gulstonian lecture; taking for his subject those parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body which serve for the secretion and discharge of the urine; and the causes, symptoms, and cure of the diseases occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. In 1739, he delivered the anniversary Harveian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>. In 1743, he married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, youngest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the celebrated Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>, by whom he had five children, two of whom died young. Two sons and a daughter survived him. In 1748, Dr Nicholls undertook the office of chirurgical lecturer, beginning with a learned and elegant dissertation on the Anima Medica. About this time, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr John Cunningham, one of the elects of the college, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> was chosen to succeed him in preference to our author, who was his senior, without any apparent reason. With a just resentment, he immediately resigned the office of chirurgical lecturer, and never after attended the meetings of the fellows, except when business of the utmost importance was in agitation. In 1751, he took some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> in an anonymous pamphlet, entitled "The petition of the Unborn Babes to the Censors of the Royal College of Physicians of London?" in which Dr Nefit (Pocus), Dr Maule (Maulus), Dr Barrowby (Barboune), principally, and Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, Sir Edward Hulfe, and the Scots incidentally, are the objects of his satire. In 1753, on the death of Sir Hans Sloane, Bart. in his 94th year, Dr Nicholls was appointed to succeed him as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s physicians, and held that office till the death of his royal master in 1760; when this most skilful physician was superseded with something like the offer of a pension, which he rejected with disdain. The causes, &c. of the uncommon disorder of which the late king died, viz. a rupture of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ventricle of the heart, our author explained in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Macclesfield, president of the Royal Society, which was published in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. I. In 1772, to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of his treatise De Anima Medica, he added a dissertation De motu cordis et sanguinis in homine nato et non nato, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to his learned friend and coadjutor the late Dr Lawrence. Tired at length of London, and also desirous of superintending the education of his son, he removed to Oxford, where he had spent most agreeably some years in his youth. But when the study of the law recalled Mr Nicholls to London, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Epsom, where he passed the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a literary retirement, not inattentive to natural philosophy, especially the cultivation of grain, and the improvement of barren soils, and contemplating also with admiration the internal nature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, as taught by Linnaeus. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> never was robust. In his youth, at Oxford, he was with difficulty recovered from a dangerous fever by the skill of Doctors Frampton and Frewen; and afterwards at London he had frequently been afflicted with a catarrh, and an inveterate asthmatic cough, which, returning with great violence at the beginning of the year 1778, deprived the world of this valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 7th, in the 80th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Dr Lawrence, formerly president of the college of physicians, who gratefully ascribed all his physiological and medical knowledge to his precepts, and who, while he Nicias he lived, loved him as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and revered him as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, two years after printed, and gave to his friends, a few copies of an elegant Latin Life of Dr Nicholls (with his head prefixed, a striking likeness, engraved by Hall from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of Golfei, 1779); from which, through the medium of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, the above particulars are chiefly extracted.

NICIAS

Pages 9-9

a celebrated painter of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, flourished about 322 years before the Christian era; and was universally extolled for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety and noble choice of his subjects, the force and relievo of his figures, his skill in the distribution of the lights and shades, and his dexterity in representing all sorts of four-footed animals, beyond any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His most celebrated piece was that of Tartarus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">Hell</a>, as it is described by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, for which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> the son of Lagus offered him 60 talents, or 11,250l. which he refused, and generously presented it to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He was much esteemed likewise by all his contemporaries for his excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>.

NICKEL

Pages 9-9

a metallic substance; for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for an account of its ores, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

NICOBAR ISLANDS

Pages 9-11

the name of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, lying at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. The largest of these islands is about 40 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and the inhabitants are said to be a harmless sort of people, ready to supply the ships that stop there with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The fourth end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Nicobar is placed in east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 94° 23' 30"; and we collect from Mr Rennell's Memoir, that it is within the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. Of the northernmost <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is called Carnicobar, we have, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the Asiatic Researches, some interesting information respecting both the produce and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the manners of its inhabitants. The author of the memoir is Mr G. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, who, in his account of this island, says, "It is low, of a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, about 40 miles in circumference, and appears at a distance as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> entirely covered with trees; however, there are several well cleared and delightful spots upon it. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> kind of clay, and marshy. It produces in great abundance, and with little care, most of the tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, such as pine apples, plantains, papayas, cocoa-nuts, and areca-nuts; also excellent yams, and a root called cachu. The only four-footed animals upon the island are, hogs, dogs, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rats, and an animal of the lizard kind, but large, called by the natives tolongui; these frequently carry off fowls and chickens. The only kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> are hens, and those not in great plenty. There is an abundance of snakes of many different kinds, and the inhabitants frequently die of their bites. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> upon the island is of many sorts, in great plenty, and some of it remarkably large, affording excellent materials for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> repairing ships. "The natives are low in stature, but very well made, and surprisingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and strong; they are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-coloured, and their features have a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of the Malay, quite the reverse of elegant. The women in particular are extremely ugly. The men cut their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> short, and the women have their heads shaved quite bare, and wear no covering but a short petticoat, made of a sort of rush or dry grass, which reaches half way <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the thigh. This grass is not interwoven, but hangs round the person something like the thatching of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Such of Nicobar. them as have received presents of cloth petticoats from the ships, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> tie them round immediately under the arms. The men wear nothing but a narrow strip of cloth about the middle, in which they wrap up their privacies so tight that there hardly is any appearance of them. The ears of both sexes are pierced when young; and by squeezing into the holes large plugs of wood, or hanging heavy weights of shells, they contrive to render them wide, and disagreeable to look at. They are naturally disposed to be good humoured and gay, and are very fond of fitting at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with Europeans, where they eat everything that is set before them; and they eat most enormously. They do not care much for wine, but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> drink bumpers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARRACK">arrack</a> as long as they can feel. A great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is spent in feasting and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>. When a feast is held at any village, every one that chooses goes uninvited, for they are utter strangers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. At those feasts they eat immense quantities of pork, which is their favourite food. Their hogs are remarkably fat, being fed upon the cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> kernel and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; indeed all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, fowls, dogs, &c., are fed upon the same. They have likewise plenty of small sea fish, which they strike very dexterously with lances, wading into the sea about knee deep. They are sure of killing a very small fish at 10 or 12 yards distance. They eat the pork almost raw, giving it only a hasty grill over a quick fire. They roast a fowl, by running a piece of wood through it, by way of spit, and holding it over a brisk fire until the feathers are burnt off, when it is ready for eating, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. They never drink water; only cocoa-nut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and a liquor called soura which oozes from the cocoa-nut tree after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the young sprouts or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. This they suffer to ferment before it is used, and then it is intoxicating; to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they add much by their method of drinking it, by sucking it slowly through a small straw. After eating, the young men and women, who are fancifully dressed with leaves, go to dancing, and the old people surround them smoking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> and drinking soura. The dancers, while performing, sing some of their tunes, which are far from wanting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, and to which they keep exact time. Of musical instruments they have only one kind, and that the simplest. It is a hollow bamboo about two feet and a half long and three inches in diameter, along the outside of which there is stretched from end to end a single string made of the threads of a split <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under the string is hollowed a little to prevent it from touching. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is played upon in the same manner as a guitar. It is capable of producing but few notes; the performer, however, makes it speak harmoniously, and generally accompanies it with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. "Their houses are generally built upon the beach; in villages of 15 or 20 houses each; and each house contains a family of 20 persons and upwards. These habitations are raised upon wooden pillars about 10 feet from the ground; they are round, and, having no windows, are like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-hives, covered with thatch. The entry is through a trap door below, where the family mount by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, which is drawn up at night. This manner of building is intended to secure the houses from being infested with snakes and rats; and for that purpose the pillars are bound round with a smooth kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>," leaf, which prevents animals from being able to mount; besides which, each pillar has a broad round flat piece of wood near the top of it, the projecting of which effectually prevents the further progress of such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> as may have passed the leaf. The flooring is made with thin strips of bamboos, laid at such distances from one another as to leave free admittance for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and the inside is neatly finished and decorated with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> lances, nets, &c. "The art of making cloth of any kind is quite unknown to the inhabitants of this island; what they have is got from the ships that come to trade in coconuts. "They purchase a much larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of cloth than is consumed upon their own island. This is intended for the Choury market. Choury is a small island to the southward of theirs, to which a large fleet of their boats sails every year about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of November, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> cloth for canoes; for they cannot make these themselves. This voyage they perform by the help of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and stars, for they know nothing of the compass. "In their disposition there are two remarkable qualities. One is their entire neglect of compliment and ceremony; and the other, their aversion to dishonesty. A Caribocobarian travelling to a distant village, upon business or amusement, passes through many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in his way without speaking to any one; if he is hungry or tired, he goes into the nearest house, and helps himself to what he wants, and sits till he is fed, without taking the smallest notice of any of the family unless he has business or news to communicate. Theft or robbery is so very rare amongst them, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> going out of his house never takes away his ladder or shuts his door, but leaves it open for any body to enter that pleases without the least <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of having anything stolen from him. "Their intercourse with strangers is so frequent, that they have acquired in general the barbarous Portuguese so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> quite different from most others, their words being pronounced with a kind of stop, or catch in the throat, at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. "They have no notion of a God, but they believe firmly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, and worship him from fear. In every village there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> pole erected with long strings of ground rattans hanging from it, which, it is said, has the virtue to keep him at a distance. When they see any signs of an approaching storm, they imagine that the devil intends them a visit, upon which many superstitious ceremonies are performed. The people of every village <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> round their own boundaries, and fix up at different distances small sticks split at the top, into which split they put a piece of cocoa-nut, a whip of tobacco, and the leaf of a certain plant; whether this is meant as a peace offering to the devil or a scarecrow to frighten him away, does not appear. "When a man dies, all his live stock, cloth, hatchets, fishing lances, and in short every moveable thing he possessed, is buried with him, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is mourned by the whole village. In one view this is an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, seeing it prevents all disputes about the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the deceased amongst his relations. His wife must conform to custom by having a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> cut off from one of her fingers; and if she refuses this, she must submit to have a deep notch cut in one of the pillars of her house. "I was once present at the funeral of an old woman. When we went into the house which had belonged to the deceased, we found it full of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> relations; some of them were employed in wrapping up the corpse in leaves and cloth, and others tearing to pieces all the cloth which had belonged to her. In another house hard by, the men of the village with a great many others from the neighbouring towns, were fitting drinking jars and smoking tobacco. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time two stout young fellows were busy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> in the sand near the house. When the women had done with the corpse, they set up a most hideous howl, upon which the people began to assemble round the grave, and four men went up into the house to bring down the body; in doing this they were much interrupted by a young man, son to the deceased, who endeavoured with all his might to prevent them; but finding it in vain, he clung round the body, and was carried to the grave along with it; there, after a violent struggle, he was turned away and conducted back to the house. The corpse being now put into the grave, and the lashings which bound the legs and arms cut, all the live stock which had been the property of the deceased, consisting of about half a dozen hogs, and as many fowls, was killed, and hung in above it; a man then approached with a bunch of leaves stuck upon the end of a pole, which he swept two or three times gently along the corpse, and then the grave was filled up. During the ceremony, the women <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make the most horrible vocal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> imaginable: the men said nothing. A few days afterwards, a kind of monument was erected over the grave, with a pole upon it, to which long strips of cloth of different colours were hung. "Polygamy is not known among them; and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> is not less severe than effectual. They cut, from the man's offending member, a piece of the foreskin proportioned to the frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> or enormity of the crime. "There seems to subsist among them a perfect equality. A few persons, from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, have a little more respect paid to them; but there is no appearance of authority one over another. Their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> seems bound rather by mutual obligations continually conferred and received; the simplest and best of all ties." It is our wish to take all opportunities of laying before our readers every authentic fact which can throw light upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. In this narrative of Mr Hamilton's respecting the natives of Caribocobar, there is however one circumstance at which we stumble. It is known to the learned, that the philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, admitted two self-existent beings, a good and an evil (see Polytheism); but we never before read of any people who had no notion of a God, and yet firmly believed in the devil. We could give instances of men worshipping the evil principle from fear, and neglecting the worship of the benevolent principle from a persuasion that he would do them all the good in his power without being bribed by sacrifices. Nicodemus, critics and oblations; but this is the only instance of which we have ever heard, of a people, under the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, who had no notion of a God! As good as is least as apparent in the world as evil, it appears to us so very unnatural to admit an evil and deny a good principle, that we cannot help thinking that Mr Hamilton, from his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the language of Carnicobar, (which he acknowledges to be different from most others), has not a perfect acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> creed of the natives: and that they believe in a good as well as in an evil principle, though they worship only the latter, from a persuasion, that to adore the former could be of no advantage either to him or to themselves. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NANCOWRY">Nancowry</a> or Soury, and Comerty, two other of the Nicobar islands, are said to be the best peopled, containing not less than 800 inhabitants. Between these islands there is a safe and spacious harbour. On the north point of Nancowry, within the harbour, the Danes have long retained a fixed settlement, protected by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> and a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and slaves.

NICODEMUS

Pages 11-11

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, a Jew by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and by feet a Pharisee (John iii. 1. &c.) The Scripture calls him a ruler of the Jews, and our Saviour gives him the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Israel. When our Saviour began to manifest himself by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, at the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> that he celebrated there after his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, Nicodemus made no doubt but that he was the Messiah, and came to him by night, that he might learn of him the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. Jesus told him, that no one could see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven except he should be born again. Nicodemus taking this in the literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, made answer, "How can a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that is old be born again?" Can he enter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> into his mother's womb?" To which Jesus replied, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a man be not born of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and of the spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit." Nicodemus asks him, "How can these things be?" Jesus answered, "Are you a master of Israel, and are you ignorant of these things? We tell you what we know, and you receive not our testimony. If you believe not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> things, and which may be called earthly, how <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> you believe me if I speak to you of heavenly things? Nobody has ascended into heaven but the Son of God, who came <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from thence. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as Moses lifted up the brazen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. For God so loved the world that he has given his only Son, so that no man who believes in him shall perish, but shall have eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>." After this conversation Nicodemus became a disciple of Jesus Christ; and there is no doubt to be made, but he came to hear him as often as our Saviour came to Jerusalem. It happened on a time, that the priests and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a> had sent officers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> Jesus (John vii. 45. &c.), who returning to them, made their report, that never man spoke as he did; to which the Pharisees replied, "Are you also of his disciples? Is there any one of the elders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pharisees that have believed in him?" Then Nicodemus thought himself obliged to make answer, saying, "Does the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> permit us to condemn any one before he is heard?" To which they replied, "Are you also a Galilean? Read the Scriptures, and you will find that never any prophet came out of Galilee." After this the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> was dismissed. At last Nicodemus declared himself openly a disciple of Jesus Christ (John xix. 39, 40.), when he came with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> of Arimathea to pay the last duties to the body of Christ, which they took down from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, embalmed, and laid in a sepulchre. We are told, that Nicodemus received baptism from the disciples of Christ; but it is not mentioned whether before or after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. It is added, that the Jews being informed of this, deposed him from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of senator, excommunicated him, and drove him from Jerusalem; but that Gamaliel, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german, took him to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and maintained him there till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when he had him buried honourably near St Stephen. There is still extant an apocryphal gospel under the name of Nicodemus, which in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> bears the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Acts of Pilate.

NICOLAITANS

Pages 11-11

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics, who assumed this name from Nicholas of Antioch; who, being a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> by birth, first embraced Judaism and then Christianity; when his zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> recommended him to the church of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, by whom he was chosen one of the first deacons. Many of the primitive writers believe that Nicholas was rather the occasion than the author of the infamous practices of those who assumed his name, who were expressly condemned by the Spirit of God himself, Rev. ii. 6. And indeed their opinions and actions were highly extravagant and criminal. They allowed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of wives, and made no distinction between ordinary meats and those offered to idols. According to Eusebius, they subsisted but a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but Tertullian says, that they only changed their name, and that their heresies passed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Cainites.

NICOLAS

Pages 11-11

St., an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and one of the most considerable of those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Verde, lying between Santa Lucia and St Jago. It is of a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and about 75 miles in length. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is stony, mountainous, and barren; there are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many goats in a valley inhabited by the Portuguese. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33° 33'. N. Lat. 17° O.

NICOLO

Pages 11-11

St., the most considerable, strongest, and best peopled of the isles of Tremei in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, to the east of St Domino, and to the south of Caparata. It has a harbour defended by several towers; and a fortress, in which is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, with a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 37'. N. Lat. 42° 10'.

NICOMEDES

Pages 11-12

the name of several kings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Bithynia. See BITHYNIA. NICOMEDES I. had no sooner taken possession of his father's throne, before Christ 270, than, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which has in all ages been too prevalent among the depots of the east, he caused two of his brothers to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The youngest, Zibaces, having saved himself by timely flight, landed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Bithynia, which was then known by the names of Thracia Thynica, and Thracia Asiatica, and there maintained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. Nicomedes being informed that Antiochus Soter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, was making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> preparations to attack him at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, called in the Gauls to his assistance; and on this occasion that people first passed into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>—Nicomedes having with their assistance repulsed Antiochus, Nicomedes, thus, overcame his brother, and acquired the possession of all his father's dominions, bestowed upon them that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> which from them was called Gallo-Grecia, and Gallatia. Having now no enemies to contend with, he applied himself to the enlarging and adorning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Aflacus, which he called after his own name <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOMEDIA">Nicomedia</a>. He had two wives, and by one of them he was persuaded to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to her son, in preference to his elder brothers; but when <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> how he died is not certainly known. Nicomedes II., the grandson of the former, began his reign like him, by sacrificing his brothers to his jealousy, after having waded to the throne in the blood of Prusias his father. He assumed the name of Epiphanes, or "the Illustrious," though he performed nothing worthy of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, or even of notice, during the whole time of his long reign. He was succeeded by his son— Nicomedes III., named by antiphrasis, Philopater, because he had murdered his father to get possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This monarch having entered into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> the Great king of Pontus, invaded Paphlagonia; and having seized on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he attempted likewise to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Cappadocia. This country, however, was at that time subject to his powerful ally; who thereupon marching into Bithynia at the head of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, drove Nicomedes from the throne, and raised his brother <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> to it in his room. The dethroned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who expelled the usurper, and restored him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions. For this favour they preferred him, and at length prevailed upon him, contrary to his own inclination, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his friends, to make incursions into the territories of Mithridates, with whom Rome wanted a subject of dispute. The king of Pontus bore for some time the devastations committed by Nicomedes with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, that he might not seem to be the aggressor; but at last he routed his army on the banks of the Amnus, drove him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time from his dominions, and obliged him to seek for shelter in Paphlagonia, where he led a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> till the time of Sylla, who replaced him on the throne. He was succeeded by his son— Nicomedes IV., who performed nothing which the many writers who flourished in his time have thought worth transmitting to posterity. As he died without issue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, he left his kingdom by his last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the Romans, who reduced it to the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. Sallust, disagreeing with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, tells us, that Nicomedes left a son named Mula or Myra; and introduces Mithridates as complaining of the Romans to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARSACES">Arsaces</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, for seizing on the kingdom of Bithynia, and excluding the son of a prince who had on all occasions shown himself a steady friend to their republic. But this Mula was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and not the son of Nicomedes, as we are told in express terms by Suetonius, Velleius Paterculus, and Appian. All we know of her is, that upon the death of her father she claimed the kingdom of Bithynia for her son, as the next male heir to the crown, but without success; no motives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> being of such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> with the ambitious Romans as to make them part with a kingdom.

NICOMEDIA

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Bithynia, built by Nicomedes the grandfather of Prusias. It is situated on a point of the Sinus Aflacenus (Pliny); named the Beautiful, (Athenæus): the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bithynia, (Paulianas), who says it was formerly called Aflacus; though Pliny distinguishes Aflacus and Nicomedia as different cities. Nicomedia was very famous, not only under its own kings, but under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: it was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Diocletian, and of Constantine while Constantinople was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> Nicephorus. It is still called Nicomedia, at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Propontis in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32°. N. Lat. 41°. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; carries on a trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton, glads, and earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and is the see of a Greek archbishop.

NICOMEDUS

Pages 12-12

a geometrician, famous on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the curve called conchoid, which is equally useful in resolving the two problems of doubling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> and trisecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. It appears that he lived soon after Eratothenes, for he rallied that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> on the mechanism of his mecanabe. Geminus, who lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, has written on the conchoid, though Nicomedus was always esteemed the inventor of it. Those who <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> him four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five centuries after Jesus Christ must be ignorant of these facts, by which we are enabled to ascertain pretty nearly the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in which he lived.

NICON

Pages 12-13

a native of Russia, was born in 1613, in a village of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Nihnei Novgorod, of such obscure parents, that their names and station are not transmitted to posterity. He received at the baptismal font the name of Nikita, which afterwards, when he became monk, he changed to Nicon, the appellation by which he is more generally known. He was educated in the convent of St Macarius, under the care of a monk. From the course of his studies, which were almost solely directed to the Holy Scriptures, and the exhortations of his preceptor, he imbibed at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and was only prevented from following the bent of his mind by the persuasions and authority of his father. In conformity, however, to the wishes of his family, though contrary to his own inclination, he entered into matrimony; and, as that state precluded him from being admitted into a convent, he was ordained a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. With his wife he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ten years, partly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and partly at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, officiating as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> priest. The loss of three children, however, gave him a total disgust to the world; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, his wife was persuaded to take the veil, and he became a monk; his retreat was in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> establishment was formed, as remarkable for the austerities of its rules as the situation was in its solitude. There were about 12 monks, but they all lived in different cells. Such a system, combined with the most gloomy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, occasioned so much cloistered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> as tarnished his character, when he was afterwards called up to fulfil the duties of a public and exalted station. Our limits do not permit us to be minute in our account of his life, we must therefore be contented with barely reciting general facts. Within less than the space of five years, Nicon was successively successively created archimandrite, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of the Novofpatkoi convent, archbishop of Novogorod, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Ruffia. That he was worthy of these rapid promotions, few <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> doubt who are acquainted with his character; for he was possessed of very extraordinary qualities, such as even his enemies allow and admire. His courage was undaunted, his morals irreproachable, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> extensive and exalted, his learning deep and comprehensive, and his eloquence commanding. When archbishop, he obtained the respect of the inhabitants by his unwearied affability in the discharge of his trust; and conciliated their affections by acts of unbounded charity: Nor was he less conspicuous in the discharge of the office of patriarch, to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> he was appointed in 1652, in the 39th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Nor was he only distinguished in his own profession, for he shone even as a statesman. At length, however, he fell a victim to popular discontents; which misfortune, though he was far from deserving it, was certainly the effect of imprudence. He abdicated the office of patriarch, which would otherwise have been taken from him, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1658, and bore his reverse of fortune with heroic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>: he returned to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, and commenced his former austeritys. His innocence, however, could not protect him from further malice: his enemies obtained him to be formally deposed in 1666. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> was followed by imprisonment, which was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very rigorous, because he, conscious of his own innocence, refused to accept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for crimes of which he was not guilty. In 1676, however, he was removed to the convent of St Cyril, and enjoyed perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Nicon survived his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> 15 years. In 1681, he requested and obtained permission to return to the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, that he might end his days in that favourite spot; but he expired upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> near Yaroslav, in the 66th year of his age. His remains were transported to that convent, and buried with all the ceremonies used at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of patriarchs.

NICOPOLI

Pages 13-13

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and in Bulgaria, famous for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought between the Turks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in 1306; and where the latter were defeated with the loss of 20,000 men. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25. 33. N. Lat. 43. 46.

NICOSIA

Pages 13-13

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, where a Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> resides. It is delightfully situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Olympus and a chain of others, and was formerly well fortified by the Venetians; but the works are now in ruins. It is about 31 miles in circumference; and there are plantations of olives, almonds, lemons, oranges, mulberries, and cypress trees, interspersed among the houses, which give the town a delightful appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Sancta Sophia is an old Gothic structure, which the Turks have turned into a mosque, and destroyed the ornaments. It is 100 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and 160 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34. 45. N. Lat. 34. 54.

NICOT

Pages 13-13

John, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Villeneuve, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, was born at Nîmes, and was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> in 1559; whence he brought the plant which, from his name, was called <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOTIANA">Nicotiana</a>, but is now more generally known Nicotiana by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1603. He wrote a French and Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> in folio; a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and other works.

NICOTIANA

Pages 13-16
TOBACCO, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandra clas, and in the natural method ranking under the 28th order, Luridae. See Botany Index.—There are seven species, of which the most remarkable is the tabacum, or common tobacco plant. This was first discovered in America by the Spaniards about the year 1560, and by them imported into Europe.
