These different opinions, however, seem perfectly reconcilable; for it appears at least probable, that ancient Nineveh took in the whole of the ground which lies between these two ruined places. Mr Ives adds, that "what confirms this conjecture is, that much of this ground is now hilly, owing no doubt to the rubbish of the ancient buildings. There is one mound of 200 or 300 yards square, which stands some yards north-east of Jonah's tomb, wherein it is likely a fortification once stood. It seems to have been made by nature, or perhaps both by nature and art, for such an use." NIO semblage of every thing most agreeable in the city and the court; and mothers were extremely desirous of sending their sons to that school of politeness and good taste, that they might learn sentiments of honour and probity, and those other virtues that render men amiable in society. But the illustrious Madame de Sevigné with great justness remarks in her letters, that this school was dangerous to religion and the Christian virtues; because Ninon L'Enclos made use of seducing maxims, capable of depriving the mind of those invaluable treasures. Ninon was esteemed beautiful even in old age; and is said to have inspired violent passions at 80. She died at Paris in 1705. This lady had several children; one of whom, named Chevalier de Villiers, excited much attention by the tragic manner in which he ended his life. He became in love with Ninon, without knowing that she was his mother; and when he discovered the secret of his birth, stabbed himself in a fit of despair. There have been published the pretended Letters of Ninon L'Enclos to the Marquis de Sevigné.

NINUS

Pages 33-33

the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Assyrians, was, it is said, the son of Belus. It is added, that he enlarged <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>; conquered Zoroaster king of the Bactrians; married Semiramis of Alcald; subdued almost all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and died after a glorious reign of 52 years, about 1150 B.C.; but all these facts are uncertain. See SEMIRAMIS.

NIO

Pages 33-34

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, between Naxi to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Armago to the east, Santerino to the south, and Sikino to the west, and is about 35 miles in circumference. It is remarkable for nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, which they pretend is in this island; for they affirm that he died here in his passage from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The island is well cultivated, and not so steep as the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and the wheat which it produces is excellent; but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and wood are scarce. It is subject to the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 25. 35. N. Lat. 36. 43. NIobe, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, according to the fictions of the poets, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANTALUS">Tantalus</a>, and wife of Amphion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes; by whom she had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons and as many daughters. Having become so proud of her fertility and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> birth, as to prefer herself before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, and to slight the sacrifices offered up by the Theban matrons to that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, the children of Latona, resented this contempt. The former slew the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> children and the latter the females; upon which Niobe was struck dumb with grief, and remained without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. Cicero is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that on this account the poets feigned her to be turned into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The story of Niobe is beautifully related in the fifth book of the Metamorphoses of Ovid. That poet thus describes her transformation into stone. Widow'd and childless, lamentable state! A doleful sight, among the dead thy seat; Harden'd with woes, a statue of despair, To ev'ry breath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> unmov'd her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; Her cheek still redd'ning, but its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> dead, Faded her eyes, and set within her head. No more her pliant tongue its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> keeps, But stands congeal'd within her frozen lips. Stagnate and dull, within her purple veins, Its current stopp'd, the lifeless blood remains. Her feet their usual offices refuse, Her arms and neck their graceful gestures lose: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> are gone, And ev'n her entrails turn to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> stone. Yet still she weeps; and whirl'd by stormy winds, Borne thro' the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, her native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> finds; There fix'd, she stands upon a bleak hill; There yet her marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> eternal tears distil. Niobe in this statue is represented as in an ecstacy of grief for the loss of her offspring, and about to be converted into stone herself. She appears as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> deprived of all sensation by the excess of her sorrow, and incapable either of shedding tears <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of uttering any lamentations, as has been remarked by Cicero in the third book of his Tusculan Questions. With her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the clasps one of her little daughters, who throws herself into her bosom; which attitude equally shows the ardent affection of the mother, and expresses that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> confidence which children have in the protection of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. The whole is executed in such a wonderful manner, that this, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of her children, is reckoned by Pliny among the most beautiful works of antiquity: but he doubts to whom of the Grecian artists he ought to ascribe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of them (a). We have no certain information at what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> this celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was transported from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to Rome, nor do we know where it was first erected. Flamininius Vacca only says, that all these statues were found in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> not far from the gate of St John, and that they were afterwards placed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Ferdinand in the gardens of the Villa de Medici near Rome.—An ingenious and entertaining traveller (Dr Moore), speaking of the statue of Niobe, says, "The author of Niobe has had the judgement not to exhibit all the distresses which he might have placed in her countenance. This consummate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> was afraid of disturbing her features too much, knowing full well that the point where he was to expect most sympathy was there, where distress co-operated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and where our pity met our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Had he sought it one step farther in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, he had lost it." In the following epigram this statue is ascribed to Praxiteles: Ἐκ Ξών με Θεῖον ἀναστήσω. Ἐκ δὲ λίθῳ Ζωὴν Πραξιτέλης ψυχαλίνη σύγκρατος. While for my children's fate I vainly mourn'd, The angry gods to maffy stone me turn'd; Praxiteles a nobler feat has done, He made me live again from being stone. The author of this epigram, which is to be found in the 4th book of the Anthology, is unknown. Scaliger the father, in his Farrago Epigrammatum, p. 172, ascribes it to Callimachus, but this appears to be only conjecture. (a) Par hæsitatio in templo Apollinis Sofiani, Niobem cum liberis morientem, Scopas an Praxiteles fecerit. NIS Cælius Calcagninus has made a happy translation of it into Latin. Vivam olim in lapidem verterunt numina; sed me Praxiteles vivam reddidit ex lapide. And perhaps the following French version of it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear no less happy: De vivre que j’étois, les Dieux Mont changée en pierre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a>; Praxitele a fait beaucoup mieux, De pierre il m’a fait rendre vive.

NIPHON

Pages 34-34

the largest of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, being 600 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. See JAPAN.

NIPPERS

Pages 34-34

in the manege, are four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>’s mouth, two in the upper, and two in the lower jaw. A horse puts them forth between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third year.

NIPPLES

Pages 34-34

in Anatomy. See MAMMÆ, ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NIPPLE-WORT. See LAPSANA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index.

NISAN

Pages 34-34

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Hebrews, answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and which sometimes takes from February <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> April, according to the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. It was the first month of the sacred year, at the coming out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> (Exod. xii. 2.), and it was the seventh month of the civil year. By Moses it is called Abib. The name Nisan is only since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>, and the return from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. On the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of this month the Jews fasted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the children of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> (Lev. x. 1, 2, 3.) On the tenth day was celebrated a fast for the death of Miriam the sister of Moses; and every one provided himself with a lamb for the paschal. On this day the Israelites passed over Jordan under the conduct of Joshua (iv. 19.) On the fourteenth day in the evening they sacrificed the paschal lamb; and the day following, being the fifteenth, was held the solemn paschal (Exod. xii. 18. &c.) The sixteenth they offered the sheaf of the ears of barley as the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> of that year (Lev. xxiii. 9. &c.) The twenty-first was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> of the paschal, which was solemnized with particular ceremonies. The twenty-fifth the Jews fasted in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the death of Joshua. On this day they began their prayers to obtain the rains of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. On the twenty-ninth they called to mind the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>.

NISI PRIUS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a judicial writ which lies in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> being impannelled and returned before the justices of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, one of the parties requests to have such a writ for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in order that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> may come before the justices in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> on their coming thither. The purport of a writ of nisi prius is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> is thereby commanded to bring to Westminster the men impannelled, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, before the justices, “nisi prius judicarii domini regis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> officia requiendas venerint.”

NISIBIS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> both very ancient, very noble, and of very considerable strength, situated in a district called Mygdolonia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Mesopotamia, towards the Tigris, from which it is distant two days journey. Some ascribe its origin to Nimrod, and suppose it to be the A-had of Moses. The Macedonians called it Antiochia of Mygdolonia (Plutarch); situated at the foot of Mount Masius (Strabo). It was the Roman bulwark against the Parthians and Persians. It sustained three memorable sieges against the power of Sapor, A.D. 338, 346, and 350; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Jovianus, by an ignominious peace, delivered it up to the Persians, A.D. 363.—A colony called Septimia Nisibiana.—Another Nisibis, of Arias, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>) near the lake Arias. Mr Ives, who passed through this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1758, tells us, that “it looked pretty at a distance, being seated on a considerable eminence, at the foot of which runs a river, formerly called the Mygdolonia, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of eleven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> built over it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a> by the river, at the foot of the hill, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hills (for the town is seated on two), begin the ruins of a once more flourishing place, which reach quite up to the present town. From every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this place the most delightful prospects would appear, were the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> but properly cultivated and planted; but instead of those extensive woods of fruit trees, which Ravolfe speaks of as growing near the town, not above thirty or forty straggling trees of any kind can be perceived; and instead of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> on which he dwells so much, a very inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of acres are now remaining. The town itself is despicable, and streets extremely narrow, and the houses, even those which are of stone, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. It suffered grievously by the famine of 1757, losing almost all its inhabitants either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or desertion. The streets presented many miserable objects, who greedily devoured rinds of cucumbers, and every other refuse article of food thrown out into the highway. Here the price of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> had risen near 4000 per cent. within the last 14 years.

NISMES

Pages 34-34

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and flourishing town of France, in the department of Garde, with a bishop’s see, and an academy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth both of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and of stuffs formerly known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERGE">serge</a> of Nîmes, exceed that of all the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. There are several monuments of antiquity, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The maison carrée, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the Corinthian order, and one of the finest in the world. The temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> gone to ruin. It was taken by the English in 1417. The inhabitants were all Calvinists; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. demolished their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in 1685, and built a castle to keep them in awe. It is seated in a delightful plain, abounding in wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> and cattle. It contains a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of venerable relics of Roman antiquity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, which it is not our business to describe, though it is chiefly remarkable for these and its delightful situation. It owed much to M. de Beccelievre, a late bishop there: “A prelate (says Mr Townend) equally distinguished for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, benevolence, and piety; who, by his wisdom and beneficence, in the space of 45 years, much more than doubled the number of inhabitants of Nîmes; for, having found only 20,000, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of seeing 50,000 rise up to call him blest.” Mr Wraxal says “it is an ill built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, containing in itself nothing extraordinary or remarkable.” A hundred fables are related concerning its origin, which is carried into times anterior by many centuries to the Roman conquests. It probably does not occupy at present the fourth part of the ground on which it formerly stood. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 26. N. Lat. 43. 51.

NISROCH

Pages 34-35

a god of the Assyrians. Sennacherib was killed by two of his sons while he was paying his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to his god Nisroch in his temple (2 Kings xix. 37.) It is not known who this god Nisroch was. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> calls him Melech, Josephus calls him Arakes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> of Tobit published by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> calls him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>. The Jews have a strange notion concerning this deity, and fancy him to have been a plank of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s ark. Some think the word signifies a dove; and others understand by it an eagle, which has given occasion to an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Belus, from whom the Assyrian kings pretended to be derived, was worshipped by them under the form of an eagle, and called Nisroch. Our poet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> gives this name to one of the rebel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. —In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> next up stood Nisroch, of principalities the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Par. Lost, book vi. 447.

NISSOLIA

Pages 35-35

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 3rd order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NITHRARIA

Pages 35-35

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NITHSDALE

Pages 35-35

Nithsdale, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Niddisdale, a district of Dumfriesshire in Scotland, lying to the westward of Annandale. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and mountainous tract, deriving its name from the river Nid, which rises on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>, and running by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANQUHAR">Sanquhar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>, discharges itself into the Solway frith. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was formerly famed with noble forests, which are now almost destroyed; so that at present, nothing can be more naked, wild, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>. Yet the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and, as is said, silver and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are covered with sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; and here are still some considerable remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> woods, particularly that of Holywood, three miles from Dumfries, noted for a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, built out of the ruins of an ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; and also for being the birthplace of the famous astrologer, hence called Johannes de Sacro <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSCO">Bosco</a>. Mr Pennant calls it a beautiful vale, improved in appearance by the bold curvatures of the meandering stream, and for some space, he says, it is adorned with groves and gentlemen's seats.

NITOCRIS

Pages 35-35

the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a> (whose father was Evil Merodach and his grandfather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>), was a woman of extraordinary abilities: she took the burden of all public affairs upon herself; and, while her son followed his pleasures, did all that could be done by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to sustain the tottering empire. She perfected the works which Nebuchadnezzar had begun for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>; raised strong fortifications on the side of the river, and caused a wonderful vault to be made under it, leading from the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to the new, 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 15 wide. She likewise built a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and accomplished several other works, which were afterwards ascribed to Nebuchadnezzar. Philostratus, in describing this bridge, tells us, that it was built by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, who was a native of Media; whence we may conclude this illustrious queen to have been by birth a Mede. Nitocris is said to have placed her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> over one of the most remarkable gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with an inscription to the following effect: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Babylon after me shall be in distress for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, he may open this sepulchre, and take out as much as may serve him; but if he be in no real <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, let him forbear, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> he shall have cause to repent of his presumption. This monument and inscription are said to have remained untouched till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>, who, considering the gate was useless, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> caring to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under a dead body, and being invited by the hopes of an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, broke it open; but, instead of what he sought, is said to have found nothing but a corpse; and another inscription, to the following effect: Hadst thou not been most insatiably avaricious and greedy of the most forlorn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, thou wouldst never have violated the abode of the dead.

NITRE

Pages 35-35
or Saltpetre. See Chemistry, No 938, et seq. Calcaceous Nitre. See Lime, Nitrate of, Chemistry Index.

NITROUS

Pages 35-35

anything impregnated with nitrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Nitrous Air. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NIVELLE

Pages 35-35

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brabant, remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of canonesses. Here is a manufacture of canvases, and the town enjoys <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> privileges. The abbey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned is inhabited by young ladies of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, who are not confined therein as in nunneries, but may go out and marry whenever they see convenient, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> offers. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 36' N. Lat. 50° 35'. NIVELLE de la Chauffée (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a>), a comic poet, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; acquired great reputation by inventing a new kind of entertainment, which was called the Weeping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">Comedy</a>. Instead of imitating <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, Terence, Molière, and the other celebrated comic poets who had preceded him; and instead of exciting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> the different ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, giving strokes of humour and absurdities in conduct; he applied himself to represent the weaknesses of the heart, and to touch and soften it. In this manner he wrote five comedies: 1. La fausse Antipathie. 2. Le Prejugé à la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>; this piece met with great success. 3. Melanide. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">Amour</a> pour Amour; and, 5. L'Ecole des Mères. He was received into the French academy in 1736; and died at Paris in 1754, at 63 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He also wrote a tragedy, entitled Maximianus; and an epistle to Clio, an ingenious didactic poem.

NIVERNES

Pages 35-35

an inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, lying on the west side of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and between it, Bourbonnois, and Barri. It is pretty fertile in wine, fruit, and corn; except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> called Morvan, which is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and barren. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wood, and several <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; as also mines of pit coal, which serves to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> their forges. This province is watered by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YONNE">Yonne</a>, are navigable. It now forms the department of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, which is also the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

NIWEGAL

Pages 35-36

NIWEGAL, a village lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in Pembrokehire, South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, remarkable only for the discovery of an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the flumps of trees appearing below low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark, after and during a storm in the year 1599, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> all round is now entirely barren of wood.

NIXAPA

Pages 36-36

a rich and considerable town in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, with a rich convent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 97. 15. N. Lat. 16. 42.

NIZAM

Pages 36-36

one of the most illustrious ministers of the east, was honoured by the caliph as an oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and science; he was trusted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> as the faithful vicegerant of his power and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. After an administration of 30 years, the fame of the vizier, his wealth, and even his services, were transformed into crimes. He was overthrown by the insidious arts of a woman and a rival; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> was hastened by a rash <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, the badges of his office, were connected by the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> with the throne and diadem of the sultan. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 93 years, the venerable statesman was dismissed by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, accused by his enemies, and murdered by a fanatic: the last words of Nizam attested his innocence, and the remainder of Malek's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was short and inglorious.

NOAH

Pages 36-37
or Noe, the son of Lamech, was born in the year of the world 1656. Amidst the general corruption into which all mankind were fallen at this time, Noah alone was found to be just and perfect in his generation, walking with God (Gen. vi. 9). This extraordinary person having therefore found favour in the eyes of the Lord, and God seeing that all flesh had corrupted their ways, told Noah, that he was resolved to destroy mankind from the face of the earth, by a flood of waters; and not them alone, but all the beasts of the earth, and every creeping thing, as well as the fowls of the air (Ibid. 7.). The Lord therefore directed Noah, as a means of preserving him and his family (for he had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, who were all married before the flood), to build an ark or vessel, of a certain form and size fitted to that end, and which might besides accommodate such numbers of animals of all sorts, that were liable to perish in the flood, as would be sufficient to preserve the several species, and again replenish the earth; together with all necessary provisions for them; all which Noah performed, as may be seen more particularly under the article Ark. In the year of the world 1656, and in the 600th year of his age, Noah, by God's appointment, entered the ark, together with his wife, his three sons, their wives, and all the animals which God caused to come to Noah; and being all entered, and the door of the ark being shut upon the outside, the waters of the deluge began to fall upon the earth, and increased in such a manner, that they were fifteen cubits above the tops of the highest mountains, and continued thus upon the earth for 150 days; so that whatever had life upon the earth, or in the air, was destroyed, except such as were with Noah in the ark. But the Lord remembering Noah, sent a wind upon the earth, which caused the waters to subside; so that upon the seventeenth day of the seventh month the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat; and Noah having uncovered the roof of the ark, and observing the earth was dry, he received orders from the Lord to come out of it, with all the animals that were therein; and this he did in the five hundred and first year of his age, on the 27th day of the second month. But the history of the deluge is more circumstantially related already under the article DELUGE. Then he offered as a burnt sacrifice to the Lord one of all the pure animals that were in the ark; and the Lord accepted his sacrifice, and said to him, that he would no more pour out his curse upon the whole earth, nor any more destroy all the animals as he had now done. He gave Noah power over all the brute creation, and permitted him to eat of them, as of the herbs and fruits of the earth; except only the blood, the life of which God did not allow them. He bid him increase and multiply, made a covenant with him, and God engaged himself to send no more an universal deluge upon the earth; and as a memorial of his promise, he let his bow in the clouds, to be as a pledge of the covenant he made with Noah (Gen. ix.). Noah, being a husbandman, began now to cultivate the vine; and having made wine and drank thereof, he unwarily made himself drunk, and fell asleep in his tent, and happened to uncover himself in an indecent posture. Ham, the father of Canaan, having observed him in this condition, made himself sport with him, and acquainted his two brothers with it, who were without. But they, instead of making it a matter of sport, turned away from it, and going backwards they covered their father's nakedness, by throwing a mantle over him. Noah awaking, and knowing what Ham had done, said, that Canaan the son of Ham should be accursed, that he should be a slave of slaves in respect of his brethren. It is thought he had a mind to spare the person of his son Ham, for fear the curse might light upon upon the other children of Ham, who had no part in this action. He cursed Canaan by a spirit of prophecy, because the Canaanites his descendants were after this to be rooted out by the Israelites. Noah added, Let the Lord, the God of Shem, be blessed, and let Canaan be the servant of Shem. And he was so in effect, in the person of the Canaanites subdued by the Hebrews. Lastly, Noah said, Let God extend the possession of Japheth; let Japheth dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant. This prophecy had its accomplishment, when the Grecians, and afterwards the Romans, being descended from Japheth, made a conquest of Asia, which was the portion of Shem. But Noah lived yet after the deluge three hundred and fifty years; and the whole time of his life having been nine hundred and fifty years, he died in the year of the world 2056. He left three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, of whom mention is made under their several names; and according to the common opinion, he divided the whole world amongst them, in order to repopulate it. To Shem he gave Asia, to Ham Africa, and Europe to Japheth. Some will have it, that besides these three sons he had several others. The spurious Berosus gives him thirty, called Titans, from the name of their mother Titaea. They pretend that the Teutons or Germans are derived from a son of Noah called Thuiticon. The false Methodius also makes mention of Jonithus or Jonicus, a pretended son of Noah. St Peter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter ii. 5.), because before the deluge he was incessantly preaching and declaring to men, not only by his discourses, but by his unblameable life, and by the building of the ark, in which he was employed five score years, that the wrath of God was ready to pour upon them. But his preaching had no effect, since, when the deluge came, it found mankind plunged in their former enormities (Mat. xxiv. 37.). Several learned men have observed, that the Heathens confounded Saturn, Deucalion, Ogyges, the god Cebus or Uranus, Janus, Proteus, Prometheus, &c. with Noah. The wife of Noah is called Noria by the Gnostics; and the fable of Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha is manifestly invented from the history of Noah. The Rabbins pretend, that God gave Noah and his sons (all who are not of the chosen race of Abraham they call Noachidae) certain general precepts, which contain, according to them, the natural right which is common to all men indifferently, and the observation of which alone will be sufficient to save them. After the law of Moses, the Hebrews would not suffer any stranger to dwell in their country, unless he would conform to the precepts of the Noachidae. In war they put to death, without quarter, all that were ignorant of them. These precepts are seven in number. The first directs, that obedience be paid to judges, magistrates, and princes. By the second, the worship of false gods, superstition, and sacrilege, are absolutely forbidden. The third forbids cursing the name of God, blasphemies, and false oaths. The fourth forbids all incestuous and unlawful connexions, as sodomy, bestiality, and crimes against nature. The fifth forbids the effusion of blood of all sorts of animals, murder, wounds, and mutilations. The sixth forbids thefts, cheats, lying, &c. The seventh forbids to eat the parts of an animal still alive, as was practised by some Pagans. To these the Rabbins have added some others; but what inclines us to doubt the antiquity of these precepts is, that no mention is made of them in Scripture, or in the writings of Josephus or Philo; and that none of the ancient fathers knew anything of them.

NOB

Pages 37-37

a sacerdotal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the tribe of Benjamin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ephraim. St Jerome says, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was entirely destroyed, and that the ruins of it might be seen not far from Diospolis. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> was driven away by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, he went to Nob, and asking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> Ahimelech for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and arms, the priest gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> which had been lately taken off the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of Goliath. Saul being informed of this by Doeg, caused all the priests of Nob to be slain, and the city to be destroyed, 1 Sam. xxii. xxii.

NOBAH

Pages 37-37

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> beyond Jordan. It took the name of Nobah from an Israelite of this name who had made a conquest of it, (Num. xxxvi. 42.). Gideon pursued the Midianites as far as this city, (Judg. viii. 2.). Eusebius says, that there is a desolate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this name about eight miles from Heshbon towards the south. But this could not be the Nobah now mentioned, because it was much farther to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>.

NOBILIARY

Pages 37-37

in literary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a book containing the history of the noble families of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>: such are Choricius's Nobiliary of Dauphine, and Caumartin's Nobiliary of Provence. The Germans are said to be particularly careful of their Nobiliaries, in order to keep up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of their families.

NOBILITY

Pages 37-41

in general, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> greatness; more particularly, it signifies antiquity of family, joined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>: in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation of the word, it means that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> or dignity which raises a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a>. At a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the public mind is so much agitated on this subject, or subjects nearly allied to it, perhaps the least that is said on it the better. We should therefore (as far as concerns the question about its expediency in civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, or the contrary) most cheerfully <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it over in silence, did we not esteem it our duty to give our readers at least some idea of it, and were it not our business to lay before them a few of those arguments which of late have been so copiously retailled both for and against this illustrious order of civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>: leaving them, however, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> which every man unquestionably ought to be allowed of judging for themselves as they shall see most proper. Whether that equality of rank and condition which has of late been so loudly contended for would be more agreeable to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or more conducive to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and prosperity of mankind, may indeed be made a question; but it is a question, we apprehend, which cannot receive different answers from men capable of reflecting without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> and partiality. A state of perfect equality can subsist only among Nobility among beings possessing equal talents and equal virtues; but such beings are not men. Were all mankind under the constant influence of the laws of virtue, a distinction of ranks would be unnecessary; but in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> itself would likewise be unnecessary, because men would have attained all that perfection to which it is the object of civil government as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to guide them: every man then would be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> unto himself. But whilst, in so many breasts, the selfish passions predominate over those which are social, violence must be restrained by authority; and there can be no authority without a distinction of ranks, such as may influence the public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. It is well observed by Hume, that government is founded only on opinion; and that this opinion is of two kinds, opinion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and opinion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. When a people are persuaded that it is their interest to support the government under which they live, that government must be very stable. But among the worthless and unthinking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, this persuasion has seldom <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. All men, however, have a notion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>—of a right to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and a right to power: and when the majority of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> considers a certain order of men as having a right to that eminence in which they are placed, this opinion, call it prejudice or what we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, contributes much to the peace and happiness of civil society. There are many, however, who think otherwise, and imagine that "the society in which the greatest equality prevails must always be the most secure. These men conceive it to be the business of a good government to distribute as equally as possible those blessings which bounteous nature offers to all." It may readily be allowed that this reasoning is conclusive; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> question returns, "How far can equality prevail in a society which is secure? and what is possible to be done in the equal distribution of the blessings of nature?" Till these questions be answered, we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> nothing by declaiming on the rights and equality of men; and the answers which have sometimes been given to them suppose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were real, would make all civil institutions useless, as well as the reveries of those reformers. The conduct of the democratic states of Pagan antiquity, together with the oppressive anarchy and shameful violences which we have seen and still see in a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, will be considered by many as a full and satisfactory answer, deduced from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, to all the schemes of the visionary theorist: such facts at least render the abolition of the order of nobility a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of more importance, and of infinitely greater difficulty, than those who plead for it are disposed to allow. It is an opinion not uncommon, and at least plausible, that the nobility of a well regulated state is the best security against monarchical despotism or lawless usurpation on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the confusion of democratic insolence on the other. Self interest is the most powerful principle in the human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and it is obviously the interest of such men to preserve that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of power in society upon which the very existence of their order depends. Corrupted as the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> confessedly is, a very recent instance could be given, in which the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> rescued at once the sovereign and the people from the threatened tyranny of a factious junto. As it is our business, however, to exhibit all opinions of any celebrity, we shall lay before our readers a short extract from Du Laure's Critical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the French Nobility, which contains, in few but forcible words, some of the common arguments against this distinction of ranks. "Nobility (says he), a distinction equally impolitic and immoral, and worthy of the times of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and of rapine, which gave it birth, is a violation of the rights of that part of the nation that is deprived of it; and as equality becomes a stimulus towards distinction, so on the other hand this is the radical vice of a government and the source of a variety of evils. It is almost impossible that there should be any uncommon instances of virtue in a state, when reputations belong exclusively to a certain class of society, and when it costs them no more to obtain these than the trouble of being born. Amongst this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of privileged persons, virtues, talents, and genius, must of course be much less frequent than in the other classes, since, without the possession of any of these qualities, they who belong to it are still honoured and rewarded. Those who profit by this absurd subversion of principles, and those who lose by this unjust distribution of favours, which seem to have grown into a right, cannot have any other than false, immoral, and pernicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> concerning merit." A perfect equality, however, in rank and fortune has seldom been contended for, except by the most ignorant enthusiasts. It is indeed doubtful whether it could possibly exist. The more moderate and rational reformers have acknowledged, that as these differences have always existed in some way or other, so, from the infinite variety of talents and attainments in the world, we have reason to expect they will exist in every form of government and among every people. The question, therefore, is reduced to this: Whether the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of distinction, or any other which could be instituted in its stead, be upon the whole the best? That the present is not perfect, or wholly without faults, few will be sanguine enough to contradict: and a wise man in the sober <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of philosophical reflection will scarce presume to assert, that any other scheme which human ingenuity can <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> would be wholly without imperfection, or altogether free from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. The case is, the errors of our own system are present, and on this account we see and feel them with peculiar force: the other plan we look forward to perhaps in too sanguine a manner, and we probably forget, in the delusive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of imagination, that if distinction depended entirely on merit, we should scarce find a society of men so honest, or so able, as always to reward it according to its deserts; or if this were possible, as perhaps in the nature of things it is not, such is the self-partiality of the generality of men, that few would think he were dealt justly by if he were not promoted as well as his neighbour; and it is clearly impossible to promote every one. For such reasons then, and many more which our limits oblige us to omit, many think (and we are inclined to think with them), that it is safer to remain as we are, as we know the evils that attend our situation, and are still able to bear them, rather than to hazard a change, which, Nobility, which, with some benefits, might also perhaps increase the troubles, and destroy many of the pleasures of social life. Perhaps it may not be amiss to lay before our readers the following observations from that most judicious commentator on the laws of England, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> Blackstone, on this important subject. "The distinction of rank and honours (says he) is necessary in every well-governed state, in order to reward such as are eminent for their services to the public, in a manner the most desirable to individuals, and yet without burden to the community; exciting thereby an ambitious, yet laudable ardour, and generous emulation, in others. And emulation, or virtuous ambition, is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which, however dangerous or invidious in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> republic or under a despotic sway, will certainly be attended with good effects under a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>; where, without destroying its existence, its excesses may be continually restrained by that superior power from which all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is derived. Such a spirit, when nationally diffused, gives life and vigour to the community; it sets all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of government in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, which, under a wise regulator, may be directed to any beneficial purpose; and thereby every individual may be made subservient to the public good, while he principally means to promote his own particular views. A body of nobility is also more peculiarly necessary in our mixed and compounded <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, in order to support the rights of both the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and the people, by forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to withstand the encroachments of both. It creates and preserves that gradual <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of dignity, which proceeds from the peasant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; rising like a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> foundation, and diminishing to a point as it rises. It is this ascending and contracting proportion that adds stability to any government; for when the departure is sudden from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to another, we may pronounce that state to be precarious. The nobility, therefore, are the pillars, which are reared from among the people, more immediately to support the throne; and, if that falls, they must also be buried under its ruins. Accordingly, when in the 17th century the commons had determined to extirpate monarchy, they also voted the house of lords to be useless and dangerous. And since titles of nobility are thus expedient in the state, it is also expedient that their owners should form an independent and separate branch of the legislature. If they were confounded with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the people, and like them had only a vote in electing representatives, their privileges would soon be borne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and overwhelmed by the popular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, which would effectually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> all distinctions. It is therefore highly necessary that the body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> should have a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, distinct deliberations, and distinct powers from the commons."—These remarks, at a time like the present, deserve our serious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; nor do we suppose our readers will be displeased, if we add the following observations on the subject from a periodical publication of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> standing and very considerable merit. "Birth and nobility are a stronger obligation to virtue than is laid upon meaner persons. A vicious or dishonourable nobleman is in effect perjured; for his honour is his oath. "Under the patriarchal scheme, and at the first setting out of the tribes, the heads of families had their Nobility, particular escutcheons, and their genealogies recorded with the utmost exactness: Even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> of Days confirmed this; he often put his people in mind of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and virtues of their forefathers; and hath set a precedent for attainders, by visiting the third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. "It is a vulgar error to suppose, that his blest Son chose his followers out of the meanest of the people, because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>; for this was part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of every Jewish nobleman: Two of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, being his kinsmen, were of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>; one was a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and another of the royal family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; and for the rest, he had the same right of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> as his Father and his vicegerents, of advancing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> to honour, and of exalting the lowly and meek. "The ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> paid great regard to nobility; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> principle obtained, and the people shared power and honour, those states soon dwindled and came to ruin. And in present Rome, great respect is paid to the renowned families of Colonna and Caesarei. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the notion of nobility is carried so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to become inconsistent with a republican scheme. The Spaniards pay more regard to their old nobles than to their old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; and the French are but little behind them. What was said of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTMORENCY">Montmorency</a> by Henry IV. "That he was a better gentleman than himself," was, perhaps, the reason why the last heir of so illustrious a family was cut off, to make the house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> the first in France.—The Welsh, Irish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, are remarkable for their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to blood and pedigree. "It is for the sake of the meanest of our people, that the high value and regard for quality should be kept up; for they are best governed by those who seem formed for power: the robe of authority fits easily upon them, and submission is as much our choice as our duty; but upstarts prove the worst of tyrants. "The ancient legislators, who studied human nature, thought it advisable, for the better government of states, that the people should be divided into the noble and the common. They judged it for the universal good of mankind, that the valiant and the wise should be separated from the rest, and appointed for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and command. "To this I take it that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of nobility is owing in all countries; even those nations which we are pleased to call <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, distinguish the wise and the valiant, obey them as counsellors and commanders, which is placing them in the rank of nobles. "Some, I know, look upon the institution of nobility to be one of the grossest impositions upon the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of mankind; they confine it indeed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> nobility; they allow, that those who have done the commonwealth any signal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> should be distinguished with honours, but it seems an absurdity to them that a man should be born a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, as if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> or a knowledge of government ran in the blood. But if they would consider how strong the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of posterity is planted in human nature, they must allow that nothing can be a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to great and worthy actions, than the notion that a man's posterity will reap the honour and profit of his labours." Nobility. Besides, we are to suppose that men born to honours and a high fortune may be bred up in generous sentiments, and formed for the station they are to fill; that they must be strangers to those vicious falsehoods and corruptions which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> first, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, puts men upon practising, whose lives are spent in pursuit of their fortunes. I will own, notwithstanding all these advantages, that many of them are like rocks whose heads are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, but are so barren that they are quite incapable of producing anything; but in general, were their minds only upon a level with those of other men, we should expect better fruit from them. "As authority is founded in opinion, all wise commonwealths have been extremely jealous in keeping up the honour of their nobility. Wherever they become base, effeminate, cowardly, or servile, their authority finks, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into contempt; then the people begin to consider them as useless to government, and look upon their privileges as a grievance to society, and perhaps they think how to get rid of them, as happened in the commonwealth of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, where, after the expulsion of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, a petty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, many of the nobility having behaved fervently to him, and insolently to the people, were degraded from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and the magistracy, and rendered incapable of holding any employment in the commonwealth. "Father Paul, the Venetian, says, that you must either keep your nobility free from taint, or have no nobility at all: That the high employments of the commonwealth should be bestowed amongst the most ancient families, unless where a person should distinguish himself by some signal service to the state. Such a man would think himself sufficiently rewarded by the honour of being put upon a footing with the ancient nobility; and the nobility would be pleased to find that no commoner, except some of great reputation and merit, was to hold any of the employments usually possessed by their body. If the person so preferred should not be rich enough to support the dignity of the office, the state may give him a pension, but by no means should employments be made lucrative; which not only exhaust and weaken the commonwealth, but wherever the high employments are sought for profit, the nobility lose their generous sentiments, and it is a means of introducing corruption amongst them." The origin of nobility in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is by some referred to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; who, after they had seized a part of Europe, rewarded their captains with titles of honour, to distinguish them from the common people. We shall only in this place further consider the manner in which in our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> they may be created, and the incidents attending them; referring for a fuller account of their origin in Europe to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Revolution, and Civil Society. 1. The right of peerage seems to have been originally territorial; that is, annexed to lands, honours, castles, manors, and the like; the proprietors and possessors of which were (in right of those estates) allowed to be peers of the realm, and were summoned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and service to their sovereign; and, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> was alienated, the dignity passed with it as appendant. Thus in England the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> still sit in the house of lords in right of succession to certain ancient baronies annexed, or supposed to be Nobility annexed, to their episcopal lands; and thus in Henry VI., the possession of the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a> was adjudged to confer an earldom on its possessor. But afterwards, when Alienations grew to be frequent, the dignity of peerage was confined to the lineage of the party ennobled, and instead of territorial became personal. Actual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> became no longer necessary to constitute a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of parliament; but the record of the writ of summons to him or his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> was admitted as a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the tenure. Peers of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> are now created either by writ or by patent; for those who claim by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> must suppose either a writ or patent made to their ancestors; though by length of time it is lost. The creation by writ or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> is a summons to attend the house of peers, by the style and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of that barony which the king is pleased to confer: that by patent is a royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to a subject of any dignity and degree of peerage. The creation by writ is the more ancient way; but a man is not ennobled thereby, unless he actually take his seat in the house of lords; and some are of opinion that there must be at least two writs of summons, and a fitting in two distinct parliaments, to evidence a hereditary barony; and therefore the most usual, because the surest way, is to grant the dignity by patent, which endures to a man and his heirs according to the limitation thereof, though he never himself makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. Yet it is frequent to call up the eldest son of a peer to the house of lords by writ of summons, in the name of his father's barony, because in that case there is no danger of his children's losing the nobility in case he never takes his seat; for they will succeed to their grandfather. Creation by writ has also one advantage over that by patent; for a person created by writ holds the dignity to him and his heirs, without any words to that purport in the writ; but in letters patent there must be words to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the inheritance, else the dignity endures only to the grantee for life. For a man or woman may be created noble for their own lives, and the dignity not descend to their heirs at all, or descend only to some particular heirs: as where a peerage is limited to a man and the heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of his body by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> his present lady, and not to such heirs by any former or future wife. 2. Let us next take a view of a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> incidents attending the nobility,—exclusive of their capacity as members of parliament, and as hereditary counsellors of the crown; for both which we refer to the articles Lords and Parliament. And first we must observe, that in criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> a nobleman shall be tried by his peers. The great are always obnoxious to popular envy: were they to be judged by the people, they might be in danger from the prejudice of their judges; and would moreover be deprived of the privilege of the meanest subjects, that of being tried by their equals, which is secured to all the realm by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>, c. 29. It is said, that this does not extend to bishops, who, though they are lords of parliament, and fit there by virtue of their baronies which they hold jure ecclesiastic, yet are not ennobled in blood, and consequently not peers with the nobility. As to peersesses, no provision was made for their their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> when accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony, till after Eleanor duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, wife to the lord protector, had been accused of treason, and found guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a>, in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, through the intrigues of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>. This very extraordinary trial gave occasion to a special statute, 20 Hen. VI. c. 9, which enacts, that peers, either in their own right or by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, shall be tried before the same judicature as peers of the realm. If a woman, noble in her own right, marries a commoner, she still remains noble, and shall be tried by her peers; but if she be only noble by marriage, then by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriage with a commoner she loses her dignity; for as by marriage it is gained, by marriage it is also lost. Yet if a duchess dowager marries a baron, she continues a duchess till; for all the nobility are peers, and therefore it is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>. A peer or peeress (either in her own right or by marriage) cannot be arrested in civil cases; and they have also many peculiar privileges annexed to their peerage in the course of judicial proceedings. A peer fitting in judgement, gives not his verdict upon oath, like an ordinary jurymen, but upon his honour; he answers also to bills in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> upon his honour, and not upon his oath; but, when he is examined as a witness either in civil or criminal cases, he must be sworn; for the respect which the law shows to the honour of a peer does not extend so far as to overturn a settled maxim, that in judicio non creditur nisi juratus. The honour of peers is however so highly tendered by the law, that it is much more penal to spread false reports of them, and certain other great officers of the realm, than of other men: scandal against them being called by the peculiar name of scandalum magnatum, and subjected to peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ancient statutes. A peer cannot lose his nobility but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or attainder; though there was an instance, in the reign of Edward IV., of the degradation of George Neville duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, on account of his poverty, which rendered him unable to support his dignity. But this is a singular instance, which serves at the same time, by having happened, to show the power of parliament; and, by having happened but once, to show how tender the parliament hath been in exerting so high a power. It hath been said indeed, that if a baron wastes his estate, so that he is not able to support the degree, the king may degrade him; but it is expressly held by later authorities, that a peer cannot be degraded but by act of parliament. Antonius Matthaeus observes, that nobility, among the Romans, was a quite different thing from what it is among us. The nobles, among the Romans, were either those raised to the magistrature, or descended from magistrates: there was no such thing as nobility by patent. Bartoli says, that doctors, after they have held a professor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in an university for 20 years, become noble; and are entitled to all the rights of counts. But this claim is not admitted at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, &c. though Bartoli's sentiments be backed with those of several other authors, particularly Chaffanoux in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUCIUS">Confucius</a>-din Burgundicus; Royer for la Coutume de Berry; Faber C. de Dig. Def. 9. &c. which last, however, restrains Bartoli's rule to doctors in law, and princes physicians. By an edict of the French king in 1669, it is declared, that trade shall not derogate from nobility, provided the person do not fall by retail. In Bretagne, by ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, a nobleman loses nothing by trading even in retail; but he realiurnes all his rights as soon as he ceases traffic, his nobility having slept all the time. In Germany, a woman, not noble by birth, doth not become, v. gr. a countess or baroness by marrying a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> or baron: a lady of the higher degree indeed becomes a princess by marrying a prince; but this does not hold of a lady of the lower nobility. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, children are only capable of being noble by the mother's side; it being allowed them to take as many husbands as they please, and to quit them whenever they think proper.

NOBLE

Pages 41-42

Nobilitis, a person who has a privilege which raises him above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, either by birth, by office, or by patent from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The word comes from the Latin nobilitas; formed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nobilitas, "distinguihable, remarkable."
