In England, the word noble is of a narrower import than in other countries, being confined to persons above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of knights; whereas, abroad, it comprehends not only knights, but what we simply call gentlemen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> of England are also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> regni, as being nobilitatis pares, though gradu impares. The Venetian noblesse is famous; it is in this that the sovereignty of the state resides. It is divided into three classes. The first only comprehends 24 families. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> includes the descendants of all those who were entered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Book, in 1280, and destined to govern the state, which then began to be aristocratic. The third consists of such as have bought the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of noble Venetians. This last class is only admitted to the inferior employ; the two former to all indifferently. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of noble Venetian is sometimes also given to foreign kings, princes, &c. Nobles, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were such as had the jus imaginum, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of using the pictures or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; a right which was allowed only to those whose ancestors had borne some curule office, that is, had been curule edile, censor, praetor, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. For a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, none but the patricii were the nobles, because no person but of that superior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> could bear any curule office; hence in Livy, Sallust, &c. nobilitas is used to signify the patrician order, and opposed to plebs. To make the true meaning of nobilitas fill more clear, let it be observed, that the Roman people were divided into nobiles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">novi</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNOBILES">ignobiles</a>. Nobiles were they who had the pictures, &c. of their ancestors; novi were such as had only their own; ignobiles were such as had neither. See Jus Imaginis. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, by way of distinction, wore a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> upon their shoes, especially those of patrician rank. The Grecian nobility were called Eumegides, as being descended from those old heroic ancestors so famous in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Such were the Praxiergidae, Etrobutidae, Alexanidae, &c. all which had many privileges annexed to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; amongst which was this, that they wore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GRIFFON">griffon</a> heads in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> as a badge of nobility. Noble, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account containing six shillings and eight pence. The noble was anciently a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> struck in the reign of Edward III. and then called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; but but it was afterwards called a rofe-noble, from its being stamped with a rofe: it was current at 6s. 8d.

NOCERA

Pages 42-42

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as he is more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, the king of the Two Sicilies. It is an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but might with greater propriety be styled a cluster of villages; its several parts being extended along the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, form the Città Sotana, or low town; and the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, together with some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> embowered in cypresses groves, cover the peak of a single hill in a very picturesque manner, and compose the Città Sopra. Nocera (A), it is reported, contains near 30,000 inhabitants; they are dispersed in forty patches of habitation. Their houses are constructed of two kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> walls are built with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tufa dug out of the hills that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> to the east of the town; which stone seems unquestionably to have been formed by a conglomeration of substances thrown out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, because, on opening these quarries, the workmen have frequently discovered tombs, vases, and coins locked up in the body of the stony stratum. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of their doors and windows are made of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stone drawn from the hill of Fiano, two miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>: it lies eight feet below the surface, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> or vein 140 feet thick, resting upon a base of sand. This seems evidently to be a stream of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> congealed. Nocera is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of very considerable antiquity: in the 13th century it was called de Pagani, to distinguish it from a city in Umbria of a similar name; this addition was in allusion to a colony of Saracens which Frederick of Swabia brought from Sicily, and settled here, that they might be out of the way of their dangerous connexions with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>: hence Nocera has often been confounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCERA">Lucera</a> by the negligent or ignorant chroniclers of the succeeding ages. The most remarkable event that occurs in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is the siege of its castle, A.D. 1384. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 49'. N. Lat. 43° 1'. Terra NOCERIANA, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a> of Nocera, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, remarkably heavy, of a grayish-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, of an insipid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and generally with some particles in it which grit between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. It is much esteemed by the Italians as a remedy for venomous bites, and in fevers; but, excepting as an absorbent and astringent, no dependence is to be had on it.

NOCTAMBULI

Pages 42-42

Noctambulones, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Night-walkers; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of equal import with somnambuli, applied to persons who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of rising and walking about in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. The word is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">nox</a>, "night," and ambulo, "I walk." Schenkius, Horitius, Clauderus, and Hildanus, who have written of sleep, give us <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> unhappy histories of such noctambuli. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is moderate, the persons affected with it only repeat the actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on getting out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and go quietly to the places they frequented at other times; but those who have it in the most violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, go up to dangerous places, and do things which would terrify them to Noctiluca, think of when they are awake. These are by some called lunatic night-walkers, because fits are observed to return with the most frequency and violence at the changes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>.—For the cure some recommend purging and a cooling regimen: others are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the best method is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at the patient's bedside in such a manner that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> naturally step into it when he gets out of bed; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that should fail, a person should fit up to watch and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it happens. See Sleep-walkers, or Somnambuli.

NOCTILUCA

Pages 42-42

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of phosphorus, so called because it shines in the dark without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> being thrown upon it.

NOCTURNAL

Pages 42-42

something relating to the night, in contradistinction to diurnal. Nocturnal, Nocturnalium, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> chiefly used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of some stars about the pole, in order to find the latitude and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night. Some nocturnals are hemispheres, or planispheres, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the equinoctial. Those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among seamen are two; the one adapted to the polar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, and the first of the guards of the Little Bear; the other to the pole star, and the pointers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bear. This instrument consists of two circular plates, applied to each other. The greater, which has a handle to hold the instrument, is about 2½ inches diameter, and is divided into twelve parts, agreeing to the twelve months; and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> subdivided into every fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and so as that the middle of the handle corresponds to that day of the year wherein the star here regarded has the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ascension with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the instrument be fitted for two stars, the handle is made moveable. The upper left circle is divided into twenty-four equal parts for the twenty-four hours of the day, and each hour subdivided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. These twenty-four hours are noted by twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> to be told in the night. Those at the hour 12 are distinguished by their length. In the centre of the two circular plates is adjusted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>, moveable upon the upper plate; and the three pieces, viz. the two circles and index, are joined by a rivet which is pierced through the centre with a hole, through which the star is to be observed. To use the nocturnal, turn the upper plate till the long tooth, marked 12, be against the day of the month on the under plate; then, bringing the instrument near the eye, suspend it by the handle with the plane nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equinoctial, and viewing the pole star through the hole of the centre, turn the index about, till, by the edge coming from the centre, you see the bright star or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the Little Bear, (if the instrument be fitted to that star): then that tooth of the upper circle, under the edge of the index, is at the hour of the night on the edge of the hour circle, which may be known without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, by counting the teeth from the longest, which is for the hour 12. (a) Anciently, Nuceria Alphaterna, a word of unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>. It was a Roman colony, and had its mint. Num. Nucerin. 1. Caput virile imberbe—Equus stans <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a> reflexo inter crura. A.. IN..

NOD

Pages 42-43
or the Land of Nod. It was to this country that Cain withdrew after his fratricide, (Gen. iv. 16.). The Septuagint, as well as Josephus, read Naid instead of Nod, and have taken it for the name of a place. It is not easily known what country this was, unless perhaps it was the country of Nyle or Nylea, towards Hyrcania. St Jerome and the Chaldee interpreters have taken the word Nod in the sense of an appellative, for vagabond or fugitive; "He dwelt a fugitive in the land." But the Hebrew reads, "He dwelt in the land of Nod" (Gen. iv. 16.).

NODAB

Pages 43-43

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> bordering upon Iturea and Idumæa, but now unknown. We read in the Chronicles, that the tribe of Reuben, afflicting those of Gad and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Hagarites, the Jeturites, and the people of Nephilim, and of Nodab, in which the Israelites had the advantage (1 Chr. v. 19.). But the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and the other particulars of this war are unknown.

NODATED HYPERBOLA

Pages 43-43

a name given by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton to a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>, which, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round, decapitates <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> croffes itself. NODDY. See STERNA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NODES

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> where the orbit of a planet intersects the ecliptic. Such are the two points C and D, fig. 1, of which the node C, where the planet ascends northward above the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic, is called the ascending node, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the dragon's head, and is marked thus Ω. The other node D, where the planet descends to the south, is called the descending node, or the dragon's tail, marked thus Ψ. The line CD, wherein the two circles CEDF and CGDH intersect, is called the line of nodes. It appears from observation, that the line of the nodes of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> constantly changes its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and shifts its situation from east to west, contrary to the order of the signs; and that the line of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s nodes, by a retrograde <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, finishes its circulation in the compass of 19 years; after which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, either of the nodes having receded from any point of the ecliptic, returns to the same again; and when the moon is in the node, she is also seen in the ecliptic. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the line of nodes were immovable, that is, if it had no other motion than that whereby it is carried round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, it would always look to the same point of the ecliptic, or would keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to itself, as the axis of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> does. From what hath been said, it is evident, that the moon can never be observed precisely in the ecliptic, but twice in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; that is, when she enters the nodes. When she is at her greatest distance from the nodes, viz. in the points E, F, she is said to be in her limits. The moon must be in or near one of the nodes, when there is an eclipse of the sun or moon. To make the foregoing account of the motion of the moon's nodes still clearer, let the plane of fig. 2. represent that of the ecliptic, S the sun, T the centre of the earth, L the moon in her orbit DN dn. Nn is the line of the nodes falling between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> Q and the moon's place L, in her last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Let now LP, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> LS, represent the excess of the sun's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at T; and this being resolved into the force LR, perpendicular to the plane of the moon's orbit, and PR parallel to it, it is the former only that has any effect to alter the position of the orbit, and in this it is wholly exerted. Its effect is twofold: 1. It diminishes its inclination by a motion which we may conceive as performed round the diameter Dd, to which LT is perpendicular. 2. Being compounded with the moon's tangential motion at L, it gives it an intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> Lt, through which and the centre a plane being drawn, must meet the ecliptic nearer the conjunction C than before.

NODUS

Pages 43-43
or NODE, in Dialling, a certain point or pole in the gnomon of a dial, by the shadow or light whereof either the hour of the day in dials without furniture, or the parallels of the sun's declination, and his place in the ecliptic, &c., in dials with furniture are shown. See Dialling.

NOEOMAGUS LEXUVIORUM

Pages 43-43

(Ptol.) thought to be the Civitas Lexuviorum of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Now Lifieux, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Normandy.—Another of the Truculini; a town of Gallia Narbonensis; thought to be S. Pol. de Trois Châteaux, six miles to the west of Nyons in Dauphiné.

NOETIANS

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics in the third century, followers of Noetus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of Ephesus, who pretended that he was another Moses sent by God, and that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> was a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> consisted in affirming that there was but one person in the Godhead; and that the Word and the Holy Spirit were but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> denominations given to God in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of different operations: that, as Creator, he is called Father; as Incarnate, Son; and as descending on the apostles, Holy Ghost.

NOLA

Pages 43-43

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, formerly populous and strong, situated in a plain to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, in Campania, said to be built by the Chalcidians; (Justin, Silius Italicus); according to others, by the Tuscani. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> met with the first check by Marcellus. Vespasian added the appellation Augusta Colonia, (Frontinus). At this place, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in its neighbourhood, Augustus is said to have expired. It is also said that bells were first invented there in the beginning of the 5th century; hence their Latin names Nola or Campania. It retains its old name to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, but it hath vastly fallen short of its ancient splendour. A town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. N. Lat. 41. 5.

NOLANA

Pages 43-43

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 41st order, Aperiflorae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NOLLE PROSEQUI

Pages 43-43

is where a plaintiff in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> does not declare in a reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is usual for the defendant's attorney to enter a rule for the plaintiff to declare, after which a non pro se may be entered. A nolle prosequi is esteemed a voluntary confession, that the plaintiff has no cause of action; and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a plaintiff enters his nolle prosequi, he shall be amerced; and if an informer cause the same to be entered, the defendant shall have costs.

NOLLET

Pages 43-44

Jean <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a>, a deacon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, preceptor to the Enfans de France for physics and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, regius professor of physics in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre, member of the Academy of Sciences. Nollet. Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, and of the Academy of Sciences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERFURT">Erfurt</a>; was born at Pimbré, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Noyon, on the 17th of November 1700, of respectable but not wealthy parents. To make up the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, they determined to give their son a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. They sent him to the college of Clermont in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a>, and afterwards to Beauvais, there to finish his introductory studies. The progress which he made in the different classes, determined them to send him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at Paris. Thenceforward they intended him for the clerical order; and they considered the strictness and purity of his morals, together with his unwearied application to study, as sufficient proofs of his vocation. The young Nollet yielded without reluctance to the wishes of his parents. As soon as he was capable of showing an inclination for any thing, he had discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for physics; but this was not become his ruling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; he therefore sacrificed it to the study of scholastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, to which he wholly dedicated himself during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of probation in 1728. No sooner had he been invested with the deaconship, than he solicited and obtained a license to preach. This new occupation, however, did not make him entirely lose sight of those studies which had first engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. They insensibly began to occupy a greater portion of his time, which was now more equally divided between theology and the sciences. The latter, however, prevailed; and thenceforth he entered into the study of physics with an ardour which was only increased by that kind of privation to which he had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> subject. He was received into the Society of Arts, established at Paris under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Clermont. In 1730, the abbe Nollet was engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> conductedly with Reaumur and du Fay of the Academy of Sciences. In 1734, he went to London in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with M. M. du Fay, du Hamel, and de Juffieu. His merit procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society without any solicitation. Two years after, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he formed an intimate connection with Desaguliers, Gravefendt, and Mouchenbroeck. On his return to Paris, he resumed the course of experimental physics which he had begun in 1735, and which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1760. These courses of physics first suggested the idea of particular courses in other branches of science, such as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, anatomy, natural history, &c. In 1738, the count de Maurepas prevailed on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Fleury to establish a public class for experimental physics; and the abbe Nollet was appointed the first professor. In the beginning of the year 1739, he was admitted a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April following, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> intending to establish a professorship of physics at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, invited the abbe Nollet into his dominions. From thence he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. In 1744, he was honoured with an invitation to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, to instruct the dauphin in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>; the king and royal family were often present at his lectures. The qualities as well of his understanding as of his heart gained him the esteem and confidence of his pupil. Going one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in state to Paris, he caused intimation to be made that he was to dine at the Tuileries. M. Nollet having gone thither to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the dauphin no sooner perceived him, than he had the goodness to say, "Binet has the advantage of me, he has been at your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>." Till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> showed marks of the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> and favour for this ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He would have wished that he had been a little more attentive to the improvement of his fortune. He prevailed upon him to go and pay court to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in power, whose patronage might have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him. The abbe Nollet accordingly waited upon the placeman, and made him a present of his works. "I never read any works of that kind," said the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> coldly, and casting a look at the volumes before him. "Sir (replied the abbe), <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> you allow them to remain in your antechamber? There perhaps there may be found men of genius who will read them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>." In the month of April 1749, he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> tour into Italy, being sent thither for the purpose of making observations. At Turin, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and Bologna, the abbe Nollet appeared as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> from the philosophers of the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. During his short stay in Italy, the wonders of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> were not the only object of his researches; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of physics, the arts, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, &c. came equally under his notice. Upon his return through Turin, the king of Sardinia, always truly sensible of his merit, offered him the order of Saint Maurice, which he did not think proper to accept without his sovereign's permission. In 1753, the king instituted a class of experimental philosophy in the royal college of Navarre, and appointed the abbe Nollet professor. In 1757, he received from the king a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREVET">brevet</a> appointing him preceptor in physics and natural history to the Enfans de France. In the month of August, the same year, he was appointed professor of experimental philosophy in the school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, at that time established at la Fere. In the month of November following, he was admitted as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a> of the Royal Academy of Sciences. M. de Cremillo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> general of artillery and fortification, having founded a class of experimental philosophy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEZIERES">Mezieres</a> in 1761, the abbe Nollet was appointed professor. This celebrated and laborious philosopher, who has rendered the most important services to physics by the discoveries with which he has enriched every branch of this science, but particularly electricity, died at Paris on the 25th of April 1770, aged 70; much regretted by the literary world, and by his friends, of whom his gentle character and benevolent heart had procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. He often retired from the gay and splendid <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of Paris, to give affluence to his relations, who were by no means affluent circumstances. His works are, 1. Several papers inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences; among which one on the Hearing of Fifths is particularly valuable. 2. Leçons de Physique Experimentale, 6 vols. 12mo; a book well composed, and uniting pleasure with instruction. 3. Recueil de Lettres sur l'Electricité, 3 vols. 12mo, 1753. 4. Essai sur l'Electricité des corps, 1 vol. 12mo. 5. Recherches sur les causes particulières des Phénomènes Électriques, 1 vol. 12mo. 6. L'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a> experiences, 3 vols 12mo, with figures, 1770.

NOMADES

Pages 44-45

a name given, in antiquity, to several nations, whose whole occupation was to feed and tend their flocks; and who had no fixed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of abode, but were constantly shifting, according to the conveniences of pasturage.—The word comes from the Greek νομάς, παίκτης, "I feed." The most celebrated among the Nomades were those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, who inhabited between Africa properly so called, to the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> to the west. They are also called Numides <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Numidians—Sallust says, they were a colony of Persians brought into Africa with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. The Nomades of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> inhabited the coasts of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The Nomades of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a> were the inhabitants of Little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>; who still retain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner of living.

NOMARCHA

Pages 45-45

in antiquity, the governor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> commander of a nome or nomos.—<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> was anciently divided into several regions or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, called nomes, from the Greek νόμος, taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; and the officer who had the administration of each nome or nomos, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, was called nomarcha, from νόμος and ἀρχά, "command."

NOMBRE-DE-DIOS

Pages 45-45

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, a little to the eastward of Porto-Bello. It was formerly a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but it is now abandoned, on account of its unhealthy situation. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 78. 35. N. Lat. 9. 43.

NOMBRIL POINT

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is the next below the fess point, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the very centre of the escutcheon. Supposing the escutcheon divided into two equal parts below the fess, the first of these divisions is the nombril, and the lower the base.

NOMENCLATOR

Pages 45-45

in Roman antiquity, was usually a slave who attended upon persons that stood candidates for offices, and prompted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suggested to them the names of all the citizens they met, that they might <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> them and call them by their names, which among that people was the highest piece of civility. Nomenclators, among botanical authors, are those who have employed their labours about settling and adjusting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> names, synonyms, and etymologies of names, in regard to the whole vegetable world.

NOMENCLATURE

Pages 45-45

NOMENCLATURA, a catalogue of several of the more useful words in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with their significations, compiled in order to facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such words to those who are to learn the tongue: such are our Latin, Greek, French, &c., nomenclatures: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a> a system of technical language by which the objects of any science are denoted, as, for instance, the present language of chemical science, usually called the new chemical nomenclature, from its recent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>.

NOMENEY

Pages 45-45

a town in Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Lorraine, situated on the river Seille, 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a>.

NOMINALS

Pages 45-45
or Nominalists, a sect of school philosophers, the disciples and followers of Occam, or Ocham, an English Cordelier, in the 14th century. They were great dealers in words, whence they were vulgarly denominated Word-sellers; but had the denomination of Nominalists, because, in opposition to the Realists, they maintained, that words, and not things, were the object of dialectics. This sect had its first rise towards the end of the 11th century, and pretended to follow Porphyry and Aristotle; but it was not till Ocham's time that they bore the name. The chief of this sect, in the 11th century, was a person called John, who, on account of his logical subtlety, was called the sophist; and his principal disciples were Robert of Paris, Roscelin of Compiègne, and Arnoul of Laon. At the beginning, the Nominals had the upper hand; but the Realists, though greatly divided among themselves, were supported by men of great abilities; such as Albertus Magnus, T. Aquinas, and Duns Scotus. The nominal sect came hereby into disrepute; till William Occam, in the 14th century, again revived it, and filled France and Germany with the flame of disputation. Having joined the party of the Franciscan monks, who strenuously opposed John XXII., that pope himself, and his successors after him, left no means untried to extirpate the philosophy of the Nominalists, which was deemed highly prejudicial to the interests of the church: and hence it was, that, in the year 1339, the university of Paris, by a public edict, solemnly condemned and prohibited the philosophy of Occam, which was that of the Nominalists. The consequence was, that the Nominalists flourished more than ever. In the 15th century, the controversy was continued with more vigour and animosity than before; and the disputants were not content with using merely the force of eloquence, but had frequently recourse to more hostile and dangerous weapons; and battles were the consequence of a philosophical question, which neither side understood. In most places, however, the Realists maintained a manifest superiority over the Nominalists. While the famous Germon, and the most eminent of his disciples were living, the Nominalists were in high esteem and credit in the university of Paris. But upon the death of these patrons, the face of things was much changed to their disadvantage. In the year 1473, Louis XI., by the instigation of his confessor, the bishop of Avranches, issued out a severe edict against the doctrines of the Nominalists, and ordered all their writings to be seized and secured, that they might not be read by the people; but the same monarch mitigated this edict the year following, and permitted some of the books of that sect to be delivered from their confinement. In the year 1481, he not only granted a full liberty to the Nominalists and their writings, but also restored that philosophical sect to its former authority and lustre in the university. The Nominalists were the founders of the university of Leipzig: and there are many yet abroad who pique themselves on being Nominals. The Nominals, with the Stoics, admit the formal conceptions or ideas of things, as the subject and foundation of universality: but to this they add names, which represent and signify, after the same univocal manner, and without any distinction, a great variety of single things alike in genus and species. Whence it is that they are called Nominals; as pretending, that to become learned, it is not enough to have just ideas of things, but it is likewise required to know the proper names of the genera and species of things, and to be able to express them clearly and precisely, without confusion or ambiguity.

NOMINATIVE

Pages 45-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> which are declinable. The simple position, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> laying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of a noun, or name, name, is called the nominative case; yet it is not so properly a case, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> or ground whence the other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are to be formed, by the several changes and inflections given to this first termination. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to be placed in discourse before all verbs, as the subject of the proposition or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a>.

NONA

Pages 46-46

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, remarkable at present only for its ruins, which might furnish abundant materials to gratify the curiosity of antiquaries; but indeed they are so buried by repeated devastations, to which that unhappy city has been exposed, that rarely any vestige of them appears above ground. "I went thither (says Fortis in his Travels), in hopes of finding something worthy of notice, but was disappointed. Nothing is to be seen that indicates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the Roman times; neither are there any remains of barbarous magnificence, to put one in mind of the ages in which the kings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Slavi had their residence there. It lies on a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, surrounded by a harbour, which in former times was capable of receiving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships; but is now become a field pool by means of a little muddy river that falls into it, after a course of about six miles through the rich abandoned fields of that district. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants turned this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into another channel, and made it run through the valley of Drausnich into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and the remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> raised by them for that purpose are still to be seen. Notwithstanding, however, the depopulation of this district, and the dreary situation of Nona in particular, the new inhabitants have not lost courage; and animated by the privileges granted to them by the most serene republic, are endeavouring to bring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> once more into a flourishing state. Proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> for the water would not only render that rich territory habitable, but moreover very fertile; and the brackish marsh that surrounds the walls of Nona is well calculated to supply a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fish, especially eels. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> generously granted the inviolability to private persons, who already draw no inconsiderable advantage from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; and did they but adopt better methods, they might every year <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> many thousands of eels, which would greatly antiver our internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> at least a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> that goes out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for foreign salt fish. To the left of the city of Nona, the walls of some ancient ruinous buildings appear; which probably in ancient times were situated on the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, though now surrounded by water. The sea forms a narrow channel in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which is easily fordable, and, at low water, the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> can scarcely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>."

NONAGE

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, generally signifies all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a person continues under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21; but in a special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is all the time that a person is under the age of 14.

NONAGESIMAL

Pages 46-46
or Nonagesimal Degree, called also the Mid Heaven, is the highest point, or 90th degree of the ecliptic, reckoned from its intersection with the horizon at any time; and its altitude is equal to the angle which the ecliptic makes with the horizon at their intersection, or equal to the distance of the zenith from the pole of the ecliptic. It is much used in the calculation of solar eclipses.

NONAGON

Pages 46-46

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> having <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> sides and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. In a regular nonagon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that whose angles and sides are all equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> each side be 1, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be $6.181824^2 = \frac{3}{2}$ of the tangent of $75^\circ$, to the radius 1.

NONCONFORMISTS

Pages 46-53

those who refuse to join the established worship. Nonconformists, in England, are of two sorts. First, Such as absent themselves from divine worship in the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> through total irreligion, and attend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of no other persuasion. These, by the statute 1 Eliz. c. 2. 23 Eliz. c. 1. and 3 Jac. I. c. 4. forfeit one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> they so absent themselves, and 2d. to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they continue such default for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> together. And if they keep any innate thus irreligiously disfavored in their houses, they forfeit 10l. per month. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of nonconformists are those who offend through a mistaken <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perverse zeal. Such were esteemed, by the English laws enacted since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Reformation, to be Papists and Protestant dissenters: both of which were supposed to be equally schismatics, in not communicating with the national church; with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the Papists divided from it upon material, though erroneous, reasons; but many of the dissenters upon matters of indifference, or, in other words, for no reason at all. "Yet certainly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a> (says Sir William Blackstone) our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were mis-conceived taken in their plans of compulsion and intolerance. The sin of schism, as such, is by no means the object of temporal coercion and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. If, through weakness of intellect, through midedirected piety, through prejudices and acerbity of temper, or (which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>) through a prospect of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> advantage in herding with a party, men quarrel with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> establishment, the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> has nothing to do with it; unless their tenets and practice are such as threaten ruin or disturbance to the state. He is bound indeed to protect the established church: and if this can be better effected by admitting none but its genuine members to offices of trust and emolument, he is certainly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to do; the disfranchisal of offices being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of favour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. But this point being once secured, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> for diversity of opinions, however ridiculous or absurd they may be, is contrary to every principle of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy and civil freedom. The names and subordination of the clergy, the posture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, the materials and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the minister's garment, the joining in a known or unknown form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and other matters of the same kind, must be left to the option of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s private judgement. "With regard therefore to Protestant dissenters, although the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of their turbulent disposition in former times occasioned several disabilities and restrictions (which I shall not undertake to justify) to be laid upon them by abundance of statutes; yet at length the legislature, with a true spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, extended that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to these sectaries, which they themselves, when in power, had held to be countenancing schism, and denied to the church of England. The penalties are conditionally suspended by the statute 1 W. & M. ii. c. 18. "for exempting their majesties Protestant subjects, dissenting from the church of England, from the penalties of certain laws," <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called called the toleration <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; which declares, that neither the laws above mentioned, nor the statutes 1 Eliz. c. 2. § 14. 3 Jac. I. c. 4. and 5, nor any other penal laws made against Popish recusants (except the test acts), shall extend to any dissenters, other than Papists and such as deny the Trinity: provided, 1. That they take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy, (or make a similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a>, being <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>), and subscribe the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. 2. That they repair to some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> certified to and registered in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the bishop or archdeacon, or at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> sessions. 3. That the doors of such meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> shall be unlocked, unbarred, and unbolted; in default of which, the persons meeting there are still liable to all the penalties of the former acts. Dissenting teachers, in order to be exempted from the penalties of the statutes 13 and 14 Car. II. c. 4. 17 Car. II. c. 2. and 22 Car. II. c. 1., are also to subscribe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> mentioned in the statute 13 Eliz. c. 12. (viz. those which only concern the confession of the true Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and the doctrine of the sacraments), with an express exception of those relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and powers of the church, and to infant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. And by stat. 10 Ann. c. 2. this toleration is ratified and confirmed; and it is declared, that the said act shall at all times be inviolably observed for the exempting such Protestant dissenters as are thereby intended from the pains and penalties therein mentioned. Thus, though the offence of non-conformity is by no means universally abrogated, it is suspended, and ceases to exist with regard to these Protestant dissenters, during their compliance with the conditions imposed by the act of toleration: and, under these conditions, all persons, who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> approve themselves no Papists or oppugners of the Trinity, are left at full liberty to act as their consciences shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them in the matter of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship. And if any person shall wilfully, maliciously, or contemptuously disturb any congregation assembled in any church or permitted meeting-house, or shall mischievously preach or teach there, he shall (by virtue of the same statute) be bound over to the sessions of the peace, and forfeit 20l. But by statute 5 Geo. I. c. 4., no mayor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> magistrate must appear at any dissenting meeting with the ensigns of his office, on pain of disfavour to hold that or any other office: the legislature judging it a matter of propriety, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship, set up in opposition to the national, when allowed to be exercised in peace, should be exercised also with decency, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, and humility. Neither doth the act of toleration extend to enervate those clauses of the statutes 13 & 14 Car. II. c. 4. and 17 Car. II. c. 2. which prohibit (upon pain of fine and imprisonment) all persons from teaching school, unless they be licensed by the ordinary, and subscribe a declaration of conformity to the liturgy of the church, and reverently frequent divine service established by the laws of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. "As to Papists what has been said of the Protestant dissenters would hold equally strong for a general toleration of them; provided their separation was founded only upon difference of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in religion, and their principles did not also extend to a subversion of the civil government. If once they could be brought to renounce the supremacy of the Pope, they might quietly enjoy their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments; their purgatory, and auricular confession; their worship of relics and images; nay, even their transubstantiation. But while they acknowledge a foreign power, superior to the sovereignty of the kingdom, they cannot complain, if the laws of that kingdom will not treat them upon the footing of good subjects. "The following are the laws that have been enacted against the Papists; who may be divided into three classes, persons professing Popery, Popish recusants convict, and Popish priests. 1. Persons professing the Popish religion, besides the former penalties for not frequenting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church, are disfavored from taking any lands either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> or purchase, after 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, until they renounce their errors; they must at the age of 21 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> their estates before acquired, and all future conveyances and wills relating to them; they are incapable of presenting to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a>, or granting to any person any avoidance of the same; they may not keep or teach any school, under pain of perpetual imprisonment; and, if they willingly say or hear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, they forfeit the one 200l., the other 100 marks, and each shall suffer a year's imprisonment. Thus much for persons, who, from the misfortune of family prejudices, or otherwise, have conceived an unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Romish church from their infancy, and publicly profess its errors. But if any evil industry is used to rivet these errors upon them; if any person lends another abroad to be educated in the Popish religion, or to reside in any religious house abroad for that purpose, or contributes to their maintenance when there; both the lender, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a>, and the contributor, are disfavored to sue in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, to be executor or administrator to any person, to take any legacy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of gift, and to bear any office in the realm; and shall forfeit all their goods and chattels, and likewise all their real estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. And where these errors are also aggravated by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a> or perversion; where a person is reconciled to the see of Rome, or procures others to be reconciled, the offence amounts to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. 2. Popish recusants, convicted in a court of law of not attending the service of the church of England, are subject to the following disabilities, penalties, and forfeitures, over and above those before mentioned. They are considered as persons excommunicated; they can hold no office or employment; they must not keep arms in their houses, but the same may be seized by the justices of the peace; they may not come within 10 miles of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on pain of 100l.; they can bring no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at law or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> in equity; they are not permitted to travel above five miles from home, unless by license, upon pain of forfeiting all their goods; and they may not come to court, under pain of 100l. No <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of such recusant, or baptism of his child, shall be had otherwise than by the ministers of the church of England, under other severe penalties. A married woman, when recusant, shall forfeit two-thirds of her dower or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a>, may not be executrix or administratrix to her husband, or have any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his goods; and during the coverture may be kept in prison, unless her husband redeems her, at the rate of 10l. a month, or the third part of all his lands. And lastly, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> recusant may be imprisoned, so all others must, within three months after conviction, either submit and renounce their errors, or, if required to do by four justices, must abjure and renounce the realm: and if they do not depart, or if they re- turn without the king's licence, they shall be guilty of felony, and suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as felons, without benefit of clergy. There is also an inferior species of recusancy, (refusing to make the declaration against Popery enjoined by statute 30 Car. II. c. 2. when tendered by the proper magistrate;) which, if the party resides within ten miles of London, makes him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> recusant convict; or, if at a greater distance, suspends him from having any seat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, keeping arms in his house, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> above the value of £1. 3. Popish priests are in a still more dangerous condition. By statute 11 & 12 W. III. c. 4. Popish priests, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, celebrating mass or exercising any part of their functions in England, except in the houses of ambassadors, are liable to perpetual imprisonment. And by the statute 27 Eliz. c. 2. any Popish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, born in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, who shall come over hither from beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> (unless driven by storms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and tarrying only a reasonable time), or shall be in England three days without conforming and taking the oaths, is guilty of high treason: and all persons harbouring him are guilty of felony without the benefit of clergy. "This is a short summary of the laws against the Papists; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Montesquieu observes, that they are so rigorous, though not professedly of the sanguinary kind, that they do all the hurt that can possibly be done in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood. But in answer to this, it may be observed (what foreigners who only judge from our statute book are not fully apprized of), that these laws are seldom exerted to their utmost rigour: and indeed, if they were, it would be very difficult to excuse them. For they are rather to be accounted for from their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and the urgency of the times which produced them, than to be approved (upon a cool review) as a standing system of law. The nefarious machinations of the Jesuits during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, the turbulence and uneasiness of the Papists under the new religious establishment, and the boldness of their hopes and wishes for the succession of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots, obliged the parliament to counteract so dangerous a spirit by laws of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and then perhaps necessary, severity. The powder-treason, in the succeeding reign, struck a panic into James I. which operated in different ways: it occasioned the enacting of new laws against the Papists; but deterred him from putting them in execution. The intrigues of Queen Henrietta in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., the protest of a Popish successor in that of Charles II., the allusion-plot in the reign of King William, and the avowed claim of a Popish pretender to the crown in subsequent reigns, will account for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of these penalties at those several periods of our history." But now that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> fears of a pretender may be said to have vanished, and the power and influence of the pope has become feeble, ridiculous, and despicable, not only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but in almost every kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: and as in fact the British Catholics solemnly disclaim the dangerous principles ascribed to them; the British legislature, giving way to that liberality of sentiment becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, have lately repealed the most rigorous of the above edicts, viz. The punishment of Popish priests or Jesuits who should be found to teach or officiate in the services of that church; which acts were felony in foreigners, and high treason in the natives of this kingdom:—The forfeitures of Nonconformists heirs, who had received their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> abroad; and whose estates went to the next Protestant heir:—The power given to the son, or other relation, being a Protestant, to take possession of the father's or other relation's estate, during the life of the real proprietor:—And the debarring Papists from the power of acquiring any legal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> by purchase.—In proposing the repeal of these penalties, it was observed, That, besides that some of them had now ceased to be necessary, others were at all times a disgrace to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. The imprisonment of a Popish priest for life, only for officiating in the services of his religion, was horrible in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: And although the mildness of government had hitherto softened the rigour of the law in the practice, it was to be remembered that the Roman Catholic priests constantly lay at the mercy of the basest and most abandoned of mankind—of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> informers; for on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of any of these wretches, the magisterial and judicial powers were of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> bound to enforce all the shameful penalties of the act. Others of these penalties held out the most powerful temptations for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of acts of depravity, at the very thought of which our nature recoils with horror: They seemed calculated to loosen all the bands of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>: to dissolve all civil, moral, and religious obligations and duties, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> the sources of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity, and to annihilate every principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The encouragement given to children to lay their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the estates of their parents, and the restriction which bars any man from the honest acquisition of property, need only to be mentioned to excite indignation in an enlightened age. In order the better to secure the English established church against perils from nonconformists of all denominations, Infidels, Turks, Jews, Heretics, Papists, and Sectaries, there are, however, two bulwarks erected; called the corporation and test acts: By the former of which, no person can be legally elected to any office relating to the government of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or corporation, unless, within a twelvemonth before, he has received the sacrament of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the church of England; and he is also enjoined to take the oath of allegiance and supremacy at the same time that he takes the oath of office: or, in default of either of these requisites, such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> shall be void. The other, called the test act, directs all officers civil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> to take the oaths and make the declaration against transubstantiation, in any of the king's courts at Westminster, or at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions, within six <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> months after their admission; and also within the same time to receive the sacrament of the Lord's supper, according to the usage of the church of England, in some public church immediately after divine service and sermon, and to deliver into court a certificate thereof signed by the minister and church warden, and also to prove the same by two credible witnesses; upon forfeiture of £500l. and disqualification to hold the said office. And of much the same nature with these is the statute 7 Jac. I. c. 2. which permits no persons to be naturalized or restored in blood, but such as undergo a like test: which test having been removed in 1753, in favour of the Jews, was the next session of parliament restored again with some precipitation. Non-naturals, in Medicine, so called, because by their abuse they become the causes of diseases. Physicians have divided the non-naturals into six classes, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, meats and drinks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> and watching, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and rest, the passions of the mind, the retentions and excretions. See Medicine, passim. Non-obstante (notwithstanding) a clause frequent in statutes and letters patent, importing a license from the king to do a thing, which at common law might be lawfully done, but being restrained by act of parliament cannot be done without such license. Non-Pro. See Nolle Prosequi. Non-Suit, signifies the dropping of a suit or action, or a renouncing thereof by the plaintiff or defendant; which happens most commonly upon the discovery of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the plaintiff's proceedings when the cause is so far proceeded in, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> is ready at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to deliver in their verdict. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NONES">Nones</a>, (nonæ), in the Roman calendar, the fifth day of the months <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, February, April, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, August, September, November, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>; and the seventh of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and October. March, May, July, and October, had six days in their nones; because these alone, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the year by Numa, had 31 days apiece, the rest having only 29, and February 30: but when Caesar reformed the year, and made other months contain 31 days, he did not allot them five days of nones. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONJURORS">Nonjurors</a>, those who refused to take the oaths to government, and who were in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> under certain incapacities, and liable to certain severe penalties. It can scarcely be said that there are any nonjurors now in the kingdom; and it is well known that all penalties have been removed both from Papists and Protestants, formerly of that denomination, as well in Scotland as in England. The members of the Episcopal church of Scotland have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been denominated Nonjurors; but perhaps they are now called so improperly, as the ground of their difference from the establishment is more on account of ecclesiastical than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONIUS">Nonius</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, in Spanish Nunez, a learned Portuguese, and one of the ablest mathematicians of the 16th century, was born at Alcacer. He was preceptor to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Henry, King Emmanuel's son, and taught the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>. He published the following works, by which he gained great reputation: 1. De arte Navigandi. 2. Annotations in theorias planetarum Purbachii; which are greatly esteemed. 3. A treatise De Crepulculis. 4. A treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>. It is observed in Furetiere's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, that Peter Nonius, in 1530, first invented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of 45 degrees made in every meridian, and that he called them rhumbs in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and calculated them by spherical triangles. Nonius died in 1577, aged 80. Nonius, the name which was not many years ago given to the common device for subdividing the arcs of quadrants and other astronomical instruments, from the persuasion that it was invented by Nonius or Nunez, of whom some account has been given in the preceding article. The generality of astronomers of the present age transferring the honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> from Nunez to Peter Vernier, a native of Franche Comte, have called this method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> by his name. (See Vernier.) Mr Adams, however, in his Geometrical and Geographical Essays, has lately shown that Clevis the Jesuit may dispute the invention with them both. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> seems to be, that Nunez started the idea, Clevis improved it, and Vernier carried it to its present state of perfection. The method of Nunez, described in his treatise De Crepulculis, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> 1542, consists in describing within the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> 45 concentric circles, dividing the outermost into 90 equal parts, the next within into 80, the next into 88, &c. till the innermost was divided into 46 only. On a quadrant thus divided the plumb line or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> must <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one or other of the circles very near a point of division; whence, by computation, the degrees and minutes of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> might be easily ascertained. This method is also described by Nunez in his treatise De arte atque ratione Navigandi, where he would fain persuade himself, that it was not unknown to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. But as the degrees are thus divided very unequally, and as it is very difficult to attain exactness in the division, especially when the numbers into which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> are to be divided are incomposite (of which there are no less than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>), the method of diagonals, first published by Thomas Digges, Esq. in a treatise entitled Ayle seu facie mathematicae, printed at London in 1573, and said to be invented by one Richard Chenefler, was substituted in its room. Nonius's method was, however, improved at different times and by different persons; and it must be acknowledged, that if Vernier <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> either the original or any of the improvements (and there can be little doubt of his having seen them all), his merit is only that of having applied to an useful practical purpose the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> invention of another person. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONNUS">Nonnus</a>, a Greek poet of the 5th century, and native of Panopolis in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the author of an heroic poem in 48 books, entitled Dionysiaca, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of St John's Gospel, which may serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon it. Nonupla, in the Italian music, denotes a quick time, peculiar to jigs.
