This species of time is otherwise called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of nine times, which requires two falls of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and one rise. There are three sorts of nonupla. 1. Nonupla di semi minimæ, or dupla semifiquarta, thus marked \( \frac{2}{3} \), where nine crotchets are to be in the bar, of which four make a semibreve in common time, i.e. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stroke fix, and but three up: it is usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> adagio. 2. Nonupla di crone, or semifiquarta, marked thus \( \frac{3}{8} \), wherein nine quavers make a bar instead of eight in common time, i.e. fix down and three up: it is beat presto. 3. Nonupla di semifiorcione or super feti parte <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONA">nona</a>, thus distinguished \( \frac{3}{8} \), in which nine semifiorciones are contained in a bar, whereof sixteen are required in common time, fix down, and three up: it is ordinarily beat prestissimo. Besides these, there are two other species of nonupla, for which see Triple. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOOTKA">Nootka</a> Sound, or, as it was called by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, King George's Sound, lies in N. Lat. 49° 33' W. Long. 153° 12'. It is an entrance or strait to a vast inland sea on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and is said to resemble the Baltic or Mediterranean in Europe. Upon the sea-coast the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is tolerably high and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; but within the sound it rises into steep hills, which have an uniform appearance. The trees of which the woods are composed, are the Canadian pine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cypress, Nootka Sound. Cypress, and two or three other sorts of pine. In general, the trees grow here with great vigour, and are of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size. About the rocks and borders of the woods were seen some strawberry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and raspberry, currant, and gooseberry bushes, all in a flourishing state. The principal animals seen here were raccoons, martens, and squirrels. Birds are far from being numerous, and those that are to be seen are remarkably shy, owing perhaps to their being continually harried by the natives, either to eat them, or to become possessed of their feathers to be worn as ornaments. The quercuslactucifera, thongs, and gulls, were seen off the coast; and the two last were also frequent in the sound. Though the variety of fish is not very great, yet they are in greater quantities than birds. The principal sorts are the common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, a river coloured <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>, and another of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour. Captain Cook and Mr King, who visited this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, consider it as an excellent shelter for ships: and in the account of A Voyage to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>, they give some directions for sailing into it. These and other matters of that kind we shall not trouble our readers with; and perhaps the generality of them will be better pleased with the following extract from Meares's Voyages to the North-west Coast of America. "The people of the Nootka <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> are, in general, robust and well-proportioned:—their faces are large and full, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> high and prominent, with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes—-their noses are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and flat, their lips thick, and they have generally very fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and of the most brilliant whiteness. "The manner in which the children of Nootka are treated, when young, is not more extraordinary from its strange, and, as it should appear, total insufficiency, as from its agreement with the customs of the Chinese and Tartars, to whom this practice gives these people a considerable resemblance. The head of the infant is bound by the mother with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a> of several folds, as low down as the eyes, in order to give it a certain form, which, at this tender age, it is capable of receiving. It might be supposed, that such a tight drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> must cause considerable pain to the child; but we never observed that any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, in such a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-loaf heads, suffered any visible pain or inconvenience. "Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of compressing the head in this manner gives them an unpleasing appearance, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the eyebrows, and sometimes producing the disagreeable effect of squinting, as well as of flattening the nose and distending the nostrils, they are by no means an ill-looking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people. They have also the custom, which is known to prevail in so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> nations, of plucking out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> by the roots, on its first appearance; and, as it continues to sprout, to keep it down by the same practice. It is one of the domestic employments assigned to their wives, to watch this appearance of manhood, and to eradicate the hairs as they come forth; which they do in a very dexterous manner with their fingers, and without giving the least pain in the operation.—Some of them, however, though we saw but very few of this disposition, when they advance in years and become infirm, suffer their beards to grow without interruption. But notwithstanding they have to great an aversion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of their chin, that of the head is an object of their attentive vanity: it is strong, black, and glossy; grows to a considerable length; and is either tied in a kind of knot on the top of their heads, or suffered to hang down their backs in flowing negligence. "In their exterior form they have not the symmetry or elegance which is found in many other Indian nations.—Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, though stout and athletic, are crooked and ill shaped; their skin, when cleansed of filth and ocre, is white; and we have seen some of the women, when in a state of cleanliness (which, however, was by no means a common sight, and obtained with difficulty), who not only possessed the fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of Europe, but features that would have attracted notice, for their delicacy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, in those parts of the world where the qualities of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form are best understood. But these examples of beauty are by no means numerous among the women of Nootka, who are calculated rather to disgust than to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> an European beholder. Their hair, like that of the men, is black; their eyes are of the same colour; and, in exterior appearance, they are not to be immediately distinguished from the men. In their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> they are reserved and chaste; and examples of loose and immoral conduct were very rare among them. There were women in St George's Sound, whom no offers could tempt to meretricious submissions." All reports concerning Nootka Sound agree in characterizing the inhabitants as "a very motile race of people."—Inoffensive, however, as they are, a custom of a very unnatural, and we should imagine cruel, kind prevails among them: for, together with many other articles which they exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> to Captain Cook's ships, they brought human skulls and hands (part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> still remaining on them), which they acknowledged they had been feeding on; and some of them, we are told, had evident marks of the fire. From hence it is too apparent, that the horrid practice of devouring their enemies exists here as well as at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> and other South Sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>: and hence, too, appears what men of even the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> dispositions will be, if left entirely to the freedom of their own will, without law to control or religion to instruct them. As there are but two villages of the Sound inhabited, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people cannot be many; perhaps they are about 2000 in all. Our limits prevent us from being so minute as we could wish to be, respecting the form of their houses and their manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> them; of their furniture, decorations, and other things of that kind: we can therefore only refer those who wish for further information on this subject to Cook, and other voyagers and travellers, &c. The employment of the men is chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, &c., whilst the women manufacture their garments. Their ingenuity in this and in the mechanic arts is far from being inconsiderable; and in the imitative arts their skill is very great. On these subjects, however, we cannot enlarge: we have in general made it our business, and it certainly is our duty, to dwell, where it can be done, on the manners or religion of the inhabitants of the several places which come under our notice; and they who know the utility of this in developing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the human mind, the most important of all sciences, will not blame our intentions, even if they should not approve of the execution. In Cook's Cook's Voyages before referred to, we find the following observations on the religion and language of the inhabitants of Nootka Sound. "Little knowledge we can be supposed to have acquired of the political and religious institutions established among these people. We discovered, however, that there were such men as chiefs, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Acweeke, to whom the others are, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, subordinate. But the authority of each of these great men seems to extend no farther than to his own family, who acknowledge him as their head. As they were not all elderly men, it is possible this title may be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. "Nothing that we saw could give us any insight into their notions of religion, except the figures already mentioned, called Kuma. These, perhaps, were idols; but as the word Acweeke was frequently mentioned when they spoke of them, we may suppose them to be the images of some of their ancestors, whose memories they venerate. This, however, is all conjecture; for we could receive no information concerning them; knowing little more of their language than to enable us to ask the names of things, and being incapable of holding any conversation with the natives relative to their traditions or their institutions. "Their language is neither harsh nor disagreeable, farther than proceeds from their pronouncing the k and h with less softness than we do. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of their language, we are enabled to say but little. It may, however, be inferred from their flow and distinct method of speaking, that it has few prepositions or conjunctions, and is destitute of even a single interjection to express surprise or admiration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> it may bear to other languages, we have not been able sufficiently to trace, not having proper specimens to compare it with; but from the few Mexican words we have procured, there is an obvious agreement throughout the language, in the frequent terminations of the words in l, ll or x. "The word waka/b was frequently in the mouths of the people of Nootka. It seemed to express approbation, applause, and friendship. Whenever they appeared to be pleased or satisfied at any sight or occurrence, they would call out waka/b! waka/b!—It is worthy of remark, that these people do essentially differ from the natives of the islands in the Pacific ocean, in their persons, customs, and language, we cannot suppose their respective progenitors to have belonged to the same tribe, when they emigrated into those places where we now find their descendants." We cannot finish this article without taking notice of a circumstance, which at the time made a great noise in Europe, and which it is probable will find a place in the future histories of the contending countries. A small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> resident in the East Indies had, early in the year 1786, formed the project of opening a trade to this part of the world, for the purpose of supplying the Chinese market with furs. The principal point towards which these expeditions were directed, was Port Nootka, or King George's Sound; and the adventurers, being in some degree satisfied with their traffic, took <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, in the year 1788, to secure to themselves a permanent settlement; at the same time that the shipping employed in this expedition was generally two, and never exceeded the amount of four, small vessels. The Spaniards conceived some jealousy of the intrusion of the English into a part of the world which they had long been desirous to regard as their exclusive property; and accordingly a Spanish frigate of 26 guns was despatched from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, for the purpose of putting an end to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The Spanish frigate arrived in May 1789, and captured two English vessels in the following July, at the same time taking possession of the little settlement which had been formed upon the coast. Such, in short, is the circumstance which was likely to involve us in an expensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Happily, however, for both countries, and perhaps for Europe, the matter was at length, after great altercation, amicably settled; and it must still be so fresh in the memories of our readers, that we trust they will excuse us from enlarging further upon it—the whole article having extended perhaps to more than a sufficient length.

NOPAL

Pages 53-53

RAQUETTE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fig; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> so named by the Indians, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> insect breeds in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. See COCHINEAL, DYING <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

NOPALCOCHUETZALLI

Pages 53-53
or NOPALCOCHUETZALLI, the prickly pear of Mexico, which is common over all the West Indies. See CACTUS, BOTANY INDEX. NOPH. See MEMPHIS.

NORBURY

Pages 53-53

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, in England, on the south-west side of Eccleshall. Here is a surprising <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">echo</a>, which, taken 440 yards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, near a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> under a wood side, repeats in a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 11 syllables very distinctly, or 12 or 13, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> spoke very quick. It is remarked that the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Meer, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, grow forward every year over the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, at the rate of three or four yards every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years.

NORDEN

Pages 53-53

Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, an ingenious traveller and naval officer in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, was born at Glückstadt in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in the year 1728. He was well skilled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and especially in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; and in 1732 obtained a pension to enable him to travel, for the purpose of studying the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of ships, particularly the galleys and other rowing vessels used in the Mediterranean. He spent near three years in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and Christian VI., being desirous of obtaining a circumstantial account of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, Mr Norden while at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> received an order to extend his travels to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. How he acquitted himself in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, appears from his Travels into Egypt and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a> in folio, 1756; and which were soon after translated into English by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Templeman. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, Mr Norden, then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, attended <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Ulric Adolphus, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> captain, to England; and they went out volunteers under Sir John Norris, and afterwards under Sir Chaloner Ogle. During his stay in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Mr Norden was made a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and gave the public drawings of some ruins and colossal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> at Thebes in Egypt, with an account of the same in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the Royal Society, 1741. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was declining; and taking a tour to France, he died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1742.

NORDHEIM

Pages 53-54

a town in Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>... Of the four larger <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this principality, it is the third in order. It is situated on the Rhume, which runs into the Leine. It contains 500 houses, and, besides a secularized Lutheran <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, has one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and some charitable foundations, and also enjoys some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>.

NORES

Pages 54-54

JASON DE, a scholar, poet, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Nicola in Cyprus. He lost his fortune when the Turks made themselves masters of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in 1570. He retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; where he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by teaching <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. His character had that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of severity which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of scholastic habits. He was one of those men who discuss every thing without being capable of feeling anything. The Pastor Fido of Guarini made its appearance; and pastoralists became a fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Nores, who did not relish works of this kind, attacked the production of Guarini, who entirely confuted him in a little piece printed at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> in 1588. Nores made a reply two years after; and the poet was preparing an answer still more severe than the former, when his antagonist died of grief, occasioned by the banishment of his only son for having killed a Venetian in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>. He left behind him a great many works, some in Italian, and others in Latin. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of his Italian works, are, 1. The Poeticks, Padua, 1588, 4to; this edition is rare. 2. A Treatise on Republics, 1578, 4to; which he forms on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that of the Venetians, his matters. 3. A Treatise on the World and its Parts, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1571, 8vo. 4. Introduction to three books of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, Venice, 1584, 4to, valuable. 5. A Treatise on what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">Comedy</a>, Tragedy, and Epic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, may receive from Moral Philosophy. His Latin works are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a> in Philosophiam Ciceronis, Padua, 1576, 8vo. 2. Brevis et difficilis summa praecoptorum de arte defendi, ex libris Ciceronis collecta, Venice, 1553, 8vo.; a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. 3. De Constitutione partium humanae et civilis philosophiae, &c., 4. Interpretatio in artem poeticaem Horatii, &c. In all his works we remark great perspicuity and accuracy, profound erudition, happy expressions, an elevated and sometimes forcible style.—His son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Nores, successively secretary to several cardinals, at once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters and a man of buffoons, left behind him different <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; among others, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Paul IV. in Italian.

NORFOLK

Pages 54-54

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, so called from its northern situation in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, is bounded on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the German ocean; on the south by Suffolk, from which it is parted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Waveney and the Leffer Ouse; and on the west it is separated from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a> by the Greater Ouse, and from a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> by the Withes. According to Templeman, it extends in length 57 miles, in breadth 35, and 140 in circumference. It contains an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 1426 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 32 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 711 villages, according to the book of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, though some make them 1500, and 273,371 inhabitants. It is divided into 31 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 164 vicarages, and 660 parishes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> differs in different parts of the county according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which in some places is marshy, especially on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and there the air is foggy and unwholesome; in others it is clayey and chalky, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, lean, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and there the air is good. The county is almost all champaign, except in some places, where rye gentle hills. The marsh lands yield rich pasture for cattle; the clay grounds pease, rye, and barley; and the sandy heaths feed vast flocks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sheep, of which some villages are said to keep 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 5000. These heaths abound also in rabbits of a silver gray <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALSINGHAM">Walsingham</a> is noted for producing the best saffron. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> quantities of mackerel and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> are caught upon the coasts of this county, the former in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the latter in September; especially at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a>, where they are cured in a particular manner, and to great perfection. Wood and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> are also very plentiful in this county; and on the coasts jet and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a> are sometimes found. The inhabitants are generally strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, sagacious and acute. That they are so robust, is the more to be wondered at, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people live much on puddings, Norfolk dumplings. They are for the most part in easy circumstances, and were formerly very quarrelsome and litigious. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this disposition, lawyers swarmed among them to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that a statute was made so early as the reign of Henry VI. to restrain their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the county, which is exceedingly populous, are chiefly woollen and worsted stuffs and stockings, for which they are well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> from the vast flocks of sheep bred in it. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the elder branch of the family of Howard, lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and sends twelve members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two knights for the shire, two citizens for Norwich, and two burgesses for each of the boroughs of Lynn Regis, Great Yarmouth, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a>, and Cattle-rifling. The county is well watered, and supplied with fish by the rivers Yare, Thurn, Waveney, the Greater and Leffer Ouse, and the Bure, besides rivulets. The Bure abounds in excellent perch, and the Yare has a fish peculiar to it called the ruffe. The latter rises about the middle of the county; and after being joined by the Waveney and Bure, falls into the sea at Yarmouth. At the equinoxes, especially the autumnal, the Ouse is subject to great inundations, being forced back by the sea, that enters it with great fury. This county was famous at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, which were extensive and valuable, and seem to have been carried on with spirit. It has also been remarkable, for at least 400 years past, for the manufacture of fine worsted stuffs.

NORFOLK ISLAND

Pages 54-55

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying in 29° 12' 30" south latitude, and 168° 16' east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. A colony was lately settled on it: and the following account of it is given in Governor Phillip's Voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTANY_BAY"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, &c. "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> island is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues in circumference; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not originally formed, like many other small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, by the eruption of volcanic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the sea, must doubtless have contained a volcano. This conclusion is formed from the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pumice <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which is scattered in all parts of it, and mixed with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least some traces of its former existence, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be found at the summit of a small mountain, which rises..." rises near the middle of the island. To this mountain the commandant has given the name of Mount Pitt. The island is exceedingly well watered. At or near Mount Pitt rises a strong and copious stream, which flowing through a very fine valley, divides itself into several branches, each of which retains sufficient force to be used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; and in various parts of the island <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> have been discovered. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is pure, salubrious, and delightful; preserved from oppressive heats by constant breezes from the sea, and of so mild a temperature throughout the winter, that vegetation continues there without interruption, one crop succeeding another. Refreshing showers from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time maintain perpetual verdure; not indeed of grass, for none has yet been seen upon the island; but of the trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and other vegetables, which in all parts grow abundantly. On the leaves of these, and of some kinds in particular, the sheep, hogs, and goats, not only live, but thrive and fatten very much. To the salubrity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> every individual in this little colony can bear ample testimony, from the uninterrupted state of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> which has been, in general, enjoyed. "When our settlers landed, there was not a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> clear of wood in the island, and the trees were so bound together by that kind of creeping shrub called supple jack, interwoven in all directions, as to render it very difficult to penetrate far among them. The commandant, small as his numbers were at first, by indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> soon caused a space to be cleared sufficient for the requisite accommodations, and for the production of excellent vegetables of all kinds in the greatest abundance. When the last accounts arrived, three acres of barley were in a very thriving state, and ground was prepared to receive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn. In the wheat there had been a disappointment, the grain that was sown having been so much injured by the weevil as to be unfit for vegetation. But the people were all at that time in commodious houses; and, according to the declarations of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> himself, in his letters to Governor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, there was not a doubt that this colony would be in a situation to support itself entirely without assistance in less than four years; and with very little in the intermediate time. Even two years would be more than sufficient for this purpose, could a proper supply of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle be sent. "Fish are caught in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty, and in the proper season very fine turtle. The woods are inhabited by innumerable tribes of birds, many of them very gay in plumage. The most useful are pigeons, which are very numerous; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> not unlike the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> fowl, except in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> (being chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>), both of which were at first so tame as to suffer themselves to be taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that afford vegetables for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> are cabbage palm, the wild plantain, the fern tree, a kind of wild spinach, and a tree which produces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> fruit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to a currant. This, it is hoped, by transplanting and care, will be much improved in size and flavour. "But the productions which give the greatest importance to Norfolk Island are the pines and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> plant; the former rising to a size and perfection unknown in other places, and promising the most valuable supply of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> and spars for our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> in the East Indies; the latter not less estimable for the purposes of making sailcloth, cordage, and even the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, growing in great plenty, and with such luxuriance as to attain the height of eight feet. The pines <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> frequently 160, or even 180 feet in height, and are sometimes 9 or 10 feet in diameter at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>. They rise to about 80 feet without a branch: the wood is said to be of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as that of the best <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> masts; and the turpentine obtained from it is remarkable for purity and whiteness. The fern tree is found also of a great height for its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, measuring from 70 to 80 feet, and affords excellent food for the sheep and other small cattle. A plant producing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and supposed to be the true oriental pepper, has been discovered lately in the island, growing in great plenty; and specimens have been sent to England in order to ascertain this important point." Norfolk <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, according to the account of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> George Dixon, is situated in 57° 3' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and 135° 36' west longitude. It is a very extensive <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but how far it stretches to the northward is not known. There may possibly be a passage through to the Bay of Islands, but neither is this certain. The shore, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, abounds with pines; there are also great quantities of the witch hazel. There are various kinds of flowering trees and shrubs, wild gooseberries, currants, and raspberries; wild parsley is found here in great plenty, and it eats excellently either as a salad or boiled amongst soup. The faramee, or wild lily root, grows also in great plenty and perfection. There are a very few wild geese or ducks seen here, but they are shy and difficult of approach.

NORHAM

Pages 55-55

a town in England, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, on the river Tweed, near the mouth of the Till, under the castle, which was anciently erected on a steep rock moated round, for the better security against the incursions of the Scotch mos troopers. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity; and its old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has lately received repairs, and been made a decent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of worship. Antiquities have been discovered here. The church had the privilege of a sanctuary. The castle has been frequently honoured with the presence of sovereigns, particularly Edward I., who received the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> from John Baliol of Scotland. It has been a formidable structure, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is in ruins; the site of which, with its demesnes, consisted of 1,330 acres.

NORIA

Pages 55-56

a hydraulic machine much used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It consists of a vertical wheel of 20 feet diameter, on the circumference of which are fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little boxes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buckets, for the purpose of raising the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> out of the well, communicating with the canal below, and to empty it into a reservoir above, placed by the side of the wheel. The buckets have a lateral office to receive and to discharge the water. The axis of this wheel is embraced by four small beams, crossing each other at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, tapering at the extremities, and forming eight little arms. This wheel is near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> walk, contiguous to the vertical axis, into the top of which the horse beam is fixed; but near the bottom it is embraced by four little beams, forming eight arms similar to those above described, on the axis of the water wheel. As the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> goes round, round, these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> arms, supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of cogs, take hold, each in succession, of those arms which are fixed on the axis of the water wheel, and keep it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>. This machine, than which nothing can be cheaper, throws up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water; yet undoubtedly it has two defects: the first is, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the water runs out of the buckets and falls back into the well after it has been raised nearly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the reservoir; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is, that a considerable proportion of the water to be discharged is raised higher than the reservoir, and falls into it only at the moment when the bucket is at the highest point of the circle, and ready to descend. Both these defects might be remedied with ease, by leaving these square buckets open at one end, making them swing on a pivot fixed a little above their centre of gravity, and placing the trough of the reservoir in such a position as to stop their progress whilst perpendicular; make them turn upon their pivot, and so discharge their contents. From the reservoir the water is conveyed by channels to every part of the garden; these have divisions and subdivisions or beds, some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, others very small, separated from each other by little channels, into which a boy with his shovel or his hoe directs the water, first into the most distant trenches, and successively to all the rest, till all the beds and trenches have been either covered or filled with water. Mr Townsendl, from whom we have taken the above account, thinks, that on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> simplicity of this machine, it is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the most remote antiquity. By means of it the inhabitants every morning draw as much water from the well as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and in the evening distribute it to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their crops. The reservoirs into which they raise the water are about 20, 30, or even 40 feet square, and three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above the surface of the ground, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> coping on the wall, declining to the water for the women to wash and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their clothes upon. Our limits preclude us from following Mr Townsendl farther in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a particular noria used at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>; which he conceives to be the original chain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, or at least its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. He compares it with similar instruments, and shows its advantages and disadvantages. **NORICUM (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Tacitus); a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, situated between the Danube on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and thus separated from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germany; the Alpes Noricae on the south; the river Aenius on the west, which separates it from Vindelicia; and Mons Cetius on the east, which divides it from Pannonia. Now containing a great part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, Styria, and Carinthia. It was anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> under its own kings (Caesar, Velleius, Suetonius). Norici the people, subduced by Tiberius under Augustus, as allies of the Pannonii (Dio, Velleius). Tacitus reckons Noricum among those provinces which were governed by procurators, officers sent by the emperors to receive and dispose of the public revenue according to order. It was divided into two provinces, but at what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> uncertain; supposed as low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as Diocletian and Constantine, viz., the Noricum Ripense, running along the south side of the Danube; and the Noricum Mediterraneum, extending towards the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. How far each of these extended in breadth does not appear: all the account we have of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being from Sextus Rufus, and the Notitia Imperii Occidentalis. Anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> (Horace); as is Stiria at this day, a part of Noricum. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and more sparingly fruitful (Solinus).

NORIN

Pages 56-56

a river which rises in a corner of the Venetian confines, that runs between the rugged marble hills, and is left entirely to itself from its very source; hence a vast tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is overflowed by it, and encumbered with reeds, willows, and wild alders. A small space of ground only remains dry between the roots of the hills and the marsh at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Prud, and that is all covered with pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, fragments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, columns, and capitals, and bas-reliefs of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, worn and deformed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and the barbarism of the northern people, who begun on that side to destroy Narona. The inhabitants, who go often to cut reeds in the marsh, affirm, that the vestiges of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> may still be seen under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It appears to have been extended over the plain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way, and undoubtedly it was three miles in length at the foot of the hills. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is now under water; and it is necessary to ascend a very steep road, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the point of a craggy hill, on which, probably before the Roman times, those fortifications were erected that cost Vetinius so much labour.

NORIS

Pages 56-57

Henry**, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ornament of the order of the monks of St Augustine, was descended from the presiding Jason, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> James de Noris, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> 1631. He was carefully educated by his father Alexander Noris, originally of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and well known by his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Germany. He discovered from his infancy an excellent understanding, great vivacity, and a quick <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>. His father instructed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and procured an able professor of Verona, called Maffoleim, to be his preceptor. At 15 he was admitted a pensioner in the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>, where he studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; after which he applied himself to the writings of the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, particularly those of St Augustine: and taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in the convent of the Augustinian monks of Rimini, he distinguished himself among that fraternity in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by his erudition: inasmuch, that as soon as he was out of his novitiate or time of probation, the general of the order sent for him to Rome, in order to give him an opportunity of improving himself in the more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> branches of learning. He did not disappoint his superior's expectations. He gave himself up entirely to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and spent whole days, and even nights, in the library of the Angeliques of St Augustine. His constant course was to stick to his books 14 hours a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and this course he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he became a cardinal. By this means he became qualified to instruct others; and on this errand he was sent first to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>, and thence to Perugia, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; after which, proceeding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, he applied himself to finish his History of Pelagianism. He had begun it at Rome at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 26; and, having completed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, the book was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and published in 1673. The great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> invited him the following year to Noris, to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, made him his chaplain, and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history in the university of Pifa, which his highness had founded with that view. In his history he set forth and defended the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> pronounced, in the eighth general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> and Mopstetia, the first authors of the Pelagian errors; he also added an account of the Schism of Aquileia, and a Vindication of the Books written by St Augustine against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> had procured him a great reputation, but met with several antagonists, to whom he published proper answers; the dispute grew warm, and was carried before the sovereign tribunal of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>. There the history was examined with the utmost rigour, and the author dismissed without the least censure. It was reprinted twice afterwards, and Mr Noris honoured by Pope Clement X. with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Qualifier of the Holy Office. Notwithstanding this, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> was renewed against the Pelagian History, and it was dilated afresh before the inquisition in 1676; but it came out again with the same success as at first. Mr Noris was now suffered to remain in peace for fifteen years, and taught ecclesiastical history at Pifa, without any molestation, till he was called to Rome by Innocent XII. who made him under-librarian of the Vatican in 1692. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> was the way to a cardinal's hat; his accusers, therefore, took fresh fire, and published several new pieces against him. Hence the Pope appointed some learned divines, who had the character of having taken neither side, to re-examine Father Noris's books, and make their report of them. Their testimony was so advantageous to the author, that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> made him counsellor of the inquisition. Yet neither did this hinder one of his adversaries, the most formidable on account of his erudition, to rise up against him, and attack him warmly, under the assumed title of a Scrupulous Doctor of the Sorbonne. Noris tried to remove these scruples in a work which appeared in 1695, under the title of An Historical Dissertation concerning one of the Trinity that suffered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">Flesh</a>; wherein, having justified the monks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, he vindicated himself also from the imputation of having attacked the Pope's infallibility, of having abused Vincentius Lirinensis, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, as favourers of Semi-Pelagianism, and of having himself gone into the errors of the bishop of Ypres. His answers to all these accusations were so much to the satisfaction of the pope, that at length his holiness honoured him with the purple in 1695. After this, he was in all the congregations, and employed in the most important affairs; so that he had little time to spend in his study, a thing of which he frequently complained to his friends. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cardinal Catanati, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> library keeper of the Vatican in 1700; and two years afterwards nominated, among others, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>: but he died at Rome in 1704 of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>. He was one of the most learned men in the last century: his writings abound with erudition, and are very elegantly finished. He was a member of the Academy; whence he assumed the name of Eucrates Agoreto. His works are numerous, and were published at Verona, in 1729 and 1730, in five volumes folio.

NORKOPING

Pages 57-57

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of East Gothland, in east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 15° 30', latitude 58° 20'. Its name signifies "the northern market" in Normandy, the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It stands on the banks of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river called Motola, which coming from the lake Vetter, falls a little lower into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> called Brawicken. It is the largest and most populous town in Sweden, next to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, conveniently situated near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on a navigable river, which brings large vessels up to the middle of the town. There are some handsome streets, and the houses in general are neatly built. Some of the churches are worth seeing; but the greatest curiosity are the famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, where there is a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people constantly at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In this article the town carries on a very good trade; as also in several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, and guns, which they make the best in Sweden. It covers a large space of ground, being ten miles in circumference; but the houses are small and scattered, and the inhabitants do not exceed 10,000. The river Motola flows through the town, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of cataracts, and is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streams, which encircle several rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, covered with houses and manufactories. At the extremity of the town it is navigable for small vessels. Several manufactories are established in the town; 55 factories of cloth, which employ 1,500 men; 3 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-houses; 1 of flour; 50 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn, which is exported in large quantities; and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> foundry. A salmon fishery gives employment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to many of the inhabitants.

NORMANDY

Pages 57-57

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the English channel; on the east by Picardy and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France; on the south by Perche and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Bretagne; and on the west by the ocean. It is about 155 miles in length, 85 in breadth, and 600 in circumference. It is one of the most fertile, and brings in the largest revenue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It abounds in all things except wine, but they supply that defect by cider and perry. There are vast meadows, fat pastures, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> yields plenty of fish. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and harbours. It carries on a great trade, is very populous, and comprehends a vast number of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages. It is divided into the Upper and Lower; the Upper borders upon Picardy, and the Lower upon Bretagne. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> dioceses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bishoprics, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, Bayeux, Avranches, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, Sées, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISIEUX">Lisieux</a>, and Coustances, in which they compute 4189 parishes, and 80 abbeys. The inhabitants are ingenious, and capable of understanding any arts and sciences, but they are chiefly fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The Normans, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, having entered France under Rollo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Simple ceded this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to them in 912, which from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was called Normandy, and contains about 8,200 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is Rouen. Rollo was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, and held it as a fief of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France, and several of his successors after him, till William, the seventh duke, conquered England in 1066; from which time it became a province of England, till it was lost in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> John, and reunited to the crown of France; but the English still keep the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the coasts of Normandy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rivers are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, the Iton, the Dive, the Andelle, the Risle, the Touque, the Drôme, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORNE">Orne</a>; among the sea ports, the principal are those of Dieppe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAVRE">Havre</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONFLEUR">Honfleur</a>, Cherbourg, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANVILLE">Granville</a>. Rouen is the principal city.

NORMANS

Pages 57-58

a fierce warlike people of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>. They at different times overran and ravaged most countries in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; to the reflective histories of those countries we therefore refer for a fuller account of them, as it is impossible to enlarge upon particulars in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> without repeating what has been already said, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> may be said, in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. NORMAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> introduced into England by William I. From some old <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> the Norman writing appears to have been composed of letters nearly Lombardic. In regal grants, charters, public instruments, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> proceedings, this character was used with very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from the reign of the Conqueror to that of Edward III. See Writing.

NORTH

Pages 58-60
Right Honourable Frederick, earl of Guildford, Lord North, lord warden and admiral of the Cinque Ports, governor of Dover castle, lord lieutenant and custos rotulorum of Somersetshire, chancellor of the university of Oxford, recorder of Gloucester and Taunton, an elder brother of the Trinity house, president of the Foundling hospital and of the Asylum, a governor of the Turkey Company and of the Charter house, K.G., and L.L.D. was born April 13, 1732; and married, May 20, 1766, Miss Ann Speke, an heiress of the ancient family of Dillington in Somersetshire, by whom he has left two sons and three daughters: the eldest son George Augustus, born September 11, 1759, and married, September 30, 1785, to Miss Hobart, succeeds to the earldom and estates. The late earl succeeded his father August 4, 1790. His lordship succeeded the celebrated Mr Charles Townend as manager of the house of commons and chancellor of the exchequer; and in 1779, on the resignation of the duke of Grafton, was made first lord of the treasury; in which office he continued until the close of the American war, or rather until the formation of the Rockingham ministry, which began the business of peace with the colonies. He was a man of strong mental faculties; and as an orator, at once commanded attention and enforced conviction; but taking the helm at a time when the king's party were unpopular, and when it was supposed that the late earl of Bute was the great machine by which the cabinet was moved, so he continued in that state of unpopularity until he resigned the seals. During the whole of his premiership (and to conduct the helm at that time required uncommonly great abilities) he studiously avoided imposing any taxes that should materially affect the lower class of people. The luxuries, and not the necessaries, of life were repeated objects of his budget. As a financier, he stood high, even in the opinion of opposition; and they were a combination of all the great talents in the kingdom: but, fatally wedded to the destructive plan of subduing the republican spirit of the Americans, his administration will not only stand marked in the page of history with an immense waste of public treasure, but it will appear bejewelled with the kindred blood of thousands of British subjects. To the very last moment he spoke in the senate, however; he defended that war; and said, he was then, as he was formerly, prepared to meet the minutest investigation as to his conduct in that business; which nothing but the unforeseen intervention of France could have prevented from being crowned with success. His lordship was one of the firmest and most strenuous supporters of the constitution in church and state. He died on the 6th of August 1792. His recollection he retained to his last moments: his family, except Lord North, who came within a few minutes afterwards, were assembled round his bed, and he took leave of them individually. Their grief did not suffer them to leave the room for some time after the event; North Cape event, and Lady Caroline Douglas was at last forced from it. Even Dr Warren, who must be strengthened as far as habit can operate against nature to endure such scenes, ran from this, convulsed with sorrow. If any extent of sympathy can lessen affliction, this family may find such relief; for perhaps no man was ever more generally beloved by all who had access to him than the earl of Guildford. We may form an opinion of the estimation the celebrated university of Oxford entertained of their chancellor while living, by the very great honour they paid to his remains. About five o'clock in the afternoon of the 1st, the great bell at St Mary's church at Oxford rang out, which was a signal that the funeral procession had arrived in the environs of that city. The officers of the university, and the whole body of resident students, were previously assembled in Magdalen College, in order to pay some tribute to the memory of their deceased chancellor. They joined the procession at Magdalen Bridge, and paraded on foot before the hero up the high street to Carfax; from thence down the corn market to St Giles's church at the town's end, in a most solemn manner. Here they halted, and opening to the right and left, the hero and other carriages passed through, the whole university being uncovered. The hero and attendants then proceeded to Banbury, where his lordship's remains were deposited in the family vault. **NORTH Cape**, the most northerly promontory in Europe, on the coast of Norway. E. Long. 21°. N. Lat. 78°. **NORTH Ferry**, a small village, on the north side of the firth of Forth, at the Queen's Ferry passage. There was here formerly a chapel, served by the monks of Dunfermline, and endowed by Robert I. Near it are large whinstone quarries, which partly supply London with paving stones, and employ many vessels for the conveyance. "The granite (whinstone) (Mr Pennant says) lies in perpendicular strata, and above is a reddish earth, filled with micaceous friable nodules." **NORTH Foreland**, a cape or promontory of Kent, in the Isle of Thanet, four miles east of Margate. Between this and the South Foreland are the Downs, through which all ships pass that are bound to or from the west. E. Long. 1°. 25°. N. Lat. 51°. 25°. **NORTH-West Passage**, a passage to the Pacific ocean through Hudson's class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay or Davis's straits, and which hath been frequently attempted without success; notwithstanding which, many people are still of opinion that it is practicable. The idea of a passage to the East Indies by the north pole, or through some opening near to it, was suggested as early as the year 1527. The person who had the honour to conceive this idea was Robert Thorne, a merchant of Bristol, who addressed two papers on the subject, the one to King Henry VIII., the other to Dr Ley, ambassador from that monarch to the emperor Charles V. To remove any objection to the undertaking, which might be drawn from the supposed danger, he insists, in his address to the king, upon the great advantages of constant daylight in the polar seas, and the probability of the climate being in those regions temperate during the summer months. In the paper addressed to Dr Ley, he observes that cosmographers may as probably be mistaken in the opinion which they entertain of the polar regions being impassable from extreme cold, as it has been found they were in supposing the countries under the line to be uninhabitable from excessive heat. The possibility of the passage was, in consequence of these addresses, very generally supposed; and in 1557, Sir Martin Frobisher failed to 62° north latitude, where he discovered the straits which have since borne his name. In 1577, Barne, in a book entitled the *Regiment of the Sea*, mentions a north-west passage as one of the five ways to Cathay; and dwells on the mildness of the climate, which, from the constant presence of the sun during summer, he imagines must be found near the pole. In 1578, George Best, a gentleman who had been with Sir Martin Frobisher in his voyages of discovery, wrote a very ingenious discourse to prove all parts of the world habitable. It does not, however, appear that any voyage was undertaken, for the express purpose of attempting to fail to India in a north-west direction, till the year 1607, when Henry Hudson was sent, at the expense of some merchants in London to discover a passage by the north pole to Japan and China. He failed from Graveend on the 1st of May, and on the 21st of June fell in with the land to the westward, in latitude 73°, which he named *Hold-with-hope*. On the 27th he discovered Spitzbergen, and met with much ice. The highest latitude in which he made an observation was 80° 27'. See HUDSON. In March 1609, Jones Poole was sent by Sir Thomas Smith, and the rest of the Muscovy Company, to make further discoveries towards the north pole. After great severity of weather, and much difficulty from ice, he made the fourth part of Spitzbergen on the 16th of May; and failing along and founding the coast, he made many accurate discoveries; but was not in that voyage able to proceed beyond 79° 50'. He was again employed (1611), in a small vessel called the *Elizabeth*, to attempt the north-west passage; but after surmounting numberless difficulties, and penetrating to 80° of latitude, he lost his ship at Spitzbergen. Two voyages, equally unsuccessful, were made in 1614 and 1615, by Baffin and Fotherby; the latter of whom concludes the account of his discoveries and dangers, with exhorting the company which employed him not to adventure more than £50l. or £200l. at most on yearly voyages to these seas. Hitherto nothing had been done in this great undertaking; but by private adventurers, fitted out for the double purpose of discovery and present advantage; and the polar regions were suffered to remain unexplored in that direction, from the year 1615 till 1773, when the earl of Sandwich, in consequence of an application which had been made to him by the Royal Society, laid before his majesty a proposal for an expedition to try how far navigation is practicable towards the north pole. Upon receiving this proposal, his majesty was pleased to direct that the voyage should be immediately undertaken, with every assistance that could contribute to its success. Accordingly, the Racehorse and Carcass bombs were fitted out for the purpose, and the command of the expedition given to Captain Phipps, now Lord Mulgrave. His Lordship's instructions were to proceed up to the pole, or as far towards it as possible, and as nearly upon a meridian as the ice or other obstructions should admit; and during the course of the voyage, to make such observations... North-westerns of every kind as might be useful to navigation, or tend to the promotion of natural knowledge. A very accurate account of this voyage was published by his Lordship in 1774. He had, by exerting all the powers of a skilful and intrepid seaman, forced his way, on the 1st of August, to 80° 37′; but could proceed no farther, as he was there opposed by one continued plain of smooth unbroken ice, bounded only by the horizon. Many other attempts have been made to discover this passage, by sailing along the western coast of America; but hitherto none of them has been crowned with success. So early as 1579, Sir Francis Drake assured Queen Elizabeth that he had sailed some leagues up the straits of Anian (see ANIAN), and discovered New Albion, to the north of California; but the strait is now known to have no existence; and Drake's real discoveries were not improved. In 1638, King Charles I. sent Captain Luke Fox in one of his pinnaces to attempt the passage; but of his proceedings we know nothing, but that he reached Port Nelson in Hudson's bay, where he found some remains of former navigators. Next year Captain James was fitted out by the merchants of Bristol for the same purpose. James was one of the ablest navigators that ever sailed from England or any other country; and his voyages to the north were printed in 1633. After all the experiments he had made, he concluded that there was no such passage; or if there be, he affirmed that the discovery of it would not be attended with those advantages which are commonly expected. His reasons, however, for these opinions have been answered, and many subsequent attempts have been made to perform what he thought impossible. The arguments for a north-west passage were so plausible, that, in 1744, an act of parliament was passed to encourage the discovery of it. Among many others, Captain Cook attempted the discovery in vain, and thence adopted James's opinion. (See COOKE'S Discoveries, No. 153.) This celebrated navigator, after having proceeded northwards to the western extremity of America, and ascertained the proximity of the two great continents of Asia and America, returned to the Sandwich islands, firmly persuaded of the impracticability of a passage in that hemisphere from the Atlantic into the Pacific ocean, either by an eastern or a western course. Later voyagers, however, have pretended to detect some errors in Cooke's discoveries; and the author of a small tract, entitled An authentic Statement of all the Facts relative to Nootka Sound, goes a great way to make the discovery not yet hopeless. In his account of the expedition under the direction of Mr. Etches, he says, that "one of the first discoveries made by these ships was, that what was by the immortal Cook laid down as a continuation of the north-west continent of America, and lying between the northern latitudes of 48° and 57°, is on the contrary an extensive cluster of unexplored islands inhabited by numerous tribes of friendly Indians, with whom a regular connexion was formed." These islands they discovered, contrary to the assertion of Captain Cook, to conceal the opening of a vast inland sea, or archipelago, in all probability equal to the Mediterranean or Baltic seas, and dividing the great northern continent of America. The Prince's Royal penetrated some hundred leagues among them, in a north-east course, to within 200 leagues of Hudson's house, but had not then an opportunity to explore the North-east extreme termination of that archipelago, their commercial concerns obliging them to return to the China market; but the commanders had the strongest reasons to believe, had the time favoured their survey, that they should have been able to discover the long wished for passage between the Atlantic and South Sea.
