They conceived, that should neither the inland arm of the sea through which the Prince's Royal penetrated, nor a large strait named Sir Charles Middleton's about three degrees to the southward, be found to reach across the continent, yet that the land barrier must be very inconsiderable; and that at the extremity of this bay a practicable passage, either by rivers or lakes, will, by perseverance, be found terminating towards Hudson's bay. The last attempt to discover this passage was made by Vancouver between the years 1790 and 1795; but the result of this voyage renders the existence of such a passage still more doubtful. Upon the whole, however, it appears to us extremely doubtful whether there be such a passage; but it is much more likely to be discovered, if discovered at all, by the progressive advances of mercantile enterprise than by any immediate expedition undertaken for that purpose.

NORTH ROCKS

Pages 62-62

(otherwise called St Patrick's rocks, from a seat of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> amongst them called St Patrick's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, whence the rocks have taken this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> name;) situated in the harbour of Donaghadee, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. From <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south they are about two thirds of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, between which is clean good ground. But care must be taken of the fourth rock, on which many ships have perished: for it is overflowed by every tide, and no crew can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> their lives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. This rock stands a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the flore. NORTH <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">SEA</a>. See North Sea.

NORTH-EAST PASSAGE

Pages 60-61

a passage to the East Indies along the northern coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which, like the former, hath frequently been attempted, but hitherto without success. The first attempt was made in 1553, by Sir Hugh Willoughby, who commanded three ships. He departed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> and sailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, where one of his ships left him, and returned home. The other two ships being separated, Sir Hugh proceeded farther northward, and discovered that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> which the Dutch have since called Spitzberg; but the severity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> obliging him to return to the southward, he was forced, by bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, into the river Arzina, in Mulcovite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, where, not being able to come out, he was found the next <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with all his ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; having the notes of his voyage and his last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> lying before him, whereby it appeared that he lived till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. But Richard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>, in the third ship, with better success, in the meanwhile entered Wardhuys, where he waited some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for his companions to no purpose; uncertain whether they were lost, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> driven farther by treas of weather. He held a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> on what he should do; whether to return, or pursue his voyage. Whatever danger might be in the last, every one agreed to it, that they might not seem to have less courage than their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. They therefore set sail, and in a few days found themselves in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> where they could no longer perceive any night. This ship, wandering about, entered soon after into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>. Here they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, in sight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and while they were examining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, they discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. Chancellor getting into his floop, went towards it; but the fishermen took to flight. He followed, and, overtaking them, showed them such civilities as conciliated their affections to him; and they carried him to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where now is the famous port of St Michael the Archangel. These people immediately spread through all the coasts an account of the arrival of those strangers; and people came from several parts to see them, and ask them questions. They, in their turn, examined the others, and found North-east found that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> they were in was Ruffia, governed by the mighty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> John Bafflowitz. Chancellor from Archangel travelled on sledges to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; from whom, overjoyed at the prospect of opening a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he obtained privileges for the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and letters to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward VI, who was not, however, alive to receive them. In 1585, Mr John Davis in two barks discovered Cape Defolation, which is supposed to be part of Greenland; and two years after advanced as far as Lat. 72°, where he discovered the strait which still bears his name. To enumerate all the attempts which have been made to discover a north-east passage, would swell the article to very little purpose. The English, Dutch, and Danes, have all attempted it without success. The last voyage from England for this purpose was made in 1676, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. That unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who was on all occasions <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> for the promotion of commerce, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Berkeley, &c., fitted out a ship, commanded by Captain Wood, for an attempt once more to find a north-east passage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, accompanied with a ship of the king's. They were encouraged to this attempt, after it had been so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> despised of, by several new reports and reasonings: some of which seem not to have been very well grounded—As, "1. On the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COREA">Corea</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, whales had been found with English and Dutch harpoons sticking in them. This is no infallible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that ships could get thither by a north-east passage, although whales might. "2. That, 20 years before, some Dutchmen had sailed within one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the north pole, and found it temperate weather there: and that therefore William Barents, the Dutch navigator who wintered at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a> in the year 1596, should have failed further to the north before <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> eastward; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, said they, he would not have found to much obstruction from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. "3. That two Dutch ships had lately sailed 300 leagues to the eastward of Nova Zembla; but their East India Company had stifled that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, as against their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>:—and such like other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> reports. But this attempt proved very unfortunate. They doubled the North Cape, and came among much ice and drift wood, in 76° of north latitude, steering to the coast of Nova Zembla, where the king's ship struck upon the rocks, and was soon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to pieces; and Captain Wood returned home with an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, "that such a passage was utterly impracticable, and that Nova Zembla is a part of the continent of Greenland." These <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, however, are not yet deemed impracticable by all. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Buffon holds it for certain, that there is a passage from Europe to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> by the North sea. The reason why it has been so often attempted in vain, he thinks, is, that fear prevented the undertakers from keeping at a sufficient distance from land, and from approaching the pole, which they probably imagined to be an immense rock. Hence he affirms, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any farther attempts be made to find a passage to China and Japan by the north seas, it will be necessary to keep at a distance from the land and the ice; to steer directly towards the pole; and to explore the most open seas, where unquestionably, says he, there is little or no ice. This opinion has been lately revived by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Daines Barington, who says, that if the passage be attempted by the pole itself, he has very little doubt of its being accomplished. See North Pole.

NORTHAMPTON

Pages 62-62

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, forming the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Virginia.

NORTHAMPTONSHIRE

Pages 62-62

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, is situated in the very heart of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>: bounded on the east by the counties of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> and Huntingdon; on the south by those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, Rutland, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, which are separated from it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, and the Welland. Its greatest length is about 50 miles, its greatest breadth about 20, and its circumference about 130. It contains 330 parishes. There are in it one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 11 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 25,000 houses, and 131,757 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> members are returned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for this county, viz. two knights for the shire, two for the city of Peterborough, two for each of the towns of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a> and Brockley, and one for Higham Ferrers. It lies in the midland circuit, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Peterborough. As this county is dry, well cultivated, free from marshes, except the fens about Peterborough, in the centre of the kingdom, and of course at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it enjoys a very pure and wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this it is very populous, and so full of towns and churches, that 30 spires <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> steeples may be seen in many places at one view; and even in the fens, the inhabitants seem to enjoy a good state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and to be little affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which frequently overflows their grounds, especially in winter, but is never suffered to remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> upon it. Its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is exceeding fertile both in corn and pasture; but it labours under a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, as it doth not produce much wood, and, by lying at a distance from the sea, cannot be easily supplied with coal. Its commodities, besides corn, are sheep, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-petre; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are ferges, tammies, shalloons, boots, and shoes. Besides many lesser brooks and streams, it is well watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Nen, Welland, Ouse, and Lerm; the three first of which are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> navigable.

NORTHERN LIGHTS

Pages 62-62

the same with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis, under which article we have given a copious account of this phenomenon, and of the supposed causes of it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> science, however, does not arrive at perfection at once, and it is well it does so after trials repeated for years with care and accuracy. How far the causes that have been assigned for this appearance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> account for it; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whether they will be able to remove all difficulties, it is not for us to determine; but it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of philosophers to hear all sides, and to attend with patient fidelity to every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, rejecting or receiving, as reason, after the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, shall seem to favour the one side or the other. We shall here notice a hypothesis which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Stearns, an American, formed, about the year 1788, to account for the appearances called aurora borealis, and aurora australis. Doctor Stearns supposes that these phenomena originate from aqueous, nitrous, sulphurous, bituminous, and other exhalations, from the fumes of various kinds of earths or other minerals, vegetables, animals, fires, volcanoes, &c. These, he thinks, become rarefied, and being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with electrical fluid, become specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the circumambient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; hence, of course, they ascend; and being elevated to the upper regions of the air, and driven by the winds from warmer to colder climates, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> makes them combine and stiffen. When they are afterwards agitated by different currents of air, they sparkle and crackle like the hairs of cats and other animals when stiffened with cold. This concretion in quite cold atmospheres, and in those which are more temperate, appears in different positions in the horizon, zenith, or otherwise, according to the situation of the spectator, and the position of the elevated exhalations. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of colours the doctor supposes to arise from the different qualities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> combined, those of the most inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> shining with the greatest lustre. The doctor likewise tries to account for these lights not appearing, or but seldom appearing, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, he thinks, was not impregnated with materials proper to produce them. He imagines that the increased consumption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in particular, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of volcanoes, and the approach of blazing stars, whose atmospheres have been expanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> that part of them have fallen into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s atmosphere, and communicated to it new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, have so changed and prepared our air, that whenever its confidence is proper, then, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is not too powerful, the aurora borealis will appear.

NORTHUMBERLAND

Pages 62-64

the most northerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, and formerly a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west by the river Tweed, which divides it from Scotland, the Cheviot hills, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; washed on the east by the German ocean; and separated from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tyne and Derwent. This county, which gives gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to a nobleman who married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Algernon duke of Somerset, whose mother was heiress of the Percy family, extends about 66 miles in length from north to south, and about 47 in breadth from east to west. It is remarkably populous, containing 12 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 280 villages, and 460 parishes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, especially towards the west, is roughened with huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the most remarkable of which are the Cheviot hills, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ridge called Redesdale; but the lands are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side and the borders of Durham. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, like that of every other mountainous country in the neighbourhood of the sea, is moist and disagreeable: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, however, is pure and healthy, as being well ventilated by breezes and strong gales of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and in winter mitigated by the warm vapours from the two seas, the Irish and the German ocean, between which it is situated. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> varies in different parts of the county. Among the hills it is barren; though it affords good pasture for sheep, which cover those mountains. The low country, when properly cultivated, produces plenty of wheat, and all sorts of grain; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of it is laid out in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> lands and rich enclosures. Northumberland is well watered with many rivers, rivulets, and fountains: its greatest rivers are the Tweed and the Tyne. The Tyne is composed of two streams called South and North Tyne: the first rises on the verge of Cumberland, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a> moor; enters Northumberland, running north to Haltwhistle; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> easterly, and receiving the two small rivers East and West Alon, unites above <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEXHAM">Hexham</a> with the other branch, taking its rise at a mountain called Fane-head in the western part of the county, thence called Tyne-dale; is swollen in its course by the little river Shele; joins the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEES">Tees</a> near Billingham; and running in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line to the south-east, is united with the southern Tyne, forming a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river that washes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and falls into the German ocean near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYNEMOUTH">Tynemouth</a>. In all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the mountains of Northumberland contain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore, and other mineralized <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in their bowels, as they in all respects resemble those parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> and Scotland where lead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> have been found and prosecuted. Perhaps the inhabitants are diverted from inquiries of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by the certain profits and constant employment they enjoy in working the coal pits, with which this county abounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the greatest part of England, are supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> from these stores of Northumberland, which are inexhaustible, enrich the proprietors, and employ an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and shipping. About 658,958 chaldrons are annually shipped for London. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> woods of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in this county; but many plantations belonging to the seats of noblemen and gentlemen, of which here is a great number. As for pot herbs, roots, saladings, and every article of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden and orchard, they are here raised in great plenty by the usual means of cultivation; as are also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of more delicate flavour, such as the apricot, peach, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECTARINE">nectarine</a>. The spontaneous fruits it produces in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, are the crab-apple, the sloe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bullace, the hazel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, the acorn, hips, and haws, with the berries of the bramble, the juniper, wood strawberries, cranberries, and bilberries. Northumberland raises a good number of excellent horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, and affords pasture for numerous flocks of sheep; both the cattle and sheep are of a large breed, but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is coarser than that which the more southern counties produce. The hills and mountains abound with a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deer, foxes, hares, rabbits, heathcock, grouse, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>, plover, teal, and woodcock: indeed, this is counted one of the best sporting counties in Great Britain. The sea and rivers are well stocked with fish; especially the Tweed, in which a vast number of salmon is caught and carried to Tynemouth, where being pickled, they are conveyed by sea to London, and sold under the name of Newcastle salmon. The Northumbrians were anciently stigmatized as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, barbarous people, addicted to cruelty, and inclined to rapine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, before the union of the two crowns of England and Scotland, the borderers on each side were extremely licentious and ungovernable, trained up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> from their infancy, and habituated to plunder by the mutual incursions made into each kingdom; incursions which neither truce nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> could totally prevent. People of a pacific disposition, who professed to earn their livelihood by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, would not on any terms remain in a country exposed to the first violence of a bold and desperate enemy; therefore the lands lay uncultivated, and in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> deserted by every body but lawless adventurers, who subsisted by theft and rapine. There was a tract 50 miles in length and six in breadth, between Berwick and Carlisle, known by the name of the debatable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, to which both nations laid claim, though it belonged to neither; and this was occupied by a set of banditti who plundered on each side, and what they stole in one kingdom, they sold openly in the other: nay, they were so dexterous in their occupation, that by means of hot <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> applied to the horns of the cattle which they stole, they twisted them in such a manner, that, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> owners <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them in the market, they did not know their own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Wardens were appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the marches or borders in each kingdom; and these offices were always conferred on noblemen of the first character for influence, valour, and integrity. The English border was divided into three marches, called the east, west, and middle marches; the gentlemen of the country were constituted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> wardens, who held <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> courts, regulated the watches, disciplined the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and took <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for assembling them in arms at the first alarm: but in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of peace between the two nations, they were chiefly employed in suppressing the insolence and rapine of the borderers. Since the union of the crowns, however, Northumberland is totally changed, both with respect to the improvement of the lands, and the reformation of the inhabitants. The grounds, being now secure from incursion and insult, are settled by creditable farmers, and cultivated like other parts of the kingdom. As hostilities have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ceased, the people have forgotten the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> themselves in the more eligible avocations of peace, in breeding sheep and cattle, manuring the grounds, working at the coal pits, and in different branches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and manufacture. In their persons they are generally tall, strong, bold, hardy, and fresh coloured; and though less polished than their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, not quite so civilized as their southern Northwick's northern neighbours. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> are well fed, lodged, and clothed; and all of them remarkably distinguished by a kind of shibboleth or whurle, being a particular way of pronouncing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> R, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they hawked it up from the windpipe, like the cawing of rooks. In other respects, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> they speak is an uncoast mixture of the English and Scottish dialects. There is no material distinction between the fashionable people of Northumberland and those of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in other parts of the kingdom; the same form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce the same effects in all countries. The gentlemen of Northumberland, however, are distinguished for their industry, knowledge of rural affairs, and hospitality. The number of inhabitants is reckoned 157,101; of houses 22,740. A great number of Roman monuments have been found in this county; but the most remarkable curiosity of that kind consists in the remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>'s wall and the wall of Severus. See ADRIAN, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> (A), and SEVERUS'S WALL. The most noted towns in Northumberland, are Newcastle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORPETH">Morpeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a>, Berwick, Hexham, and North Shields. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

NORTHWICK

Pages 64-64

a small town of Cheshire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for its rock <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> pits. The stratum of salt lies about 40 yards deep; and some of the pits are hollowed into the form of a temple. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> is through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> supported by rows of pillars about two yards thick, and several in height; and when illuminated with a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of candles, they make a most magnificent appearance. Above the salt is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of whitish clay (Argilla cerula-cinerea), used in making the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a> earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is also dug a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the gypsum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The fossil salt is generally <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and semipellucid, sometimes defaced with a dull greenish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and is often found, but in small quantities, quite clear and colourless. The town is situated near the river Dane, and is tolerably handsome: it has a market on Fridays. It is 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and 173 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. Long. 2° 36'. N. Lat. 53° 16'.

NORTON

Pages 64-64

in Cheshire, a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> almshouse, founded by P—y Brooke, Esq., on the site of a priory of canons regular of St Augustine, founded by William, son of Nigellus, A.D. 1135, who did not live to complete his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; for Euftace de Burgaville granted to Hugh de Catherine pasture for 100 sheep, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he finished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in all respects conformable to the intent of the founders. It was granted afterwards to R. Brooke, Esq.

NORTON'S SOUND

Pages 64-64

was discovered, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook's last voyage, and was so named in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Sir Fletcher <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Grantley), a near relation of Mr afterwards Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>. It extends as far as N. Lat. 64° 55'. There is no good station for ships, nor even a tolerable harbour in all the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. Mr King, on his landing here, discerned many spacious valleys, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> flowing through them, well wooded, and bounded with hills of a moderate height. One of the rivers towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west seemed to be considerable; and he was inclined to suppose, from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, that it discharged itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. Some of his people, penetrating beyond this into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, found the trees to be of a larger size the further they proceeded. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 197° 13'. N. Lat. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, 64° 31'.

NORWAY

Pages 64-72

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> (for the map see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">DENMARK</a>), lying between the 57th and 72d degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between the 5th and 31st degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> east from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; extending in length about 1000 miles, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line from Lindefnaes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Christiania, to the North <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, at the extremity of Finnmark. Its breadth, from the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> westward to Cape Statt, may amount to about 300 miles; but from thence the country becomes gradually narrower towards the north. On the south it is bounded by the Schagen rock, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Categate, the entrance into the Baltic; on the east it is divided from Sweden by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and on the west and north it is washed by the northern ocean. In the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Norway, the country is craggy, abrupt, and mountainous, diversified sometimes with fertile and even delightful spots. In these respects it resembles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>: the prospects and the meteorological phenomena seem to be very similar. The range of the thermometer is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> having risen to 88°, and in the winter fallen to —40°: in general it is between 80° and —22°. Respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Norway it is difficult to attain to certainty. An author of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> (Coxe) seems to think it amounts to 750,000; but he appears to have over-rated it considerably. The Norwegian peasants are free, well clothed, well lodged, spirited, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, frank, open, and undaunted. They are said to have a very considerable resemblance to the peasants of Switzerland. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is too thin for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>: corn is therefore obtained from the neighbouring flats; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment of the peasants of Norway is grazing. The following extract from Mr Coxe, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> near Christiana, is not beside our purpose, and may not perhaps be disagreeable to our readers. "As we approached Christiana, the country was more wild and hilly, but still very fertile and agreeable; and about two miles from the town we came to the top of a mountain, and burst upon as fine a view as ever I beheld. From the point on which we stood in raptures, the grounds laid out in rich enclosures, gradually sloped to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; below us appeared Christiana, situated at the extremity of an extensive and fertile valley, forming a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> along the shore of a most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, which, being enclosed by hills, uplands, and forests, had the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake. Behind, before, and around, the inland mountains of Norway rose on mountains covered with dark forests of pines and fir, the inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the north. The most distant summits were capped with eternal snow. From the glow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, the warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the variety of the productions, and the mild beauties of the adjacent scenery, I could scarcely believe that I was nearly in the 60th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of northern latitude." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Norway, extending above 300 leagues, is studded with a multitude of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, affording habitation to fishermen and pilots, and pasture to a few cattle. They form an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of narrow channels, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> of rocks, which renders Norway inaccessible to the naval power of its enemies. Attempts of this kind are the more dangerous, as the shore is generally bold, steep, and impeding; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the rocks the depth of the sea amounts to 100, 200, or 300 fathoms. The perils of the north sea are moreover increased by sudden storms, sunk rocks, violent currents, and dreadful whirlpools. The most remarkable vortex on this coast is called Mofkoe-fjord, from the small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Mofkoe, belonging to the district of Lofoten in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Nordland. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, the stream runs up between Lofoden and Mofkoe with the most boisterous rapidity; but in its ebb to the sea, it roars like a thousand cataracts, so as to be heard at the distance of many leagues. The surface exhibits different vortices; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in one of these any ship or vessel is absorbed, it is whirled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bottom, and dashed in pieces against the rocks. These violent whirlpools continue without intervals, except for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, at high and low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, in calm weather; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> gradually returns as the flood or ebb advances. When its fury is heightened by a storm, no vessel ought to venture within a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of it. Whales have been frequently absorbed within the vortex, and howled and bellowed hideously in their fruitless endeavours to disengage themselves. A bear, in attempting to swim from Lofoten to Mofkoe, was once hurled into this whirlpool, from whence he struggled in vain for deliverance, roaring so loud as to be heard on shore; but notwithstanding all his efforts, he was borne down and destroyed. Large trees being absorbed by the current are sucked down, and rise again all shattered into splinters. There are three vortices of the same kind near the islands of Ferroe. Norway is divided into the four governments of Aggerhus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRONTHEIM">Drontheim</a>, and Wardhus, besides that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAHUS">Bahus</a>, which is now subject to Sweden. The province of Aggerhus comprehends the south-east part of Norway, extending in length about 300 miles. Its chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Christiana, the see of a bishop, suffragan to the metropolitan see of Drontheim, where the sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is held, in presence of the viceroy and the governor of the province; Aggerhus, about 15 miles to the south-west of Christiana; Fredericksthall or Frederikstad, in the siege of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. of Sweden lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; Saltzberg, Tonberg, Alleen, Hammar, and Hollen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Bergen lies in the most southerly and westerly part of Norway, including the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, which is an episcopal see, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade; and Staffanger, situated in the bay of Buckenfor, about 80 miles to the southward of Bergen. The third province, called Drontheim or Trondheim, extends about 500 miles along the coast; and is but thinly peopled. The chief town, Drontheim, seated on a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> at the mouth of the river Nider, is the only metropolitan see in Norway; and carries on a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, deals, tar, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Leetfrund, Stronden, Scoerdale, Opdal, Romildal, and Solendael, are likewise places of some traffic. The northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Drontheim, called the sub-government of Salten, comprehends the towns Melanger and Scheen. The province of Wardhus, extending to the North Cape, and including the islands, is divided into two parts; namely, Finnmark and Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>. The chief town, which is very insignificant, stands upon an island called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, from whence the place and the government derive their name, Norway. The province of Bahus, though now yielded to the Swedes, is reckoned part of Norway, being a narrow tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, about 90 miles in length, lying on the coast of the Categate. The great chain of Norway mountains, running from north to south, called indifferently Rudfield, Snudefield, Skarsfield, and Scoreberg, is known in different parts by other appellations; such as Dofrefield, Lamfied, Sagufield, Filefield, Halnefield, Hardangerfield, Joklefield, Bygglefield, Hicklefield, and Hangfield. The height and breadth of this extensive chain likewise vary in different parts. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the mountain Hardanger, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> must travel about 70 English miles, whereas Filefield may be about 50 over. This last rises about two miles and a half in perpendicular height; but Dofrefield is counted the highest mountain of Norway, if not of Europe. The river Drivane winds along the side of it in a fertile course, so as to be met <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times by those who travel the winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the other side of the chain. The bridges are thrown over roaring cataracts, and but indifferently fastened to the steep rocks on either side; so that the whole exhibits a very dreadful appearance, sufficient to deter the traveller from hazarding such a dangerous passage; for which reason, people generally choose the road over Filefield, which is much more tedious. This, however, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> road used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The way is distinguished by posts fixed at the distance of 200 paces from each other, that, in snowy or dark weather, the traveller may not be bewildered. For the convenience of resting and refreshing, there are two mountain stoves or houses maintained on Filefield, as well as upon other mountains, at the expense of the public, and furnished with fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensils. Nothing can be more dismal and dreary than those mountains covered with eternal snow, where neither <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, tree, nor living creature is to be seen, but here and there a solitary rein deer, and perhaps a few wandering Laplanders. In travelling from Sweden to Nordenfields, there is only one way of avoiding this chain of mountains; and that is, where it is interrupted by a long deep valley, extending from Romfdale to Guldbranddalen. In the year 1612, a body of 1000 Scots, commanded by Sinclair, and sent over as auxiliaries to the Swedes, were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in this defile, by the peasants of Guldbrand, who never gave quarter. Besides this chain, there is a great number of detached mountains over all the country, that form valleys and ridges, inhabited by the peasants. Some of these are of incredible height, and others exhibit very remarkable appearances. In sailing up Joering Creek on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the sight is astonisbed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of mountains, resembling the prospect of a city, with old Gothic towers and edifices. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Oerfkong is the high mountain Skopfhorn, the top of which represents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a fortification, with regular walls and bastions. In the district of Hilgeland appears a very high range of mountains, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pinnacles or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, known by the appellation of the Seven <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a>, discernible a great way off at sea. To the southward of this range, though in the same district, rises the famous mountain Torghatten, so called because the summit resembles a man's head with a hat on, under which appears a single eye, formed by an aperture through the mountain. Norway. mountain, 150 ells high, and 3000 ells in length. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> may be seen through this surprising cavity, which is passible by the foot of travellers. On the top of the mountain we find a reservoir of water, as large as a moderate fish pond; in the lower part is a cavern, through which a line 400 fathoms in length, being let down, did not reach the bottom. At Herroe in Sundmoer is another cavern called Doffeen, supposed to reach under the sea to Scotland; which, however, is no more than an idle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. In the year 1752, two clergymen entered this subterranean cavity, and proceeded a considerable way, until they heard the feet dashing over their heads; the passage was as wide and high as an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the sides perpendicular, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> vaulted. They descended one flight of natural stairs; but arriving at another, they were afraid to penetrate farther; they had gone so far, however, that two candles were consumed in their progress and return. A cavern of a very curious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, serving as a conduit to a stream of water, penetrates through the sides of the mountain Limur. In the district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">Rake</a>, in the neighbourhood of Frederichshall, are three cavities in a rock; one of which is so deep, that a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> dropped down, does not reach the bottom in less than two minutes; and then the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> it produces is pleasant and melodious, not unlike the sound of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. The vast mountains and rugged rocks that deform the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this country are productive of numberless inconveniences. They admit of little arable ground; they render the country in some parts impassable, and everywhere difficult to travellers; they afford shelter to wild beasts, which come from their lurking holes, and make terrible havoc among the flocks of cattle; they expose the sheep and goats, as well as the peasants, to daily accidents of falling over precipices; they occasion sudden torrents, and falls of snow, which descend with incredible impetuosity, and often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> away the labours of the husbandman; and they are subject to dreadful disruptions, by which huge rocks are rent from their sides, and, hurling down, overwhelm the plains below with inevitable ruin. The peasants frequently build their houses on the edge of a steep precipice, to which they must climb by ladders, at the hazard of their lives; and when a person dies, the corpse must be let down with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, before it can be laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>. In winter the mail is often drawn up the sides of steep mountains. Even in the king's road, travellers are exposed to the frequent risks of falling over those dreadful rocks; for they are obliged to pass over narrow pathways, without rails or rising on the sides, either thored up with rotten planks, or suspended by iron bolts fastened in the mountains. In the narrow pass of Naeroe is a remarkable way of this kind, which, above 600 years ago, the famous King Sverre caused to be made for the passage of his cavalry; and even this would have been found impassable by any other horses than those of Norway, which are used to climb the rocks like goats. Another very difficult and dangerous road is that between Shogstadt and Vang-in-Volders, along the side of a steep mountain, in some places so narrow, that if two travellers on horseback should meet in the night, they would find it impracticable either to pass each other, or turn back. In such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> their lives could not be saved, unless one of them should alight, and throw his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> headlong into the lake below, and then cling to the rock, until the other could pass. When a sheep or goat makes a false step to the projection of a rock, from whence it can neither ascend nor descend, the owner hazards his own life to preserve that of the animal. He directs himself to be lowered down from the top of the mountain, sitting on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> stick, tied to the end of a long rope; and when he arrives at the place where the creature stands, he fastens it to the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, and it is drawn up with himself. Perhaps the other end of the rope is held by one person only; and there are some instances in which the assistant has been dragged down by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his friend, so that both have perished. When either man or beast has had the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> over very high precipices, they have not only been suffocated by the repercussion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, but their bodies have been always burst before they reached the ground. Sometimes entire crests of rocks, many fathoms in length and breadth, have fallen down at once, creating such a violent agitation of the air, as seemed a prelude to the world's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. At Steenbroe in Laerdal, a stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, larger than any castle in the universe, appears to have been fevered and tumbled from the mountain in large, sharp, and ragged fragments, through which the river rears with hideous bellowing. In the year 1731, a promontory on Sundmoer, called Ramsfjeld, that hung over Nordal Creek, suddenly gave way, and plunged into the water; which swelled to such a degree, that the church of Strand, though half a league on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, was overflowed; the creek, however, was not filled up; on the contrary the fishermen declare they find no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the depth, which is said to exceed 900 fathoms. The remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Norway are these: The Nied, issuing from Tydalmen, on the borders of Sweden, runs westward into the lake Selboe; and afterwards, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the northward, passes by the city of Drontheim, to which it anciently gave the name of Nidero; and Nidqo: Sule <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, that descending from Sulefield, runs with a rapid course through Nordale into the sea; Gulen, which rises near Sifferfeld in the north; and running 20 leagues westward, through Aalen, Hlotaalen, Storen, and Meihus, discharges itself into the sea, about a league to the west of Drontheim. In the year 1344, this river buried itself under ground; from whence it again burst forth with such violence, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> thrown up by the eruption filled the valley, and formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>; which, however, was soon broken and washed away by the force of the water. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> churches, 48 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> houses, with 250 persons, were destroyed on this occasion.—Otteren, a large river, taking its rise from the mountain Agde, runs about 30 leagues through Seesterdale and Efde, and discharges itself into the cataract of Wiland. The river Syre rises near the mountain Lang, and winds its course through the vale of Syre into the lake of Lande in the diocese of Christiania; thence it continues its way to the sea, into which it discharges itself through a narrow strait formed by two rocks. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> augments its impetuosity, so that it shoots like an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> into the sea, in which it produces a very great agitation. Nid and Sheen are two considerable rivers, issuing out of Tillemark. Their water-falls have been diverted, with infinite labour, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> cut through the rocks, for the convenience of floating down the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. Tyreford or Dramme, is in the neighbourhood of Ho- Norway nifosse, joined by two rivers from Osdale and Hadsland, and disembogues itself into the sea near Bragernes. Loven rises in the highest part of Nummedal, and runs through Konnerberg to the sea near Laurvig. Glaamnen is the largest river of Norway, distinguished by the name of Stor Elvin, or the great river. It derives its origin from the mountain Dofre, from whence it winds all along the plains of Oesterdalen and Soloe; then joins the Vorme, another considerable river rising out of Mioss and Guldbranddalen. These being joined, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the lake Oeyern; and thence issuing, run on to Sarp near Fredericksfadt. Norway abounds with fresh-water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are Ryfvan in Nordland, Snalen, Selboe, the Greater and Lesser Mioss, Shirevand, Sperdille, Rand, Vefta, Saren, Modum, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">Lund</a>, Norfoe, Huidfoe, Farifvand, and Oeyevand: all these are well stocked with fish, and navigable for large vessels. Wars have been formerly carried on upon these inland seas; in some of which are small floating islands, or parcels of earth, with trees on them, separated from the main land, and probably preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> masses by the roots of trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and grass, interwoven in the soil. In the year 1722, the family seat of Borge, near Fredericksfadt, being a noble edifice, with lofty towers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, suddenly sunk into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> 100 fathoms deep, which was instantaneously filled by a piece of water 300 ells in length and about half as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Fourteen persons, with 200 head of cattle, perished in this catastrophe, which was occasioned by the river Glaamnen precipitating itself down a waterfall near Sarp, and undermining the foundation. Of all the waterfalls in Norway this of Sarp is the most dangerous for its height and rapidity. The current drives 17 miles; and roars with such violence, that the water, being dashed and comminuted among the rocks, rises in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, where a beautiful rainbow may be always seen when the sun shines. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times this cataract was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for the execution of traitors and other malefactors: they were thrown down alive, that they might be dashed in pieces on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of rocks, and die in a dreadful commotion, analogous to those they had endeavoured to excite in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. Great part of Norway is covered with forests of wood, which constitute the principal article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in this country. They chiefly consist of fir and pine, for which great sums are received from foreigners, who export an immense number of masts, beams, planks, and boards. Besides, an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is consumed at home in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, ships, bridges, piles, moles, and fences; over and above the vast demand for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> to the foundries, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> uses.—Nay, in some places, the trees are felled for no other purpose but to clear the ground and to be burned into ashes for manure. A good quantity of timber is yearly exported to Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but this is inconsiderable when compared to the vast exports from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRAMMEN">Drammen</a>, Frederickshall or Fredericksfadt, Christiana, Skeen, Arendal, Christiania, Chriffian's Bay, and Drontheim. The masts and large beams are floated down the rivers, and the rest is divided into boards at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. These works supply a vast number of families with a comfortable subsistence.—A tenth part of all sawed timber belongs to his Danish majesty, and makes a considerable branch of his revenue. The forests in Norway are so vast and thick, that the people seem to think Norway there can never be a scarcity of wood, especially as the soil is peculiarly adapted for the production of timber; they therefore destroy it with a wasteful hand; insomuch that more wood rots in Norway than is burned in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Denmark. The best timber grows in the provinces of Saltan, Helleland, Komfdale, Guldbranddalen, Oesterdalen, Soloe, Valders, Hallingdale, Sogniford, Telemark, and the lordship of Nedenes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Norway is very different in different parts of the kingdom. At Bergen the winter is so moderate, that the seas are always open and practicable both to mariners and fishermen, except in creeks and bays, that reach far up into the country towards Filefield, when the keen north-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the land. On the east side of Norway, from the frontiers of Sweden to Filefield, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> generally sets in about the middle of October with great severity, and lasts till the middle of April; during which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> the waters are frozen to a very considerable thickness, and the face of the country is covered with snow. In the year 1719, 7500 Swedes, who intended to attack Drontheim, perished in the snow on the mountain of Ruden or Tydel, which separates Jempleteland in Sweden from the diocese of Drontheim. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of 200 Norwegian fledge-men under <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Emahus, found them all frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> on the ridge of the mountain, where they had been surprised by a storm accompanied with snow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cold. Some of these unhappy victims appeared fitting, some lying, and others kneeling in a posture of praying. They had cut in pieces their muklets, and burned the little wood they afforded.—The generals Labarre and Zoega lost their lives; and of the whole corps, consisting originally of 10,000, no more than 250 survived this dreadful catastrophe. The cold is still more intense in that part of Norway called Finnmark, situated in the frigid zone near the polar circle. But if the winter is generally cold, the summer is often excessively hot in Norway. The rays of the sun are reverberated from the sides of the mountains so as to render the weather close and sultry in the valleys; besides, the sun's absence below the horizon is so short, that the atmosphere and mountains have not time to cool. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so great, that vegetation is remarkably quick. Barley is sown, grows, ripens, and is reaped, in the space of six weeks or two months. The longest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at Bergen consists of 19 hours; the sun rising at half an hour after two, and setting at half an hour after nine. The shortest day does not exceed five hours; for the sun rises at nine in the morning, and sets at three in the afternoon.—In the beginning of the year the daylight increases with remarkable celerity; and, at the approach of winter, decreases in the same proportion. In summer one may read and write at midnight by the light of the sky. Christian V., while he resided at Drontheim, used to sup at midnight without candles. In the district of Tromfen, at the extremity of Norway, the sun is continually in view at midsummer. It is seen to circulate day and night round the north pole, contracting its orbit, and then gradually enlarging it, until at length it leaves the horizon. In the depth of winter, therefore, it is for some weeks invisible; and all the light perceived at noon is a faint glimmering for about an hour and a half, proceeding from the reflection of the sun's rays from the highest mountains. Norway. mountains. But the inhabitants of these provinces are supplied with other lights that enable them to follow their employments in the open air. The sky being generally serene, the moonlight is remarkably bright, and, being reflected from the mountains, illuminates the valleys. They are also afflicted by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis, which is very frequent in the northern parts of Europe. The air of Norway is generally pure and salubrious. On the sea coasts, indeed, it is rendered moist by vapours and exhalations; but in the midland parts of the country, towards the mountains, the climate is so dry, that meat may be kept for many years without being worm-eaten or damaged in the least. The inhabitants have no idea of sickness, except what is occasioned by excesses. It is said, that in the vale of Guldbrand the inhabitants live to such extreme old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that they become weary of life, and cause themselves to be removed to a less salubrious climate, whereby they may have a chance of dying sooner. In consumptions, however, the moist air on the sea side is found to be most agreeable to the lungs in respiration. Norway, being a mountainous country intersected by creeks, abounding with lakes, rivers, and snow, must be subject to frequent rains; and from sudden thaws the inhabitants are sometimes exposed to terrible dilatations. Vast masses of snow falling from precipices overwhelm men, cattle, boats, houses, nay even whole villages. About two centuries ago, a whole parish was covered and destroyed by an immense mass of snow; and several domestic utensils, as teapots, knives, and basins, have been at different times brought to light by a rivulet that runs under the snow, which has been gradually hardened and increased by repeated frosts and annual accretions. The winds that chiefly prevail on the western coast are those that blow from the south; whereas, on the other side of Fifefield, the winds that produce and continue the hard frosts are always northerly. In the summer, there is a kind of regular trade-wind on the coast of Bergen. In the forenoon the sea begins to be cooled with a westerly breeze, which continues till midnight. Then the land breeze begins from the east, and blows till about ten in the morning. The coast is likewise subject to sudden squalls and storms. Hurricanes sometimes rise at sea; and in these latitudes the phenomenon called a water-spout is not uncommon. One of these in the neighbourhood of Ferro is said to have sucked up with the water some last of herrings, which were afterwards dropped on Kolter, a mountain 1200 feet high. The fresh water of Norway is not very light or pure; but on the contrary, is generally turbid, and deposits a sediment of adventitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, being sometimes impregnated with ochre and particles of iron.—Nevertheless it is agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and remarkably salubrious; as appears from the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, who drink little or no other liquor. The soil of Norway varies in different places according to the situation of rock or valley. The mountains, here, as in every other country, are bare and barren; but the earth washed down from them by the rains enriches and fertilizes the valleys. In these the soil generally consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mould, sand, loam, chalk, and gravel, lying over one another in unequal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, and sometimes in three or four successions: the mould that lies uppermost is very fine and mellow, and fit to nourish all sorts of vegetables. There is also clay found in different parts of this kingdom, of which the inhabitants begin to make earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; but bricks and tiles are not used in building. The face of the country is in many places deformed by large swamps and marshes, very dangerous to the traveller. Near Leefoe in the diocese of Christiania, a wooden causeway is extended near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> over a morass; and if a horse or any other animal should make a false step, he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> sink at once into the abyss, never to rise again. In a cold country like Norway, stony with rocks and mountains, interspersed with bogs, and covered with forests, we cannot expect to find <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in perfection. The ploughed lands, in respect to mountains, woods, meadows, and wastes, do not exceed the proportion of 1 to 80; so that the whole country does not produce corn to maintain above half the number of its inhabitants. The peasants are discouraged from the practice of husbandry by the frequency of accidents that seem peculiar to the climate. Even in the fruitful provinces of Guldbrandsfjeld, Oesterdale, and Soloe, as well as in the other places, when the corn appears in the most flourishing condition, the whole hope of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is sometimes destroyed in one night by a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> that nips the blade and extinguishes the vegetation. The kingdom is moreover visited by some unfavourable years, in which the sun seems to have lost his genial power; the vegetables are blighted; the trees bud and bloom, yet bear no fruit; and the grain, though it rises, will yet produce nothing but empty ears and straw. This calamity, however, rarely occurs; and in general the cultivated parts of Norway yield plentiful crops of excellent rye, barley, and oats. The most fruitful provinces are Nordland, Inderbarre, and Numedale, in the diocese of Drontheim; Sognfjord and Vaas, in that of Bergen; Jeddere, Ryefylk, Raabygdalag, the lordship of Nedenes, in the diocese of Christiania; Hedemark in the diocese of Aggerhus; Hadeland, Toten, Romerige, Ringerige, and Guldbrandsfjeld: these territories not only produce grain enough for their own consumption, but likewise support their neighbours, and even supply part of Sweden.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">Peat</a> is likewise propagated in this country, together with wheat, buckwheat, hops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, but not to any considerable advantage. The meadows are well stored with pasturage for sheep and cattle, and the fields are productive of those vegetables which are common in other northern countries. Within these 50 years the people of Norway have bestowed some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the culture of gardens, which in former times was so neglected, that the cities and towns were supplied with leeks, cabbage, and roots, from England and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. At present, however, the Norwegians raise their own culinary and garden roots and vegetables, which thrive there as well as in any other country. The scarcity being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that prevails along the sea coast, Nature has scattered upon it a variety of herbs efficacious in the cure of that distemper; such as angelica, rofe-wort, gentian, cretis, trefoil, forrel, scurvy-grafts, and a plant called erich's grafs, that grows in great plenty on the islands of Nordland: from whence the people of the continent fetch away <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> loads of it, to be preserved in barrels as a succedaneum for cabbage. There are also a few noxious vegetables little known in any country but Norway. In Guldbranddalle is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grass called *selfnape*, the root of which is so poisonous, that any beast which eats of it dies immediately, the belly bursting; nay, the carnivorous fowls that prey upon the carcals of the beast meet with the same fate: children have been more than once poisoned by this root, which nevertheless is sometimes used externally as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMULET">amulet</a> for arthritic disorders. Another vegetable pernicious to the cattle is the *Gramen offfragum Norwegienfe*, which is said to mollify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the cattle which feed upon it. Among the noxious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of Norway we may also reckon the *gle-glas*, fatal to sheep and goats; the *tour-gras*, which affects horses and cows with a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>; and the plant *torboe*, or little-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, which produces nearly the same effect on horses, but is not at all prejudicial to cows, sheep, or any ruminating animals. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> *turte*, not unlike angelica, operates nearly in the same manner: yet the bears are said to feed upon it with peculiar relish; and when their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> begins to fall off by feeding upon this plant, they cure themselves by eating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of animals. The common fruit trees thrive tolerably well in Norway, the inhabitants of which have plenty of cherries, apples, and pears. Some kinds of plums attain maturity; which is seldom the case with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, apricots, and peaches. But even the apples and pears that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> here are summer fruit; that which grows till the winter seldom coming to perfection.
