Great variety of agreeable berries is produced in different parts of this kingdom; such as the hagebar, a kind of floes; an infusion of which in wine makes a pleasant cooling liquor; juniper berries, corinths <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, foelbar or sunberries, raifberries, goofeberries, blackberries, strawberries, &c. with many other species that seem to be natives of Norway and Sweden. Among those are the transebar, the produce of the myrtillus repens, red and auster, found in the spring in perfection under the snow, and much relished by the reindeer; crakebeer, resembling bilberries, deemed a powerful anticoagulant; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">ager</a>-beer, larger and blacker than bilberries, of a pleasant acid, ripened by cold, and used as cherries for an infusion in wine; and finally tytlebeer, a red pleasant berry growing on a short stem, with leaves like those of box; they are plucked off by handfuls, and sent to Denmark to be preferred for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, where they are eaten by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESSERT">dessert</a>. Of the trees that grow wild in Norway, the principal are the fir and the pine. The first yield an annual revenue of 1,000,000 of rixdollars, if we include the advantages resulting from the saw mills and the masts; one of which last has been known to sell for 200 rixdollars. The red fir tree, which grows on the mountains, is so rich in turpentine as to be almost incorruptible. Some of the houses belonging to the Norway peasants, built of this timber, are supposed to be above 400 years standing. In Guldbranddalle the house is still to be seen standing in which King Olaf lodged five nights, above 700 years ago, when he travelled round the kingdom to convert the people to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Even 100 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the fir tree has been cut down, the peasants burn the roots for tar, which is a very profitable commodity. In the fens, the resin of the fir tree is by nature transformed into a substance which may be called *Norway frankincense*. The buds or pine apples of this tree, boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> beer, make an excellent medicine for the scurvy; less unpleasant to the taste, though as efficacious, as tar-water. The pine tree is more tall and beautiful than the fir, though inferior to it in strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; for which reason the planks of it are sold at an inferior price, and the peasants waste it without remorse. Norway likewise produces some forests of oak, which is found to be excellent for ship-building. Here also grow plenty of elm trees; the bark of which, being powdered, is boiled up with other food to fatten hogs, and even mixed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> among their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>; also the ash, from which the peasants distill a balm used in certain disorders, and which is used both externally and internally. Many other trees flourish in this country, an enumeration of which would prove too tedious. Hazels grow here in such abundance, that 100 tons of the nuts are annually exported from Bergen alone. A great diversity of stones is found in Norway, some of which are of a surprising figure. Several mountains consist chiefly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> pebble, which decays with age; nay, it sometimes dissolves, and drops into the sea, and the cement being thus loosened, a terrible dilution ensues. In some places the gray and black pebbles are intermixed with iron, copper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The ground in certain districts is covered with the fragments of rocks that have been precipitated from the summits of mountains, and broken by their fall into innumerable shivers. Between 20 and 30 years ago, in the neighbourhood of Bergen, a man was suddenly overwhelmed with such a mass, which formed a kind of vault around him. In this dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> he remained alive for several weeks. By his loud cries the place of his confinement was discovered: but it was found impossible to remove the huge stones by which he was inclosed. All that his friends could do for him was, to lower down meat and drink through some crevices; but at length the stones fell in, and crushed him to death. In Norway are inexhaustible quarries of excellent marble, black, white, blue, gray, and variegated; together with some detached pieces of alabaster, several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, chalk-stone, cement-stone, <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-stone</a>, millstone, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>-stone, flate, talc, magnets, and wine-stone, a production natural to Norway and Sweden, of a brown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, fetid smell, in texture resembling crystal, and deriving its name from a supposed efficacy in curing a distemper incident to swine. Here also is found the amianthus or stone-flax, of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a> cloth may be made. Norway, however, affords no flints, but plenty of pyrites or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, beautiful crystals, granites, amethysts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>-stones, and eagle-stones. Gold has formerly been found in a small quantity in the diocese of Christianland, and coined into ducats. There is at present a very considerable silver mine wrought at Kongsherg on the account and at the risk of his Danish majesty: the ore is surprisingly rich, but interrupted in such a manner, that the vein is often lost. Many masses of pure silver have been found; and, among the rest, one piece weighing 560 pounds, preserved in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. Such is the richness of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, that the annual produce amounts in value to a ton and a half in gold. About 5000 people are daily employed, and earn their subsistence, in these stupendous works. Norway. works (a). Other silver mines are prosecuted at Jarlberg, but not to the same advantage; and here the ore is mixed with lead and copper. In many parts of this country copper mines have been discovered; but the principal, and perhaps the richest in all Europe, is at Rorasaas, about 100 English miles from Drontheim. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> yields annually about 1100 ship pounds of pure copper; the founderies belonging to it consume yearly about 14,000 lasts of coal, and 500 fathoms of wood. The next in importance is the copper work at Lykken, about 20 miles from Drontheim. A third mine is carried on at Indet or Quickne, at the distance of 30 miles from the same place; and here they precipitate the copper from its mercurium, by means of iron. There is a fourth copper work at Silboe, about 30 miles distant from Drontheim, though the least considerable of the four. Other copper mines of less note are worked in different parts of the kingdom. Iron is still in greater plenty, and was the first metal wrought in this country. Many hundred thousand quintals are annually exported, chiefly in bars, and part of it in stoves, pots, kettles, and cannon; the national profit arising from this metal is estimated at 300,000 rixdollars. There is a species called moor-iron, found in large lumps among the morasses: of this the peasants make their own domestic tools and utensils, such as knives, scythes, and axes. The lead found mixed in the silver ore is an article of small importance in Norway; yet some mines of this metal have been lately opened in the district of Soloe by the proprietors of the copper work at Oudal. A vitriol work has been begun near Kongberg: the mines yield great plenty of sulphur; which, however, the Norwegians will not take the trouble to melt and depurate, because immense quantities are found at a cheaper rate in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">Alum</a> is found between the slate flakes near Christiania in such plenty, that works have been set up for refining this mineral, though they have not yet brought it to any degree of transparency. His Danish majesty has established <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Valoe, about six English miles from Tonberg, where this mineral is extracted in large quantities from the sea water. Besides the animals common to other countries, Norway is said to contain many of the uncommon and dubious kind; such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KRAKEN">kraken</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERMAID">mermaid</a>, sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, &c. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Many Danish, English, Scotch, Dutch, and German families have now settled in Norway; and indeed form no inconsiderable part of the trading people: but the original inhabitants are the descendants of those ferocious Normanni, who harried almost all the coasts of Europe with piratical armaments in the 8th, 9th, and 10th centuries. "Our first certain knowledge of the inhabitants of this country (says Pennant *) was from the defoliation they brought on the southern nations by their piratical invasions. Their country had before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the name of Nortmanland, and the inhabitants Normans, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> which included other adjacent people. Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> were ravaged by them in 845; and they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their invasion till they effected the conquest of England, under their leader Canute the Great. They went up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, burnt the town, and forced its weak monarch to purchase their absence at the price of fourteen thousand marks. They plundered Spain, and at length carried their excursions through the Mediterranean to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and even into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. They used narrow vessels, like their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> the Sitones; and, besides oars, added the improvement of two sails; and victualled them with salted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, biscuit, cheese, and beer. Their ships were at first small; but in after times they were large enough to hold 100 or 120 men. But the multitude of vessels was amazing. The fleet of Harold Blageland consisted of 700. A hundred thousand of these savages have at once sailed from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, so justly styled Officina gentium, aut certe velut <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> nationum. Probably <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, more than ambition, caused them to displace their country of its exuberant numbers. Multitudes were destroyed; but multitudes remained, and peopled more favourable climates. "Their king, Olaus, was a convert to Christianity in 904; Bernard an Englishman had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of baptizing him, when Olaus happened to touch at one of the Scilly islands. He plundered with great spirit during several years; and in 1066 received the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of martyrdom from his pagan subjects. But <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> zeal first gave the rest of Europe a knowledge of their country and the sweets of its commerce. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> towns poured in their missionaries, and reaped a temporal harvest. By the year 1204, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> obtained from the wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Suer every encouragement to commerce; and by that means introduced wealth and civilization into his barren kingdom. England by every method cherished the advantages resulting from an intercourse with Norway, and Bergen was the emporium. Henry III. in 1217, entered into a league with its monarch Haquin; by which both princes stipulated for free access for their subjects into their respective kingdoms, free trade, and security to their persons. In 1269, Henry entered into another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with Magnus; in which it was agreed, that no goods should be exported from either kingdom except they had been paid for; and there is, besides a humane provision on both sides, for the security of the persons and effects of the subjects who should suffer shipwreck on their several coasts." The inhabitants now speak the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> that is used in Denmark, through their original tongue is the dialect now spoken in Iceland. They profess the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, under an archbishop established at Drontheim. (a) Mr Coxe tells us, that he visited those mines, but at present yield little more than 50,000l. The expenses generally exceed the profits; and government gains only by the number of miners employed. The mines of cobalt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of Prussian blue, are much more productive. The latter goes through 270 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and the number of men employed is 365. It is supposed, that, at this period (1793), it may produce to government a profit of 16,000l. a-year. Drontheim, with four suffragans; namely, of Bergen, Staffanger, Hammer, and Christiana. By the union of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALMAR">Calmar</a>, the two kingdoms of Norway and Denmark were united under one monarch; and then the people of both nations enjoyed considerable privileges: but the Danish government soon became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>; and Norway was ruled despotically by a viceroy, who resided in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and presided in the supreme court, to which appeals were made from the subordinate courts of judicature. A great change has, however, taken place since the present amiable and accomplished prince of Denmark had part of the government; and more may be expected from his virtue and affability when the power shall come wholly into his own hands. The Norwegians are generally well formed, tall, sturdy, and robust, brave, hardy, honest, hospitable, and ingenious; yet <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, rash, quarrelsome, and litigious. The same character will nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the inhabitants of every mountainous country in the northern climates. Their women are well shaped, tall, comely, remarkably fair, and obliging. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Norway have been chiefly removed by the kings of Denmark, in order to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> and opposition to the court; or are long ago degenerated into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of peasants: some families, however, have been lately raised to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Every freeholder in Norway enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of primogeniture and power of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and it is very usual to see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> inhabiting the same house which has been possessed 400 years by his ancestors. The adels-gods, or freehold, cannot be alienated by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> or otherwise from the right heir, called adels-mand: if he is not able to redeem the estate, he declares his incapacity every 10th year at the sessions; and if he, or his heirs to the third <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, should acquire wealth enough for that purpose, the possessor pro tempore must resign his possession. The mountaineers acquire surprising strength and dexterity by hard living, cold, laborious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, climbing rocks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SKATING">skating</a> on the snow, and handling arms, which they carry from their youth to defend themselves against the wild beasts of the forest. Those who dwell in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> parts of Norway exercise the employments of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and become very expert mariners. The peasants of Norway never employ any handicraftsmen for necessaries to themselves and families: they are their own hatters, shoemakers, tailors, tanners, weavers, carpenters, smiths, and joiners: they are even expert at ship-building; and some of them make excellent violins. But their general turn is for carving in wood, which they execute in a surprising manner with a common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> of their own forging. They are taught in their youth to wrestle, ride, swim, skate, climb, shoot, and forge iron. Their amusements consist in making verses, blowing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, or playing upon a kind of guitar, and the violin: this last kind of music they perform even at funerals. The Norwegians have evinced their valour and fidelity in a thousand different instances. The country was always disturbed by intestine quarrels, which raged from generation to generation. Even the farmers stand upon their puntillo, and challenge one another to single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> with their knives. On such occasions they hook themselves together by their belts, and fight until one of them is killed or mortally wounded. At weddings and public feasts they drink to intoxication, quarrel, fight, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> generally ensues. The very common people are likewise passionate, ambitious of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and independence, and vain of their pedigree. The nobility and merchants of Norway fare sumptuously; but the peasant lives with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and frugality, except at festivals: his common <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is made of oatmeal, rolled into broad thin cakes, like those used in Scotland. In time of scarcity, they boil, dry, and grind the bark of the fir tree into a kind of flour which they mix with oatmeal; the bark of the elm tree is used in the same manner. In those parts where a fishery is carried on, they knead the roes of cod with their oat meal. Of these last, mixed with barley meal, they make hasty pudding and soup, enriched with a pickled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> or salted mackerel. Fresh fish they have in plenty on the sea coast. They hunt and eat grouse, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, hare, red deer, and reindeer. They kill cows, sheep, and goats, for their winter stock: these they pickle, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or dry for use. They make cheese of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and a liquor called syre of their four whey: this they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> drink mixed with water; but they provide a store of strong ale for Christmas, weddings, christenings, and other entertainments. From their temperance and exercise, joined to the purity and elasticity of their air, they enjoy good health, and often attain to a surprising degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a>. Nothing is more common than to see a hearty Norwegian turned of 100. In the year 1733, four couples danced before his Danish majesty at Frederikshald; their ages, when joined, exceeded 800 years. Nevertheless the Norwegians are subject to various diseases; such as the scab, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, the scurvy, the catarrh, the rheumatism, gout, and epilepsy. The dress of the Norway peasants consists of a wide loose jacket made of coarse cloth, with waistcoat and breeches of the same. Their heads are covered with flapped <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, or caps ornamented with ribbons. They wear shoes without outer soles, and in the winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> buskins. They have likewise snow shoes and long skates, with which they travel at a great pace, either on the land or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. There is a corps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> thus accoutred, who can outmatch the swiftest horses. The Norwegian peasant never wears a neckcloth, except on extraordinary occasions: he opens his neck and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to the weather, and lets the snow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> into his bosom. His body is girt round with a broad leather belt, adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> plates, from which depends a brass chain that sustains a large knife, gimlet, and other tackle. The women are dressed in close laced jackets, having leather girdles decorated with ornaments of silver. They likewise wear silver chains round their necks, to the ends of which are fixed gilt medals. Their caps and handkerchiefs are almost covered with small plates of silver, brass, and tin, large rings, and buttons. A maiden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> appears with her hair plaited, and, together with her clothes, hung full of such jingling trinkets. The churches, public edifices, and many private houses in Norway, are built of stone: but the people in general live in wooden houses, made of the trunks of fir and pine tree laid upon each other, and joined by mortises at the corners. These are counted more dry, warm, and healthy, than stone or brick buildings. In the whole diocese of Bergen, one hardly fees a farm house with a chimney or window: they are generally lighted by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole in the top of the house, which lets in the light, and lets out the smoke. In summer Norway, this hole is left quite open; in the winter, it is covered with what they call a fiau; that is the membrane of some animal, stretched upon a wooden frame that fits the hole, and transmits the rays of light. It is fixed or removed with a long pole occasionally. Every person that enters the house, upon business or courtship, takes hold of this pole, according to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. The ceiling is about eight feet high in the middle; and, being arched like a cupola, the smoke of the fire underneath rolls about, until it finds a vent at the hole, which is called liur. Under this opening stands a thick table with benches, and a high seat at the upper end for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the family: he has likewise a small cupboard for his own use, in which he locks up his most valuable effects. The boards of the roof are coated with the bark of the birch trees, which is counted incorruptible: this again is covered with turf, which yields a good crop of grass for goats and sheep, and is often mowed as hay by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>. The Norwegians carry on a considerable trade with foreign nations. The duty on the produce of their own country exported, amounts annually to 100,000 rix-dollars. These commodities are, copper wrought and unwrought; iron <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into cannon, floves, and pots, or forged into bars; lead, in small quantity; masts, timber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> boards, planks, marble, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, herring, cod, ling, salmon, lobsters, flounders, cow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, goat skins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> skins, the furs of bears, wolves, foxes, beavers, ermines, martens, &c., down, feathers, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, tallow, train <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, tar, juniper and other sorts of berries, and nuts; salt, alum, glaas, vitriol, and pot ashes. All other commodities and articles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> the Norwegians import from different nations. The nature of the ground does not admit of much improvement in agriculture: nevertheless, the farmers are not deficient in industry and skill to drain marshes, and render the ground arable and fit for pasture. Many are employed in grazing and breeding cattle; but a much greater number is engaged in felling wood, floating timber, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> charcoal, and extracting tar from the roots of the trees which have been cut down in the silver, copper, and iron mines; in the navigation and fishery. A considerable number of people earn a comfortable livelihood by hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-catching. Every individual is at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to pursue the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, especially in the mountains and commons; therefore every peasant is expert in the use of fire arms; and there are excellent marksmen among the mountains, who make use of the bow to kill those animals, whose skins, being valuable, would be damaged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of fire arms. Norway can produce above 14,000 excellent seamen. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of this country amounts to 30,000 effective men; and the annual revenue exceeds 800,000 rix-dollars. Norway <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">Rat</a>. See Mus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NORWICH

Pages 72-73

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 26', N. Lat. 52° 40'. It is supposed to have had its name, which signifies "a castle to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>," from its situation in respect of Cæsar, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Venta Icenorum, three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four miles to the south of it, out of whose ruins it seems to have risen. In its infancy, in the reign of Etheldred, it was plundered and burnt by Sueno the Dane, when he invaded England with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Afterwards it recovered; and in the reign of Edward the Confessor was a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, having 1320 burgheers. But it suffered again much in the reign of William I. by being the seat of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which Ralph <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> raised against that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. So much was it impaired by the siege it then underwent, that there were scarce 360 burgheers left in it, as appears from Doomsday book. From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> forward it began by little and little to recover, especially after Bishop Herbert translated the episcopal see hither from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a> in the reign of William Rufus in 1096; and built a beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, of which he himself laid the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, with this inscription, Dominus Herbertus posuit primum lapidem, in nomine Patrii, Filii, et Spiritus Sancti, Amen, i.e. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> (Bishop) Herbert laid the first stone, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost." And by a licence from Pope Paschal, declared it the mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Norfolk and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. After this, as Malmesbury has it, it became a town famous for merchandise and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants. Yet it was miserably harassed in the reign of Henry II. by Hugh Bigod earl of Norfolk, who was an adherent of Henry's son, called the junior king. In the time of Edward I. it was walled round by the citizens, who had presented a petition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to do it. Henry IV. allowed them, instead of bailiffs, which they had before, to elect a mayor yearly, and made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> a county of itself. In the year 1348, near 18,000 persons were carried off by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>; and in 1505, the city was almost consumed by fire. For the flourishing state to which the city is now arrived, they are much indebted to the Flemings, who fled hither from the tyranny of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, and taught them the manufacture of those striped and flowered damasks, camlets, druggets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> crape, for which the place is now so noted, and which have been computed to yield sometimes 200,000l. a-year. In the year 1583, the citizens, by the help of an engine, conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> to the highest parts of the city, which is pleasantly seated along the side of a hill, extending a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length from north to south; but the breadth is much less, and it contracts itself by degrees towards the south. It is now one of the most considerable cities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> for wealth, populousness, neat buildings, beautiful churches, (of which it had once 38, but now only 36), and the industry and civility of the inhabitants. The cathedral is a very venerable structure, with a curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, adorned with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in little images, carved to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and a lofty steeple 105 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The wall of flint stone, beautified with 40 towers and 12 gates, finished in 1309, is now much decayed. The city, though there is a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of waste ground within the walls, was computed, about 60 years ago, to contain 8000 houses and 50,000 inhabitants. Besides the cathedral already mentioned, the most remarkable buildings are, the duke of Norfolk's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, one of the largest in England; the castle, which is now the county gaol, and stands in the heart of the city, with a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> round it, over which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of one very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; the town <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; the guild hall, formerly the church belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Black Friars; the house of correction; the shire house, where the assizes are held; a lofty market <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, built after the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>; the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the king's school, founded by Edward VI. the boys of which are nominated by the mayor for the time being, with the consent Norwich. consent of the majority of aldermen. There having been formerly many thatched houses, an order was made, that all houses that should hereafter be built should be covered with tiles. The city is interspersed with gardens, orchards, and trees, which make it both pleasant and healthful. It has four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, in which a great number of old men and women, boys and girls, are maintained; and a dozen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Here are two churches for the Dutch and French Flemings; who have particular privileges, and are very numerous. Some of the churches are thatched, and all of them crafted with flint stone curiously cut; which is the more wonderful, as Norwich stands in a clay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and has no flint within 20 miles of it. It is now governed by a mayor, recorder, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, two sheriffs, 24 aldermen, 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, with a town clerk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and other inferior officers. The mayor is chosen on May-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the freemen, and sworn in on the Tuesday before Midsummer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>. The sheriffs are also chosen annually, on the first Tuesday in August, one by the freemen, the other by the aldermen, and sworn in on Michaelmas day. The freemen of the several wards choose each their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. The common council is chosen in Mid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. The mayor is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace and quorum, during his year (as are also the recorder and steward) within the city and liberties; and after his mayoralty, he is a justice during life. The trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the city are very considerable. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> they export large quantities of their manufactures, most of which are sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and import a great deal of wine, coal, fish, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c. All the city and country round are employed in the worsted manufacture, brought hither, as already observed, by the Flemings, in which they not only consume the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of their own county, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, &c. but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> many thousand packs of yarn which they receive from other parts of England, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>. There are eight wardens of the weavers chosen annually, and sworn to take care that there be no frauds committed in spinning, weaving, or dying the stuffs. It is computed that there are not less than 120,000 people employed in and about the city in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and woollen manufactures. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are thought to be the greatest in England, and furnished with a surprising plenty and variety of goods and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. At a small village to the north of the city, called St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>'s, not less than 40,000 head of Scotch cattle are said to be yearly bought up by the Norfolk graziers, and fattened in their meadows and marshes. Its markets are on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. It has a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, lends two members to parliament, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the duke of Gordon. Few cities or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> seem to have suffered more than Norwich has done at various periods, and few seem to have felt it less; for though quite burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Sueno as above, it was of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in Edward the Confessor's time; nor did it long feel the evils of the insurrection and siege in William the Conqueror's time, for it was rebuilt in Stephen's reign, and made a corporation. The city of Norwich has long been famous for its manufactures; which are not, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, at present in so flourishing a state as formerly. In addition to the manufacture of camlets, druggets, and crapes, it is also remarkable for baize, ferges, shalloons, stockings, and woollen cloths. The inhabitants of Norwich are generally so employed in their manufactures within doors, that the city has the appearance of being deserted, except on Sundays and holidays, when the streets swarm with people. Caister, near Norwich, was the Venta Icenorum, or capital city of the Iceni, the broken walls of which contain a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of about 30 acres. In those walls may still be perceived the remains of four gates and a tower. Several Roman urns, coins, and other relics of antiquity, have been found in this place.

NOSE

Pages 73-74

the organ of smell. See ANATOMY. The uses of the nose are, its giving us the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of smelling; its serving in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> office of respiration, and in modelling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>; in receiving the abundant humours from the eyes, and in adding to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The nose was by the augurs particularly attended to in forming conjectures concerning future good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ill success. The tingling of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or left side of it, for instance, was thought to have different significations as it happened to different sexes, or persons in different conditions. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, the greatest beauties are those who have the least noses. Ruybrock mentions the wife of the great Jenghiz Khan as a celebrated beauty, because she had only two holes for a nose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRIM_TARTARS">Crim Tartars</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the noses of their children while young, as thinking it a great piece of folly to have their noses stand before their eyes. In most other countries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> excepted, great noses are an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. In what the beauty of the nose consists, different nations have different opinions: and the following reflections of Sir Joshua Reynolds on this subject, are perhaps the most philosophical account of the beauty of form that is to be found in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. "I suppose (says Sir Joshua) it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be easily granted, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can judge whether any animal be beautiful in its kind, or deformed, who has seen only one of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>: that is as conclusive in regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a man born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> was to recover his sight, and the most beautiful woman was brought before him, he could not determine whether she was handsome or not; nor, if the most beautiful and most deformed were produced, could he any better determine to which he should give the preference, having seen only those two. To distinguish beauty, then, implies the having seen many individuals of that species. If it is asked, how is more skill acquired by the observation of greater numbers? I answer, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of having seen many, the power is acquired, even without seeking after it, of distinguishing between accidental blemishes and excrescences, which are continually varying the surface of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>'s works, and the invariable general form which Nature most frequently produces, and always seems to intend in her productions. "Thus amongst the blades of grass or leaves of the same tree, though no two can be found exactly alike, yet the general form is invariable: a naturalist, before he chose one as a sample, would examine many, since, if he took the first that occurred, it might have, by accident..." accident or otherwise, such a form as that it would scarce be known to belong to that species; he selects, as the painter does, the most beautiful, that is, the most general form of nature. "Every species of the animal as well as the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> may be said to have a fixed or determinate form, towards which nature is continually inclining, like various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> terminating in the centre; or it may be compared to pendulums vibrating in different directions over one central point; and as they all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the centre, though only one passes through any other point, so it will be found that perfect beauty is oftenest produced by nature than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>: I do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> than deformity in general, but than any one kind of deformity. To instance in a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a feature: the line that forms the ridge of the nose is beautiful when it is straight; this then is the central form, which is oftener found than either concave, convex, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> form that shall be proposed. As we are then more accustomed to beauty than deformity, we may conclude that to be the reason why we approve and admire it, as we approve and admire customs and fashions of dress for no other reason than that we are used to them; so that though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> cannot be said to be the cause of beauty, it is certainly the cause of our liking it: and I have no doubt, but that if we were more used to deformity than beauty, deformity would then lose the idea now annexed to it, and take that of beauty; as if the whole world should agree that yes and no should change their meanings, yes would then deny, and no would affirm. "Whoever undertakes to proceed further in this argument, and endeavours to fix a general criterion of beauty respecting different species, or to show why one species is more beautiful than another, it will be required from him first to prove that one species is really more beautiful than another. That we prefer one to the other, and with very good reason, will be readily granted; but it does not follow from thence that we think it a more beautiful form; for we have no criterion of form by which to determine our judgement. He who says a swan is more beautiful than a dove, means little more than that he has more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in seeing a swan than a dove, either from the flatnesses of its motions, or its being a more rare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>; and he who gives the preference to the dove, does it from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of innocence that he always annexes to the dove; but if he pretends to defend the preference he gives to one or the other, by endeavouring to prove that this more beautiful form proceeds from a particular gradation of magnitude, undulation of a curve, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a line, or whatever other conceit of his imagination he shall fix on as a criterion of form, he will be continually contradicting himself, and find at last that the great mother Nature will not be subjected to such narrow rules. Among the various reasons why we prefer one part of her works to another, the most general, I believe, is habit and custom: custom makes, in a certain sense, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and black white; it is custom alone determines our preference of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the Europeans to the Ethiopians; and they, for the same reason, prefer their own colours to ours. I suppose nobody will doubt, if one of their painters was to paint the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of beauty, but that he would represent her black, with thick lips, flat nose, and woolly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; and it seems to me he would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> very unnaturally if he did not; for by what criterion will any one dispute the propriety of his idea? We indeed say, that the form and colour of the European is preferable to that of the Ethiopian; but I know of no other reason we have for it, but that we are more accustomed to it. It is absurd to say, that beauty is possessed of attractive powers, which irresistibly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the corresponding mind with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and admiration, since that argument is equally conclusive in favour of the white and the black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. "The black and white nations must, in respect of beauty, be considered as of different kinds, at least a different species of the same kind; from one of which to the other, as I observed, no inference can be drawn. "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">Novelty</a> is said to be one of the causes of beauty: that novelty is a very sufficient reason why we should admire, is not denied; but because it is uncommon, is it therefore beautiful? The beauty that is produced by colour, as when we prefer one bird to another, though of the same form, on account of its colour, has nothing to do with this argument, which reaches only to form. I have here considered the word beauty as being properly applied to form alone. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of fixing this confined sense; for there can be no argument, if the sense of the word is extended to every thing that is approved. A rose may as well be said to be beautiful, because it has a fine smell, as a bird because of its colour. When we apply the word beauty, we do not mean always by it a more beautiful form, but something valuable on account of its rarity, usefulness, colour, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is said to be a beautiful animal; but had a horse as few good qualities as a tortoise, I do not imagine that he would be then esteemed beautiful. "A fitness to the end proposed is said to be another cause of beauty; but supposing we were proper judges of what form is the most proper in an animal to constitute strength or swiftness, we always determine concerning its beauty before we exert our understanding to judge of its fitness. "From what has been said, it may be inferred, that the works of nature, if we compare one species with another, are all equally beautiful; and that preference is given from custom, or some association of ideas; and that in creatures of the same species, beauty is the medium or centre of all various forms. See the article Beauty, towards the end.

NOSOLOGY

Pages 74-74

is a Greek word signifying a discourse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> treatise of diseases; otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATHOLOGY">pathology</a>. The importance of a comprehensive and accurate nosology has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and generally allowed. Baglivi, Boerhaave, Gorter, Gaubius, and Sydenham, have expressed their desire of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this kind, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> object of which is to fix pathognomies to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; or in which all diseases are divided into certain classes, orders, and genera, founded on distinctions taken from the symptoms only, without regard to remote or proximate causes. See Medicine.

NOSTOCH

Pages 74-76
shot stars; tremella nostrac, (Lin. Spec. Plant. Dillenius de Mucris, tab. 10, fig. 14; Flor. Danica, tab. 885, fig. 1.) tremella intestinalis vel meenterica, A writer in the Gentleman's Magazine gives this account of it: "The substance in question is not unfrequent in England, nor in all other parts of Europe, after rains, both in spring and autumn. Very large spots of it are seen in gravelly soils, and particularly on the tops of hills, and on open downs, and often it is found on gravel walks. "It is met with in some of the old authors, under the name of nofoch, as in Paracelsus and others; and the alchemists fancied there was something wonderful in it, and that it would afford a menstruum for gold. Nofoch is said to be a word synonymous to Jaculum aliquicis stellae, vel patris ejus repurgatione dejectum quid in terram; flores aeris; fragmentum nimbis; as this substance was believed to fall from the sky with the meteors that we often see, and call falling-stars. Hence the country people in Sweden have called it sky-fall; and in England it is known by the name of witches butter, in common with some of the gelatinous liverworts. "Paracelsus, Helmont, and others, ranked it with the terniabin, or manna, and thought it dropped, as that did, from heaven. It is described, and the chemical analysis thereof given, by M. Geoffroy, in the Paris Memoirs for 1703, and is there said to yield, besides an acid phlegm, a portion of concrete volatile salt and some fixed salt. The distilled water from it was believed by some to possess singular virtues, in allaying pains of the joints; but there is certainly no room to attribute any extraordinary qualities to it. "Since the days of Paracelsus it has been considered as a vegetable production; but the botanists have had difficulty to assign its place or genus in their several systems. Our own countryman, Dr Merret, seems to have been among the first authors who ranked it among vegetables, and he calls it Lichen humiditate intumeens, ficcitate evanescens (Pin. page. 71.) Others have retained it among the plants of that genus to this day; as does the celebrated Dr Haller, in his Historia Stirp. Helvetiae, who calls it Lichen gelatinosus, plicatus, undulatus; lacinis crinitis, granulosus; No 2041, as there are several of the liverworts that have a gelatinous texture and appearance; though they differ much from the nofoch, in not being so instantly dried up. It was put into Ray's Synopsis, by Dr Dillenius, under the name of Ulva terrefricta pinguis et fugax, p. 64.; but he afterwards changed that name for tremella, in his Historia Muscorum, where he calls it tremella terrefricta pinguis pinguis et fugax, p. 52. tab. 10. f. 14., and reduces the lavers to the same genus. Michel, an Italian botanist, famous for his attention to the Cryptogamia clasps of plants, makes it a fungus, as Magnol and Dr Morison had done before him, and describes and figures it, in his Nova Plantarum Genera, under the name of Linbia terrefricta gelatinosa, membranacea, vulgarisima, p. 126. t. 67. f. 1. He describes the seeds as lying in the form of little strings of beads, coiled up within the plant, or rather in the folds thereof, and only to be discovered by the microscope. Linnaeus mentions it, first under the name of Byflis gelatinosa fugax terrefricta, in his Flora Lapponica, No 520; but he afterwards adopted Dillenius's term, though he does not make it a layer. Linnaeus has called it, in all his subsequent works, tremella (nofoch) plicata, undulata, under which name it stands in his Species Plantarum, p. 1157, and in Hudson's Flora Anglicana, p. 463, as also in a numerous set of other authors who follow his system." Another writer in the same work gives this account of it. "This substance is very rarely seen between the middle of April and the month of October. It is most frequently to be found in the high pasture lands, where the ground is inclined to wet, and on the moors and commons in the north of England. The time we always meet with it is after a very wet night, when the air in the morning suddenly clears up, and a sharp frost ensues. The frogs that then happen to be out are immediately seized by the frost, and turned into this jelly-like substance. For as I have had occasion sometimes to go out very early, I have found several parts of the frog not yet dissolved among the jelly, such as feet, legs, and thighs, yet in a little time afterwards the change was fully completed. The quantity of jelly produced from one single frog is almost beyond belief, even to five or six times its bulk when in its natural state. "I communicated this discovery to an acquaintance, who has since had frequent opportunities of observing and examining this production; and we are fully assured, that whatever opinion the learned may have of it, it certainly proceeds from the above-mentioned cause wherever found. "Most people that I have conversed with on the subject, are of opinion that this jelly falls from the stars, or out of the higher regions of the air; which notion, however absurd, many are credulous enough to believe." Naturalists had for some years begun to doubt whether these gelatinous substances were of a vegetable or animal nature, when at length Mr J. Pratt of Oxford, in a letter printed in the Gentleman's Magazine for 1776, page 402, threw such light on the subject as to us, at least, is perfectly satisfactory. "From a child I remember seeing the meteors shooting in the air, which appearance, by my comrades, was called star-shooting, believing the stars no larger than their apparent magnitude. This jelly-like substance mentioned in your magazine, was believed to be the drops of these meteors, and took the name of star-shot, which passed for certain with me till I had arrived at the age of 24, when I was engaged in business that required me frequently passing over both meadows and pasture-grounds, where in spring and autumn I saw many portions of this supposed alga or nofoch, but never more than one or two contiguous, mostly near the water, when the meadows were or had been just before flooded. My conjectures were various, until I saw a crow pecking at something in a field, which I heard to cry; when turning my horse to the place, I found a frog of the common size, which the crow (of the carrion kind) would soon have killed and gorged, had I not disturbed her, and chafed her away. "About this time I found in a meadow the bowels of a frog indigested, and compact as the chitterlings of a calf or pig; but white as the paper I write upon, though not translucid. I took it up, and placed it in a paper exposed to the air; leaving it in some grass where I found it, till my return that way in three days' time," NOS Nostradamus, when I saw it changed to that tremulous jelly-like substance, the alga or star-shot. I was much pleased with this discovery, and took it home in my pocket wrapped in a paper, where I showed it to a society of young persons of which I was a member, who agreed with my sentiments of its being the indigestible part of a frog digested by some bird of prey. "To corroborate my sentiments of this alga being the bowels of a frog, I luckily saw some of it lying by the side of a brook, where I lighted and took it up, and to my great surprise found attached to the jelly the head, heart, liver, and one leg of the frog, which had been (I presume) digested by some carrion crow, who frequented the flooded grounds to pick up worms and other vermin. There was also some of it found on an apple tree at Wyton Magna, near Leicester, where I then lived, which, no doubt, was digested by some owl." Dr Darwin, in his Poem on the Loves of the Plants, is of the same opinion with Mr Platt, that these gelatinous substances are of an animal nature, and that the different appearances they put on are owing to various circumstances, viz. the different birds who feed on frogs, the quantity they devour at a time, and the state of digestion before they are voided.

NOSTRADAMUS

Pages 76-77

MICHEL, an able physician and a celebrated astrologer, was a Provençal, and descended of a noble family, and born Dec. 14, 1503, at St Remy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>. By his grandfather he was initiated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He afterwards completed his course of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at Avignon; and, going thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>, he there applied himself to physic, till being forced away by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1525, he took his route towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, and paffed on till he came to Bordeaux. This course held him five years, during which he undertook the cure of all such patients as were willing to put themselves under his care. After this he returned to Montpellier, and was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> in 1529, and then revisited the same places where he had practised physic before. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a> he contracted an acquaintance with Julius Caesar Scaliger, which induced him to make some stay in that town, and there he entered into matrimony; but having buried his wife, and two children which she brought him, he quitted Agen after a residence of about four years. He returned into Provence, and fixed himself first at Marfeilles; but his friends having provided an advantageous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for him at Salon, he transported himself thither in 1544. In 1546, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> being afflicted with the plague, he went thither at the solicitation of the inhabitants, and was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; particularly by a powder of his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>: so that the town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> gave him a considerable pension for several years after the contagion ceased. Returning afterwards to Salon, he became a recluse, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his leisure to apply himself to his studies. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> followed the trade of a conjurer occasionally; and now he began to think himself inspired, and miraculously illuminated with a prospect into futurity. As fast as these illuminations had discovered to him any future event, he entered it in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in simple prose, but by enigmatical sentences, as he declared himself; but reviving them afterwards, he thought the sentences would appear more respectable, and would favour more of a prophetic spirit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were expressed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. Nostradamus. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> determined him to throw them all into quatrains, and he afterwards ranged them into centuries. When this was done, he hesitated about making them public, till reflecting that the time of many events which he had foretold was very near at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he determined to print them. This he did with a dedication addressed to his son Caesar, an infant only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months old, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, dated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1, 1555. This first edition, which is included in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> centuries, was printed by Rigault at Lyons. He prefixed his name in Latin, but gave to his son Caesar the name as it is pronounced, Notrada-me. The public were divided in their sentiments of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>: many looked upon the author as a simple visionary or a fool; while he was accused of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> art, or black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, by others, and treated as an impious person, who held a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>: at the same time there were not wanting such, and those in great numbers, who believed him to be really and truly endowed with the supernatural gift of prophecy. Lastly, some were found who remained in suspense, and refrained from giving any judgment at all upon the point. However, Henry II. and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catharine of Medicis his mother, were resolved to see our prophet; and, receiving orders to that effect, he presently repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He was very graciously received at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and, besides the extraordinary respect that was paid to him, received a present of 200 crowns. He was sent afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>, to make a visit to his majesty's children there, and report what he should be able to discover concerning their destinies. No doubt he exerted himself to the utmost on the occasion; but what his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was is not known; however, it is certain, he returned to Salon loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and presents. Animated with his success, he augmented his work from 300 quatrains to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of a complete millade, and published it with a dedication to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> in 1558. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> dying the next year of a wound which he received, as is well known, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a>, the book of our prophet was immediately consulted; and in the 37th quatrain of the first century this unfortunate event was found predicted in the following verse: Le lion jeune le vieux surmontera, En champ bellique par singulier <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, Dans cage d'or les yeux lui crevera, Deux classes une puis mourir, mort cruelle. So remarkable a prediction added new wings to his fame; and he was honoured shortly after with a visit from Emanuel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy and the princess Margaret of France his consort. From this time Nostradamus found himself even overburdened with visitors, and his fame made every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> new acquisitions. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., coming to Salon, was eager above all things to have a sight of him. Nostradamus, who then was in waiting as one of the retinue of the magistrates, being instantly presented to his majesty, complained of the little esteem his countrymen had for him; whereupon the monarch publicly declared, that he should hold the enemies of Nostradamus to be his enemies, and desired to see his children. Nor did that prince's favour stop here; in passing, not long after, through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, he sent for Nostradamus, presented him with a purse of 200 crowns, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREVET">brevet</a>, constituting him his physician in ordinary, with the same appointment as the reft. But our prophet enjoyed these honours only for the space of fifteen months, for he died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 2, 1566, at Salon. Besides his "Centuries," we have the following compositions of his: A Treatise de Fardemens et de Senteurs, 1552.—A Book of singular Receipts, pour Entretenir la Santé du Corps, 1556.—A piece des Confitures, 1557.—A French Translation of the Latin of Galen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a>, exhorting Menodolas to Study, especially to that of Physic, 1552. Some years before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he published a small instruction for husbandmen, flowing the best seasons for their several labours, which he entitled, The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a> of Notradamus. Lastly, After his death there came out The eleventh and twelfth Centuries of his Quatrains, added to the former ten, which had been printed three times in two separate parts. It is only in these first editions that our author's Centuries are found without alterations, additions, &c. It is to this work that the following distich of Stephen Jodelle alludes. *Notra damus cum falsa damus, nam fallere nostrum est.* *Et cum falsa damus, nil nisi Notra damus.*

NOSTRE

Pages 77-77

Andrew le, comptroller of the buildings of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and designer of his gardens, distinguished himself by carrying the art of laying out gardens to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1631; and was near 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> when M. Fouquet, superintendent of the finances, gave him an opportunity of becoming known by the fine gardens of Vaux-le-Vicomte. He was afterwards employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, Trianon, St Germain, &c. and discovered an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in all his works. In 1678 he went to Rome, with the permission of the French king, to improve his skill; but he found nothing there comparable to what he himself had done. Pope Innocent XI. resolved to see Le Nostre, and gave him a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> audience; at the conclusion of which Le Nostre said, "I have seen the two greatest men in the world, your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, and the king my <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>." "There is a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>," answered the pope: "The king is a great victorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and I am a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the servants of God." Le Nostre, charmed with this answer, and forgetting who he was with, clasped the pope on the shoulder, saying, "Reverend father, you look extremely well, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> live to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> all the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>." The pope laughed at his prediction. Le Nostre, charmed more and more at the goodness of the sovereign pontiff and the singular esteem he showed for the king, threw his arms about the pope's neck and kissed him. It was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to behave in the same manner to all who spoke in praise of Louis XIV., and he even embraced the king himself whenever that prince returned from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Le Nostre had also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. He preserved his good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and vivacity of mind to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and died at Paris, in 1700, aged 87. NOTÆ, signs used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, which have the force of many letters. This contrivance for expedition is of great antiquity. It was known to the Greeks, and from them derived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. By whom the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> was brought into Rome is not precisely ascertained; but the most general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that in matters of importance Tully first made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of notes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shorthand writing, when Cato made an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> in order to oppose Julius Caesar relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of Catiline. Cicero, who was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, placed notarii, or expert shorthand writers, in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the speech; and this was the first public occasion which we find recorded of employing shorthand writers among the Romans. It is unnecessary to observe, that hence proceeded the name of notary still in use. There were three kinds of notes for shorthand writing used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, either for dispatch or secrecy. The first and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> was that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, which are rather images or representations of things than of words. (See Hieroglyphics.) The Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are of this kind, and may with greater propriety be called nota than literæ, as appears from what hath been already advanced. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of notes were called singulares, from their expressing words by single letters. Servius Ursatus has compiled a very copious collection of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> there are several editions. The third kind of notes were called nota Tironianæ, from Tiro the freed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of Cicero, who was excellently skilled in this art; and it is to him that we are indebted for the preservation of Cicero's letters, of which a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> still remain, and one entire book of them written to Tiro himself. From books it appears, that notes were very frequent among the Romans, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in use to the 10th and 11th centuries. We have indeed but few books remaining that are written in shorthand; but this is not surprising, when such was the unhappy situation of early ages, that either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> condemned them to the flames as the works of impious magicians or necromancers, or they were left to be devoured by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and stupidity, which was so very great, that some people, as Trithemius affirms, looked upon notes in those days as the elements of the Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It is probable, however, that there are writings of this sort still extant, which might contribute to enrich the republic of letters. There are several MSS. and instruments written in these kind of nota, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> library at Paris. In the year 1747, the learned and ingenious Monf. Charpentier, engraved and published at Paris a capitulary, and 54 charters of Louis the Pious, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and king of France, written in these nota Tironianæ. To this work the learned editor hath prefixed an Alphabetum Tironianum, together with a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and variety of notes or marks for the different parts of speech, and rules for acquiring the art of writing in these kind of notes. Valerius Probus, in his book De Literis Antiquis, explains many of the characters used by the shorthand writers; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of them set forth by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Gruterus. See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STENOGRAPHY">Stenography</a>.

NOTARI

Pages 77-78

persons employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to take, by nota, trials and pleadings in their courts of judicature, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to write as amanuenses from the mouth of an author. These notarii were of servile condition. Under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, they were formed into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> or corporate body. Notarii were also appointed to attend the prefects, to transcribe for them. There were likewise notarii domici, who were employed in keeping... keeping the accounts of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and when the empire became Christian, there were notaries for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs, who attested the acts of archbishops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and other spiritual dignitaries. We find ecclesiastical notaries at Rome, under Pope Julius IV. and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Antioch, about the year 370. From these notaries is derived the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> to the bishops; afterwards almost every advocate was admitted a notary. **NOTARY (Notarius),** signifies a person, usually some scrivener, who takes notes, or frames short draughts of contracts, obligations, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> parties, or other writings.
