NOVGOROD Serpikoi, a strong town of the Russian empire, and capital of a province of Siberia of the same name, seated on the river Dubica, in E. Long. 33° 20'. N. Lat. 52° 30'.

NOVOGORODECK

Pages 87-87

a town of Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the same name. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and situated in a vast plain, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 30'. N. Lat. 53° 45'. NOURISHMENT. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTRITION">Nutrition</a>. NOURISHMENT of Vegetables. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NOWED

Pages 87-87

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies "knotted," from the Latin nodatus; being applied to the tails of such creatures as are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and sometimes represented in coat armour as tied up in a knot.

NOX

Pages 87-87

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deities among the heathens, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a>. From her union with her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, she gave birth to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>. She was also the mother of the Parce, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESPERIDES">Hesperides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">Dreams</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">Discord</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOMUS">Momus</a>, Fraud, &c. She is called by some of the poets the mother of all things, of gods as well as of men; and she was worshipped with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. She had a famous statue in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>'s temple at Ephesus. It was usual to offer her a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sheep, as she was the mother of the Furies. The cock was also offered to her, as that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> proclaims the approach of day during the darkness of the night. She is represented as mounted on a chariot, and covered with a veil bespangled with stars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> generally went before her as her constant messengers. Sometimes she is seen holding two children under her arms; one of which is black, representing Death, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, representing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">Sleep</a>. Some of the moderns have described her as a woman veiled in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, and crowned with poppies, and carried on a chariot drawn by owls and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a>.

NOYON

Pages 87-88

a town of France, situated on the declivity of a hill on the rivulet Vorfe, which at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>'s distance falls into the Oyfe, in the department of Oyfe, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3°. N. Lat. 49° 38' about 66 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being the Noviodunum Belgarum of the Latins. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and is well situated for inland trade, which consists here in wheat and oats, which they send to Paris. Paris. They have also manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloths, lawns, and tanned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. There are eight parishes in it, two abbeys, and several monasteries of both sexes. It is the see of a bishop, suffragan to the metropolitan of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>; he has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> and peer of France, and his income is said to amount to about 15,000 livres per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a cloister where the canons of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dwell, and the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The latter is regularly built in a large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in the middle of which there is a fountain, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> conveyed to it from a neighbouring mountain runs continually through three conduits, and is received in a large basin built of very hard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. They have also many other fountains, several market places, and two public gardens. Noyon is particularly remarkable for the birth of the famous John Calvin, who was born here on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1502, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> the 27th of May 1564.

NUAYHAS

Pages 88-88

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">Ague</a> tree; a name given by the Indians to a sort of bamboo <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the leaves of which falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, are said to regenerate it with such virtue, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in it afterwards cures the ague. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> also a decoction of the leaves to dissolve coagulated blood, giving it internally, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> rubbing the bruised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> externally with it. It is said that this plant bears its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> only once in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; that it lives 60 years before those make their appearance; but that when they begin to show themselves, it withers away in about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> afterwards; that is, as soon as it has ripened the seed. There seems to be something of fiction in the account of many other particulars relating to this tree in the Hortus Malabaricus; but it seems certain, that the length of the stalks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, must be very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; for, in the gallery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, there is preserved a cane of it 28 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and another not much shorter in the Ashmolean <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and which is more than eight inches in diameter: yet both these appear to be only parts of the whole trunk, they being nearly as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> at one end as at the other.

NUBA

Pages 88-88

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> Pagans, in the neighbourhood of Sennaar, of whom we know nothing but what we have learned from Mr Bruce. That celebrated traveller passed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two among them, in his way from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; and he tells us, that they are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the Mek or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sennaar, cantoned in villages, which to the distance of four or five miles surround the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. They are not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; but "are either purchased or taken by force from Fanuelo, and the provinces to the south upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Dyre and Tegla." Though the slaves of a cruel and treacherous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, Mr Bruce represents them as a gentle, honest, and hospitable people; and he says expressly, that on a journey he had seldom passed a more comfortable night, than one in which he took refuge from a storm in a village of those Nuba. He had a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, and a clean neat hut to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in, while some of the Nuba watched for him all night, and took care of his beasts and his baggage. "Having settlements and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> given them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Sennaar, as also arms put into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, they never wish to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, but live a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> and sober <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and are a much gentler sort of negro than their masters." (See Sennaar.) Though the established <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Sennaar is that of Mahomet, the government has never attempted to convert the Nuba. On the contrary, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Pagan priests is maintained for them in every village, who have soldiers in pay to assist them in the affairs of their religion. This is a very singular instance of toleration among Mahometans, and what we should little have expected from such barbarous and languid wretches as those who have the supreme power in Sennaar, had not our observing traveller informed us, that these men themselves knew almost nothing of the religion which they profess, and are in their hearts rather Pagans than Mahometans. The idolatry of the Nuba is described as a mixture of Sabism and statue worship: but what is very uncommon, their worship is chiefly paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, while they pay no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> either rising or setting, advancing to the meridian or receding from it. It is an old observation, that the worship of every people is tinged by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> dispositions; and this is verified in the Nuba. "That their worship is performed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and satisfaction, is obvious (says our author) every night that the moon shines. Coming out from the darkness of their huts, they say a few words upon seeing her brightness, and testify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> joy, by motions of their feet and hands, at the first appearance of the new moon." This is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> what we should have expected from their gentleness and hospitality. They worship likewise a tree and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but our author could never discover what tree or stone; only he learned that neither of them exists in Sennaar, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where the Nuba are born. Such of them as are natives of the villages where he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them, become, like their masters, nominal Mahometans.—The rest practice the idolatrous worship of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and are much under the influence of their priests, from fear rather than from affection. They are immoderately fond of swine's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and maintain great herds of small hogs, marked with black and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots. Few of the Nuba advance higher than to be soldiers and officers in their own corps; and the Mek maintains about 12,000 of them near Sennaar to keep the Arabs in subjection. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> so violent as that which they inhabit, there is very little need of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; and it is happy for them that such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, for in the whole country there is not a single tree, or turf, or any thing resembling it. They do not, however, "eat their meat raw like the Abyssinians; but with the stalk of the dora or millet, and the dung of camels, they make ovens under ground, in which they roast their hogs whole, in a very cleanly manner, keeping their skins on till they are perfectly baked. They have neither flint nor <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> with which to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> their fire at first; but do it in a manner still more expeditious, by means of two sticks, brought, we are led to think, from Sennaar, and there picked out of the river when flooded. They make a small hole in one of these sticks, and point the other: then laying the former in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, they apply the point of the latter to the hole; and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the perpendicular stick between their hands, as we do a chocolate mill, both sticks take fire and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> in a moment; so perfectly dry and prepared to take fire is everything there on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>."

NUBECULA

Pages 89-89
or Nubea, is also used for what is otherwise called albigo. See ALBUGO. NUBECULA is used likewise for a matter in form of a cloud, suspended in urine.

NUBIA

Pages 89-89

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, on the west by the kingdoms of Tagua, Gaoga, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Gerham. The river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> runs through it; on the banks of which, and those of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, it is pretty fruitful, but in other places barren, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and in want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. To the west of the Nile is the desert of Bahouda, which is five days journey over, being the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Egypt to Abyssinia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">Money</a> is of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the way of trade, it being all carried on by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and drink is made of a small round seed, called doca <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> jeff, which is very ill tasted. Their houses have mud walls, being very low, and covered with reeds. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the better sort is a vest without sleeves; and they have no coverings for their heads, legs, and feet. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people wrap a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth about them, and the children go quite naked. They are a stupid debauched sort of people, having neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, civility, nor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, though they profess to be Mahometans.—The productions of this country are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, civet, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood; and they send a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many slaves into Egypt. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> known to the Europeans are Dangola and Sennar. It is famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of horses the most powerful and docile in the world. These animals are generally about fifteen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and by Mr Bruce, who has given the most scientific account of them, they are said to be the breed which was introduced into Nubia at the Saracen conquest, and has been preserved unmixed to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Our author represents this as a much nobler animal than the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. "What <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> (says he) the Nubian horse would make in point of fleetness is very doubtful, his make being so entirely different from that of the Arabian; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> beautiful symmetry of parts, great size and strength, the most agile, nervous, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> movements, great endurance of fatigue, docility of temper, and seeming <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to men beyond that of any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal, can <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> anything for a stallion, the Nubian is above all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> the most eligible in the world." He thinks, and justly thinks, that an attempt should at least be made to import them into this kingdom. "The expense (he says) would not be great, though there might be some trouble and application necessary: but if adroitly managed, there would not be much even of that. The Nubiens are very jealous in keeping up the pedigree of their horses, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, but a vast proportion of the former to the latter." Our author never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which we call gray, i.e., dappled; but he has seen some bright bays, and some inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAN">roan</a>. All noble horses in Nubia are said to be descended of one of the five upon which Mahomet and his four immediate successors, Abu Bekr, Omar, Atmen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, fled from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> to Medina the night of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>. No one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> pay much regard to this legendary tale, or believe that the strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this breed of horses is owing to any virtue communicated to the first of them by the prophet and his apostles. Mr Bruce accounts for their excellence upon rational principles. "The best horses of the Arabian breed are found (he says) in the tribe of Mowelli and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNECY">Annecy</a>, which is about 36° north latitude. Dangola, which is in 20° latitude, seemed to him to be the centre of excellence for this noble animal." Hence he infers, that the bounds in which the horse is in greatest perfection, are between the 20th and 36th degrees of latitude, and between 30 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> east from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> and the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. If to the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> we add the manner of feeding the Nubian horses, we shall perhaps have the true cause of their superiority over all others. "They are kept fat upon dora, and suffered to eat nothing green but the short roots of grass that are to be found by the side of the Nile, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> has withered it. This is dug out where it is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and appears blanched, and laid in small heaps once a day on the ground before them."

NUBIAN DESERT

Pages 89-90

a vast tract of barren rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sands, extending from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYENE">Syene</a> in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to Geon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Berber in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>. As Syene is in latitude 24° 0' 45" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and Geon in latitude 17° 57' 22", the length of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> from north to south is 6° 3' 23", <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upwards of 420 English miles. Its breadth from east to west has not, as far as we know, been precisely ascertained. Through this horrid region, where nothing is to be seen which has the breath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, mult all travellers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from Sennar to Egypt; in danger every moment of perishing by thirst, being overwhelmed by moving columns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, suffocated by a hot and poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or cut in pieces by troops of wandering Arabs. The last European of whom we have heard that made the journey and lived to give an account of it, is Mr Bruce; and the person must have neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> who can read unmoved his manly narrative. No single traveller, nor even a caravan, can enter with safety into this desert, but under the protection of a Hybear; whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and office are thus explained by Mr Bruce: "A Hybear is a guide, from the Arabic word Hubbar, which signifies to inform, instruct, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, because they are used to do this office to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> travelling through the desert in all directions. They are men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> consideration, knowing perfectly the situation and properties of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to be met with on the route, the distance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, whether occupied by enemies or not; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> so, the way to avoid them with the least inconvenience. It is also necessary that they should know the places occupied by the Siroom, and the seasons of its blowing (see Siroom), as well as those occupied by moving sands."—Under the conduct of one of these men, Mr Bruce, with infinite fortitude and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, passed through the desert in the year 1772, surmounting dangers at which one shudders in his closet. Of these, the following, which we shall give in the nervous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the author, may serve as an instance. "We were here (at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Wezhi al Helleb) NUC at once surprized and terrified by a sight surely one of the most magnificent in the world. In that vast expanse of desert, from W. and to NW. of us, we <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prodigious pillars of sand at different distances, at times moving with great celerity, at others stalking on with a majestic slowness. At intervals we thought they were coming in a very few minutes to overwhelm us; and small quantities of sand did actually more than once reach us. Again they would retreat so as to be almost out of sight; their tops reaching to the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. There the tops often separated from the bodies; and these once disjointed, dispersed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and did not appear more. Sometimes they were broken in the middle as if struck with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cannon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. About noon they began to advance with considerable swiftness upon us, the wind being very strong at north. Eleven, of them ranged alongside of us about the distance of three miles. The greatest diameter of the largest appeared to me at that distance as if it would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 10 feet. They retired from us with a wind at SE. leaving an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon my mind to which I can give no name; though surely one ingredient in it was fear, with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of wonder and astonishment. If it be true, as the author of A Philosophical Inquiry into the Origin of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">Ideas</a> of the Sublime and Beautiful affirms, that "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> raised by the sublime is astonishment, and that astonishment is that state of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> in which all its motions are suspended with some degree of horror," surely a more sublime spectacle was never presented to mortal eyes, than that which was on this occasion presented to Mr Bruce. It must have been awfully majestic; but few, we believe, would choose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of contemplating such a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of magnificence at the hazard of that dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> with which at every moment it threatened our traveller and his attendants. He, indeed, had firmness of mind to stand still and admire it; but his companions shrieked out; while some of them exclaimed that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgement, and others that it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a> or the world set on fire. But for a more particular account of this phenomenon, as well as of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the desert and the proper way of passing it, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> from which this short sketch is taken.

NUCLEUS

Pages 90-90

in general, denotes the kernel of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even any seed enclosed within a husk. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> nucleus is also used for the body of a comet, otherwise called its head.

NUCTA

Pages 90-90

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, which falling in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> about St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, is by the superstitious natives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> considered as miraculous, and the peculiar gift of that saint. Its effects are indeed so beneficial, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> is little surprising among a people so totally ignorant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Egyptians, for it is acknowledged, by the most enlightened travellers, to stop the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, and announce a speedy and plentiful inundation of the country. These effects are thus rationally accounted for by Mr Bruce. "In February and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is on its approach to the zenith of one extremity of Egypt, and of course has a very considerable influence upon the other. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> having now fallen low, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in certain old cisterns, which, though they still exist, are suffered to accumulate all the filth of the river, becomes putrid, and the river itself has lost all its finer and volatile parts by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a vertical fun; so that instead of being subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, it grows daily more and more inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. About St John's day it receives a plentiful mixture of the fresh and fallen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from Ethiopia, which dilutes and refreshes the almost corrupted river; and the fun near at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> exerts its influence upon the water, which is now become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> enough to be exhaled, though it has still with it a mixture of the corrupted fluid. It is in February, March, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> April only, that the plague begins in Egypt." Our philosophical traveller does not believe it an endemic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; but affirms very sufficient reasons for thinking that it comes from Constantinople with merchandise or with passengers at the very <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> absence of dews, has attained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of putridity proper to receive it. In this state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, the infection continues to rage till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of St John's day, when it is suddenly checked by the dews occasioned by a refreshing mixture of rain water, which is poured into the Nile at the beginning of the inundation. The first and most remarkable sign of the change effected in the air, is the sudden stopping of the plague. Every person, though shut up from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for months before, buys, sells, and communicates with his neighbour without any sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>; and as far as our author could learn upon fair inquiry, it was never known that one fell sick of the plague after the anniversary of St John. He admits that some have died of it after that period; but of them the disease had got such hold, under the most putrid influence of the air, that they could not recover. To corroborate this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, which attributes so much to the benign influence of the falling dew, he observes, that immediately after St John's day, the clothes of the many thousands who have died during the late continuance of the plague are publicly exposed in the market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and that all these, though consisting of furs, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and woollen cloths, which are the stuffs most retentive of infection, imbibing the moist air of the evening and the morning, are handled, bought, put on and worn, without any apprehension of danger, and without a single accident being known to have happened to any one professed of this happy confidence.

NUDITIES

Pages 90-90

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, those parts of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which are not covered with any drapery; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those parts where the carnation appears.

NULLITY

Pages 90-90

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies any thing that is null <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> void; thus there is a nullity of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, where persons marry within the degrees, or where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> marry without consent of their parents or guardians.

NUMA POMPILIUS

Pages 90-91

the fourth son of Pompilius Pompo, an illustrious Sabine. He had married Tatia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Tatius, and together with her remained in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, preferring the tranquillity of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the splendour of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his wife, with whom he had lived thirteen years, he gave himself up entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and, leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cures, confined himself to the country, wandering from solitude to solitude, in search only of those woods and fountains which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> had made sacred. His recluse life gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, which was very early received among the Sabines, that Numa lived in familiarity with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGERIA">Egeria</a>. Upon the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>... Numa senate and people strongly solicited him to be their king. They despatched Julius Proculus and Valerius Volefus, two senators of distinction, to acquaint Numa with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and make him an offer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The Sabine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> rejected at first their proposal; but being at last prevailed upon by the arguments and entreaties of the deputies, joined with those of his father and of Martius his near relation, he yielded; and having offered sacrifices to the gods, set out for Rome, where he was received by all ranks of people with loud shouts of joy. Spurius Vettius, the interrex for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, having assembled the curiae, he was elected in due form, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was unanimously confirmed by the senate. The beginning of his reign was popular; and he dismissed the 300 bodyguards which his predecessor had kept around his person, and observed, that he did not distrust a people who had compelled him to reign over them. He was not, like Romulus, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> expeditions, but he applied himself to tame the ferocity of his subjects, to inculcate in their minds a reverence for the Deity, and to quell their dissensions by dividing all the citizens into different classes. He established different orders of priests, and taught the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> not to worship the Deity by images; and from his example no graven <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> painted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> appeared in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> or sanctuaries of Rome for the space of 160 years. He encouraged the report that was spread of his paying regular visits to the nymph Egeria, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of her name to give sanction to the laws and institutions which he had introduced. He established the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the vestals, and told the Romans that the safety of the empire depended upon the preservation of the sacred ancyle or shield, which, as was generally believed, had dropped from heaven. He dedicated a temple to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, which, during his whole reign, remained shut as a mark of peace and tranquillity at Rome. After a reign of 42 years, in which he had given every possible encouragement to the useful arts, and in which he had cultivated peace, Numa died in the year of Rome 82. Not only the Romans, but also the neighbouring nations, were eager to pay their last offices to a monarch whom they revered for his abilities, moderation, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. He forbade his body to be burnt according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Romans; but he ordered it to be buried near Mount Janiculum, with many of the books which he had written. These books were accidentally found by one of the Romans, about 400 years after his death; and as they contained nothing new or interesting, but merely the reasons why he had made innovations in the form of worship and in the religion of the Romans, they were burnt by order of the senate. He left behind him one daughter called Pomponia, who married Numa Marcius, and became the mother of Ancus Marcius the fourth king of Rome. Some say that he had also four sons; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is ill founded. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> laws of King Numa, mentioned by different authors, are, 1. That the gods should be worshipped with corn and a salted cake. 2. That whoever knowingly killed a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, should be held as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>. 3. That no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a> should touch the altar of Juno; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she did, that she should sacrifice a ewe-lamb to that goddes, with dishvelled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. 4. That whoever removed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-mark should be put to death. 5. That wine should not be poured on a funeral pile, &c.

NUMANTIA

Pages 91-91

a very noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the ornament of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, (Florus); celebrated for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 20 years which it maintained against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The baseness and injustice of the Romans during this war were truly disgraceful to them, and altogether unworthy of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and powerful people. The inhabitants obtained some advantages over the Roman forces, till Scipio Africanus was empowered to finish the war and to see the destruction of Numantia. He began the siege, with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 60,000 men, and was bravely opposed by the beleaguered, who were no more than 4000 men able to bear arms. Both armies behaved with uncommon valour, and the courage of the Numantines was soon changed into despair and fury. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> began to fail, and they fed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of their horses, and afterwards on that of their dead companions, and at last they were obliged to draw lots to kill and devour one another. The melancholy situation of their affairs obliged them to surrender to the Roman general. Scipio demanded them to deliver themselves up on the morrow; they refused, and when a longer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> had been granted to their petitions, they retired and set fire to their houses and destroyed themselves, so that not even one remained to adorn the triumph of the conqueror. Some historians, however, deny that; and assert, that a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Numantines delivered themselves into Scipio's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and that 50 of them were drawn in triumph at Rome, and the rest sold as slaves. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Numantia was more glorious than that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Corinth, though the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was much inferior to them. It was taken by the Romans, A.U.C. 629; and the conqueror obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Numanicus.

NUMBER

Pages 91-93

an assemblage of several units, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> things of the same kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No 205—208. Number, says Malcolm, is either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> or applicate: Abstract, when referred to things in general, without attending to their particular properties; and applicate, when considered as the number of a particular sort of things, as yards, trees, or the like. When particular things are mentioned, there is always something more considered than barely their numbers; so that what is true of numbers in the abstract, or when nothing but the number of things is considered, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be true when the question is limited to particular things: for instance, the number two is less than three; yet two yards is a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> than three inches: and the reason is, because regard must be had to their different natures as well as number, whenever things of a different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are considered; for though we can compare the number of such things abstractedly, yet we cannot compare them in any applicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. And this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is necessary to be considered, because upon it the true sense, and the possibility or impossibility, of some questions depend. Number is unlimited in respect of increase; because we can never conceive a number so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> but still there is a greater. However, in respect of decrease, it is limited; unity being the first and least number, below which therefore it cannot descend. Kinds and distinctions of Numbers. Mathematicians, considering number under a great many relations, have established the following distinctions. Broken numbers are the same with fractions. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> numbers are those which express the quantity of units, as 1, 2, 3, 4, &c., whereas ordinal numbers are those which express order, as 1st, 2nd, 3rd, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">Compound</a> number, one divisible by some other number besides unity; as 12, which is divisible by 2, 3, 4, and 6. Numbers, as 12 and 15, which have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> besides unity, are said to be compound numbers among themselves. Cubic number is the product of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> number by its root; such is 27, as being the product of the square number 9 by its root 3. All cubic numbers, whose root is less than 6, being divided by 6, the remainder is the root itself; thus 27 ÷ 6 leaves the remainder 3, its root; 215, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> of 6, being divided by 6, leaves no remainder; 343, the cube of 7, leaves a remainder 1, which added to 6, is the cube root; and 512, the cube of 8, divided by 6, leaves a remainder 2, which added to 6, is the cube root. Hence the remainders of the divisions of the cubes above 216, divided by 6, being added to 6, always give the root of the cube so divided till that remainder be 5, and consequently 11, the cube root of the number divided. But the cubic numbers above this being divided by 6, there remains nothing, the cube root being 12. Thus the remainders of the higher cubes are to be added to 12 and not to 6, till you come to 18, when the remainder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> must be added to 18; and so on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> infinitum. Determinate number is that referred to some given unit, as a ternary or three: whereas an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> one is that referred to unity in general, and is called quantity. Homogeneous numbers are those referred to the same unit; as those referred to different units are termed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a>. Whole numbers are otherwise called integers. Rational number is one commensurable with unity; as a number, incommensurable with unity, is termed irrational, or a surd. In the same manner, a rational whole number is that whereof unity is an aliquot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; a rational broken number, that equal to some aliquot part of unity; and a rational mixed number, that consisting of a whole number and a broken one. Even number, that which may be divided into two equal parts without any fraction, as 6, 12, &c. The sum, difference, and product, of any number of even numbers, is always an even number. An evenly even number, is that which may be measured, or divided, without any remainder, by another even number, as 4 by 2. An unevenly even number, when a number may be equally divided by an uneven number, as 20 by 5. Uneven number, that which exceeds an even number, at least by unity, or which cannot be divided into two equal parts, as 3, 5, &c. The sum or difference of two uneven numbers makes an even number; but the factum of two uneven ones makes an uneven number. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> an even number be added to an uneven one; or if the one be subtracted from the other, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the sum, in the latter the difference, is an uneven number; but the factum of an even and uneven number is even. The sum of any even number of uneven numbers is an even number; and the sum of any uneven number of uneven numbers is an uneven number. Primitive or prime numbers are those divisible only by unity, as 5, 7, &c. And prime numbers among themselves, are those which have no common measure besides unity, as 12 and 19. Perfect number, that whose aliquot parts added together make the whole number, as 6, 28; the aliquot parts of 6 being 3, 2, and 1, = 6; and those of 28, being 14, 7, 4, 2, 1, = 28. Imperfect numbers, those whose aliquot parts added together make either more or less than the whole. And these are distinguished into abundant and defective: an instance in the former case is 12, whose aliquot parts 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, make 16; and in the latter case 16, whose aliquot parts 8, 4, 2, and 1, make but 15. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">Plane</a> number, that arising from the multiplication of two numbers, as 6, which is the product of 3 by 2; and these numbers are called the sides of the plane. Square number is the product of any number multiplied by itself; thus 4, which is the factum of 2 by 2, is a square number. Even square number added to its root makes an even number. Figurate numbers, are such as represent some geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, in relation to which they are always considered; as triangular, pentagonal, pyramidal, &c. numbers. Figurate numbers are distinguished into orders, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, being all produced one from another, viz. by adding continually the terms of any one, the successeive sums are the terms of the next order, beginning from the first order which is that of equal units 1, 1, 1, 1, &c.; then the 2d order consists of the successeive sums of those of the 1st order, forming the arithmetical progression 1, 2, 3, 4, &c.; those of the third order are the successeive sums of those of the 2d, and are the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, &c.; those of the 4th order are the successeive sums of those of the 3d, and are the pyramidal numbers 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, &c.; and so on as below: | Order | Names | Numbers | |-------|----------------|---------| | 1 | Equals | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, &c. | | 2 | Arithmeticals | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &c. | | 3 | Triangulars | 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, &c. | | 4 | Pyramidal | 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, &c. | | 5 | 2d Pyramidal | 1, 5, 15, 35, 70, &c. | | 6 | 3d Pyramidal | 1, 6, 21, 56, 126, &c. | | 7 | 4th Pyramidal | 1, 7, 28, 84, 210, &c. | The above are all considered as different sorts of triangular numbers, being formed from an arithmetical progression whose common difference is 1. But if that common difference be 2, the successeive sums will be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of square numbers; if it be 3, the series will be pentagonal numbers, or pentagons; if it be 4, the series will be hexagonal numbers, or hexagons; and so on. Thus: Arithmeticals. And the reason of the names triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, &c. is, that those numbers may be placed in the form of these regular figures or polygons. But the figurate numbers of any order may also be found without computing those of the preceding orders; which is done by taking the successive products of as many of the terms of the arithmeticals, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &c. in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, as there are units in the number which denominates the order of figurates required, and dividing those products always by the first product: thus, the triangular numbers are found by dividing the products \(1 \times 2\), \(2 \times 3\), \(3 \times 4\), \(4 \times 5\), &c. each by the first product \(1 \times 2\); the first pyramids by dividing the products \(1 \times 2 \times 3\), \(2 \times 3 \times 4\), \(3 \times 4 \times 5\), &c. by the first \(1 \times 2 \times 3\). And, in general, the figurate numbers of any order \(n\) are found by substituting successively 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &c. instead of \(x\) in this general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>: \[ \frac{x(x+1)}{2} + \frac{x(x+1)(x+2)}{6} \] where the factors in the numerator and denominator are supposed to be multiplied together, and to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the number in each be less by 1 than that which expresses the order of the figurates required. See MacLaurin's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>, art. 351, in the notes; also Simpson's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, p. 213; or Malcolm's Arithmetic, p. 396, where the subject of figurates is treated in a very extensive and perspicuous manner. Hutton's Mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. Polygonal or polygonous numbers, the sums of arithmetical progressions beginning with unity: where the common difference is 1, are called triangular numbers; where 2, square numbers; where 3, pentagonal numbers; where 4, hexagonal numbers; where 5, heptagonal numbers, &c. Pyramidal numbers, the sums of polygonous numbers, collected after the same manner as the polygons themselves, and not gathered out of arithmetical progressions, are called first pyramidal numbers; the sums of the first pyramidal are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> pyramidal, &c. If they arise out of triangular numbers, they are called triangular pyramidal numbers; if out of pentagons, first pentagonal pyramidal. From the manner of summing up polygonal numbers, it is easy to conceive how the prime pyramidal numbers are found, viz. \[ \frac{(a-2)n^3 + 3n^2 - (a-5)n}{6} \] expresses all the prime pyramidal. The number <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> has a very curious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, its products always composing either 9 or some lesser product of it. We have already given an account of this, with the examples from Hume, under the article Nine; and we need not repeat them. Did our limits permit us, we could instance in a variety of other properties numbers both curious and surprising. Such speculations are indeed by some men considered as trifling and useless; but perhaps they judge too hastily; for few employments are more innocent, none more ingenious, nor, to those who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for them, more amusing. Numbers were by the Jews, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, expressed by letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>: hence we may conceive how imperfect and limited their arithmetic was, because the letters could not be arranged in a series, or in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, conveniently enough for the purposes of ready calculation. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the cipher, or arithmetical figures, which we now make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, has given us a very great advantage over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> in this respect. Mankind, we may reasonably suppose, first reckoned by their fingers, which they might indeed do in a variety of ways. From this digital arithmetic, very probably, is owing the number 10, which constitutes the whole set of arithmetical figures. The letters chiefly employed by the Romans to express numbers were, M, for 1000; D, for 500; C, for 100; L, for 50; V, for five; X, for 10; and I, for one.—M, probably signified 1000, because it is the initial of mille; D stands for 500, because it is the diminution of mille; C signifies 100, as being the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the word centum; L stands for 50, because it is the half of C, having formerly been wrote thus L; V signifies 5, because V is the fifth vowel; X stands for 10, because it contains twice X or V in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> form; I stands for one, because it is the first letter of initium. These however are fanciful derivations. See NUMERAL LETTERS. The Jewish cabalists, the Grecian conjurors, and the Roman augurs, had a great veneration for particular numbers, and the result of particular <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of them. Thus three, four, six, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, nine, ten, are full of divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, and of great efficacy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> NUMBER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>, No. 27.

NUMBERS

Pages 93-94

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, Oratory, &c., are certain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, proportions, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cadences, which render a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, or song, agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Poetical numbers consist in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> in the order, quantities, &c. of the feet and syllables, which make the piece musical to the ear, and fit for singing, for which all the verses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were intended. See POETRY.—It is of these numbers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> speaks in his ninth Eclogue, when he makes Lycidas say, Numeros memini, si verba tenerem; meaning, that although he had forgot the words of the verses, yet he remembered the feet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of which they were composed. Rhetorical or profane numbers are a sort of simple unaffected harmony, less glaring than that of verse, but such as is perceived and affects the mind with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The numbers are that by which the style is said to be easy, free, round, flowing, &c. Numbers are things absolutely necessary in all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and even in all speech. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Tully, Quintilian, &c. lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> abundance of rules as to the best manner of intermixing dactyls, spondees, anaepeta, &c. in order to have the numbers perfect. The substance of what they have said, is reducible to what follows: 1. The style becomes numerous by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> disposition and temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables, so as that the multitude of short ones neither render it too halting, nor that of long ones too... Numbers too slow and languid; sometimes, indeed, long and short syllables are thrown together designedly without any such mixture, to paint the flowness or celerity of anything by that of the numbers; as in these verses of Virgil: "Illi inter se se magna vi brachia tollunt; and Radit iter liquidum, celere neque commovet alas." 2. The style becomes numerous, by the intermixing words of one, two, or more syllables; whereas the too frequent repetition of monosyllables renders the style pitiful and grating. 3. It contributes greatly to the numerousness of a period, to have it cloathed by magnificent and well-founded words. 4. The numbers depend not only on the nobleness of the words in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, but of those in the whole tenor of the period. 5. To have the period flow easily and equally, the harsh concurrence of letters and words is to be studiously avoided, particularly the frequent meeting of rough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>; the beginning the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> of a word with the last of the preceding; the frequent repetition of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> or syllable; and the frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the like ending words. Lastly, The utmost care is to be taken, lest, in aiming at oratorical numbers, you should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into poetical ones; and instead of prose, write verse. Book of NUMBERS, the fourth book of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, taking its denomination from its numbering the families of Israel. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this book is historical, relating to several remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Israelites' <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> through the wilderness. It contains a distinct relation of their several movements from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, or their flags through the wilderness, and many other things, whereby we are instructed and confirmed in some of the weightiest truths that have immediate reference to God and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> in the world.—But the greatest part of this book is spent in enumerating those laws and ordinances, whether civil or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, which were given by God, but not mentioned before in the preceding books.

NUMERAL LETTERS

Pages 94-95

those letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> which are generally used for figures; as I, one; V, five; X, ten; L, fifty; C, a hundred; D, five hundred; M, a thousand, &c. It is not agreed how the Roman numerals originally received their value. It has been supposed, as we have observed in the end of the article <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">NUMBER</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used M to denote 1000, because it is the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of mille, which is Latin for 1000; and C to denote 100, because it is the first letter of centum, which is Latin for 100. It has also been supposed, that D, being formed by dividing the old M in the middle, was therefore appointed to stand for 500, that is, half as much as the M stood for when it was whole; and that L being half a C, was, for the same reason, used to denote 50. But what reason is there to suppose, that 1000 and 100 were the numbers which letters were first used to express? And what reason can be assigned why D, the first letter in the Latin word decem, ten, should not rather have been chosen to stand for that number, than for 500, because it had a rude resemblance to half an M?—But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these questions could be satisfactorily answered, there are other numeral letters which have never yet been accounted for at all. These considera- tions render it probable that the Romans, did not, in their original intention, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> letters to express numbers at all; the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> seems to be this: The Romans probably put <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a single stroke, I, for one, as is still the practice of those who score on slate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with chalk: this stroke, I, they doubled, trebled, and quadrupled, to express 2, 3, and 4: thus, II. III. IIII. So far they could easily number the strokes with a glance of the eye. But they presently found, that if more were added, it would soon be necessary to tell the strokes one by one: for this reason, then, when they came to 5, they expressed it by joining two strokes together in an acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> thus, V; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear the more probable, if it be considered that the progression of the Roman numbers is from 5 to 5, i.e., from the fingers on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the fingers on the other.—Ovid has touched upon the original of this in his Fastorum, lib. iii. and Vitruvius has made the same remark. After they had made this acute angle V. for five, they added the single stroke to it to the number of 4, thus, VI. VII. VIII. VIII. and then as the strokes could not be further multiplied without confusion, they doubled their acute angle by prolonging the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> beyond their intersection thus, X., to denote two fives, or ten. After this they doubled, trebled, and quadrupled, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> acute angle thus, XX. XXX. XXXX. they then, for the same reason which induced them first to make a single and then to double it, joined two single strokes in another form, and instead of an acute angle, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> angle L, to denote fifty. When this 50 was doubled, they then doubled the right angle thus R, to denote 100, and having numbered this double right angle four times, thus LLL, LLLL, LLLLL, when they came to the fifth number, as before, they reverted it, and put a single stroke before it thus IX, to denote 900; and when this 900 was doubled, they also doubled their double right angle, setting two double right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> opposite to each other, with a single stroke between them, thus XIX to denote 1000: when this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for 1000 had been four times repeated, then they put down XXX for 3000, XXXX for 4000, XXXIX for 5000, and LXXXIX for 100,000, XXXL for 500,000, and LXXXIX for 1 million. That the Romans did not originally write M for 1000, and C for 100, but <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as they are written above, we are expressly informed by Paulus Manutius; but the corners of the angles being cut off by the transcribers for dispatch, these figures were gradually brought into what are now numeral letters.—When the corners of LXX were made round, it stood thus CXX, which is so near the Gothic m, that it soon deviated into that letter; so IX having the corner made round, it stood thus IX, and then easily deviated into D. It also became a plain C by the same means; the single rectangle which denoted 50, was, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> L; the double acute angle was an X; the single acute angle a V consonant; and a plain single stroke, the letter I; and thus these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> letters, M, D, C, L, X, V, I, became numerals. NUMERAL Characters of the Arabs, are those figures which are now used in all the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. We have elsewhere shown that the Arabs derived the use of them most probably from NUMERAL from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, (See Arithmetic, No. 5.) This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, however, though very generally received, has been controverted with some ingenuity. A writer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when that miscellany was in its highest reputation, thus endeavours to prove that the Arabs derived their notations from the Greeks. "I maintain (says he) that the Indians received their numeral characters from the Arabians, and the Arabians from the Greeks, as from them they derived all their learning, which in some things they improved, but for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> have altered. The numerical figures which they received from the Greeks are proofs of this alteration; which is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that without particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> one can scarce discover in them the vestiges of their origin. But when we compare them carefully and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, we find in them manifest traces of the Greek figures. The Greek numerical figures were no other than the letters of their alphabet. A small stroke was the mark of unity. The B, being abridged of its two extremities, produced the 2. If you incline the γ a little on its left side, and cut off its foot, and make the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> round towards the left side, you will produce a 3; the Δ makes the 4, by raising the right leg perpendicularly, and lengthening it a little below the base, and lengthening the base on the left side. The Σ forms the 5; by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> towards the right, which before was turned towards the left side. The number 6 forms the 6 by having its head taken off, and its body rounded. Ζ, by taking away the base, makes the 7. If we make the top and bottom of H round, we shall form an 8. The Θ is the 9 with very little alteration. The cypher ω was only a point, to which one of the figures was added to make it stand for ten times as much. It was necessary to mark this point very strongly; and in order to form it better, a circle was made, which was filled up in the middle; but that circumstance was afterwards neglected. Theophanes, an historian of Constantinople, who lived in the ninth century, says expressly, that the Arabians retained the Greek figures, having no characters in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to represent all the numbers. The Greeks observed in their numbers the decuple progression, which the Arabians have retained. Certain characters are found in the Greek alphabet, which are not used in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, but only in calculation, and for this reason they are styled Epiphanes, that is to say, notes, marks, in order to distinguish them from letters. The number 6 derives its form from one of these epiphanes, which was called επιφανεις βασιλευοντος. This epiphane forms the letter F among the Æolians and among the Latins. This was called the Digamma, so styled from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which seems to have been one Γ placed upon another. That this reasoning is plausible will hardly be questioned; but whether it be conclusive our readers must determine. It has not convinced ourselves; but through the whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we wish to state candidly the different opinions held on every subject of curiosity and usefulness.

NUMERATION

Pages 95-95
or Notation, in Arithmetic, the art of expressing in characters any number proposed in words, or of expressing in words any number proposed in characters. See Arithmetic, No. 7.

NUMERICAL

Pages 95-95

Numerous, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Numerical, something belonging to numbers; as numerical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a> is that which makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of numbers, instead of letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>.—Also numerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is that by which one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is distinguished from another. Hence a thing is said to be numerically the same, when it is so in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word.

NUMIDA

Pages 95-95

a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NUMIDIA

Pages 95-104

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the south by Gaetulia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior; on the west by the Mulucha, a river which separated it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>; and on the east by the Tufca, another river which bounded it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with Africa Propria. Dr Shaw has rendered it probable, that the river which formerly went under the denominations of Malwa, Malgana, Mulucha, and Molochah, is the same with that now called Mulloolah by the Algerines; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the kingdom of Numidia must have extended upwards of 500 miles in length; its breadth, however, cannot be so well ascertained; but supposing it to have been the same with that of the present kingdom of Algiers, in the narrowest part it must have been at least 40 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and in the widest upwards of 100. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> included two districts; one inhabited by the Maffyli, and the other by the Massiflyli; the latter being also called in after times, Mauritania Caesariensis, and the former Numidia Propria. The country of the Maffyli, or, as some call it, Terra Metagoria, was separated from the proper territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> by its eastern boundary the river Tufca, and from the kingdom of the Massiflyli, or Mauritania Caesariensis, by the river Ampfla. It seems to correspond with that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Constantine lying between the Zaine and the Med al Kheer, which is above 130 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and more than 100 broad. The sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of this province is for the most part mountainous and rocky, answering to the appellation given to it by Abulfeda, viz. El Edwaa, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or lofty. It is far from being equal in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to the ancient country of the Maffyli, which, Strabo informs us, was yet inferior to the country of the Maffyli. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was Cirta, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The most celebrated antiquarians agree, that the tract, Peopled by extending from the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a> to the lake Triton, the defendants, was chiefly peopled by the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIZRAIM">Mizraim</a>, and that the posterity of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Put, or Phut, spread themselves all over the country between that lake and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. To this notion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> countenance: for he tells us, that the Libyan Nomades, whose territories to the west were bounded by the Triton, agreed in their customs and manners with the Egyptians; but that the Africans, from that river to the Atlantic ocean, differed in almost all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> from them. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> called Putea near Adrametum; and Pliny, a river of Mauritania Tingitana, known by the name of Fu, or Phut; and the district adjacent to this river was called Regio Phutenis, which plainly alludes to the name of Phut. That word signifies scattered, or dispersed, which very well agrees with what Mela and Strabo relate of the ancient Numidians; so that we may, without any scruple, admit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a> of this country to have been the descendants of Phut.
