Thus the nundinal day being under A on the first, ninth, seventeenth, and twenty-fifth days of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> D <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the nundinal letter of the year following. These nundinals bear a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance to the dominical letters, which return every eight days, as the nundinals did every nine.

NUNDOCOMAR

Pages 105-105

a Rajah in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, and head of the Brahmans, who, in 1775, was condemned to an ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by English laws newly introduced, in an English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> newly established, for a forgery <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to have been committed by him many years before. That he was guilty of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> cannot be questioned; but there was surely something hard in condemning a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by an ex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> facto <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He bore his fate with the utmost fortitude, in the full confidence that his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> would soon be reunited to the universal spirit whence it had sprung. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. Chap. IV. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">Immortality</a> of the Soul.

NUPERTIAL RITES

Pages 105-106

the ceremonies attending the solemnization of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, which are different in different ages and countries. We cannot omit here a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which was practised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> on these occasions; which was this: Immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ceremonies were over, the new married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> threw nuts about the room for the boys to scramble for. Various reasons have been assigned for it; but that which most generally prevails, and seems to be the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, is, that by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> the bridegroom signified his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to abandon trifles, and commence a serious course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; whence nucibus relicitis in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> became a proverb. They might also be an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of fertility. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks had a person to conduct the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> from her own to the bridegroom's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and hence he was called by the Greeks Nymphagoge, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was afterwards used both by the Romans and the Jews.

NUREMBERG

Pages 106-106

an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. N. Lat. 47. 30. It stands on the Regnitz, over which it has several bridges, both of wood and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, at the bottom of a hill, 60 miles from Augsburg, 87 from Munich, 46 from Wurtzburg, and 50 from Ratibon; and is thought by some to be the Segodium, and by others the Castrum Noricum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The city has derived its name from the hill, upon which stands this castle, called, in Latin, Castrum Noricum, round which the city was begun to be built, and where the emperors formerly lodged; and here they lodge still, when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by that city. They there preserve, as precious relics, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, sceptre, clothes, buckles, and other ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> (A), which served also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Leopold, when he went thither after his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, to receive the homage of the city. The small river Regnitz, which runs through it, and those of Rednitz and Schwarzack, which pass by its walls, furnish the inhabitants, besides other advantages, with the means of making all sorts of stuffs, dyes, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> (B), and toys, which are carried and sold even in the Indies. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well-built town, but not very populous. Its fortifications are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall, flanked with towers mounting cannon, and a deep ditch. The magistrates, and most of the inhabitants, are Lutherans. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many churches and chapels in it. In that of St Sebald is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> monument of the saint; and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world, by the celebrated Albert Durer, who was a native of the town; but the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the town is that of St Giles. In that of the Holy Ghost are kept most of the jewels of the empire, together with the pretended spear with which our Saviour's side was pierced, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a> of his crown, and a piece of the manger wherein he was laid. Here are also a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, one in particular for foundlings, and another for pilgrims; with a gymnasium, an anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a>, a fine public library, the old imperial forts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> castles, some remains of the old citadel of the burggraves of Nuremberg, several Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, an academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, a well furnished arsenal, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in which the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is tolerated, and a mint. Mr Keyser says, there are upwards of 500 streets in it, about 140 fountains, 16 churches, 44 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, 12 bridges, 10 market places, and 25,000 inhabitants; and that its territories, besides the capital and four other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, contain above 500 villages, and about 160 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> on the Regnitz. The trade of this city, though upon the decline, is still very great, many of its manufactures being still exported to all parts of the world; among which may be reckoned a great variety of curious toys in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, wood, and metal, already mentioned. The city has also distinguished itself in the arts of painting and engraving. When the emperor Henry VI. assisted at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> in Nuremberg, he raised 38 burghers to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, the defendants of whom are called patricians, and have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the city entirely in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, except eight masters of companies, who are summoned only on extraordinary occasions, consisting of them. Among the fine brass cannon in the arsenal, is one that is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> at the breech, and may be fired eight times in a minute; and two that carry balls of eighty pounds. The city keeps, in constant pay, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> companies, consisting each, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of peace, of 100 men, but, in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, of 185; two troops of cuirassiers, each consisting of 85 men; and two companies of invalids. There are also 24 companies of burghers, well armed and disciplined. On the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which is said to have cost 100,000 guilders, are two pyramids, on the top of one of which is a dove with an olive branch in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, and on the other an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eagle. Music also flourishes greatly in Nuremberg; and those who delight in mechanic (A) These ornaments are, a mitred crown, enriched with rubies, emeralds, and pearls; the dalmatic of Charlemagne, richly embroidered; the imperial mantle powdered with embroidered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, and its border thick set with large emeralds, sapphires, and topazes; the buckles covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the gloves embroidered; the apple, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> sceptre, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the empire is, that the emperor is bound to assemble in this city the first diet that he holds after his election and coronation. (B) There is in Nuremberg, and in the neighbouring villages depending upon it, an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of workmen, very ingenious in making several kinds of toys of wood, which are carried through all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of Germany, and from thence through all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. These toys are called Nurembergs; and they have so great a fame, that it even exceeds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. This employment affords a livelihood to the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the inhabitants of the city; and they make a very considerable profit from this traffic.

NURSERY

Pages 106-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, is a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> set apart for raising and propagating all sorts of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to supply the garden and other plantations. NURSING OF CHILDREN. See LACTATIO. The following observations and directions are said to be the result of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The child should be laid (the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>) upon a thin mattress, rather longer than itself, which the nurse <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep upon her lap, that the child may always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> straight, and only sit up as the nurse flants the mattress. To set a child quite upright before the end of the first month, hurts the eyes, by making the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the eye appear below the upper eyelid. Afterwards the nurse will begin to set it up and dance it by degrees. The child must be kept as dry as possible. The clothing should be very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and not much longer than the child, that the legs may be got at with ease, in order to have them often rubbed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> with a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, and in particular the inside of them. Rubbing a child all over takes off scurf, and makes the blood circulate. The one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> should be rubbed with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> one way, and the other the other way, night and morning at least. The ankle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and inside of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> should be rubbed twice a day; this will strengthen those parts, and make the child stretch its knees and keep them flat, which is the foundation of an erect and graceful person. A nurse ought to keep a child as little in her arms as possible, lest the legs should be cramped, and the toes turned inwards. Let her always keep the child's legs loose. The oftener the posture is changed, the better. Tossing a child about, and exercising it in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, is of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. In cities, children are not to be kept in hot rooms, but to have as much air as possible. Want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> is the cause of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heads, weak and knotted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, a contracted breast, which occasions coughs and stuffed lungs, an ill shaped person, and waddling gait, besides a numerous train of other ills. The child's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is to be kept perfectly clean, by constantly washing its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> and likewise its neck and ears; beginning with warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, till by degrees it will not only bear, but like to be washed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water. Rising early in the morning is good for all children, provided they awake of themselves, which they generally do; but they are never to be waked out of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and as soon as possible to be brought to regular sleeps in the day. When laid in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> or cradle, their legs are always to be laid straight. Children, till they are two or three years old, must never be suffered to walk long enough at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be weary. Girls might be trained to the proper management of children, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a premium were given in free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, workhouses, &c. to those that brought up the finest child to one year old. If the mother cannot suckle the child, get a wholesome cheerful woman, with young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, who has been used to tend young children. After the first six months, small broths, and innocent foods of any kind, may do as well as living wholly upon milk. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing to be always attended to is, to give young children constant exercise, and to keep them in a proper posture. With regard to the child's dress in the day, let it be a shirt; a petticoat of fine flannel, two or three inches longer than the child's feet, with a dimity top (<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a bodice coat), to tie behind; over that a surcingle made of fine buckram, two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, covered over with satin or fine ticken, with a ribbon fastened to it to tie it on, which answers every purpose of stays, and has none of their inconveniences. Over this put a robe, or a flip and frock, or whatever you like best; provided it is fastened behind, and not much longer than the child's feet, that their motions may be strictly observed. (c) Of these 42 members, there are only 34 chosen from the patrician families; the other eight are taken from among the burgheers, and make in a manner a small separate body. (n) This secret <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> is composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> principal chiefs of the republic, and for that reason is called septemvirate. It determines the most important affairs; and is the depository of the precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the empire, of the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, the ensigns, feats, and keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Two caps are to be put on the head, till the child has got most of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The child's dress for the night may be a shirt, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a> to tie on, and a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> to tie over the blanket.

NUSANCE

Pages 108-108
or NUISANCE, in Law**, a thing done to the annoyance of another. Nuisances are either public or private.—A public nuisance is an offence against the public in general, either by doing what tends to the annoyance of all the king's subjects, or by neglecting to do what the common good requires: in which case, all annoyances and injuries to streets, highways, bridges, and large rivers, as also disorderly alehouses, bawdy-houses, gaming houses, stages for rope-dancers, &c., are held to be common nuisances.—A private nuisance is, when only one person's family is annoyed by the doing of any thing; as where a person stops up the light of another's house, or builds in such a manner that the rain falls from his house upon his neighbours.

NUTATION

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a kind of tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the axis of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereby, in each annual revolution, it is twice inclined to the ecliptic, and as often returns to its former position. **NUTCRACKER.** See CORVUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **NUTHATCH.** See SITTA, ORNITHOLOGY Index.

NUTMEG

Pages 108-108

the fruit of a tree, and a well known spice. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRISTICA">MYRISTICA</a>.

NUX VOMICA

Pages 108-108

a flat, compressed, round fruit, about the breadth of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>, brought from the East Indies. It is found to be a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> for dogs, cats, &c., and it is not to be doubted that it would also prove fatal to mankind. Its surface is not much corrugated; and its texture is firm like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> grayish-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It is said to be used as a specific against the bite of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-snake. It is considerably bitter and deleterious; but has been used in doses from five to ten grains twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> so, in intermittents, particularly oliginate quartans, and in contagious dysentery. The *strychnus ignatii* is a tree of the same kind, producing gourd-like fruit, the seeds of which are improperly called St Ignatius's beans. These, as also the woods or roots of some such trees, called *lignum colubrinum*, or *snakewood*, are very narcotic bitters, like the nux vomica.

NUZZER

Pages 109-109
or NUZZERANAH; a present or offering from an inferior to a superior. In Hindoostan no man ever approaches his superior for the first time on business without an offering of at least a gold or silver rupee in his right hand; which, if not taken, is a mark of disfavour. Nuzzeranah is also used for the sum paid to the government as an acknowledgment for a grant of lands or any public office.

NYCHTHEMERON

Pages 109-109

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, signified the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> day and night, consisting of 24 hours, or 24 equal parts. This way of considering the day was particularly adopted by the Jews, and seems to owe its origin to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of Moses, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, "the evening and the morning were the first day."—Before the Jews had introduced the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> into their discourse, they used to signify this space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by the simple expression of a night and a day. It is proper here to observe, that all the eastern countries reckoned any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a day of 24 hours for a whole day; and say a thing that was done on the third or seventh day, &c., from that last mentioned, was done after three or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. And the Hebrews, Nyctalopia having no word which exactly answers to the Greek νυκτόνησος, signifying "a natural day of 24 hours," νύξ νύξ, or νύξ νύξ, for it. So that to say a thing happened after three days and three nights, was, with them, the same as to say it happened after three days, or on the third day. This, being remembered, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> explain what is meant by "the Son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>'s being three days and three nights in the heart of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>." NYCTALOPIA. See MEDICINE, No. 361.

NYCTANTHES

Pages 109-109

ARABIAN JASMINE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the diandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with the 44th order, Sepiarie. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NYCTASTRETEGI

Pages 109-109

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, were officers appointed to prevent fires in the night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to give alarm and call assistance when a fire broke out. At Rome they had the command of the watch, and were called nocturni triumviri, from their office and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

NYCTICORAX

Pages 109-109

the night raven; a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ARDEA. See ARDEA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NYL-GHAU

Pages 109-109

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of quadruped belonging to the genus <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, a native of the interior parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NYLAND

Pages 109-109

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Finland, to the west of the province of Carelia.

NYMPH

Pages 109-111

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, an appellation given to certain inferior goddesses, inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, wood, waters, &c., said to be the daughters of Oceanus and Tethys. All the universe was represented as full of these nymphs, who are distinguished into several ranks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> classes. The general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of them is into celestial and terrestrial; the former of them were called uraniae, and were supposed to be intelligences that governed the heavenly bodies or spheres. The terrestrial nymphs, called epigeiae, presided over the several parts of the inferior world; and were divided into those of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The nymphs of the water were the oceanitides, or nymphs of the ocean; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREIDS">nereids</a>, the nymphs of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; the naiads and ophrygiades, the nymphs of the fountains; and the limnades, the nymphs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The nymphs of the earth were the oreades, or nymphs of the mountains; the napaeae, nymphs of the meadows; and the dryads and hamadryades, who were nymphs of the forests and groves. Besides these, we meet with nymphs who took their names from particular countries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c., as the citheroniades, so called from Mount Citheron in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; the dodonides, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>; tiberiades, from the Tiber, &c.—Goats were sometimes sacrificed to the nymphs; but their constant offerings were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and wine. We have the following account of nymphs in Chandler's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. "They were supposed to enjoy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a>, but not to be immortal. They were believed to delight in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and fountains. They are described as sleepless, and as dreaded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people. They were susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The Argonauts, it is related, landing on the shore of the Propontis to dine in their way to Colchos, sent Hylas, a boy, for water, who discovered a lonely fountain, in which the nymphs Eunice, Malis, and Nycheia, were preparing to dance; and these feeling him were enamoured, and, seizing him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, hand as he was filling his vase, pulled him in. The del- ties, their copartners in the cave, are such as prefiged with them over rural and pastoral affairs. "The old Athenians were ever ready to cry out, A god! or a goddes! The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Pifitratrus entered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in a chariot with a tall woman drested in ar- mour to resemble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and regained the Acropolis, which he had been forced to abandon, by this stratagem; the people worshipping, and believing her to be the dei- ty whom they represented. The nymphs, it was the po- pular persuasion, occasionally appeared; and nympho- lepsy is characterized as a frenzy, which arose from ha- ving beheld them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> disposed the mind to adopt delusion for reality, and gave to a fancied vision the efficacy of full conviction. The foundation was per- haps no more than an indirect, partial, or obscure view of some harmless girl, who had approached the foun- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> on a like errand with Hylas, or was retiring after she had filled her earthen pitcher. "Among the sacred caves on record, one on Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and one by Lebadea in Boeotia of Trophonius. Both these were oracular, and the latter bore some resemblance to that we have described. It was formed by art, and the mouth surrounded with a wall. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, occasionally applied and removed. It was situated on a mountain above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>; and they related, that a swarm of bees conducted the person by whom it was first discovered. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> owners of caves were the nymphs, and these were sometimes local. On Citheron in Boeo- tia, many of the inhabitants were possessed by nymphs called Sphragitides, whose cave, once also oracular, was on a summit of the mountain. Their dwellings had ge- nerally a well or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of water; the former often a collection of moisture condensed or exuding from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and sides; and this, in many instances, being pregnant with flaky particles, concreted, and marked its passage by incrustation, the groundwork in all ages and coun- tries of idle tales framed or adopted by superstitious and credulous people. "A cave in Paphlagonia was sacred to the nymphs who inhabited the mountains about Heraclia. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and wide, and pervaded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, clear as crystal. There also were seen bowls of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and nymphs and their webs and distaffs, and curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, exciting admiration. The poet who has described this grotto, deserves not to be regarded, as fervently copying <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; he may justly lay claim to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as an original topographer. "The pity of Archidamus furnished a retreat for the nymphs, where they might find shelter and provision, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> distressed; whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> parched up their trees, or Jupiter enthroned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> upon the mountain top feared them with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and terrible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, pour- ing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a deluge of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or brightening the summits with his snow." Nymph, among naturalists, that state of winged in- sects between their living in the form of a worm and their appearing in the winged or moth perfect state. The eggs of insects are first hatched into a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> or maggots; which afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the nymph state, surrounded with shells or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of their own skins; so that, in reality, these nymphs are only the embryo insects, wrapped up in this covering; from whence they at last get loose, though not without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty. During this nymph state the creature loses its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Swammerdam calls it nympha aurelia, or simply aurelia; and others give it the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of the like import. See the article CHRYSALIS. NYMPH-Band, situated about 10 leagues off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Mun- ster in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, is a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> place, and 11 leagues S. S. E. from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> head of Dungarvan. It abounds with cod, ling, skate, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>, whiting, and other fish; which was discovered by Mr Doyle, who on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 15, 1736 sailed to it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> men, on board the Nymph, a small vessel of about 12 tons. This place is well adapted for a fishing com- pany, the great public advantages of which must be very evident. NYMPHÆ, in Anatomy, two membranaceous parts, situated on each side the rima. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NYMPHÆA, the WATER-LILY; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Miscellaneous. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index. NYMPHÆA (amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>), doubtful what structures they were; some take them to have been grottoes, deriving their name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the nymphs with which they were adorned; but that they were considerable works appears from their being exe- cuted by the emperors, (Amianus, Victor, Capitolinus) or by the city prefects. In an inscription, the term is written nymphium. None of all these nymphæa has lasted down to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Some years since, indeed, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of marble was discovered between <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, with only one entrance, and some steps that went down to it. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand as you enter, towards the head, there is a fountain of the purest water; along which, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> as it were, is laid a naked Arethusa of the whitest marble; the bot- tom or ground is of variegated marble, and encompassed with a canal fed by the water from the fountain: the walls are set round with shells and pebbles of various colours; by the setting of which, as by so many strokes in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, are expressed the 12 months of the year, and the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> virtues; also the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Proserpine; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> playing on his reed, and soothing his flock; besides the representations of nymphs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, failing, and wanton on fishes, &c. It seems pretty evident that the nymphæa were public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>; for at the same time that they were furnished with pleasing grottoes, they were also supplied with cooling streams, by which they were rendered exceed- ingly delightful, and drew great numbers of people to frequent them. Silence seems to have been a particu- lar requisite there, as appears by this inscription, Nympha, loci, libri, lata, tace. That building between Naples and Vesuvius, mentioned above, was certainly one of these nymphæa. NYMPHÆUM, (Plutarch); the name of a sacred place, near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLONIA">Apollonia</a> in Illyricum, sending forth con- tinually fire in detached streams from a green valley and verdant meadows. Dio Cassius adds, that the fire neither burns up nor parches the earth, but that herbs and trees grow and thrive near it, and therefore the place is called nymphæum; near which was an oracle of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that the fire, to show that the wish was granted NYM granted, confused the frankincense thrown into it; but repelled it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the fire was rejected. It was there that a sleeping satyr was once caught and brought to Sylla as he returned from the Mithridatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This monster had the same features as the poets ascribe to the satyr. He was interrogated by Sylla and by his interpreters; but his articulations were unintelligible; and the Roman spurned from him a creature which seemed to partake of the nature of a beast more than that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

NYMPHEUM

Pages 111-111

in antiquity, a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> magnificently decorated, for entertainments, &c. and where those who wanted convenience at home held their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> feasts; whence the name.

NYMPHIDUS

Pages 111-111

Sabinus, a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, but appointed by Nero colleague of Tigellinus in the command of the praetorian guards. About the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, that the German legions revolted from this despicable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, he was also betrayed by Nymphidius and abandoned by his guards. Nymphidius began now to entertain thoughts of seizing the sovereignty himself. However, he did not immediately declare his ambitious views; but pretending to espouse the cause of Galba, assured the guards that Nero was fled, and promised them such sums as neither Galba nor any other was able to discharge. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> secured for the present the empire to Galba, occasioned afterwards the loss of it, and, finally, produced the destruction of Nymphidius and the guards themselves. After Nero's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, however, and on the acknowledgement of Galba as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, he renewed his ambition; and having, by his immense largesses, gained the affections of the praetorian guards, and persuading himself that Galba, by reason of his infirmities and old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, would never reach the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, usurped all the authority at Rome. Presuming upon his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, he obliged Tigellinus, who commanded, jointly with him, the praetorian guards, to resign his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. He made several magnificent and extensive entertainments, inviting such as had been consuls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had commanded armies, distributed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums among the people, and with shows and other diversions, which he daily exhibited, gained so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an interest with all ranks, that he already looked upon himself as sovereign. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, dreading his power, conferred extraordinary honours upon him, styled him their protector, attended him when he appeared in public, and had recourse to him for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of their decrees, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been already invested with the sovereign power. This base compliance elated him to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he usurped, not leisurely and by degrees, but all at once, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority. He acted as sovereign indeed, but he had not as yet openly declared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of seizing the empire; his power however was great, and he used it in undermining Galba's power; he was, however, unsuccessful, and the disclosure of his designs was much against him. Galba was again acknowledged and proclaimed, and he, notwithstanding his artifices, detected and slain by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who were proclaiming Galba. See Nero.

NYSA

Pages 111-111
or NYSSA, in Ancient Geography, a town of Ethiopia, at the south of Egypt. Some place it in Arabia. This city, with another of the same name in India, was sacred to the god Bacchus, who was educated there by the nymphs of the place, and who received the name of Dionysus, which seems to be compounded of Διος and Νύσσα, the name of his father, and that of the place of his education. The god made this place the seat of his empire, and the capital of the conquered nations of the east. According to some geographers, there were no less than ten places of this name. One of these was famous on the coast of Euboea for its vines, which grew in such an uncommon manner, that if a twig was planted in the ground in the morning, it immediately produced grapes which were full ripe in the evening. A city of Thrace; another seated on the top of Mount Parnassus, and sacred to Bacchus.

NYSLOT

Pages 111-111

a strong town of Russia, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle; seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, among <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> marshes. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 55. N. Lat. 58. 46.

NYSSA

Pages 111-111

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the polygamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holoraceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NYU-CHE

Pages 111-112
or KIN, an empire which arose in Eastern Tartary in the beginning of the 13th century. From the founder of this empire the late Chinese emperor Kang-hi said that his family was descended. See China and Tartary. O. THE 14th letter and fourth vowel of our alphabet; pronounced as in the words nose, rope, &c. The sound of this letter is often so soft as to require it double, and that chiefly in the middle of words; as goosie, reproof, &c. And in some words, this oo is pronounced like u short, as in blood, flood, &c. Vol. XV. Part I. As a numeral, O was sometimes used for 11 among the ancients; and with a dash over it thus, Ō, for 11,000. In the notes of the ancients, O. CON. is read opus conductum; O. C. O. opera confliqve; O. D. M. operæ, donum munus; and O. LO. opus locatum. The Greeks had two O's; viz. omicron, ο, and omega, ω; the first pronounced on the tip of the lips with a sharper sound; the second in the middle of the mouth, with a fuller sound, equal to oo in our language. The long and short pronunciation of our O are equivalent to the two Greek ones; the first, as in suppose; the second, as in obey. O is usually denoted long by a fervile a subjoined, as moan; or by e at the end of the syllable, as bone; when these vowels are not used, it is generally short. Among the Irish, the letter O, at the beginning of the name of a family, is a character of dignity annexed to great houses. Thus, in the history of Ireland, we frequently meet with the O Neals, O Carrolls, &c., considerable houses in that island. Camden observes, that it is the custom of the lords of Ireland to prefix an O to their names, to distinguish them from the commonalty. The ancients used O as a mark of triple time; from a notion that the ternary, or number 3, was the most perfect of numbers, and therefore properly expressed by a circle, the most perfect of figures. It is not, strictly speaking, the letter O, but the figure of a circle O, or double CO, by which the modern ancients in music used to express what they called tempo perfecto, or triple time. Hence the Italians call it circolo. The seven antiphones, or alternate hymns of seven verses, &c., sung by the choir in the time of Advent, were formerly called O, from their beginning with such an exclamation. O is an adverb of calling, or interjection of sorrow or wishing.

NYUTS

Pages 108-109
Peter**, a native of Holland, and a leading character in that extraordinary transaction which happened between the Japanese and the Dutch about the year 1628. In 1627 Nyuts arrived in Batavia from Holland, and was in the same year appointed ambassador to the emperor of Japan by the governor and council of Batavia. He repaired to that empire in 1628; and being a man of a haughty disposition, and extremely vain, he believed it practicable to pass upon the natives for an ambassador from the king of Holland. Upon his affuming this title he was much more honourably received, cared for, and respected, than former ministers had been. But he was soon detected, reprimanded, and reproached in the severest manner, sent back to the port, and ordered to return to Batavia with all the circumstances of disgrace imaginable; notwithstanding which, his interest was so great, that, instead of being punished as he deserved, he was immediately afterwards promoted to the government of the island of Formosa, of which he took possession the year following. He entered upon the administration of affairs in that island with the same disposition that he had shown while ambassador, and with the most implacable resentment against against the Japanese; neither was it long before an opportunity offered, as he thought, of revenging himself to the full. Two large Japanese ships, with upwards of 500 men on board, came into the port; upon which he took it into his head to disarm and unite them, in the same manner as the Dutch vessels are treated at Japan. The Japanese did all they could to defend themselves from this ill usage; but at last, for want of water, they were forced to submit. Governor Nuyts went still farther. When they had finished their affairs at Formosa, and were desirous of proceeding, according to their instructions, to China, he put them off with fair words and fine promises till the monsoon was over. They began then to be very impatient, and desired to have their cannon and sails restored, that they might return home; but the governor had recourse to new artifices, and, by a series of false promises, endeavoured to hinder them from making use of the season proper for that voyage. The Japanese, however, soon perceived his design; and at length, by a bold attempt, accomplished what by fair means and humble entreaty they could not obtain; for, by a daring and well concerted effort, they took him prisoner, and made him and one of the council sign a treaty for securing their liberty, free departure, and indemnity, which was afterwards ratified by the whole council. Nuyts was first confined in Batavia, and afterwards delivered up to the Japanese, notwithstanding the most earnest entreaties on his part to be tried, and even to suffer any kind of death where he was, rather than to be sent to Japan. He was sent there, however, in 1634. He was submitted to the mercy or discretion of the emperor; and the consequence was, that, though imprisoned, he was well used, and could go anywhere, provided his guards were with him, which was more than he could possibly have expected. He now looked for nothing but the continuance of his confinement for life. On a particular occasion, however, i.e., at the funeral of the emperor's father, at the request of the Dutch he was set free, and returned again to Batavia, to the surprize of that people, who, however, adopted ever after a very different conduct with respect to the Japanese.

OAK

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Quercus. The oak has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of monarch of the woods, and very justly. It was well known, and often very elegantly described, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> is exquisite: Velati annofo validam cum robore quercum Alpini Boreae, nunc hinc, nunc flatibus illinc Eruere inter se certant: it fridora, et alia Confluent terram concupisco fipite frondes: Ipsa heret scopulis; et quantum vertice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> auras Ætherias, tantum radice in Tartara tendit. Aen. iv. 441. As o'er th' aerial <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> sublimely spread, Some aged oak uprears his reverend head; This way and that the furious tempests blow, To lay the monarch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> low; Th' imperial plant, though nodding at the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, Though all his scatter'd honours flew the ground; Safe in his strength, and seated on the rock, In naked majesty defies the flock: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> as the head shoots tow'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> to the skies, So deep the root in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>'s foundation lies.

OAKHAMPTON

Pages 114-114

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 5'. N. Lat. 50° 48'.

OAKHUM

Pages 114-114

OCKHAM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Oakum, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> untwisted and pulled out into loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, in order to be used in caulking the seams, tree nails, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> of a ship, for stopping or preventing leaks.

OANNES

Pages 114-114

a being in Chaldean <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, represented as half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and half a fish. According to Berossus and other fabulous writers, this monster was the civilizer of the Chaldeans; to whom he taught a system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> so perfect as to be incapable of improvement. In discharging the duties of his office, he spent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but retired every night into the ocean <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the river. See Mythology, No. 25.

OAR

Pages 114-115

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, flat at one end and round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the other; and which being applied to the side of a floating vessel, serves to make it advance upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the oar which is out of the vessel, and which enters into the water, is called the blade, or wa/b-plate; and that which is within board is termed the loom, whose extremity being small enough to be grasped by the rowers, or persons managing the oars, is called the handle. To pull the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or vessel forwards by means of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, the rowers turn their backs forward, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the blade of the oar in the water, pull the handle forward so that the blade at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> may move aft in the water: but since the blade cannot be so moved, without striking the water, this impulsion is the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the water were to strike the blade from the stern towards the head: the vessel is therefore necessarily moved according to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Hence it follows, that she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> advance with the greater rapidity, by as much as the oar strikes the water more forcibly. Thus it is evident, that an oar acts upon the side of a boat boat or vessel like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> class, whose fulcrum is the station upon which the oar rests on the boat's gunnel. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels, this station is usually called the row-port; but in lighters and boats it is always termed the row-lock.

OARISTUS

Pages 115-115
or OARISTYS, a term in the Greek poetry, signifying a dialogue between a husband and his wife; such as that in the fifth book of the Iliad between Hector and Andromache. Scaliger observes, that the oarifus is not properly any particular little poem, or entire piece of poetry; but always a part of a great one. He adds, that the passage now cited in Homer is the only proper oarifus extant in the ancient poets.

OASIS

Pages 115-115

the name of a fertile spot in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY_DESERT"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. Many of those spots, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oases, in the African deserts are remarkable for their fertility. OAT. See AVENA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mr Bruce gives the following account of the oats which he found growing wild in Arooifi, a small territory in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, not far from the source of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>: "Wild oats (says he) grow up here spontaneously to a prodigious height and size, capable often of concealing both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and his rider, and some of the stalks being little else than an inch in circumference. They have, when ripe, the appearance of small canes. The inhabitants make no sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this grain in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its growth: the uppermost thin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> of it is beautifully variegated with a changeable purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is perfectly good. - I often made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> into cakes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of Scotland." Our author informs us, that the Abyssinians could never be brought to relish these cakes, which they said were bitter, burnt their stomachs, and made them thirsty. He is, however, decidedly of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the wild oat of Arooifi is the oat in its original state; and that it has degenerated everywhere in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

OATH

Pages 115-118

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, accompanied with an invocation of God to witness what we say; and with an imprecation of his vengeance, or a renunciation of his favour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> what we affirm be false, or what we promise be not performed (A). The laws of all civilized states have required the security of an oath for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> given in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and on other occasions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> importance (B); and the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> utterly prohibits swearing, except when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> are required by legal authority. Indeed no serious and reflecting <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, whether he admits the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> or not, can look upon swearing on trivial occasions as anything else than a sin of a very heinous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. To call upon that infinite and omnipresent Being, who created and sustains the universe, to witness all the impertinence of idle conversation, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> uttered at random, betrays a spirit so profane, that nothing short of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> could make us believe it possible for a creature endowed with reason and reflection to be habitually guilty of a practice so impious. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can plead in extenuation of this crime, that he is tempted to swear by the importunity of any appetite or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> implanted in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>: for the utterance of a profane oath communicates no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and removes no uneasiness: it neither elevates the speaker nor depresses the hearer. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> and Moravians, swayed by these considerations, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which they put upon certain texts of Scripture, refuse to swear upon any occasion, even at the requisition of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and in a court of justice. These scruples are groundless; and seem to proceed from an incapacity to distinguish between the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and abuse of swearing. It is unquestionably impious to call upon God to witness impieties, or to use his tremendous name as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> expletive in conversation; but it by no means follows, that we may not piously call upon him to witness truths of importance, or invoke his name with reverence and solemnity. No individual could, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> profaneness, pray for a thousand times more wealth than he may ever have occasion to use; but it was never thought profane to pray "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by day for our daily <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from heaven, and fruitful seasons." If it be lawful to ask of God these earthly blessings, because he alone can bestow them; it cannot surely be unlawful, where the lives or properties of our (A) The word oath is a corruption of the Saxon eoth. It is often in England called a corporal oath, because, in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, the person was sworn over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> or corpus Christi. (B) The various oaths required by different nations at different times, and the various forms, &c., of imposing them, is a subject of very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and curiosity: An account of them does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the present article; it would indeed extend it to an undue length; we cannot, however, omit observing, what is doubtless very remarkable, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> impostor Mahomet taught the Moors, that their oaths might be dissolved. This wonderful doctrine is contained in the 66th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Koran; which, to free himself from his promise and oath to Hafsa his spouse, he pretended was revealed. What the use of oaths is in such circumstances, or what security they afford for performance, it is difficult to ascertain. It is also very remarkable, that an oath respecting marriages was the cause of the first divorce at Rome. The circumstance happened about the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> 525, Posthumius <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> and Spurius Carvilius being consuls. The censors of this year observing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> declining, and imagining it proceeded from interested marriages and promiscuous cohabitation, obliged all the citizens to swear, that they would not marry with any other view than that of peopling the republic. It raised, however, many scruples, and occasioned many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> ruptures. Among the rest, one Carvilius Ruga, a man of distinction, imagined that he was bound by his oath to divorce his wife, whom he passionately loved, because she was barren, which was the first instance of a divorce at Rome from its foundation, though the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> laws of the kings allowed it; it afterwards, however, became shamefully frequent. This is also a striking instance of the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid to oaths among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; it is remarked indeed by all writers, that they paid a most profound respect to them; and on that we know they founded their hopes of success in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Oath. Our neighbours, or the security of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is concerned, to invoke him with reverence to witness the truth of our assertions, or the sincerity of our intentions; because of our truth in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and of our sincerity in all, none but he can be the witness. The text of Scripture upon which the Quakers chiefly rest their argument for the unlawfulness of all swearing under the gospel, is our Saviour's prohibition (Mat. v. 34): "I say unto you, swear not at all." But whoever shall take the trouble of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and looking at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perceive, that it is only in ordinary conversation, and by no means in courts of justice, that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> prohibits his followers from swearing at all. There is no evidence whatever, that swearing by heaven, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, or by their own heads, was the form of a judicial oath in use among the Jews. On the contrary, we are told by Maimonides*, that "if any man swear by heaven, or by earth, yet this is not an oath;" which surely he could not have said, had such been the forms of judicial swearing. Indeed they could not have admitted such forms into their courts without expressly violating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses, who commands them to "Fear the Lord (<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a>) their God, to serve him, and to swear by his name." But the Jews, as everyone knows, had such a reverence for the name Jehovah, that they would not pronounce it on flight occasions, and therefore could not swear by that name in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> conversation. Hence, to gratify their propensity to common swearing, they invented such oaths as, by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of thy head, &c. and by this contrivance they thought to avoid the guilt of profaning the name Jehovah. These, however, being appeals to intangible objects, either had no meaning, or were in fact, as our Saviour justly argues, oaths by that God whose creatures they were; so that the Jew who swore them was still guilty of profaneness towards the very Jehovah whose name his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> would not permit him to pronounce. But what puts it beyond all doubt that the use of judicial oaths is not wholly prohibited in the gospel, is the conduct of our Saviour himself as well as of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> St Paul. When <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> was simply asked by the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, what it was which certain false witnesses testified against him? we are told by the evangelists, that "he held his peace:" but being adjured by the living God to declare whether he was the Christ, the Son of God, or not, he immediately answered the high priest, without objecting to the oath (for such it was) upon which he was examined. "St Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans +, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. Paley says, 'God is my witness,' that, without ceasing, I make mention of you in my prayers;" and to the Corinthians, still more strongly, "I call God for a record upon my soul, that, to spare you, I came not as yet to Corinth." Both these expressions are of the nature of oaths; and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of swearing judicially without any mark of censure or disapprobation: "Men verily swear by the greater; and an oath, for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, is to them an end of all strife." But though a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has an undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to require the security of an oath upon occasions of real importance, we do not hesitate to say, that, in our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, it is something worse than bad policy to multiply oaths, and to hold out to the people temptations to perjure themselves. The security which an oath affords, depends entirely upon the reverence which attaches to it in the mind of him by whom it is given; but that reverence is much weakened by the frequency of oaths, and by the careless manner in which they are too often administered. An excellent moralist + observes, with Mr Paley, truth, that "the levity and frequency with which oaths are administered, has brought about a general inadversity to the obligation of them, which both in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> view is much to be lamented; and it merits (continues he) public consideration, whether the requiring of oaths on so many frivolous occasions, especially in the customs, and in the qualification for petty offices, has any other effect than to make them cheap in the minds of the people. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> cannot travel regularly from the ship to the consumer without coining half a dozen oaths at least; and the same facility for the due discharge of his office, namely that of an oath, is required from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> warden and an archbishop, from a petty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justice of England. Let the law continue its own functions, if they be thought requisite; but let it spare the solemnity of an oath: and where it is necessary, from the want of something better to depend upon, to accept a man's own word or own account, let it annex to prevarication penalties proportioned to the public <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the offence." That these pernicious consequences of frequent oaths are not felt only in England, we have the evidence of another respectable writer, whose acuteness well qualified him to observe, whilst his station in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> furnished him with the best opportunities of observing, the effects of repeated swearing upon the morals of Scotchmen. "Cuffonhouse oaths (says Lord Kames)* Sketcher have become so familiar among us, as to be swallowed of the Hi without a wry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; and is it certain that bribery and forgery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a> in electing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> members are not approaching to the same cool state? Men creep on to vice by degrees. Perjury, in order to support a friend, has become customary of late years; witness fictitious qualifications in the electors of parliament-men, which are made effectual by perjury: yet such is the degeneracy of the present times, that no man is the worse thought of upon that account. We must not flatter ourselves, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> will reach no farther: a man who boggles not at perjury to serve a friend, will in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> become such an adept, as to commit perjury in order to ruin a friend when he becomes an enemy." Besides the frequency of oaths, we have mentioned the irreverent manner in which they are too often administered as one of the causes which make them cheap in the estimation of the people. In this view, the form of the oath, and the ceremonies with which it is required to be taken, are of considerable importance. "The forms of oaths in Christian countries (says Mr Paley) are very different; but in none I believe worse contrived either to convey the meaning, or to impress the obligation of an oath, than in England. In that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> the juror, after repeating the promise or affirmation which the oath is intended to confirm, adds, 'to help me God;' or more frequently the substance of the oath is repeated to the juror by the officer or magistrate who administers it; adding in the conclusion, 'to help you God.' The energy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> resides in the particle..." particle fo; fo, i.e. hac lege, 'upon condition of my speaking the truth, or performing this promise, may God help me, and not otherwise.' The juror, whilst he hears or repeats the words of the oath, holds his right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> upon a Bible, or other book containing the four gospels. The conclusion of the oath sometimes runs, 'ita me Deus adjuvet, et hoc sancta evangelia,' or 'to help me God, and the contents of this book;' which last clause forms a connexion between the words and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the juror, which before was wanting. The juror then kisses the book." This obscure and elliptical form, the excellent author justly observes, is ill calculated to impress the juror with reverence; and he seems to think great preference due to the form of judicial oaths in Scotland. In that country the juror holds up his right hand towards heaven, and swears by Almighty God, and as he shall answer to God at the great day of judgement, "that he will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so far as he knows, or it shall be asked of him." This, if administered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and reverence, is an oath sufficiently solemn and well calculated to have the proper effect upon the mind of the juror, as it brings immediately into his view the Author of his being, and the awful day of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> retribution when every man shall receive the things done in his body according to that he hath done, whether it be good or evil. But when the magistrate, as is too often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, repeats this solemn invocation without rising from his seat at the name of the Supreme Being, and in a tone of carelessness which may convey to the ignorant juror an opinion that he has himself no serious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that there ever will be a great day of judgement, the form, however excellent, makes not its full <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. But let us suppose the oath to be administered with the greatest dignity and reverence, the words of the promise itself appear to us by no means unexceptionable. In a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> on life and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, we should be glad to know what this oath binds the witness to declare. Is he to tell all that he knows touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in question? or only all that shall be asked of him? If he be obliged, in virtue of his oath, to tell all that he knows, the clause—"or it shall be asked of you" is superfluous, and calculated to mislead. If he be bound to tell nothing more of the truth than what shall be asked of him, the word or should be changed into and; he should swear "to tell the truth, &c. so far as he knows, and it shall be asked of him." The court, we believe, considers the witness as bound to declare everything which he knows touching the matter in question. The greater part of witnesses, on the other hand, consider themselves as bound no farther by their oath than to give true answers to such questions as shall be asked of them. They would do well, however, to remember that as oaths are designed for the security of the public, they must be interpreted in the sense in which the public intends them, otherwise they afford no security. But the sense of the public is the law; and as it belongs to the court to declare what the mind of the law is, the witness, who has any doubt concerning the extent of the obligation imposed on him by the words of this oath, should apply to the court for a solution of that doubt, which will be a safe guide to him respecting the evidence which he is to give. Should the court, in resolving the doubts of a witness, give an opinion concerning the sense of any other part of the oath contrary to what he apprehends to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the law in imposing it, he is bound to disregard such opinion; because it is only where he himself is doubtful that the court has a right to interfere, and because in all moral questions men must be finally determined by their own judgement and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. There is one case, and but one, in which, whatever sense be put upon the words of the oath, no witness is obliged to declare the whole truth. It is when such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> would tend to accuse himself of some legal crime; for as the laws of Scotland and England constrain no man to become his own accuser, they must be considered as imposing the oath of testimony with this tacit reservation. The exception, however, must be confined to legal crimes.
