A point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, Moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">Pride</a> of delicacy, or of reputation, may make a witness back-lost, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> to disclose some circumstance with which he is acquainted; but is no excuse for concealment, unless it could be shown, that the law which imposes the oath, intended to allow this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to such motives. The exception is also withdrawn by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> between the magistrate and the witness, when an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> is admitted to give evidence against the partners of his crime." But these are a fort of witnesses to whom a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> will always listen with a very cautious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Oaths are either affirmary or promissory. Affirmatory oaths are required both to confirm our veracity in evidence, and to give security to the public that we believe certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> conceived to be of public importance. An oath in evidence binds the juror to declare what he knows to be true, and nothing but what he knows to be true. An oath required to assure the public of our belief in the truth of any proposition, cannot, without the guilt of perjury, be taken by any man, who, at the time of swearing, has the slightest doubt whether the proposition be really true. Such an oath, however, though it unquestionably requires the sincerity of the juror's belief at the time when it is given, cannot oblige him to continue in that belief as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he may live; for belief is not in any man's power: it is the necessary consequence of evidence, which compels the assent of the mind according as it appears to preponderate on the one side or on the other. No man, therefore, can be justly accused of perjury for holding opinions contrary to those which he may formerly have sworn to believe; because his belief at the time of emitting his oath may have been the necessary result of the evidence which then appeared before him; and his change of opinion may have resulted with the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> from superior evidence which had been since thrown into the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, and made it preponderate. On this account, we cannot help thinking, that all affirmatory oaths, except such as are necessary to confirm testimony respecting facts, ought either to be abolished or expressed with great caution. Of truths intuitively certain or capable of rigid demonstration, no man of common sense can entertain a doubt; and therefore the public never requires from individuals the solemnity of an oath as an assurance of their believing such truths. But with respect to the truth of propositions which admit of nothing superior to moral evidence on either side, a man of the most steady virtue may think differently at different periods of his life; and in such cases, the effect of an oath, if it have any effect, can only be either, to shut the man's eyes against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, or to make his integrity be carelessly questioned by those who shall observe his change of belief. Promissory oaths cannot, without the guilt of perjury, be given by him, who, at the time of swearing, knows that it will not be in his power to fulfil the promise, or who does not seriously intend to fulfil it. A promissory oath cannot, without great guilt, be given by any man, who at the time of swearing believes the object of the promise to be in itself unlawful; for if he seriously <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to fulfil his oath, he calls upon Almighty God to witness his intention to commit a crime. Promissory oaths give to the public greater security than a simple promise; because the juror having the thoughts of God and of religion more upon his mind at the same time than at the other, offends with a higher hand, and in more open contempt of the divine power, knowledge, and justice, when he violates an oath, than when he breaks a promise. Yet it is certain that promissory oaths, though more solemn and sacred, cannot be binding, when the promise without an oath would not be so in an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; for the several cases of which, see Promise and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">Allegiance</a>. Coronation Oath. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>.

OATHLAW

Pages 118-118

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, about two miles from Forfar, chiefly remarkable for the remains of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a>-dykes (vulgarly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>-dykes), which is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

OBADIAH

Pages 118-118
or the Prophecy of Obadiah, a canonical book of the Old Testament, which is contained in one single chapter; and is partly an invective against the cruelty of the Edomites, who mocked and derided the children of Israel as they passed into captivity; and with other enemies, their confederates, invaded and oppressed those strangers, and divided the spoil amongst themselves; and partly a prediction of the deliverance of Israel, and of the victory and triumph of the whole church over her enemies. Obadiah, the prophet, is believed to have been the same with the governor of Ahab's house, mentioned in the first book of Kings, (xviii. 3, &c.) who hid and fed the hundred prophets whom Jezebel would have destroyed; and some say, that he was that Obadiah whom Josiah made overseer of the works of the temple, (2 Chron. xxxiv. 12). The truth is, that when he lived or prophesied is wholly uncertain: though most writers make him contemporary with Hosea, Amos, and Joel. Obadiah, a valiant man of David's army, who came to join him in the wilderness, with several others of the tribe of Gad, (1 Chron. xii. 9.). This was also the name of one of those whom King Jehoshaphat sent into the cities of Judah to instruct the people in their religion, (2 Chron. xvii. 7.). It was also the name of one of the principal men of Judah, who signed the covenant that Nehemiah renewed with the Lord, (Nehem. x. 5.).

OBED-EDOM

Pages 118-118

son of Jeduthun, a Levite, (1 Chr. xvi. 38.), and father of Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nathaniel, Ammiel, Issachar, and Peulthai. He had a numerous family, says the Scripture, (1 Chron. xxvi. 4.) because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> blessed him; and this is the occasion of the blessing. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> transferred the ark of the covenant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, Uzzah having rashly laid <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the ark, which he thought to be in danger of falling, was smitten of God, and died upon the spot. David, terrified at this accident, durst not remove the ark into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he had provided for it in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, but let it up in the house of Obededom, which was near the place where Uzzah had been struck dead. But the presence of the ark not only created no temporal misfortune to the family of this Levite, but, on the contrary, the Lord heaped upon him all sorts of blessings; which encouraged David some months after to remove it to the place he had appointed for it. Afterwards Obed-edom and his sons were assigned to be keepers of the doors of the temple, (1 Chron. xv. 18, 21.). In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Samuel, (vi. 10.) Obededom is called the Gittite, probably because he was of Gathrimmon, a city of the Levites beyond Jordan, (Joth. xxi. 24, 25.).

OBELISK

Pages 118-118

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a truncated, quadrangular, and slender <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, raised as an ornament, and frequently <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> either with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">Obelisks</a> appear to be of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and to have been first raised to transmit to posterity precepts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which were cut in hieroglyphical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>: afterwards they were used to immortalize the great actions of heroes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of persons beloved. The first obelisk mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was that of Rameses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which was 40 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Phius, another king of Egypt, raised one of 55 cubits; and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, another of 88 cubits, in memory of Arinoë. Augustus erected one at Rome in the Campus Martius, which served to mark the hours on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, drawn on the pavement. They were called by the Egyptian priests the fingers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, because they were made in Egypt also to serve as styles or gnomons to mark the hours on the ground. The Arabs still call them Pharao's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>; whence the Italians call them aquiglia, and the French aiguilles. The famous obelisks called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s arrows, now reduced to three, the fourth having been taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the last century, stand about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the town of Borough-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a> to the south-west, in three fields, separated by a lane, 200 feet apart, nearly on high ground sloping every way. Mr Drake urges many arguments for their Roman antiquity, and plainly proves them to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and brought from Plumpton quarries about five miles off, or from Ickly 16 miles off. The crofs in the town, 12 feet high, is of the same kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The easternmost or highest is 22 feet and a half high by 4 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 14½ in girth; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> 21½ by 5½; the third 16½ by 8½. Stukeley's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> differ. The flutings are cut in the stone but not through: the tallest stands alone, and leans to the south. Plot and Stukeley affirm them to be British monuments, originally hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">Gale</a> supposed that they were Mercuries, which have lost their heads and inscriptions; but in a MS. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in his Antoninus, he acknowledges that he was misinformed, and that there was no cavity to receive a bust. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENRITH">Penrith</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, are two square obelisks, of a single stone each, 11 or 12 feet high,

OBLIGATION

Pages 118-120

in general, denotes any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> where by a person becomes bound to another to do something; as to pay a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, be surety, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. Obligations are of three kinds, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, civil, and mixed. Natural obligations are entirely founded on natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>; civil obligations on civil authority alone, without any foundation in natural equity; and mixed obligations are those which, being founded on natural equity, are farther enforced by civil authority. In a legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, obligation signifies a bond, wherein is contained a penalty, with a condition annexed, for the payment of money, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between it and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is, that the latter is generally without a penalty or condition, though it may be made obligatory; and obligations are sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of record, as statutes and recognizances. See the article Bond. Moral Obligation. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, No. 58, &c. Oblique, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, something slanting, or that deviates from the perpendicular. Thus an oblique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> is either an acute or obtuse one, i.e., any angle except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> one. Oblique <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">Cases</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, are all the cases except the nominative. See Grammar. Oblique Ascension, is that point of the equinoctial which rises with the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, or any other point of the heavens, in an oblique sphere. Oblique Circle, in the stereographic projection, is any circle that is oblique to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of projection. Oblique Declination, that point of the equinoctial which falls with the centre of the sun, or star, or any other point of the heavens, in an oblique sphere. Oblique Line, that which, falling on another line, makes oblique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with it, viz. one acute, and the other obtuse. Oblique Planes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALLING">Dialling</a>, are those which decline from the zenith, or incline towards the horizon. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. Oblique Sailing, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, is when a ship sails upon some rhumb between the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, making an oblique angle with the meridian; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> she continually changes both latitude and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. See Navigation, Chap. VIII. Obliquus, in Anatomy, a name given to several muscles, particularly in the head, eyes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">Oblong</a>, in general, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that is longer than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; such is a parallelogram. Obolaria, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 40th order, Perforatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Obolus, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> silver money of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a drachma; worth somewhat more than a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-farththing farthing.—The word comes from the Greek ὀβολός, or ὀβάλης, "spit, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROACH">broach</a>;" either because it bore such an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>; or because, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a>, it was in form thereof. But those now in the cabinets of the antiquaries are round. Obolus, in Medicine, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of ten grains, or half a scruple. Oboth, an encampment of the Hebrews in the wilderness. From Punon they went to Oboth, and from Oboth to Ije-abarim, (Numb. xxi, 10. xxxiii. 43.). <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Ptolemy speaks of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> called Oboda, or Eboda, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, which is the same as Oboth. Pliny and the geographer Stephanus mention it also. Stephanus makes it belong to the Nabataeans, and Pliny to the Helmodceans, a people of Arabia. It was at Oboth that they worshipped the god Obodas, which Tertullian joins with Dufares, another god or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

OBREPTITIOUS

Pages 120-120

an appellation given to letters patent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other instruments, obtained of a superior by surprize, or by concealing from him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

OBSCRATION

Pages 120-120

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby the orator implores the affluence of God <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

OBSCURE

Pages 120-120

something that is dark and reflects little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in material objects, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is not clear and intelligible in the objects of the intellect.

OBSERVATION

Pages 120-120

among navigators, signifies the taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the stars meridian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>, in order thereby to find the latitude.

OBSERVATORY

Pages 120-121

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> defined for observing the heavenly bodies; being generally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> erected on some eminence, covered with a terrace for making astronomical observations. The more celebrated observatories are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> observatory, built in 1676, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., at the solicitation of Sir Jonas Moore and Sir Christopher Wren; and furnished with the most accurate instruments; particularly a noble sextant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet radius, with telecopic sights. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> observatory, built by the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the faubourg St Jacques. It is a very singular, and a very magnificent building, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Monfieur Perrault: it is 80 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and has a terrace at the top. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> between this and the Greenwich observatory is 2° 20'. In it is a cave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cellar, of 170 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, for experiments that are to be made far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, &c., particularly such as relate to congelations, refrigerations, indurations, conservations, &c. 3. Tycho Brahe's observatory, which was in the little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Ween, or Scarlet Island, between the coasts of Schonen and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> in the Baltic. It was erected and furnished with instruments at his own expense, and called by him Uraniburg. Here he spent twenty years in observing the stars; the result is his catalogue. 4. Pekin observatory. Father Le Compte describes a very magnificent observatory, erected and furnished by the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, at the intercession of some Jesuit missionaries, principally Father Verbeilt, whom he made his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> observer. The instruments are exceedingly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> less accurate, and the contrivance in some respects less commodious, than that of the Europeans. The chief are, An armillary zodiacal sphere of six feet diameter; an equinoctial sphere of six feet diameter; an azimuthal horizon of six feet diameter; a large <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> five feet radius; a sextant eight feet radius; and a celestial globe five feet diameter. Observatories, as they are very useful, and indeed absolutely necessary for astronomers, so they have become far more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> than they were. There is a very excellent one now at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, built by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of Dr Radcliffe, at the expense of nearly 30,000l. At <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> there is as yet no public observatory. Over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gate of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, indeed, there is one which is called Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's, because this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> had used it; but it is gone to decay. It were well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the university would repair and preserve it in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of that truly great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. In St John's, too, there is a small one. The late ingenious Mr Cotes had used to give lectures in Sir Isaac Newton's on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In Scotland there is an observatory at Glasgow belonging to the university: there is one erected on the Calton hill at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; but it is in very bad repair, (see Edinburgh); and there is an excellent one at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. 5. Bramins observatory at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>. Of this Sir Robert Barker gives the following account, (Phil. Trans. CCCLXX. vol. lxvii. p. 598.). "Benares in the East Indies, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seminaries of the Bramins or priests of the original Gentooos of Hindostan, continues still to be the place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of people; and there are many public charities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and pagodas, where some thousands of them now reside. Having frequently heard that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Bramins had a knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and being confirmed in this by their information of an approaching eclipse both of the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, I made inquiry, when at that place in the year 1772, among the principal Bramins, to endeavour to get some information relative to the manner in which they were acquainted of an approaching eclipse. The most intelligent that I could meet with, however, gave me but little satisfaction. I was told, that these matters were confined to a few, who were in possession of certain books and records; some containing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and others the tables of astronomical observations, written in the Sanscrit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which few understood but themselves: that they would take me to a place which had been constructed for the purpose of making such observations as I was inquiring after, and from whence they supposed the learned Bramins made theirs. I was then conducted to an ancient building of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which, in its present situation, was converted into a stable for horses, and a receptacle for lumber; but by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yards and apartments, it appeared that it must once have been an edifice for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of some public body of people. We entered this building, and went up a staircase to the top of a part of it, near to the river Ganges, that led to a large terrace, where, to my surprise and satisfaction, I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a number of instruments yet remaining, in the greatest preservation, stupendously large, immovable from the spot, and built of stone, some of them being upwards of 20 feet in height; and although they are said to have been erected 200 years ago, the graduations and divisions on the several arcs appeared as well cut, and as accurately divided, as if they had been the performance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The execution in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of these instruments exhibited a mathematical exactness in the fixing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, fitting of the several parts, in the necessary and sufficient supports to the very large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that composed them, and in the joining and fastening each into the other by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. "The situation of the two large quadrants of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> marked A in the plate, whose radius is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet two inches, by their being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the gnomon..." gnomons at twenty-five degrees elevation, are thrown into such an oblique situation as to render them the most difficult, not only to construct of such a magnitude, but to secure in their position for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and affords a striking instance of the ability of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> in their construction: for by the shadow of the gnomon thrown on the quadrants, they do not appear to have altered in the least from their original position; and so true is the line of the gnomon, that, by applying the eye to a small iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of an inch diameter at one end, the sight is carried through three others of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a>, to the extremity at the other end, distant 38 feet 8 inches, without obstruction; such is the firmness and art with which this instrument has been executed. This performance is the more wonderful and extraordinary, when compared with the works of the artificers of Hindoostan at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, who are not under the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of an European mechanic; but arts appear to have declined equally with science in the east. " <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Archibald Campbell, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> chief engineer in the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> that could be brought within his eye at one view; but I lament he could not represent some very large quadrants, whose radii were about 20 feet, they being on the side from whence he took his drawing. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, however, is, that they are exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of circles of different radii, the largest of which I judged to be 20 feet, constructed very exactly on the sides of stone walls, built perpendicular, and situated, I suppose, in the meridian of the place: a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> is fixed at the centre or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the quadrant, from whence, the Bramin informed me, they stretched a wire to the circumference when an observation was to be made; from which, it occurred to me, the observer must have moved his eye up or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the circumference, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> or some such contrivance, to raise and lower himself, until he had discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of any of the heavenly bodies in their passage over the meridian, so expressed on the arcs of these quadrants: these arcs were very exactly divided into nine large sections; each of which again into ten, making ninety lesser divisions or degrees; and those also into twenty, expressing three minutes each, of about two-tenths of an inch at sundown; so that it is probable they had some method of dividing even these into more minute divisions at the time of observation. "My time would only permit me to take down the particular dimensions of the most capital instrument, or the greater equinoctial sun <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, represented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> A, which appears to be an instrument to express solar time by the shadow of a gnomon upon two quadrants, one situated to the east, and the other to the west of it; and indeed the chief part of their instruments at this place appear to be constructed for the same purpose, except the quadrants, and a brass instrument that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be described hereafter. "Figure B is another instrument for the purpose of determining the exact <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day by the shadow of a gnomon, which stands perpendicular to, and in the centre of, a flat circular stone, supported in an oblique situation by means of four upright stones and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> piece; so that the shadow of the gnomon, which is a perpendicular iron rod, is thrown upon the division of the circle described on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the flat circular stone. "Figure C is a brass circle, about two feet diameter, moving vertically upon two pivots between two stone pillars, having an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round horizontally on the centre of this circle, which is divided into 360 parts; but there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> divisions on the index to subdivide those on the circle. This instrument appears to be made for taking the angle of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> at setting or rising, or for taking the azimuth or amplitude of the sun at rising or setting. "The use of the instrument, figure D, I was at a loss to account for. It consists of two circular walls; the outer of which is about forty feet diameter, and eight feet high; the wall within about half that height, and appears intended for a place to stand on to observe the divisions on the upper circle of the outer wall, rather than for any other purpose; and yet both circles are divided into 360 degrees, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> being subdivided into twenty lesser divisions, the same as the quadrants. There is a door-way to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the inner circle, and a pillar in the centre, of the same height with the lower circle, having a hole in it, being the centre of both circles, and seems to be a socket for an iron rod to be placed perpendicular into it. The divisions on these, as well as all the other instruments, will bear a nice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. "Figure E is a smaller equinoctial sun dial, constructed upon the same principle as the large one A. "I cannot quit this subject without observing, that the Bramins, without the assistance of optical glasses, had nevertheless an advantage unexperienced by the observers of the more northern climates. The serenity and clearness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> in the nighttime in the East Indies, except at the seasons of the monsoons or periodical winds changing, is difficult to express to those who have not seen it, because we have nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> to form our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> upon: it is clear to perfection, a total quietude subsists, scarcely a cloud to be seen, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the heavens, by the numerous appearance of the stars, affords a prospect both of wonder and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. "This observatory at Benares is said to have been built by the order of the emperor Akbar: for as this wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> endeavoured to improve the arts, so he wished also to recover the sciences of Hindoostan, and therefore directed that three such places should be erected; one at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, another at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, and the third at Benares." OBSIDIANUS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBSIDIAN">Obsidian</a>, a mineral substance. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

OBSIDIONALIS

Pages 121-121

an epithet applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. See the article Crown.

OBSTRUCTION

Pages 121-121

in Medicine, such an obturation of the vessels as prevents the circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, whether of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and vital, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the morbid and peccant kind, through them. OBTURATOR. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

OBTUSE

Pages 121-121

signifies blunt, dull, &c. in opposition to acute <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sharp. Thus we say, obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, obtuse-angled triangle, &c.

OBY

Pages 121-122
or OB, a large and famous river of Asiatic Russia, which flows from the Altin lake (called by the Russians Teleboi Ofero), in latitude 52 degrees, and longitude 103 degrees 30 minutes. Its name signifies Great; and accordingly in Russia it is often styled the Great River. The Calmucks and Tartars call it Umar. Its stream is very large and smooth, its current being usually slow; and it is in general between two and three hundred fathoms broad; though in some places it is much wider. It affords plenty of fish, and is navigable almost to the lake from which it springs. After a long winding course through a vast tract of land, in which it forms several islands, it empties itself in latitude 67 degrees, and longitude 86 degrees, into a bay, which, extending near 400 miles farther, joins the Icy sea, in latitude 73° 30' and longitude 92°. The springs from which this river rises, are not very copious; but it receives in its course the waters of a great number of considerable streams. Of these, the Tom and the Iris are the most considerable: the Tom falls into it in latitude 53° and the Iris in latitude 61°, and longitude 86°. The exact course of this river was unknown till the country was surveyed by the Russians; who have given us tolerable maps of it and of all Siberia. The Oby forms the boundary between Europe and Asia, and its course is upwards of 2000 miles in length.

OCCIDENT

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the westward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the horizon; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the horizon where the ecliptic, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> therein, descends into the lower hemisphere; in contradistinction to orient. Hence we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word occidental for any thing belonging to the west; as occidental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEZOAR">bezoar</a>, occidental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, &c. Occident Equinoctial, that point of the horizon where the sun sets at midwinter, when entering the sign <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>. Occident Equinoctial, that point of the horizon where the sun sets, when he crosses the equinoctial, or enters the sign Aries or Libra.

OCCIPITAL

Pages 122-122

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the parts of the occiput, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> back <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the skull.

OCCULT

Pages 122-122

something hidden, secret, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> invisible. The occult sciences are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECROMANCY">necromancy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">cabala</a>, &c. Occult qualities, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, were those qualities of body or spirit which baffled the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of philosophers, and for which they were unable to give any reason; unwilling, however, to acknowledge their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they deceived themselves and the vulgar by an empty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, calling what they did not know occult. Occult, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is used for a line that is scarce perceivable, drawn with the point of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> or a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are used in several operations, as the raising of plans, designs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, &c. They are to be effaced when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is finished.

OCCULTATION

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> planet is hid from our sight, by the interposition of the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> or some other planet.

OCCUPANCY

Pages 122-123

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the taking possession of those things which before belonged to nobody. This is the true ground and foundation of all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of holding those things in sevralty, which by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, unqualified by that of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all mankind. But, when once it was agreed that every thing capable of ownership should have an owner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> reason suggested, that he who could first declare his intention of appropriating anything to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such his intention, actually took it into possession, should thereby <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> property of it; according to that rule of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS">law of nations</a>, recognized by the laws of Rome, Quod nullius est, id ratione naturali occupanti conceditur. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of occupancy, so far as it concerns real property, hath been confined by the laws of England within a very narrow compass; and was extended only to a single instance; namely, where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was tenant pour autre vie, or had an estate granted to himself only (without mentioning his heirs) for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of another man, and died during the life of celui que vive, or him by whose life it was holden: in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he that could first enter on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, might lawfully retain the possession so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as celui que vive lived, by right of occupancy. This seems to have been recurring to first principles, and calling in the law of nature to ascertain the property of the land, when left without a legal owner. For it did not revert to the grantor, who had parted with all his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, so long as celui que vive lived; it did not descend to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee; for all estates must be of the absolute entire fee, and not of any particular estate carved out of it, much less of so minute a remnant as this: it did not belong to the grantee; for he was dead; it did not descend to his heirs; for there were no words of inheritance in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>: nor could it vest in his executors; for no executors could succeed to a freehold. Belonging therefore to nobody, like the hereditas jacea of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the law left it open to be seized and appropriated by the first person that could enter upon it, during the life of celui que vive, under the name of an occupant. But there was no right of occupancy allowed, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the lands; for the reversee hath an equal right with any other man to enter upon the vacant possession; and where the king's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and a subject's interfere, the king's shall always be preferred. Against the king therefore there could be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> occupant, because nullum tempus occurrit regi. And, even in the case of a subject, had the estate pour autre vie granted to a man and his heirs during the life of celui que vive, there the heir might, and still may, enter and hold possession, and is called in law a special occupant; as having a special exclusive right, by the terms of the original grant, to enter upon and occupy this hereditas jacea, during the residue of the estate granted; though some have thought him so called with no very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety; and that such estate is rather a defeasible freehold. But the title of common occupancy is now reduced almost to nothing by two statutes; the one, 29 Car. II. c. 3. which enacts, that where there is no special occupant, in whom the estate may vest, the tenant pour autre vie may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> it by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, or it shall go to the executors, and be affects in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for payment of debts: the other that of 14 Geo. II. c. 20. which enacts, that it shall vest not only in the executors, but, in case the tenant dies intestate, in the administrators also; and go in course of a distribution like a chattel interest. By these two statutes the title of common occupancy is utterly extinct and abolished: though that of special occupancy, by the heir at law, continues to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; such heir Occupancy heir being held to succeed to the ancestor's estate, not by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, for then he must take an estate of inheritance, but as an occupant, specially marked out and appointed by the original grant. The doctrine of common occupancy may, however, be usefully remembered on the following account, amongst others: That, as by the common law no occupancy could be of incorporeal hereditaments, as of rents, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, advowsons, commons, or the like, (because, with respect to them, there could be no actual entry made, or corporal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> had;) and therefore by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the grantee pour autre vie a grant of such hereditaments was entirely determined): to now, it is apprehended, notwithstanding those statutes, such grant would be determined likewise; and the hereditaments could not be devisable, nor vest in the executors, nor go in a course of distribution. For the statutes must not be construed so as to create any new estate, or to keep that alive which by the common law was determined, and thereby to defeat the grantor's reversion; but merely to dispose of an interest in being, to which by law there was no owner, and which therefore was left open to the first occupant. When there is a residue left, the statutes give it to the executors, &c. instead of the first occupant; but they will not create a residue on purpose to give it to the executors. They only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to provide an appointed instead of a casual, a certain instead of an uncertain, owner, of lands which before were nobody's; and thereby to supply this defectum universus, and render the disposition of the law in all respects entirely uniform; this being the only instance wherein a title to a real estate could ever be acquired by occupancy. For there can be no other case devised, wherein there is not some owner of the land appointed by the law. In the case of a sole corporation, as a parson of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, when he dies or resigns, though there be no actual owner of the land till a successor be appointed, yet there is a legal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a>, ownership, subsisting in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of law; and when the successor is appointed, his appointment shall have a retrospect and relation backwards, so as to entitle him to all the profits from the instant that the vacancy commenced. And, in all other instances, when the tenant dies intestate, and no other owner of the lands is to be found in the common course of descents, there the law vests an ownership in the king, or in the subordinate lord of the fee, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a>. So also, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, where the laws of other nations give a right by occupancy, as in lands newly created, by the rising of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in a river, or by the alluvion or dereliction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; in these instances, the law of England affirms them an immediate owner. For Bracken tells us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> an island arise in the middle of a river, it belongs in common to those who have lands on each side thereof; but if it be nearer to one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> than the other, it belongs only to him who is proprietor of the nearest shore: which is agreeable to, and probably copied from, the civil law. Yet this seems only to be reasonable, where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the river is equally divided between the owners of the opposite shores: for if the whole soil is the freehold of any one man, as it must be whenever a several fishery is claimed, there it seems <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> (and so is the usual practice) that the islets, or little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, arising in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, shall be the property of him who oweth the pircary and the soil. However, in case a new island rise in the sea, though the civil law gives it to the first occupant, yet our's gives it occupancy to the king. And as to lands gained from the sea; either by alluvion, by the washing up of sand and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, so as in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to make terra firma; or by dereliction, as when the sea shrinks back below the usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark; in these cases the law is held to be, that if this gain be by little and little, by small and imperceptible degrees, it shall go to the owner of the land adjoining. For de minimis non curat lex: and besides, these owners being often losers by the breaking in of the sea, or at charges to keep it out, this possible gain is therefore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> consideration for such possible <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> or loss. But if the alluvion or dereliction be sudden and considerable, in this case it belongs to the king: for, as the king is lord of the sea, and so owner of the soil while it is covered with water, it is but reasonable he should have the soil when the water has left it dry. So that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ground gained, and the time during which it is gained, are what make it either the king's or the subject's property. In the same manner, if a river, running between two lordships, by degrees gains upon the one, and thereby leaves the other dry; the owner who loses his ground thus imperceptibly has no remedy: but if the course of the river be changed by a sudden and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, or other hasty means, and thereby a man loses his grounds, he shall have what the river has left in any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as recompense for this sudden loss. And this law of alluvions and derelictions, with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, is nearly the same in the imperial law; from whence indeed those our determinations seem to have been drawn and adopted: but we ourselves, as islanders, have applied them to marine increases; and have given our sovereign the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> he enjoys, as well upon the particular reasons before mentioned, as upon this other general ground of prerogative, which was formerly remarked, that whatever hath no other owner is vested by law in the king. See PREROGATIVE.

OCCUPANT

Pages 123-123

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the person that first seizes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gets possession of a thing.

OCCUPATION

Pages 123-123

in a legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is taken for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>: as in deeds it is frequently said, that such lands are, or were lately, in the tenure or occupation of such a person.—It is likewise used for a trade or mystery. OCCUPIERS of WALLING, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works for the persons who are the sworn officers that allot in particular places what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of salt is to be made, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> may not be overstocked, and see that all is carried fairly and equally between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> and the tenant.

OCEAN

Pages 123-124

that huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> waters which encompasses all parts of the globe, and by means of which, in the present improved state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, an easy intercourse subsists between places the most distant. The ocean is distinguished into three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, which divides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which is generally about 3000 miles wide. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which divides America from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and is generally about 10,000 miles over. And, 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, which separates the East Indies from Africa: which is 3000 miles over. The other seas, which are called oceans, are only parts or branches of these, and usually receive their names from the countries they border upon. For the saltness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, &c. of the ocean, see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Sea, Tides, &c.

OCEANIDES

Pages 124-124

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> nymphs, daughters of Oceanus, from whom they received their name, and of the goddesses Tethys <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Theis. They were 300 according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, who mentions the names of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of them; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Styx, Elektra, Donis, Eurynome, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, and Metis. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> speaks of the eldest of them, which he reckons 41; Pithe, Admete, Pryno, Ianthe, Rhodia, Hippo, Calliope, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, Clymene, Idyia, Pafithoe, Clythia, Zeaoo, Galaxaare, Pleuxaere, Perseis, Pluto, Thoe, Polydora, Melobois, Dione, Cerceis, Xanthe, Acafa, Ianira, Teletho, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>, Menetho, Petraea, Eudora, Calypso, Tyche, Ocyroe, Crispa, Amphiro, with those mentioned by Apollodorus, except Amphitrite. Hyginus mentions 16, whose names are almost all different from those of Apollodorus and Hesiod; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> proceeds from the mutilation of the original text. The Oceanides, like the rest of the inferior deities, were honoured with libations and sacrifices. Prayers were offered to them, and they were entreated to protect sailors from storms and dangerous tempests. The Argonauts, before they proceeded to their expedition, made an offering of flour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, on the sea shore, to all the deities of the sea, and sacrificed bulls to them, and entreated their protection. When the sacrifice was made on the sea shore, the blood of the victim was received in a vessel; but when it was in open sea, they permitted the blood to run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the waters. When the sea was calm, they generally offered a lamb or a young pig; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was agitated by the winds and rough, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bull was deemed the most acceptable victim.

OCEANUS

Pages 124-124

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the son of Coelus and Terra, the husband of Thetis, and the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and fountains, called Oceanides. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called him the Father of all things, imagining that he was produced by Humidity, which, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, was the first principle from which every thing was produced. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> represents Juno visiting him at the remotest limits of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and acknowledging him and Thetis as the parents of the gods. He was represented with a bull's head, as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the rage and bellowing of the ocean when agitated by a storm. According to Homer, he was the father even of all the gods, and on that account he received frequent visits from them. He is often, indeed almost always, represented as an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> flowing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and fitting upon the waves of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. He often holds a pike in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, while ships under sail appear at a distance, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a sea monster stands near him. Oceanus presided over every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sea, and even the rivers were subjected to his power. The ancients were superstitious in their worship of him, and revered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity a deity to whose care they intrusted themselves when going on any voyage.

OCEIA

Pages 124-124

a woman who presided over the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Veja for 57 years with the greatest sanctity. She died in the reign of Tiberius, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Domitian succeeded her. OCELLUS the Lucanian, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of the school of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who lived before <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> περὶ τῶν Παντῶν, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "The Universe," is the only piece of his which is come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> entire to us; and was written originally in the Doric dialect, but was translated by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> into the Attic. William Christian, and after him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Nogarola, translated this work into Latin; and we have several editions of it, both in Greek and Latin.

OCHLOCRACY

Pages 124-124

that form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> wherein the populace have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> administration of affairs.

OCHNA

Pages 124-124

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OCHRE

Pages 124-124

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a mineral substance composed of oxide and carbonate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and clay. See Ores of Iron, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OCHROMA

Pages 124-124

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Colummiferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OCHUS

Pages 124-124

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a>. He was cruel and avaricious; and in order to strengthen himself on his throne, he murdered all his brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. His subjects revolted; but he reduced them to obedience, and added <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to his other dominions. Bagoas, his favourite eunuch, poisoned him for the insults he had offered to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> the god of the Egyptians; and he gave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> to be eaten by cats, and made handles for knives with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. It seems to be not a little remarkable, that all those monsters who disgraced <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> by their crimes, and sunk themselves below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, have met with condign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; and this in general seems true, whether we refer to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times.—A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of Cyzicus, who was killed by the Argonauts.—A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Persia, who refused to visit his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for fear of giving all the women each a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>.—A river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> or of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACTRIA">Bactria</a>.—A king of Persia: He exchanged this name for that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Nothus. See Persia.

OCRISIA

Pages 124-124

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the wife of Corniculus, was one of the attendants of Tanaquil the wife of Tarquinius Priscus. As she was throwing into the flames, for offerings, some of the meats that were served on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of Tarquin, she suddenly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, as is reported, in the fire, what Ovid calls obfacent forma virilis. She informed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of it; and when by her command she had approached near it, she conceived a son who was named Servius Tullius, and was educated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s family. He afterwards succeeded to the vacant throne. Some suppose that Vulcan had assumed that form which was presented to the eyes of Ocrida, and that this god was the father of the fifth king of Rome.

OCTAETERIS

Pages 124-124

a cycle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of eight years, in the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, at the conclusion of which three entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months were added. This cycle was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> till Meton's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or cycle of 19 years.

OCTAGON

Pages 124-126
or Octogon, in Geometry, is a figure of eight sides and angles; and this, when all the sides and angles are equal, is called a regular octagon, or one that may be inscribed in a circle. Octagon, in Fortification, denotes a place that has eight battlements. See Fortification. Octahedron, or Octaedron, in Geometry, one of the five regular bodies, consisting of eight equal and equilateral triangles. Octandra (ὀκτά "eight," and ἄνθος "a man or husband?") the 8th class in Linnaeus's sexual system; consisting of plants which are furnished with eight stamens. See Botany Index. Octant, the eighth part of a circle. Octant, or Octile, in Astronomy, that aspect of two planets wherein they are distant an eighth part of a circle, or 45° from each other. Octapla, in matters of sacred literature, denotes a Polyglot Bible, consisting of eight columns, and as many different versions of the sacred text; viz. the original Hebrew both in Hebrew and Greek characters, Greek versions, &c. Octateuch, an appellation given to the eight first books of the Old Testament. Octave, in Music. See Interval. Octavia, daughter of Caius Octavius and sister to Augustus Caesar. See the following article. She was one of the most illustrious ladies of ancient Rome; her virtues and her beauty were equally conspicuous.—Prideaux says she was much handsomer than Cleopatra. She married Claudius Marcellus, and after his death M. Antony. Her marriage with Antony was a political match, to reconcile her brother and him together. Antony proved for some time attentive to her; but when he had been Cleopatra, he neglected and despised her; and when he attempted to withdraw him from this illegal amours by going to meet him at Athens, she was rebuked and totally banished from his presence. This affront was highly resented by her brother; and though Octavia endeavoured to pacify him by palliating Antony's behaviour, yet he resolved to revenge her cause by arms. After the battle of Actium and the death of Antony, Octavia, forgetful of her own injuries, took into her house all the children of her husband, and treated them with extraordinary tenderness. Marcellus, her son by her first husband, was married to a niece of Augustus, and openly intended as a successor to his uncle. His sudden death plunged all the family into the greatest grief. Virgil, whom Augustus patronized, undertook of himself to pay a melancholy tribute to the memory of a young man whom Rome had looked upon as her future father and patron. He was desired to repeat his composition in the presence of the emperor and his sister. Octavia burst into tears even when the poet began; but when he mentioned Tu Marcellus eris, she swooned away. This tender and pathetic encomium upon the merit and the virtues of young Marcellus she liberally rewarded; and Virgil received 10,000 sesterces, according to some 78L. 2s. 6d. for every one of the verses. Octavia had two daughters by Antony, Antonia Major and Antonia Minor.—The elder married L. Domitius Ahenobarbus, by whom she had Cn. Domitius, who was the father of the emperor Nero by Agrippina the daughter of Germanicus. Antonia Minor, who was as virtuous and as beautiful as her mother, married Drusus the son of Tiberius, by whom she had Germanicus, and Claudius who reigned before Nero. The death of Marcellus constantly preyed upon the mind of Octavia, who died of grief or melancholy, about 11 years before the Christian era. Her brother paid great regard to her memory, and pronounced her funeral oration himself. The Roman people also showed their regard to her virtues, by willing to pay her divine honours.—A daughter of the emperor Claudius by Messalina. She was betrothed to Silanus, but by the intrigues of Agrippina, she was married to the emperor Nero in the 16th year of her age. She was soon after divorced under pretence of barrenness; and the emperor married Poppea, who exercised her enmity upon Octavia by procuring her to be banished into Campania. She was afterwards recalled by the people; but Poppea, who was determined on her ruin, caused her again to be banished to an island, where she was ordered to kill herself by opening her veins. Her head was cut off and carried to Poppea. Octavianus, or Octavius Caesar, was nephew of Julius Caesar the dictator, being the son of Accia his sister by Octavius a senator, and afterwards became the second emperor of Rome. He was born in the year of the city 691, during the consulship of Cicero. His uncle Julius Caesar adopted him, and left him the greatest part of his fortune. When he was but 20 years of age, he was raised to the consulship. His youth and inexperience were ridiculed by his enemies; notwithstanding which obstacle, his prudence and valour raised his consequence. He made war against his opponents on pretence of avenging the assassination of his uncle. He engaged in five civil wars with great success, viz. The wars of Mutina, Perusia, Philippi, Sicily, and Actium; the first and last of which were against M. Antony; the second against L. Antony, brother of the triumvir; the third was against Brutus and Cassius; and the fourth against Sext. Pompey, son of Pompey the Great. He united his forces with Antony's at the battle of Philippi; and had he not been supported by the activity and bravery of his colleague, he would doubtless have been totally ruined in that engagement. In this triumvirate with Antony and Lepidus, he obtained the western parts of the Roman empire; and, like his other colleagues, more firmly to establish his power, he proscribed his enemies and cut them off. The triumvirate lasted for 10 years. He had given his sister Octavia in marriage to Antony, to make their alliance more lasting; but when Cleopatra had charmed this unfortunate man, Octavia was repudiated. Augustus immediately took up arms to avenge the wrongs of his sister; but perhaps more eager to remove a man whose power and existence kept him in continual fear and constant dependence. Both parties met at Actium to decide the fate of Rome. Antony was supported by all the power of the east, and Augustus by Italy. Cleopatra fled from the battle with 60 ships; and her flight ruined the interest of Antony, who followed her into Egypt. The conqueror soon after went into Egypt likewise, besieged Alexandria, and honoured with a magnificent funeral his unfortunate colleague and the celebrated queen, whom the fear of being led in the victor's triumph at Rome had driven to commit suicide. After he had established peace all over the world, he shut the gates of the temple of Janus, A.U.C. 753. He was twice determined to lay down the supreme power and Octavianus immediately after the victory obtained over Antony, and on account of his ill health; but his two faithful friends Mecenas and Agrippa dissuaded him, and contended, that if he did he would leave it to be the prey of the most powerful, and expose himself to the greatest dangers. He died at Nola in the 76th year of his age, after he had held the sovereign power for 57 years.—He was an active emperor, and consulted the good of the Romans with the greatest anxiety and care. He visited all the provinces except Africa and Sardinia, and his consummate prudence and experience occasioned many salutary laws. He is, however, accused of licentiousness and adultery; but the goodness of his heart, the fidelity of his friendship, and the many good qualities which the poets whom he patronized have perhaps truly celebrated, made some, though in the eye of strict religion and true morality but little, amends for his natural foibles. He was ambitious of being esteemed handsome; and as he was publicly reported to be the son of Apollo according to his mother's declaration, he wished his flatterers to represent him with the figure and attributes of that god. Like Apollo, his eyes were clear, and he affected to have it thought that they possessed some divine irradiation, and was well pleased if, when he fixed his eyes upon any body, they held down their eyes as if overcome by the glaring brightness of the sun. He distinguished himself by his learning; he was a complete master of the Greek language, and wrote some tragedies, besides memoirs of his life and other works, which are now lost. He married four times; but he was unhappy in all these connexions; and his only daughter Julia disgraced herself and her father by the debauchery and licentiousness of her manners. He recommended at his death his adopted son Tiberius as his successor. He left his fortune partly to him and to Drusus, and made donations to the army and Roman people. The title of Augustus was conferred upon him by the senate after the battle of Actium and the final destruction of the Roman republic. The title continued afterwards, being given to his successors in the empire. Virgil is said to have written his Æneid at the desire of Augustus, whom he represents under the amiable and perfect character of Æneas. The name of Octavius was very common at Rome; it was the name of a variety of men of very considerable rank. October, in Chronology, the eighth month of Romulus's year, which the name implies; but tenth in the calendar of Numa, Julius Caesar, &c. The senate gave this month the name Faufinum, in compliment to Faufina, the wife of the emperor Antoninus; Commodus would have it called Invictus; and Domitian named it Domitianus; but in spite of all these attempts it still retains its original name. This month was sacred to Mars, and under his protection. October Equus, a horse annually sacrificed to Mars in the month of October, either because the horse is a warlike animal, or to punish him for the taking of Troy. A race was run with chariots, drawn by two horses, previous to the sacrifices, and he that ran quickest was adjudged to be the victim. Octostyle, in the ancient architecture, is the face of an edifice adorned with eight columns. Oculus, the eye, in Anatomy. See there, No. 145.

OCYMOPHYLLON

Pages 126-126
