a name given by Buxbaum to a new genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The flower is of the laminateous kind, having no petals; it stands upon the embryo fruit, which afterwards becomes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> quadrangular seed-vessel, divided into four cells, and containing roundish and very small seeds; its leaves are like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ocy- mum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">basil</a>, whence its name; and its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of growth is in damp marshes. Boccone has described it under the improper name of glaux, calling it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, green-flowered, marsh glaux.

OCYUM

Pages 126-126
basil; a genus of plants belonging to the didynamia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See Botany Index. Oczakow, or Oczakoff, a town of Turkey in Europe, and capital of a sanguine of the same name, inhabited by Tartars. During a late war, here was a Turkish garrison of 20,000 men. However, it was taken by the Ruffians in 1737, and all those that resisted were put to the sword. The Ruffians themselves lost 18,000 men in the assault. The Turks returned the same year with 70,000 men to retake it; but were obliged to retire, after the loss of 20,000. In 1738, the Ruffians withdrew their garrison, and demolished the fortifications. It is seated on the river Bog, to the west of the Nieper, or rather where they both unite and fall into the "xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black sea. It is 42 miles south-west of Bialagrod, and 190 north by east of Constantinople. It has been lately a subject of great contest between the Ruffians and Turks. The affair is fresh in our readers memories; but the following more particular account of the place, will not, we trust, be unacceptable to our readers.—It is called by the Turks Dzaim Crimenda, is seated at the influx of the Nieper into the Black sea, 120 miles from Bender, to the south-east. The river is here above a mile broad. Hither the Turkish galleys retire which guard the mouth of the river, to prevent the Cossacks from pirating upon the Black sea. Here is no port, but good anchorage. It is defended by a castle, surrounded with walls 25 feet high; those of the town are much lower. There are about 2,000 people at Oczakow. Below the castle are two towns or suburbs, situated on the declivity of a hill, which on the other side has nothing but precipices. To the south of these towns is another small castle, where is some artillery to prevent vessels from coming up the river. Here is also a tower, in which are always some Turks upon the watch to discover from afar any of the Cossacks at sea, and give notice of them to the galleys by a signal. The city is inhabited by Tartars, though garrisoned by Turks. E. Long. 30° 50' N. Lat. 46° 50'.

ODA

Pages 126-127

in the Turkish teraglio, signifies a class, order, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chamber. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> are divided into five classes or chambers. The first, which is the lowest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> oda, from the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons that compose it; these are the juniors, who are taught to read, write, and speak the languages. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is called the little oda, where from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14 or 15 years, till about 25, they are trained up to arms, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of all the polite learning the Turks are acquainted with. The third chamber, called kiler oda, consists of 200 pages, who, besides their other exercises, are under the command of the kilardgi-bachi, and serve in the pantry and fruiterly. ODE Oda Bachi fruitery. The fourth consists only of 24, who are under the command of the khazineda-bachi, and have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> in the grand signior's apartment, which they never enter with clothes that have pockets. The fifth is called kas oda or privy-chamber; and is composed of only 40 pages, who attend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s chamber. Every night eight of these pages keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> in the grand signior's bedchamber while he sleeps: they take care that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which is constantly kept in the room, does not glare in his eyes, lest it should awake him: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they find him disturbed with troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, they cause him to be awakened by one of their agas.

ODA BACHI

Pages 127-127
or Oddabashi, an officer in the Turkish foldery, equivalent to a serjeant or corporal among us. The common folderies and janizaries, called oddachts, after having served a certain number of years, are always preferred and made biquelairs; and of biquelairs in time become odobachs, i.e. corporals of companies, or chiefs of certain divisions, whose number is not fixed; being sometimes ten, and sometimes twenty. Their pay is six doubles per month; and they are distinguished by a large felt, a foot broad and above a foot long, hanging on the back, with two long ostrich feathers. ODDLY-ODD. A number is said to be oddly-odd, when an odd number measures it, by an odd number. So 15 is a number oddly-odd, because the odd number 3 measures it by the odd number 5.

ODED

Pages 127-127

a prophet of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, who being at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, when the Israelites of the ten tribes returned from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Pekah, together with 200,000 of the people of Judah captives, he went out to meet them, and said, "You have seen that the Lord God of your fathers was in wrath against Judah; he has therefore delivered them into your <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and you have slain them inhumanly, so that your cruelty has ascended up into heaven; and more than this, you would make slaves of the children of Judah, who are your brethren, and would add this sin to the many others you have committed: therefore, hear the counsel that I give you; send back these captives, lest the Lord should pour out his fury upon you." Oded having done speaking, some of the chiefs of Samaria seconded him, and by their remonstrances prevailed with the Israelites to set the captives at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> (2 Chron. xxviii.). See AHAZ. The enlargement of the captives being obtained, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men of Samaria took care of them, gave them clothes and food and other necessary assistance. After which they furnished them with horses, because the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them were so tired and exhausted that they were not able to walk. Thus they conducted them to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>, which was in the confines of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Judah. This is all that is come to our knowledge concerning the prophet Oded.

ODEMA

Pages 130-130
or PHLEGMATIC TUMOUR, in Medicine and Surgery, a sort of tumour attended with pustules and cold, yielding little resistance, retaining the print of the finger when pressed with it, and accompanied with little or no pain. This tumour obtains no certain situation in any particular part of the body, since the head, eyelids, hands, and sometimes part, sometimes the whole body, is afflicted with it. When the last mentioned is the case, the patient is said to be troubled with a cachexy, leucophlegmatia, or dropy. But if any particular part is more subject to this disorder than another, it is certainly the feet, which are at that time called swelled or oedematous feet.

ODENATUS

Pages 127-127

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>, who very early incurred himself to bear fatigues, and by hunting leopards and wild beasts, accustomed himself to the labours of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was a faithful friend to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and when Aurelian had been taken prisoner by Sapor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, Odenatus warmly interceded himself in his cause, and solicited his release, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the conqueror, and by sending him presents. The king of Persia was offended at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of Odenatus, he tore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and ordered the presents that were offered to be thrown into a river, and in order to punish Odenatus, who had the impudence, as he called it, to pay homage to so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a monarch as himself, he commanded him to appear before him, on pain of being devoted to instant destruction with all his family, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he dared to refuse. Odenatus despised this haughty summons of Sapor, and opposed force by force. He obtained some considerable advantages over the troops of the Persian king, and took his wife prisoner, with a great and rich booty. These services were observed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> by the Romans; and Gallienus, the then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, named Odenatus as his colleague on the throne, and gave the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Auguslus to his children, and to his wife the celebrated Zenobia. Odenatus invested with new power, resolved to signalize himself more conspicuously by conquering the barbarians of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; but his exulting was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>: he perished by the dagger of one of his own relations, whom he had slightly offended at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> entertainment. He died at Emessa about the 267th year of the Christian era. Zenobia succeeded to his titles and honours.

ODENSEE

Pages 127-127

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNEN">Funen</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity, that some Danish writers derive its foundation and name from Odin the god and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of the Gothic nations. "Its name certainly occurs (says Mr Coxe) in the earliest ages of the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and it was a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a> existed. Odensee stands upon a small river, not navigable, and about two miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Stegeflrand. Many of the houses are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> dates about the middle of the 16th century; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is newly built: it contains about 5200 inhabitants, who carry on some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, exporting chiefly grain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; the latter is much esteemed, and its goodness supposed to arise from a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RIVER_WATER">river <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, in which it is soaked for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>. The Danish cavalry are supplied from thence with the greatest part of their leathern accoutrements. "Odensee is the seat of a bishop, which was founded by Harold Blaatand in 980, and is the richest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> next to Copenhagen. It has a school, endowed by the celebrated Margaret of Valdemar, in which a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scholars, from six to 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, are instructed gratis: they live and board in the town, and each receives a yearly pension; other scholarships have been also founded by private persons. The whole number amounted to 70. There is also a gymnasiwm, instituted by Christian IV. for the admission of students at the age of 16. The seminary was still further improved by the liberality of Holberg the Danish historian, who protected letters with the same zeal with which he cultivated them. It is now greatly fallen from its former flourishing state, containing, when I passed through the town, only eight students. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old brick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which has nothing remarkable except some costly monuments of a private Danish family. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which formerly belonged to the convent of Recolets, contains the sepulchre of John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark, and of his son Christian II." E. Long. 10. 27. N. Lat. 55. 28.

ODER

Pages 127-128

a river of Germany, which has its source near near a town of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>. It runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> through that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and then into the marches of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> and Pomerania, where it forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, afterwards falling into the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by three mouths; between which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> Ufedom and Wolin. It passes by several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; as Ratibor, Oppelen, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, Glogau and Großen, in Silesia; Frankfort, Lebus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULM">Culm</a>, in Brandenburg; and Gartz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STETTIN">Stettin</a>, Cammin, Wallin, Ufedom, and Wolgast, in Pomerania.

ODEUM

Pages 128-128

in Grecian antiquity, a musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>; the inside of which was filled with seats and ranges of pillars, and on the outside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> descended sloping downwards from a point in the centre, with many bendings, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>. Here the musical prizes were contended for; and here also, according to Aritophanes was a tribunal.

ODIN

Pages 128-128

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, called also in the dialect of the Anglo-Saxons, Woden <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Wodan, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scythians to their supreme god, and assumed, about 70 years before the Christian era, by Sigge, a Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who conquered the northern nations, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> changes in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, manners, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and enjoyed great honours, and had even divine honours paid him. According to the account given of this conqueror by Snorro, the ancient historian of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and his commentator Torlaus, Odin was a Scythian, who withdrew himself, with many others in his train, by flight, from the vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, under the conduct of Pompey; and having officiated as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, as well as the civil government, of the nations which he conquered. Having subdued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and Norway, he retired to Sweden, where he died. There is nothing certain in this account; but it is probable, that the god, whose prophet or priest this Scythian pretended to be, was named Odin, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of succeeding ages confounded the deity with his priest, composing out of the attributes of the one, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the other, the character of the northern conqueror. He deluded the people by his enchantments and skill in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>: having cut off the head of one Mimer, who in his lifetime was in great reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, he caused it to be embalmed, and persuaded the Scandinavians that he had restored it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of speech; and he caused it to pronounce whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> he wanted. The Icelandic chronicles represent Odin as the most eloquent and persuasive of men; they ascribe to him the introduction of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> among the Scandinavians, and likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. He had also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to persuade his followers, that he could run over the world in the twinkling of an eye; that he had the direction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and tempests; that he could transform himself into all sorts of shapes, could raise the dead, could foretell things to come, deprive his enemies, by enchantment, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour, and discover all the treasures concealed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They add, that by his tender and melodious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, he could make the plains and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> open and expand with delight; and that the ghosts, thus attracted, would leave their infernal caverns, and stand motionless about him. Nor was he less dreadful and furious in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; changing himself into the shape of a bear, a wild bull, or a lion, and amidst ranks of enemies committing the most horrible devastation, without receiving any wound himself. Dr Henry gives this account of him: "Odin is believed to have been the name of the one true God among the first colonists who came from the east and peopled Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, and among their posterity for several ages. But at length a mighty conqueror, the leader of a new <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of adventurers from the east, overrun the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, erected a great empire, assumed the name of Odin, and claimed the honours which had been formerly paid to that deity. From thenceforward this deified mortal, under the name of Odin or Wodin, became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of the idolatrous worship of the Saxons and Danes in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, as well as of many other nations. Having been a mighty and successful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, he was believed to be the god of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, who gave victory, and revived courage in the conflict. Having civilized, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the countries which he conquered, and introduced arts formerly unknown, he was also worshipped as the god of arts and artists. In a word, to this Odin his deluded worshippers impiously ascribed all the attributes which belong only to the true God: to him they built magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, offered many sacrifices, and consecrated the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, which is still called by his name in England and in all the other countries where he was formerly worshipped. Notwithstanding all this, the founders of all the kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon heptarchy pretended to be descended from Wodin, and some of them at the distance only of a few generations." ODIN'S FIRE. We have this account of it in Gough's Camden. "In Evie <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, in the Orkneys, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, are some rocks, which frequently in the night appear on fire; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Michael there was often seen full of lights, called fires sent by Odin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their tombs, but now ceased. This may be a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, or some inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> on the cliffs, as at Charmouth, Dorset."

ODINUS

Pages 128-129

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of antiquity, who flourished about 70 years before the Christian era, in the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. He was at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, a soldier, a poet, a monarch, and a victor. He imposed upon the credulity of his superstitious countrymen, and made them believe that he could raise the dead, and that he was acquainted with futurity. When he had extended his power, and increased his fame by conquest and by artifice, he determined to die in a different way from other men. He assembled his friends, and with the sharp point of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> he made in his body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> different wounds in the form of a circle; and when expiring he declared that he was going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, where he should become an immortal god. He added, that he would prepare bliss and felicity for those of his countrymen who lived a virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, who fought with bravery, and who died like heroes in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. These injunctions had the wished-for effect: his countrymen superstitiously believed him, and constantly recommended themselves to his protection when they engaged in battle; and they entreated him to receive the souls of such as fell in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. De Odio et Atia. See False IMPRISONMENT. The writ de odio et atia was anciently used to be directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, commanding him to inquire whether a prisoner <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> was committed upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause of suspicion, or merely propter odium et atiam, for hatred and ill <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> due cause of suspicion did not then appear, then there issued another writ for the sheriff to admit him to bail. This writ, according to Bracton, ought not to be denied to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; it being expressly ordered to be made out gratis, without any denial, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>, c. 26. and statute Westm. 2. 13 Edw. I. c. 29. But the statute of Glocester, 6 Edw. I. c. 9, restrained it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of killing by misadventure or self <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and the statute 28 Edw. III. c. 9. abolished it in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> whatsoever: but as the flat. 42 Ed. III. c. 1. repealed all statutes then in being, contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the writ de odio et atia was thereby revived. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">HABEAS Corpus</a>.

ODO

Pages 129-129

Sr, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLUNY">Cluny</a> in France, was illustrious for learning and piety in the 10th century. The sanctity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> contributed greatly to enlarge the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of Cluny; and he was so esteemed, that popes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> princes, usually chose him the arbiter of their disputes. He died about the year 942, and his works are printed in the Bibliothèque of Cluny. ODO Cantianus, so called as being a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, was a Benedictine monk in the 12th century, in which order his learning and eloquence raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> and abbot. Archbishop Becket was his friend; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> was made by John of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. He composed Commentaries on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and the Second Book of Kings; Moral Reflections on the Psalms; treatises entitled, De Onore Philippii; De Moribus Ecclesiasticis; De Vitiss et Virtutibus Anima, &c.

ODOACER

Pages 129-129

according to Ennodius, was meanly born, and only a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the guards of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustulus, when (A.D. 476, under the consulship of Balbinus and Asinianus) the barbarians chose him for their leader. The barbarians thought, as they often defended <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> at least to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it; but upon demanding it they were refused, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was a revolt. Odoacer is said to have been a man of uncommon parts, capable alike of commanding an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governing a state. Having left his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> when he was very young, to serve in Italy, as he was of a stature remarkably tall, he was admitted among the emperor's guards, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that station till the above year; when, putting himself at the head of the barbarians in the Roman pay, who, though of different nations, had unanimously chosen him for their leader, he marched against Orestes, and his son Augustulus, who still refused to share any of the lands in Italy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were inferior both in numbers and valour, and were easily conquered: Orestes was ordered to be slain; but the emperor Augustulus was spared, and, though stripped of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, was treated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and allowed a liberal sum for his own support and for that of his relations. Odoacer was proclaimed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy; but assumed neither the purple nor any other mark of imperial consequence. He was afterwards defeated and slain by Theodoric the Ostrogoth. See Odoacer.

ODOMETER

Pages 129-129

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for measuring the distance passed over in travelling. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEDOMETER">PEDOMETER</a>.

ODONTOID

Pages 129-129

in Anatomy, an appellation given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> vertebra of the neck, from its resemblance to a tooth.

ODOROUS

Pages 129-129
or ODORIFEROUS, appellations given to whatever smells strongly, whether they be fetid or agreeable; but chiefly to things whose smell is brisk and pleasant.

ODYSSEY

Pages 129-130

the name of an epic poem composed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, which, when compared with the Iliad, exhibits its author as the setting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> remains without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of his meridian beams. The poet's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in the Odyssey was to paint the miseries of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in the absence of its supreme governor, and the evil consequences resulting from a disregard of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and of that subordination without which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> cannot exist. With this view he lets before his countrymen the adventures of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who had been obliged to forsake his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and to head an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of his subjects in a foreign expedition; and he artfully contrives, without interrupting the narrative, to make the reader acquainted with the state of the country in the absence of its sovereign. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> having gloriously finished the enterprise in which he was engaged, was returning with his army; but in spite of all his eagerness to be at home, he was detained on the way by tempests for several years, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon several countries differing from each other in manners and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In these dangers his companions, not strictly obeying his orders, perish through their own fault. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the grandees of his country abuse the freedom which his absence gave them; consume his estate; conspire to destroy his son; endeavour to compel his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> to accept one of them for her husband; and indulge themselves in every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of violence, from a persuasion that he would never return. In this they were disappointed. He returns; and discovering himself only to his son and some others who had maintained their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, he is an eye witness of the insolence of his enemies, punishes them accordingly to their deserts, and restores to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> that tranquillity and repose to which it had been a stranger during the many years of his absence. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the Odyssey, in which there is no opportunity of displaying that vigour and sublimity which characterize the Iliad. "It descends from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of gods and heroes, and warlike achievements; but in recompense we have more pleasing pictures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manners. Instead of that ferocity which reigns in the other poem, this presents us with the most amiable images of hospitality and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; entertains us with many a wonderful adventure; and instructs us by such a constant vein of morality and virtue which runs through the poem," sometimes in precepts, and always in the conduct of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, that we should not wonder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, which gave the appellation of wise to men who uttered fling sentences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, had given to Homer the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the father of virtue, for introducing into his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> such... Oeconomica, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of moral maxims. As a poem, however, the Odyssey has its faults. The last twelve books are tedious and languid; and we are disappointed by the calm behaviour of Penelope upon the discovery of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> lost husband.

OECONOMICS

Pages 130-130

the art of managing the affairs of a family <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; and hence the person who takes care of the revenues and other affairs of churches, monasteries, and the like, is termed oeconomus.

OECONOMISTS

Pages 130-130

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of French philosophers, who obtained this name in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of directing their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and researches to objects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy, and in particular to the improvement of the departments of finance. The views of those philosophers, among whom are reckoned the celebrated names of Voltaire, d'Alembert, Diderot, and Condorcet, have been variously represented; by some as directly hostile to all regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and by others as unfriendly to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

OECONOMY

Pages 130-130

denotes the prudent conduct, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discreet and frugal management, whether of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own estate or that of another. Animal OECONOMY, comprehends the various operations of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a> and preservation of animals*. The doctrine of the animal economy is nearly connected with physiology, which explains the operation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, &c. See ANATOMY and PHYSIOLOGY.

OECUMENICAL

Pages 130-130

signifies the same with general <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> universal; as, oecumenical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, bishop, &c.

OEDERA

Pages 130-130

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas. See BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OEDIPUS

Pages 130-130

the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is partly fabulous, flourished about 1266 B.C. It is said he was given by his father to a shepherd, who was ordered to put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in order to prevent the misfortunes with which he was threatened by an oracle. But the shepherd, being unwilling to kill him with his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, tied him by the feet to a tree, that he might be devoured by wild beasts. The infant was however found in this situation by another shepherd named Phorbas, who carried him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLYBUS">Polybus</a>, king of Corinth; where the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, having no children, educated him with as much care as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been her own son. When he was grown up, he was informed that he was not the son of Polybus; on which, by order of the oracle, he went to seek for his father in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>; but scarce was he arrived in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, when he met his father on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and killed him without knowing him. A short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, having delivered the country from the monster called the Sphinx, he married Jocasta, without knowing that she was his mother, and had four children by her; but afterwards, being informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, he quitted the throne, and, thinking himself unworthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, put out his eyes. Eteocles and Polynices, who were celebrated among the Greeks, were born of this incestuous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>.

OEGWA

Pages 130-130

a town on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated, according to Artus, on the brow of an eminence, raising itself by a gentle ascent to a considerable height, and defended by rocks, against which the waves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> with the utmost violence, the noise of which is heard at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. Barbot affirms, that Oegwa contains above 500 houses disposed by narrow crooked streets; and that from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> it has the appearance of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. Des Marchias reduces the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses to 200, in the centre of which stands a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the repository of their gold dust and other commodities. The houses are built of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and clay, but convenient, and well furnished with chairs, stools, mats, carpets, earthen pots, and even looking glasses, which they purchase from the Europeans. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the coast is better provided with all kinds of eatables, which are sent in from the adjacent cantons, and sold in public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. Everything is bought and sold with gold dust, which is the standard of all other commodities, and brought hither in great abundance from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of Feitu, Abrambo, Affeito, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANDINGO">Mandingo</a>. The gold is sold by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> determined by nice scales, made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> before it was frequented by the Europeans: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> are not wholly ignorant of the more refined principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. Next to gold, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of fish, of which they catch prodigious quantities on the coast. Although the natives are brave and warlike, yet in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of peace no people are more industrious, their whole time being employed in catching fish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cultivating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the earth. They are extremely expert in throwing the line, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> by the hook; nor is their intrepidity in combating the elements, and pursuing their employments in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, less astonishing. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, except Wednesday, which is sacred to the Fetiches, they employ in their several occupations, and no season of the year is exempted from fishing. Their canoes weather storms which would endanger the largest shipping; and the negroes have the dexterity of making their advantage of those seas, which oblige others to discontinue their labours, by throwing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> with the same success in tempestuous as in calm weather.

OELAND

Pages 130-130

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, seated in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between the continent of Gothland and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Gothland. It lies between 56° and 57° of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 17° and 18° of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is about 60 miles in length, and 15 in breadth; having a wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, with rising hills, and several castles. It has no town of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>.

OENANTHE

Pages 130-130
WATER DROPWORT, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 45th order Umbellatae. See BOTANY Index.

OENOPTAE

Pages 130-131

in Grecian antiquity, a kind of cen- OETOS at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who regulated entertainments, and took care that none drank too much, nor too little.

OENOS

Pages 131-131

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the name used by authors for the stock-dove, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood-pigeon, called also by some vinago, somewhat larger than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pigeon, but of the same shape and general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Its neck is of a fine changeable hue, as differently opposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, shoulders, and wings, are of a fine purplish hue, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine colour, from whence it has its name vinago.

OENOTHERA

Pages 131-131

TREE-PRIMROSE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the oenandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OENOTRIA

Pages 131-131

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; so called from the Oenotri, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); inhabiting between Paestum and Tarentum, (Ovid). Originally Arcadians, (Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>), who came under the conduct of Oenotrus son of Lycaon, 17 generations before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 459 years, at 27 years each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, and gave name to the people. Cato derives the name from Oenotrus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a>; but Varro from Oenotrus, king of the Latins; and Servius from the Greek name for wine, for which Italy was famous; of which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is Strabo.

OENOTRIDES

Pages 131-131

two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, over against Velia, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, called Pontia and Icchia; now Penza and Icchia, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Principato Citra, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. So called from the Oenotri, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.

OESEL

Pages 131-131

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. It is about 70 miles in length, and 50 in breadth, and contains 10 parishes. It is defended by the fortresses of Airenburg and Sonneburg. It lies between 22° and 24° of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 58° and 59° of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude.

OESOPHAGUS

Pages 131-131

in Anatomy, the Gula, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gullet, is a membranaceous canal, reaching from the fauces to the stomach, and conveying into it the food taken in at the mouth. See Anatomy, No. 92.

OESTRUS

Pages 131-131

a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OETA

Pages 131-131

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain of Thessaly, extending from Thermopylae westward to the Sinus Ambracius, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> the mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> stretching out between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> to the south, and Pindus to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. At Thermopylae it is very rough and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, rising and ending in sharp and steep rocks, affording a narrow passage between it and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from Thessaly to Locris (Strabo), with two paths over it; the one above Trachis, very steep and high; the other through the country of the Aetolians, much easier and readier for travellers; by this it was that Leonidas was attacked in rear by the Persians (Pausanias). Here <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> laid himself on the funeral pile (Silius Italicus, Ovid); the spot thence called Pyra (Livy), who says, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to the east are called Oeta; and hence the poets allege, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, night, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and stars, arose from Oeta (Seneca, Statius, Silius Italicus, Catullus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Culex)—circumstances which show the height of this mountain.

OETING

Pages 131-131

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and east by Franconia; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Neuburg; and on the west by that of Württemberg. It is about 40 miles from east to west, and 25 from north to south.

OFF-SETS

Pages 133-133

in Surveying, are perpendiculars let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and measuring from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> to the hedge, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extremity of an enclosure.

OFFA'S DYKE

Pages 131-131

an intrenchment <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up by Offa, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, to defend England against the incursions of the Welsh. It runs through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, Denbighshire, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>.

OFFANTO

Pages 131-131

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. It rises in the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in the Farther Principato; and passing by Conza, and Monte Verde, it afterwards separates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a> from the Bafllicata and the Terra-di-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, and then it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, near Salpe.

OFFENCE

Pages 131-132

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> committed against the law, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> omitted where the law requires it. OFFERINGS. The Hebrews had several kinds of offerings, which they presented at the temple. Some were free-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> offerings, and others were of obligation. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, the sin offerings, were of obligation; the peace offerings, vows, offerings of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and other things, which were made to the temple or to the ministers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, were offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The Hebrews called all offerings in general corban. But the offerings of bread, salt, fruits, and liquors, as wine and oil, which were presented to the temple, they called mincha. The sacrifices are not properly offerings, and are not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> included under that name. See CORBAN and SACRIFICE. The offerings of grain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, bread, cakes, fruits, wine, salt, and oil, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the temple. Sometimes these offerings were alone, and sometimes they accompanied the sacrifices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">Honey</a> was never offered with the sacrifices; but it might be offered alone in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of first fruits. Now these were the rules that were observed in the presenting of those offerings, called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> mincha, or kerbon mincha; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, offerings of sacrifice; and the same by St Jerome, oblationem sacrificii; but by our translators, meat offerings (Lev. ii. i., &c.). There were five sorts of these offerings: 1. Fine flour or meal. 2. Cakes of several sorts, baked in an oven. 3. Cakes baked upon a plate. 4. Another sort of cakes, baked upon a gridiron, or plate with holes in it. 5. The first fruits of the new corn, which were offered either pure and without mixture, or roasted or parched in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> or out of the ear. The cakes were kneaded with oil olive, or fried with oil in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, or only dipped in oil after they were baked. The bread offered to be presented upon the altar, was to be without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a>; for leaven was never offered upon the altar, nor with the sacrifices. But they might make presents of common bread to the priests and ministers of the temple. See CAKE, &c. The offerings now mentioned were appointed on ac- Offerings. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of the poorer sort, who could not go to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of sacrificing animals. And even those that offered living victims were not excused from giving meal, wine, and salt, which was to go along with the greater sacrifices. And also those that offered only oblations of bread or of meal, offered also oil, incense, salt, and wine, which were in a manner the feasting of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in waiting received the offerings from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of him that offered them; laid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them upon the altar, and reserved the rest for his own subsistence: that was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> as a minister of the Lord. Nothing was burnt quite up but the incense, of which the priest kept back nothing for his own share. When an Israelite offered a loaf to the priest, or a whole cake, the priest broke the loaf or the cake into two parts, setting that part aside that he referred to himself, and broke the other into crumbs; poured oil upon it, salt, wine, and incense; and spread the whole upon the fire of the altar. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> these offerings be accompanied by an animal for a sacrifice, it was all thrown upon the victim, to be consumed along with it. If these offerings were the ears of new corn, either of wheat or barley, these ears were parched at the fire or in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and rubbed in the hand, and then offered to the priest in a vessel; over which he put oil, incense, wine, and salt, and then burnt it upon the altar, first having taken as much of it as of right belonged to himself. The greatest part of these offerings were voluntary, and of pure devotion. But when an animal was offered in sacrifice, they were not at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to omit these offerings. Everything was to be supplied that was to accompany the sacrifice, and which served as a feasting to the victim. There are some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which the law requires only offerings of corn, or bread: for example, when they offered the first fruits of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, whether they were offered solemnly by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, or by the devotion of private persons. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of meal, oil, wine, or salt, which was to go along with the sacrifices, we cannot easily see that the law had determined it. Generally the priest threw an handful of meal or crumbs upon the fire of the altar, with wine, oil, and salt in proportion, and all the incense. All the rest belonged to him, the quantity depended upon the liberality of the offerer. We observe in more places than one, that Moses appoints an affaron, or the tenth part of an ephah of meal, for those that had not wherewithal to offer the appointed sin offerings (Lev. v. 11, xiv. 21.). In the solemn offerings of the first fruits for the whole nation, they offered an entire sheaf of corn, a lamb of a year old, two tenths or two affarons of fine meal mixed with oil, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an hin of wine for the libation. (Lev. xxiii. 10, 11, 12, &c.). In the sacrifice of jealousy (Numb. v. 15.), when a jealous husband accused his wife of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, the husband offered the tenth part of a fatum of barley-meal, without oil or incense, because, it was a sacrifice of jealousy, to discover whether his wife was guilty or not. The offerings of the fruits of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, of bread, of wine, oil, and salt, are the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of any that have come to our knowledge. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a> offered to the Lord of the fruits of the earth, the first fruits of his labour (Gen. iv. 3, 4.). <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> offered the firstlings of his flocks, and of their fat. The heathen have nothing more ancient in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, than these sorts of offerings made to their gods. They offered clean wheat, flour, and bread. Office, a particular charge or trust, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> attended with a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>.—The word is primarily used in speaking of the offices of judiciary and policy; as the office of secretary of state, the office of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace, &c.

OFFICE ALSO

Pages 132-133

e also signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment appointed for officers to attend in, in order to discharge their respective duties and employments; as the secretary's office, ordnance office, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a> office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> office, pipe office, fix clerks office, &c. Office, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, denotes all the apartments appointed for the necessary occasions of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, pantries, confectionaries, &c. Office, in the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is usual for a benefice, that has no jurisdiction annexed to it. Duty upon Offices and Pensions, a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s extraordinary perpetual revenue, consisting in a payment of 1s. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> (over and above all other duties) out of all salaries, fees, and perquisites of offices and pensions payable by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This highly popular <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> was imposed by stat. 31 Geo. II. c. 22. and is under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax. Officer, a person possessed of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> or office. See the preceding article. The great officers of the crown, or state, are, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, the lord high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the lord high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the lord privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, the lord chamberlain, the lord high <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> marshal; each of which see under its proper article. Non-committed Officers, are sergeants majors, quartermaster sergeants, sergeants, corporals, drum and fifes majors; who are nominated by their respective captains, and appointed by the commanding officers of regiments, and by them reduced without a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> martial. Orderly non-committed Officers, are those who are orderly, or on duty for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; who, on hearing the drum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> for orders, are to repair to the place appointed to receive them, and to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in the orderly book, what is dictated by the adjutant, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>: they are then immediately to show these orders to the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and afterwards warn the men for duty. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">Flag</a> Officers. See Flag Officers, and Admirals. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">Commission</a> Officers, are such as are appointed by the king's commission. Such are all from the general to the cornet and ensign inclusive. They are thus called in contradistinction to non-committed officers. See Non-committed Officers. General Officers, are those whose command is not limited to a single company, troop, or regiment; but extends to a body of forces composed of several regiments: such are the general, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> general, major general, and brigadier. Officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">Household</a>. See the article Household. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">Staff</a> Officers, are such as, in the king's presence, bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> staff or wand; and at other times, on their going abroad, have it carried before them by a footman bare-headed: such are the lord fleward, lord chamberlain, lord treasurer, &c. The white staff is taken for a commission; and, at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, each of these officers breaks his staff over the hearse made for the king's body, and by this means lays down his commission, and discharges all his inferior officers. Subaltern Officers, are all who administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in the name of subjects; as those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> under the earl marshal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the subaltern officers are the lieutenants, cornets, ensigns, sergeants, and corporals.

OFFICIAL

Pages 133-133

is also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> appointed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-deacon as his assistant, who sits as judge in the arch-deacon's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

OFFICINAL

Pages 133-133

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an appellation given to such medicines, whether simple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, as are required to be constantly kept in the apothecaries shops. The officinal simples are appointed, among us, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians; and the manner of making the compositions directed in their pharmacopoeia. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>.

OFFING

Pages 133-133
or OFFIN, in the sea language, that part of the sea a good distance from shore, where there is deep water, and no need of a pilot to conduct the ship: thus, if a ship from shore be seen sailing out to seaward, they say, she stands for the offing; and if a ship, having the shore near her, have another a good way without her, or towards the sea, they say, that ship is in the offing.

OGHAMS

Pages 133-133

a particular kind of steganography, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in cypher, practised by the Irish; of which there were three kinds: The first was composed of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and marks, which derived their power from their situation and position, as they stand in relation to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> line, over or under which they are placed, or through which they are drawn; the principal line is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, and serves for a rule or guide, whose upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is called the left, and the under side the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; above, under, and through which line, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> or marks are drawn, which stand in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>, diphthongs, and triphthongs. Some authors have doubted the existence of this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of writing in cypher, called Ogham among the Irish; but these doubts are perhaps ill founded: for several MSS. in this character still exist, from which Mr. Atte has given a plate of them.

OGIVE

Pages 133-133

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of a Gothic vault; which, instead of being circular, passes diagonally from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> to another, and forms a croft with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. The middle, where the ogives <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> each other, is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>; being cut in form of a roe, or a cul de lampe. The members or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> of the ogives are called nerves, branches, or reins; and the arches which separate the ogives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> arches.

OGYGES

Pages 133-133
king of the Thebans, or, according to others, of Ogygia and Attica, afterwards called Boeotia and Attica. He is recorded to have been the first founder of Thebes and Eleusis. The famous deluge happened in his time, in which some say he perished with all his subjects, 1796 B.C. OGYGIÁ (Homer), the island of Calypso; placed by Pliny in the Sinus Scylaeus, in the Ionian sea, opposite to the promontory Lacinium; by Mela in the strait of Sicily, calling it Θέας; which others place at the promontory Circeum, and call it the island of Circe. OGYgia, the ancient name of Thebes in Boeotia: so called from Ogyges, an ancient king, under whom happened a great deluge, 1020 years before the first Olympiad.

OHETEROA

Pages 133-133

one of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> lately discovered, is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 150° 47'. S. Lat. 22° 27'. It is neither fertile nor populous; nor has it any harbour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> anchorage fit for shipping, and the disposition of the people is hostile to such as visit them.

OHIO

Pages 133-133

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, having its source in the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and after them is called Alleghany, till it joins the Monongahela at Fort Pitt, where it receives the name of Ohio. It bounds the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENTUCKY">Kentucky</a>, and its only disadvantage is a rapid, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, in N. Lat. 38° 3', about 400 miles from its mouth. The breadth of this river in no one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> exceeds 1200 yards, but its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> breadth may be estimated at 600 yards, and its length almost 1200 miles, according to the measurement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hutchins. The inundations of the Ohio begin about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and subside in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, although they have been known to happen frequently in other months; so that boats which are capable of carrying 300 barrels of flour from the Monongahela above Pittsburg, have seldom very long to wait for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is thought that, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> floods, a first rate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> might sail from Louisville to New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the sudden turns of the river, and the rapidity of its current, should be found to admit of a safe steerage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the Ohio is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock, and is divided by an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> into two branches, the southern of which is about 200 yards wide, but impassable in dry seasons. It is the branch that may be most easily opened for a constant <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, as the bed of the northern branch is worn into channels by the constant course of the water, and the attrition of the pebble <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> carried along with it. OHIO is also the name of the north-westernmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, bounded on the east by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>. It contains 5,212 inhabitants, of whom 281 are slaves.

OIL

Pages 133-136

an unctuous inflammable substance, drawn from several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies, as animal and vegetable substances. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. For an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of an oil mill, see Gray's Experienced Millwright; and for an account of a very simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for expressing oils from different seeds. feeds at Bangalore in the East Indies, see Phil Mag. vol. xxx. p. 329. Rock Oil. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETROLEUM">Petroleum</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. Ointment, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>. See Unguent, Materia Medica Index. Okeham, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Rutlandshire, in England, seated in a rich and pleasant valley, called the vale of Catnus. It is pretty well built, has a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a free-school, and an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 45. N. Lat. 52. 40. Okingham, Ockingham, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Waxingham, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, in England, noted for the manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings. W. Long. o. 50. N. Lat. 51. 26. Olaus Magnus. See Magnus. Okra, the fruit of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hibiscus, which is employed in the West Indies in making soups. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Olax, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the triandra class. See Botany Index. Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">Age</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGEVITY">Longevity</a>. Many methods have been proposed for lengthening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and rendering old age comfortable. Cornaro's Treatise on this subject is known to every body, and needs not be quoted.
