To some of our readers the following set of resolutions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps be new, and may certainly be useful. The old men should resolve, except the reasons for a change be invincible, to live and die in the public profession of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in which they were born and bred. To avoid all profane talk and intricate debates on sacred topics. To endeavour to get the better of the intrusions of indolence of mind and body, those certain harbingers of enfeebling age. Rather to wear out, than to rust out. To rise early, and as often as possible to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> before midnight. Not to nod in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, nor to indulge repose too frequently on the couch in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. To waste as little of life in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> as may be, for we shall have enough in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. Not to give up walking; nor to ride on horseback to fatigue. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a>, and a late medical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, determine to ride five miles every day: Nothing contributes more to the preservation of appetite, and the prolongation of life. Cheyne's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the valetudinary, "to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their religion," to be religiously observed. To continue the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, pursued for more than fifty years, in books on all subjects; for variety is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of the mind as well as of life. Other people's thoughts, like the best conversation of one's companions, are generally better and more agreeable than one's own. Frequently to think over the virtues of one's acquaintance, old and new. To admit every cheerful ray of sunshine on the imagination. To avoid retrospection on a past friendship, which had much of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> in it; for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> often comes when she is not invited. To try to think more of the living and less of the dead; for the dead belong to a world of their own. To live within one's income, be it large or little. Not to let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of any sort run away with the understanding. Not to encourage romantic hopes nor fears. Not to drive away hope, the sovereign balm of life, though he is the greatest of all flatterers. Not to be under the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> or enthusiasm. Not willingly to undertake any thing for which the nerves of the mind or the body are not strong enough. Not to run the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of competition, or to be in another's way. To avoid being jostled too much in the street, being overcome by the noise of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, and not to be carried even by curiosity itself into a large crowd. To strive to embody that dignified sentiment, "to write injuries in dust, but kindliness in marble." Not to give the reins to constitutional impatience, for it is apt to hurry on the first expressions into the indecency of swearing. To recollect, that he who can keep his own temper may be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of another's. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> one cannot be a stoic, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> and forbearing, on every trying occasion, yet it may not be impossible to pull the check-string against the moroseness of spleen or the impetuosity of peevishness. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">Anger</a> is a short madness. Not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in love, now on the precipice of three score, nor expect to be fallen in love with. A connexion between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter is an improper one. Love, like fire, is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, but a bad master. Love is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when the animal spirits are gone. To contrive to have as few vacant hours upon one's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> as possible, that idleness, the mother of crimes and vices, may not pay its visit. To be always doing of something, and to have something to do. To fill up one's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and to have a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> to fill up: for time is the materials that life is made of. If one is not able by situation, or through the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of raising the supplies within the year, or by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> (for virtue itself is but habit), to do much ostentatious good, yet do as little harm as possible. To make the best and the most of everything. Not to indulge too much in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, nor yet to undermine the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. The gout, rheumatism, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Spectator, seem to be hovering over the dishes. Wine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> purveyor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the senses, offers his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, when love takes his leave. It is natural to catch hold of every help, when the spirits begin to droop. Love and wine are good cordials, but are not proper for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Resolve not to go to bed on a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> are the best receipts for a good night's rest, and the parents of undisturbing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>. Not to be enervated by the flatulence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>. Let the second or third morning's thought be to consider of the employment for the day; and one of the last at night to inquire what has been done in the course of it. Not to let one's tongue run at the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Not to be too communicative nor unrevealed. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> tongue, with an open countenance, are the safest passports through the journey of the world. To correct the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of too much talking, and refrain the narrativeness of the approaching climacteric. To take the good-natured side in conversation. However, not to praise everybody, for that is to praise nobody. Not to be inquisitive, and eager to know secrets, nor be thought to have a head full of other people's affairs. Not to make an enemy, nor to lose a friend. To aim at the esteem of the public, and to leave a good name behind. Not to be singular in dress, in behaviour, in notions, or expressions of one's thoughts. Never to give bad advice, and to strive not to let a bad example. Seldom to give advice till asked, for it appears like giving something that is superfluous to one's self. Not to like or dislike too much at first sight. Not to wonder, for all wonder is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> that possession falls short of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. The longing of twenty years may be disappointed in the unanticipated gratification of a single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. hour. Whilst we are willing, we see the best side; after we have taken possession, the worst. Refuse to attend to the arguments on both sides, and to hear every body against everybody. The mind ought not to be made up, but upon the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. To be affectionate to relations, which is a kind of self-love, in preference to all other acquaintance. But not to omit paying the commanding respect to merit, which is superior to all the accidental chain of kindred. Not to debilitate the mind by new and future compositions. Like the spider, it may spin itself to death. The mind, like the field, must have its fallow season. The leisure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> has created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> acquaintance, and pleased all it has wished to please. To resolve not to be too free of promises, for performances are sometimes very difficult things. Not to be too much alone, nor to read, nor meditate, or talk too much on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> that may awaken tender sensations, and be too pathetic for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. To enjoy the present, not to be made too unhappy by reflection on the past, not to be oppressed by invisible gloom on the future. To give and receive comfort, those necessary alms to a distrested mind. To be constantly thankful to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> for the plenty hitherto possessed, which has preserved one from the dependence on party, persons, and opinions, and kept one out of debt. The appearance of a happy situation, and opportunities of taking many worldly felicities (for content has seldom perverted itself into discontent), has induced many to conclude, that one must be pleased with one's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> in life; and it occasions many to look with the eye of innocent envy. To resolve more than ever to shun every public station and responsibility of conduct. To be satisfied with being master of one's self, one's habits, now a second <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and one's time. Determined not to solicit, unless trampled upon by fortune, to live and die in the harness of trade, or a profession. To take care that pity (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> is not here meant) does not find out one in the endurance of any calamity. When pity is within call, contempt is not far off. Not to wish to have a greater hold of life, nor to quit that hold. The possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of existence is of too short a possession for the long night that is to succeed: therefore not a moment to be lost. Not to lose sight even for a single day, of these good and proverbial daughters—diet—merryman—and quiet. Resolved to remember and to recommend, towards tranquillity and longevity, the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> maxims of Sir Hans Sloane—"Never to quarrel with one's self—one's wife—or one's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>." Lastly, Not to put one's self too much in the power of the elements, those great enemies to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frame; namely, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>—the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>—the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>—and the night <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> of the Mountain. See Assassins. Oldcastle, Sir John, called the Good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cobham, was born in the reign of Edward III. and was the first author as well as the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> among the English <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>: he obtained his peerage by marrying the heiress of that Lord Cobham who with so much virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> opposed the tyranny of Richard II. By his means the famous statute against profaners was revived, and guarded against by severer penalties; he was one of the leaders of the reforming party; was at great expense in procuring and dispersing copies of Wickliffe's writings among the people, as well as by maintaining a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his disciples as itinerant preachers. In the reign of Henry V. he was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; the growth of which was attributed to his influence. Being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the king delayed his prosecution that he might reason with him himself; but not being able to reclaim him to the church of Rome, he in great displeasure resigned him to its censure. He was apprehended and condemned for heresy; but escaping from the Tower, lay concealed for four years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, until the rumour of a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was raised against him, and a price set upon his head: he was at last seized and executed in St Giles's Fields; being hung alive in chains upon a gallows, and burned by a fire placed underneath. He wrote "Twelve Conclusions, addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> of England." Oldenburg, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The origin of this illustrious family, we are told, is this: On the death of Christopher king of Denmark, &c., in 1443, without issue, there was a great contest about the succession; and a variety of factions were raised, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, for the promotion of different persons; and various animosities and numerous discords were excited by the several parties, in order each to obtain their own ends. As soon as these intrigues were known in Denmark, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> resolved to proceed to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a king; for it did not appear expedient to commit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of affairs to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> dowager, at a time when they had every thing to fear from the two neighbouring crowns. At this time a lord of great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and ambition, sought the queen in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the more easily to pave his way to the throne. This is a fact mentioned by Pontanus and Meurinus, though neither takes notice of his name. But as for a great number of years there was no precedent for electing a king out of the body of nobility, though agreeable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the queen entered into the views of the senate, and declared she would give her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to no prince who should not be judged deserving of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The advantages which would have accrued from annexing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sleswick and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> to the crown, made the senate first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their eyes on Adolphus. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> required no long deliberation; all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the conveniences resulting from such an union, and gave their assent. Immediately an embassy was despatched with the offer to Adolphus; but that prince consulting the good of his subjects, whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> would have been absorbed in the superior weight of Denmark, declined it, with a moderation and disinterestedness, altogether uncommon among princes. However, that he might not be wanting in respect to the senate, he proposed to them his nephew Christian, second son to Theodoric, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Oldenburg, a prince bred up at the court of Adolphus from his infancy. The proposition was so agreeable to the senate, that, without loss of time, the ambassadors were sent to Theodoric, to demand either of his sons he should pitch upon for their king. Theodoric's answer to the ambassadors was remarkable: "I have three sons, says he, of very opposite qualities. One is passionately fond of pleasure and women; another breathes nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, without regarding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the cause; but the third is moderate in his disposition, prefers Oldenburg prefers peace to the din of arms, yet stands unrivalled in valour, generosity, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>." He said he painted these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> for the senate's information, desiring they would choose which of the young princes they believed would render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> happiest. It was a matter which would admit of no hesitation; with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> the senate declared for that prince whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> the father had so warmly drawn; and under these happy auspices commenced the origin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the house of Oldenburg, at this day seated on the throne of Denmark.

OLD-WIFE

Pages 136-136
or Wrangle. See LABRUS, Ichthyology Index. OLD-WIFE Fish. See Ballistes, Cy Index.

OLD-WOMAN'S ISLAND

Pages 136-136

a narrow slip of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, about two miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, separated from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> in the East Indies by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which, however, is passable at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It terminates at one extremity in a small eminence, on which a look-out <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is kept for vessels. Near the middle are three tombs kept constantly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, as land-marks into the harbour. From the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> a dangerous ledge of rocks flows forth, which are not very easily cleared. It produces only pasture for a few cattle.

OLDENBURG

Pages 136-136

Henry, a learned German of the 17th century, was descended from the noble family of his name, who were earls of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Oldenburg, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Westphalia, for many generations. He was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bremen in the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> for his countrymen, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, after the usurpation of Cromwell; but being discharged of that employ, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Henry O'Bryan, an Irish nobleman, whom he attended to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he was admitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in the Bodleian library in the beginning of the year 1656. He was afterwards tutor to William lord Cavendish, and was acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> the poet. During his residence at Oxford, he became also acquainted with the members of that body there, which gave birth to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and upon the foundation of this latter, he was elected fellow; and when the society found it necessary to have two secretaries, he was chosen assistant secretary to Dr Wilkins. He applied himself with extraordinary diligence to the business of his office, and began the publication of the Philosophical Transactions with No. I. in 1664. In order to discharge this task with greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to himself and the society, he held a correspondence with more than seventy learned persons, and others, upon a vast variety of subjects, in different parts of the world. This fatigue would have been insupportable, had not he, as he told Dr Lister, managed it so as to make one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> answer another; and that to be always fresh, he never read a letter before he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, ready to answer it forthwith; so that the multitude of his letters cloyed him not, nor ever lay upon his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Among others, he was a constant correspondent of Mr Robert Boyle, with whom he had a very intimate friendship; and he translated several of that ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s works into Latin. Mr Oldenburg <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to publish the Transactions, as before, to No. xxxvi. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 25, 1677. After which the publication was discontinued till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> following, when it was again resumed by his successor in the secretary's office, Mr Nehemiah Grew, who carried it on till the end of February 1678. Our author dying at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLESTON">Charleston</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August that year, was interred there.

OLDENLANDIA

Pages 136-136

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OLDHAM

Pages 136-136

John, an eminent English poet in the 17th century, son of a Nonconformist minister, was educated under his father, and then sent to Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He became usher to the free-school at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> in Surry; where he received a visit from the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> and Dorset, Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Sedley, and other persons of distinction, merely upon the reputation of some verses of his which they had seen in manuscript. He was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to several gentlemen's sons successively; and having saved a small sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and became a perfect votary to the bottle, being an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. He was quickly found out here by the noblemen who had visited him at Croydon, who brought him acquainted with Mr Dryden. He lived mostly with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> at Holme Pierpoint in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, where he died of the smallpox in 1683, in the 30th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His acquaintance with learned authors appears by his satires against the Jesuits, in which there is as much learning as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> discovered. Mr Dryden esteemed him highly. His works are printed in 2 vols 12mo. They chiefly consist of satires, odes, translations, paraphrases of Horace and other authors, elegiac verses, imitations, parodies, familiar epistles, &c.

OLDHEAD

Pages 136-136

a promontory situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, four miles south of Kinlake, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> of Courcies, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, which runs far into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on which is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> for the convenience of shipping. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from its extremity is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle of the lords of Kinlake, built from one side of the isthmus to the other, which defended all the lands towards the head; this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was formerly called Duncearma, and was the old seat of the Irish kings. The isthmus, by the working of the sea, was quite penetrated through, so as to form a stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, under which boats might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> to the other. Among the rocks of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> there are aviaries of good hawks; also the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ospreys build their nests and breed there.

OLDMIXON

Pages 136-136

John, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>: he was a violent party-writer and malevolent critic, who would scarcely have been remembered, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Pope, in resentment of his abuse, had not condemned him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> in his Dunciad. His party-writings procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the revenue at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, where he died at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the year 1745. Besides his fugitive temporary pieces, he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Stuarts, in folio; a Critical History of England, 2 vols 8vo; a volume of Poems, some dramatic pieces, &c.; none of them worthy of notice, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> being that of falsifying history.

OLEAGINOUS

Pages 136-136

something that partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> out of which oil may be expressed.

OLEANDER

Pages 136-137
or ROSE BAY, *nerium*; a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria clas. See Botany Index.

OLECRANUM

Pages 137-137
or OLECRANON, in Anatomy, the protuberance of the ulna, which prevents the joint of the elbow from being bent back beyond a certain length. See Anatomy, No. 51.

OLENUS

Pages 137-137

a Greek poet, older than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, came from Xanthe, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lycia. He composed several hymns, which were sung in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Delos upon festival days. Olenus is said to have been one of the founders of the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; to have been the first who filled at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; and to have given responses in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of these assertions is very doubtful.

OLERON

Pages 137-137

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Auvergne and Saintonge, about five miles from the continent. It is 12 miles in length, and five in breadth; and is very fertile, containing about 12,000 inhabitants, who are excellent seamen. It is defended by a castle, which is well fortified; and there is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> placed there for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of ships. It is 14 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Lat. 46. 3. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Laws of OLERON, certain laws relative to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, made in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Richard I. when he was at the island of Oleron. These laws, being accounted the most excellent sea laws in the world, and recorded in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> book of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. See Selden's Mare Claustrum.

OLEUM PALMAE CHRISTI

Pages 137-137
commonly called castor oil, is extracted from the kernel of the fruit produced by the Ricinus Americanus. See Ricinus, Botany and Materia Medica Index. OLFACATORY NERVES. See Anatomy, No. 139 and 143.

OLGA

Pages 137-137
queen of Igor, the second monarch of Russia, who flourished about the year 880, having succeeded his father Ruric, who died in 878. Olga was born in Plescow, and was of the best family in that city. She bore him one son, called Svetoslav. Igor being murdered by the Drevewes, or Dreveliani, Olga revenged his death. She went afterwards, for what reason we know not, to Constantinople, where she was baptized, and received the name of Helena. The emperor John Zimilces was her godfather, and fell in love with her as we are told; but she, alleging their spiritual alliance, refused to marry him. Her example made some impression upon her subjects, a good number of whom became converts to Christianity; but none upon her son, who reigned for a long time after her death, which happened at Pereslaw, in the 80th year of her age, 14 years after her baptism. The Russians to this day rank her among their saints, and commemorate her festival on the 11th of July.

OLIBANUM

Pages 137-137

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a gummy resin, (the product of the *juniperus lyca* Lin.), brought from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and the East Indies, usually in drops <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tears. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OLIGARCHY

Pages 137-137

a form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> wherein the administration of affairs is confined to a few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.

OLIO

Pages 137-137
or OILIO, a favourite dish, or food, composed of a great variety of ingredients; chiefly found at Spanish tables. The forms of ollios are various. To give a notion of this strange assemblage, we shall here add one from an approved author. Take rump of beef, neats tongues boiled and dried, and Bologna sausages; boil them together, and, after boiling two hours, add mutton, pork, venison and bacon, cut in bits; as also turnips, carrots, onions and cabbage, borage, endive, marigolds, sorrel, and spinach; then spices, as saffron, cloves, mace, nutmeg, &c. This done, in another pot put a turkey or goose, with capons, pheasants, pigeons and ducks, partridges, teals, and stock-doves, snipes, quails, and larks, and boil them in water and salt. In a third vessel, prepare a sauce of white wine, strong broth, butter, bottoms of artichokes, and chestnuts, with cauliflowers, bread, marrow, yolks of eggs, mace, and saffron. Lastly, dish the olio, by first laying out the beef and veal, then the venison, mutton, tongues, and sausages, and the roots over all; then the largest fowls, then the smallest, and lastly pour on the sauce.

OLISIPO

Pages 137-137

(Pliny, Antonine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>); a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>; of such antiquity, that Solinus thought it was built by Ulysses; and Mela, probably to favour this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, writes, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> copies, Ulyssippe; both of them perhaps deceived by the similarity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. It was a municipium, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Felicitas Julia, a privilege granted by the munificence of Augustus, (Inscriptions, Pliny). Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated on the north <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tagus, distant about ten miles from its mouth. See LISBON.

OLIVAREZ

Pages 137-138
Count de, by name Don Galpar de Guzman, favourite and minister to Don Philip IV. of Spain, about 1620; a man of great parts and boundless ambition. Philip no sooner became king, than he became the subject of this his favourite. The king had abilities, it is true, but they lay dormant; and whilst he spent his time in little inactivity, the whole government was under the direction of Olivarez. The count's management, indeed, was sufficiently dexterous in accomplishing his own designs; for by the best framed excuses, and on the most plausible pretexts, he removed all such as he thought stood in his way; nor did he stop there, but sometimes persecuted his rivals even to death, of which Don Rodrigo Calderona was a melancholy instance, an instance which at that time excited universal compassion. This minister, in short, had a genius of no common kind; added to which, he had a disposition which spurned all controul. He had persecuted the late ministry for their pusillanimity in the management of affairs; he therefore thought it necessary, and it was certainly prudent, to pursue new measures. His self-sufficiency, though unbounded, was concealed under the veil of assumed meekness, and he was careful to make it appear that he was wholly taken up with the things of his own province. His politics were of a refined perhaps, but not of a very useful tendency; for his imprudence, or his wrong notions on the subject, made him renew a war with Holland, contrary to the universal opinion of the council and the people. By the same imprudence, or by something worse, he provoked England, and obliged her to endeavour to humble the pride and lessen the authority of the house of Austria. Thus far he had been of little service. service to his country, having only provoked the resentment of the most powerful states, particularly England, France, Holland, &c., to conspire for its ruin. It is remarkable that Olivarez, notwithstanding this, never lost his credit; and indeed things so turned about in the end, that though Spain for a whole year was put to the severest trials, it acquired a degree of fame which sufficiently, in the general opinion, overbalanced some little losfs. Olivarez too was particularly fortunate in making the peace; in which transaction he gained a very considerable advantage over Richelieu, so that things appeared to be still in a very favourable train. Fortune, however, was not always quite so indulgent to the schemes of this minister: he again drew Spain into a war with Mantua, contrary to the sentiments of the wisest men; from which is justly dated its declension, if not its ruin. On the whole, Olivarez seems to have been always averse to peace; and with such a restless disposition, it is undoubtedly wonderful that he held his place so long and with so few complaints as he did. It was certainly owing to his ambition and obstinacy, that an almost general war was excited about the year 1627, and which, as we have said, proved so fatal to Spain. So averse, indeed, does he appear to have been to peace, that he used every means in his power to prevent the restoration of it in Italy; and for this very purpose he sent Feria into Milan, whom he knew to be a man of such a temper and abilities as suited his purposes; for he was naturally averse to quiet. He endeavoured to break the alliances of the duke of Mantua by various stratagems; but they did not succeed: the schemes of Olivarez and the intrigues of Feria being totally defeated. Our minister had soon after this another cause of mortification, on Richelieu's being created a duke and peer of France, and unanimously admitted among the Venetian nobility; which could not fail to be a severe stroke on Olivarez, who considered him as his implacable enemy. The people at length began to see and be displeased with his conduct; and with reason, had they known it all, for it was in many instances cruel and detestable. Indeed the differences which at that time had so long subsisted between France and Spain were the effect of the private animosity between him and Richelieu. Things, however, so turned about, and Spain was so unusually successful, that the faults of the minister were overlooked for the time; but this unexpected good fortune had no other effect than that of making him far more insolent than ever. He was, in every instance, one of the most headstrong and obstinate men in the world: he had set his heart on the reduction of Cafal in Italy, and he was determined on it at whatever hazard; this foolish enterprise was, however, unaccountably defeated, and the Spanish army experienced a total defeat. The revolt of the Catalans, whom he wished to deprive of their privileges, was the next consequence of his folly: he had privately employed the marquis de los Velez to extinguish this rebellion; but the cruelty of the measures used for this purpose only inflamed it more. The revolution of Portugal, another disastrous event, was also the result of his obstinacy and rigour. This series of ill fortune, which ought to have opened the eyes of the Catholic king and his ministers, seemed to infatuate both. The great secret by which Olivarez had governed his matters was being the companion, or at least the confidant, of his pleasures. While he affected to deceive the world with a specious appearance of religion and piety, he was not only immersed in vice himself, but encouraged and promoted it in his prince, to the scandal of his subjects, and the prejudice of his affairs. At this time, of all others the most improper, Olivarez produced a bastard of his, hitherto called Julian; he had taken to little care of this son, that, not able to subsist in Spain, he had passed over to the Indies, where, in very mean stations, he had scarcely got bread. On him he now bestowed the name of Don Henrico de Guzman; and bringing him with great pomp and splendour to court, either flattered or forced the constable of Castile to give him his daughter; in consideration of which alliance he was to devolve upon him his duchy of St Lucar. In the beginning of his administration, by some accident or other, he presented to the king a memorial, in relation to an affair upon which his majesty had already received one from Don Balthasar de Zuniga: upon comparing them, they contradicted each other flatly. The king ordered a person of great quality to inquire thoroughly into this business; in consequence of which Don Balthasar's memorial appeared to be the truth, and that of Olivarez the reverse of it. The king was very angry; but the count regained his favour, by procuring for him the fair actress Calderone. By this woman he had a son, of whom no great notice was taken; but now, to obscure the folly of the count duke, this youth, scarce in the 14th year of his age, was produced, with the title of Don Juan of Austria, and declared generalissimo of the army against Portugal; while the heir apparent to the crown, Don Balthasar, was left under the tuition, or rather in the custody of the counsellors of Olivarez; at which conduct the queen was chagrined, the people enraged, and the world in general affronted. His schemes now began to be entirely broken and defeated everywhere and in every kind; he fell under the displeasure of the queen, the emperor, the grandees, and the people all at once, and experienced the disgrace he had long merited. His ill fortune, which came upon him with the force of a torrent, did not, however, wholly overpower him; he was indeed obliged to conceal himself, in order to avoid the rage of the populace: but he had still confidence enough to offer an apology for his conduct, which possessed no inconsiderable share of wit and humour, well tempered with spirit and masterly reasoning. It was not, however, of any consequence to him; for he was banished to Toro, where, worn out by infirmities, or overcome by despair, he ended his days about the year 1645.

OLIVE

Pages 138-139

the fruit of the olive tree. See Olea, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. OLIVE Press. In order to obtain the olive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the olives are first bruised in a rough trough, under a mill-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, rolling perpendicularly over them; and when sufficiently mashed, put into the mave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trough, m, of an olive press, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">aa</a> are the upright beams, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>; b, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, and c, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw; f, the board on which the screw presses; g, a cubical piece of wood, called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>; h, the peel, a circular board, to be put under the block. By <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the screw, all the liquid... Olive Oil Liquor is pressed out of the mashed olives, and is called virgin oil; after which, hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> being poured upon the remainder in the press, a coarser oil is obtained. Olive oil keeps only about a year, after which it degenerates. OLIVE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

OLIVET

Pages 139-139
or Mount of Olives, in Ancient Geography, was situated to the east of the city of Jerusalem, and parted from the city only by the brook Kidron, and by the valley of Jehoshaphat, which stretches out from the north to the south. It was upon this mount that Solomon built temples to the gods of the Ammonites (1 Kings xi. 7.) and of the Moabites, out of complacence to his wives, who were natives of these nations. Hence it is that the mount of Olives is called the mountain of corruption (2 Kings xxiii. 13.). Josephus says, that this mountain is at the distance of five stadia, or furlongs, from Jerusalem, which make 625 geometrical paces, or the length of a Sabbath-day's journey, says St Luke (Acts i. 12.). The mount of Olives had three summits, or was composed of three several mountains, ranged one after another from north to south. The middle summit is that from whence our Saviour ascended into heaven. It was upon that towards the south that Solomon built temples to his idols. The summit which is most to the north is distant two furlongs from the middlemost. This is the highest of the three, and is commonly called Galilee. In the time of King Uzziah, the mount of Olives was so shattered by an earthquake, that half of the earth that was on the western side fell down, and rolled four furlongs or 500 paces from thence, towards the mountain which was opposite to it on the east; so that the earth blocked up the highways, and covered the king's gardens. Mr Maudrell tells us that he and his company going out of Jerusalem at St Stephen's gate, and crossing the valley of Jehoshaphat, began immediately to ascend the mountain; that being got above two-thirds of the way up, they came to certain grottoes cut with intricate windings and caverns under ground, which were called the sepulchres of the prophets; that a little higher up were twelve arched vaults under ground, standing side by side, and built in memory of the apostles, who are said to have compiled their creed in this place; that 60 paces higher they came to the place where Christ is said to have uttered his prophecy concerning the final destruction of Jerusalem; and a little on the right hand, to another, where he is said to have dictated a second time the Lord's prayer to his disciples; that somewhat higher is the cave of a faint called Pelagia; a little above that, a pillar denoting the place where an angel gave the Blest Virgin three days warning of her death; and at the top of all, the place of our blest Lord's ascension.

OLIVETAN

Pages 139-139

Robert, related to the famous Calvin, printed at Neuchâtel in 1535, in folio, a version of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> into French, the first which had been translated from the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Greek. It is written in an uncouth and barbarous style, and is far from being faithful. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in which it is printed are Gothic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of it is no less so. It is valued only because it is rare. Calvin is thought to have had a very considerable share in this translation. Olivetan survived his publication but a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; for he was poisoned at Rome the year after, of which his translation is alleged to have been the cause. Olivetan's Bible, revised by John Calvin and N. Malinger, was reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, in 1540, in quarto. This edition is still rarer than the former. It is called the Bible de l'Époque, because the printer had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> for his sign.

OLIVIER

Pages 139-139
Claude Matthieu, advocate of the parliament of Aix, was born at Marseille in 1701, and appeared at the bar with eclat. He had a chief hand in the establishment of the academy of Marseille, and was one of its original members. He possessed a quick and lively genius. A few hours retirement from society and from his pleasures were frequently sufficient to enable him to speak and write, even on important causes; but his works commonly bore marks of haste. Given to excel in every thing, he would employ a fortnight in studying the Code and the Digest, or in storing his mind with the beauties of Demosthenes, Homer, Cicero, or Boëtius; and then abandon himself for another fortnight, frequently a whole month, to a life of frivolity and dilapidation. He died in 1736, at the age of 35. He published, 1. L'Histoire de Philippe roi de Macédoine, et père d'Alexandre le Grand, 2 vols 12mo. No writer has so ably handled the history of the age of Philip, the interests of the different nations of Greece, and their manners and customs: but the conduct of the work is extremely defective. The digressions are too frequent, and often tedious. The style is in no respect suitable to a history. It is in general dry, unconnected, and like the style of a dissertation. Sometimes, however, we find in it passages full of fire and beauty, and turns of expression truly original. A disease of the brain, with which he was attacked, and under which he laboured several years, prevented him from putting his last hand to the work. 2. Mémoire sur les secours donnés aux Romains par les Marseillais pendant la 2de Guerre Punique. 3. Memoire sur les secours donnés aux Romains par les Marseillais durant la Guerre contre les Gaulois.

OLMUTZ

Pages 139-139

a town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, with a bishop's see, and a famous university. The public buildings are very handsome, particularly the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. It is a populous, trading, and very strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and yet it was taken, with the whole garrison, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1741. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1758 he besieged it again; and when he had almost taken the place he was obliged to raise the siege, to go and meet the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is seated on the river Morava. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 25', N. Lat. 49° 30'.

OLYMPIA

Pages 139-141

Maldachini Donna, a woman of a very uncommon character. She flourished about the middle of the 17th century. She was sister-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to Pope Innocent X. and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to acquire an unlimited power over this vain, weak, and injudicious ecclesiastic. Her son Camillo was promoted to the cardinalate, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Pamphilio; but falling in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with the princess Rosiana, a beautiful young widow, he laid aside his hat, and married. The crime, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was one, was esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in general at least venial. The pope, however, was displeased; and Olympia procured their banishment, being afraid lest her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>-in-law should lessen her authority in the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. This authority, equally unnatural and uncommon, reflected neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> on her who held it, nor on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who allowed her to hold it. Such elevated situations, Olympia's situations, however, whether they are the reward of merit, the effect of chance, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acquired by cunning, are seldom very secure. Olympia, who had procured the disgrace of many who did not deserve it, and who had herself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> merited such a fate, at length experienced both disgrace and banishment. This was obtained by means of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Panzirollo, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> favourite of the pope's. The immediate cause of it was this: The pope had determined, in order to lessen his own trouble, to adopt a nephew, and to make him a Cardinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">Patron</a>, in order to give audience to ambassadors and ministers, and in his absence to preside at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. For this purpose, at the recommendation of his favourite, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> made choice of Affalli, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the marquis Affalli, who had married a niece of Olympia. Olympia indeed was slightly consulted on the affair, and showed no disapprobation of the appointment. The pope, however, no sooner got him fixed in his new office, than he showed his own weakness by repenting of it. Olympia too was displeased, and by her solicitations procured the disgrace of Affalli, before had enjoyed either the honours or emoluments of his office. Panzirollo, however, soon managed matters so as to turn the scales: he prevailed on the pope again to countenance and honour Affalli; and, what was more, had influence sufficient to persuade him to disgrace Olympia, and to banish her court. She had indeed abused her authority in a most scandalous manner, and had gained such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> ascendant over the pope, that in everything his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> had been subservient to her dictates.—Her avarice and ambition were unbounded: she disposed of all benefices, which were kept vacant till she fully informed herself of their value: she rated an office of 1000 crowns for three years, at one year's revenue, and if for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, at 12 years purchase, one half of which sum she required to be paid in advance: she gave audience upon public affairs, enacted new laws, abrogated those of former popes, and sat in council with Innocent, with bundles of memorials in her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It was generally said that they lived together in a criminal correspondence, and that she had charmed him by some secret incantation. In the Protestant countries the loves and intrigues of Innocent and Donna Olympia were represented upon the stage; and fevere sarcasms were daily put into the hands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASQUIN">Pasquin</a> at Rome.—As she had usurped such an absolute authority, the new cardinal nephew <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of ruining her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; he therefore seconded the endeavours of Panzirollo.—He intimated to the pope, that his reputation had suffered greatly among the Catholics by her scandalous proceedings, and that his nuncios were treated with disrespect and contempt at the courts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Upon these representations, Innocent at length, but with great reluctance, banished Olympia, and was reconciled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Camillo and the princess Roffano; though some authors affirm that her banishment was no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> retreat, and that she still in private directed the affairs of the pope. A woman of Olympia's character, however, with such unbounded ambition, such an extravagant lust for power, and such an ambitious desire of wealth, and who had once possessed so great an ascendancy over such a man as Innocent, was not to be so easily put off. She was banished in 1650; but in 1653, she again assumed the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of affairs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as before her disgrace. She again accomplished the disgrace of Affalli, and procured the promotion of Azzolini to the office of secretary of the briefs. In 1654, his holiness resigned himself entirely into the hands of this affuming woman; who, observing his infirmities daily increasing, redoubled her rapacity, disposing of benefices to the highest bidders in all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. She was again, however, in hazard of being displaced by a new favourite, viz. the cardinal de Retz; and had not the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> prevented it, it would in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> quickly have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. During his last illness he received nothing but from the hands of Donna Olympia, who was at great pains to prolong his life, watched continually at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> side, and prevented the ambassadors or others from disturbing him with discourses upon business. She is said, during the last ten days of his life, when he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of reason, to have amassed about half a million of crowns. She did not find the succeeding pope (Alexander VII.) so easy to be played upon as his weak predecessor: a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of memorials were sent in against her, and his holiness was well disposed to attend to them: he ordered her to retire from Rome, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> began to examine witnesses reflecting her conduct. She was cut off, however, before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> was finished, by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which, in 1656, afflicted Rome and its neighbourhood. Her estate was not confiscated as was generally expected; and the prince Pamphilio was allowed to succeed her. The pope only referred for his own relations about a million of crowns. Olympia, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Pifatius (Strabo); so called from the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; described by Strabo, "as the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympus, before which stands a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of wild olive trees, in which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, or foot-course, so called because the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; and by which the Alpheus, coming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, runs." Olympia, however, was famous not merely for the temple of Jupiter, but also for a temple of Juno, 63 feet long, with columns round it of the Doric order; and a Metroum or temple of the mother of the gods, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Doric edifice; with holy treasuries. There, and the porticoes, a gymnastum, prytaneum, and many more buildings, chiefly in the enclosure, with the houses of the priests and other inhabitants, made Olympia no inconsiderable place. The stadium was in the grove of wild olive trees, before the great temple; and near it was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">hippodrome</a> or course for the races of horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>. The Alpheus flowed by from Arcadia with a copious and very pleasant stream, which was received on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> by the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The temple of Jupiter was of the Doric order, 68 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> to the pediment, 95 wide, and 230 long; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> encompassed with columns. It was erected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> not of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> baked, but of Pentelic marble; the slabs disposed as tiles; the way to it up a winding staircase. The two pediments were enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; and one had over the centre a statue of Victory gilded; and underneath a votive buckler of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. At each corner was a gilded vase. Above the columns were fixed 21 gilded bucklers, offered at the conclusion of the Achaean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> by the Roman general Mummius. The gates in the two fronts were Olympia, were of brafs, and over them were carved the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. Within the cell were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> colonnades, between which was the approach to the image. The Jupiter of Olympia was accounted alone sufficient to immortalize its maker, Phidias. It was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and gold, the head crowned with olive. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> was a statue of Victory; in the left a flowered sceptre, composed of various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, on which was an eagle. The sandals were of gold, as also the vestment, which was curiously embossed with lilies and animals. The throne was gold inlaid with ebony and ivory, and studded with jewels, intermixed with paintings and exquisite figures in relievo. The pillars between the feet contributed to its support. Before it were walls, serving as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, decorated principally with the exploits of Hercules; the portion opposite to the door of a blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It was the office of a family descended from Phidias, called phœdruntres or the polibiers, to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> bright and clean. The veil or curtain was cloth rich with the purple dye of Phoenicia and with Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, an offering of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Antiochus, and was let down from above by looening the strings. The image impressed on the spectator an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it was higher and wider than it measured. Its magnitude is such, that though the temple was very large, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> seemed to have erred in the proportions. The god, fitting, nearly touched the ceiling with his head; suggesting an idea, that if he were to rise up, he would destroy the roof. A part of the pavement before it was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, enclosed in a rim of Parian or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, where they poured <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> to preserve the ivory. The altar of Jupiter Olympius was of great antiquity, and composed of ashes from the thighs of the victims, which were carried up and confused in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> with wood of the white poplar tree. The ashes also of the prytaneum, in which a perpetual fire was kept on a hearth, were removed annually on a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and spread on it, being first mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the Alpheus. The cement, it was affirmed, could be made with that fluid only; and therefore this river was much respected, and esteemed the most friendly of any to the god. On each side of the altar were stone steps. Its height was 22 feet. Girls and women, when allowed to be at Olympian, were suffered to ascend the bafe- ment, which was 125 feet in circumference. The people of Elis sacrificed daily, and private persons as often as they chose. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> flourished at Olympia, and many deities were worshipped besides Jupiter. Paulanias has enumerated above 60 altars of various shapes and kinds. One of the unknown gods stood by the great altar. The people of Elis offered on all these monthly; laying on them boughs of olive; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> incense, and wheat mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and pouring libations of such liquors as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> prescribed. At the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> sometimes a form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> was used, and they sung hymns composed in the Doric dialect. Olympia was situated on an eminence, between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called Offa and Olympus. Though its ancient splendour is gone, the place reminds the traveller of what it once was. It is in the Morea, being now a small place called Longinico, 50 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>, in E. Long. 22° 5' N. Lat. 37° 40'.

OLYMPIAD

Pages 141-141

the space of four years, whereby the Greeks reckoned <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.—The first Olympiad fell, according to the accurate and learned computation of some of the moderns, exactly 776 years before the first year of Christ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 775 before the year of his birth, in the year of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> 3938, and 22 years before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome. The games were exhibited at the time of the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> next after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice; therefore the Olympiads were of unequal length, because the time of the full moon differs 11 days every year, and for that reason they sometimes began the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the solstice, and at other times four weeks after. The computation by Olympiads ceased, at some supposal, after the 304th, in the year 440 of the Christian era. It was universally adopted not only by the Greeks, but by many of the neighbouring countries; though still the Pythian games served as an epoch to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> and to the Boeotians; the Nemean games to the Argives and Arcadians; and the Isthmian to the Corinthians and the inhabitants of the Peloponnesian isthmus. To the Olympiads <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is much indebted. They have served to fix the time of many momentous events; and indeed before this method of computing time was observed, every page of history is mostly fabulous, and filled with obscurity and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>, and no true chronological account can be properly established and maintained with certainty.

OLYMPIAS

Pages 141-141

a celebrated woman, who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Epirus, and who married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, by whom she had Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. Her haughtiness, and more probably her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, obliged Philip to repudiate her, and to marry Cleopatra, the niece of King Attalus. Olympias was sensible of this injury, and Alexander showed his disapprobation of his father's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, by retiring from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to his mother. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Philip, which soon followed this disgrace, and which some have attributed to the intrigues of Olympias, was productive of the greatest extravagancies. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> paid the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to her husband's murderer. She gathered his mangled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, placed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> on his head, and laid his ashes near those of Philip. The administration of Alexander, who had succeeded his father, was in some instances offensive to Olympias; but when the ambition of her son was concerned, she did not scruple to declare publicly that Alexander was not the son of Philip, but that he was the offspring of an enormous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> who had supernaturally introduced himself into her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. When Alexander was dead, Olympias seized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Macedonia; and, to establish her usurpation, she cruelly put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> Arrideus, with his wife Eurydice, as also Nicanor the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDER">Cassander</a>, with 100 leading men of Macedon, who were inimical to her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Such barbarities did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> remain unpunished: Cassander besieged her in Pydna, where she had retired with the remains of her family, and she was obliged to surrender after an obstinate siege. The conqueror ordered her to be accused, and to be put to death. A body of 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were ordered to put the bloody commands into execution, but the splendour and majesty of the queen disarmed their courage; and she was at last massacred by those whom she had cruelly deprived of their children, about 316 years before the Christian era.

OLYMPIC GAMES

Pages 141-143

were solemn games among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks, so called from Olympian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, to whom they were dedicated; and by some said to be first instituted by him, after his victory over the sons of Titan; others ascribe their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, not the son of Alcmena, but one of much greater antiquity; others to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELOPS">Pelops</a>; and others to Hercules the son of Alcmena. By whomsoever they were instituted, we know that, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> rather early, they had fallen into disuse. The wars which prevailed among the Greeks, for a while, totally interrupted the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies and exhibitions with which they had been accustomed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> gods and heroes; but the Olympic games were restored on the following occasion. Amidst the calamities which afflicted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> threatened <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, Iphitus, a descendant of Oxylos, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Eleia had fallen in the general partition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, applied to the Delphic oracle. The priests of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, ever disposed to favour the views of kings and legislators, answered agreeably to his wish, that the festivals anciently celebrated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, on the Alpheus, must be renewed, and an armistice proclaimed for all the states willing to partake of them, and desirous to avert the vengeance of heaven. Fortified by this authority, and assisted by the advice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, Iphitus took <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, not only for restoring the Olympic solemnity, but for rendering it perpetual. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> of the oracle was speedily diffused through the remotest parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> by the numerous votaries who frequented the sacred shrine. The armistice was proclaimed in Eleia for exhibiting shows and performing sacrifices. In the heroic ages, feats of bodily strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> were destined to the honour of deceased warriors; hymns and sacrifices were offered for the gods; but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> texture of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, easily confounding the expressions of respectful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and pious veneration, enabled Iphitus to unite both in his new institution. The festival, which lasted five days, began and ended with a sacrifice to Olympian Jove. The intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was chiefly filled up by the gymnastic exercises, in which all freemen of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> were invited to contend, provided they had been born in lawful wedlock, and had lived untainted by any infamous immoral stain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the entertainment was made in the gymnasium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, a spacious edifice, surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> range of pillars, with an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> in the middle. Adjoining were various apartments, containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and other conveniences for the combatants. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was gradually adorned with porticoes, shady walks and groves, interfering with feats and benches; the whole originally destined to relieve the fatigues and anxiety of the candidates for Olympic fame; and frequented in later times, by sophists and philosophers, who were fond to contemplate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and communicate knowledge, in those delightful retreats. The order of the athletic exercises, or combats, was established by Lycurgus, and corresponded almost exactly to that described by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, in the 23rd book of the Iliad, and eighth of the Odyssey. Iphitus, we are told, appointed the other ceremonies and entertainments; settled the regular return of the festival at the end of every fourth year, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>; and gave to the whole solemnity that form and arrangement, which it preserved with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> above a thousand years; a period exceeding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the most famous kingdoms and republics of antiquity. Among the benefactors of Olympia, at a much later period, was reckoned Herod, who was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Judea.
