Seeing, on his way to Rome, the games neglected or dwindling into insignificance from the poverty of the Eleans, he displayed vast munificence as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and provided an ample revenue for their future support and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The care and management of the Olympics belonged for the most part to the Eleans; who on that account enjoyed their possessions without molestation, or fear of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> or violence. They appointed a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of judges, who were to take care that those who offered themselves as competitors should perform their preparatory exercises; and these judges, during the solemnity, sat naked, having before them a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of victory, formed of wild olive, which was presented to whomsoever they adjudged it. Those who were conquerors were called Olympionikes, and were loaded with honours by their countrymen. At these games women were not allowed to be present; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any woman was found, during the solemnity, to have passed the river Alpheus, she was to be thrown headlong from a rock. This, however, was sometimes neglected; for we find not only women present at the celebration, but also some among the combatants, and some rewarded with the crown. The preparations for these festivals were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. No person was permitted to enter the lists, if he had not regularly exercised himself ten months before the celebration at the public gymnasium of Elis. No unfair dealings were allowed; whoever attempted to bribe his adversary was subjected to a severe fine; and even the father and relations were obliged to swear that they would have recourse to no artifice which might decide the victory in favour of their friends. No criminals, nor such as were connected with impious and guilty persons, were suffered to present themselves as combatants. The wrestlers were appointed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Some little balls <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> were thrown into a silver urn, and such as drew the same letter were obliged to contend one with the other. He who had an odd letter remained the last; and he often had the advantage, as he was to encounter the last who had obtained the superiority over his adversary. In these games were exhibited running, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, wrestling, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">boxing</a>, and the throwing of the quoit, which was called altogether πυγμαχία, or quinquarium. Besides these, there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and chariot races, and also contentions in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, eloquence, and the fine arts. The only reward that the conqueror obtained was a crown of olive. This, as some suppose, was in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the labours of Hercules, which were accomplished for the universal good of mankind, and for which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> claimed no other reward but the consciousness of having been the friend of mankind. So small and trifling a reward stimulated courage and virtue, and was the source of greater honours than the most unbounded treasures. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the conquerors, called Olympionikes, were erected at Olympia in the sacred wood of Jupiter. Their return home was that of a warlike conqueror; they were drawn in a chariot by four horses, and everywhere received with the greatest acclamations. Their entrance into their native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was not through the gates; to make it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and more solemn, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> was made in the walls. Painters and poets were employed in celebrating their names; and indeed the victories Olympus, victories severally obtained at Olympia are the subjects of the most beautiful odes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. The combatants were naked. A scarf was originally tied round their waist; but when it had entangled one of the adversaries, and been the cause that he lost the victory, it was laid aside, and no regard was paid to decency. The Olympic games were observed every fifth year, or, to speak with greater exactness, after a revolution of four years, and in the first month of the fifth year, and they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for five successive days. As they were the most ancient and most solemn of all the festivals of the Greeks, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not appear wonderful, that they drew so many people, not only inhabitants of Greece, but of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and countries. Such is the account of Grecian writers, who have, doubtless, often ascribed to positive institution many inventions and usages naturally resulting from the progressive manners of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. When we come to examine the Eleusinian games in their more improved state, together with the innumerable imitations of them in other provinces of Greece, there will occur reasons for believing, that many regulations, referred by an easy solution to the legislative wisdom of Iphitus or Lycurgus, were introduced by time or accident, continued through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, improved by repeated trials, and confirmed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of their utility. Yet such an institution as the Olympiad, even in its least perfect form, must have been attended with manifest advantages to society. It is sufficient barely to mention the suspension of hostilities which took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, not only during the celebration of the festival, but a considerable time both before and after it. Considered as a religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, at which the whole Grecian name was invited, and even enjoined, to assist, it was well adapted to facilitate intercourse, to promote knowledge, to soften <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, and to hasten the progress of civilization and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. Greece, and particularly Peloponnesus, was the centre from which the adventurous spirit of its inhabitants had diffused innumerable colonies through the surrounding nations. To these widely separated communities, which, notwithstanding their common origin, seemed to have lost all connexion and correspondence, the Olympiad served as a common bond of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> and point of reunion. The celebrity of this festival continually attracted to it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> most distinguished for genius and enterprise, whose fame would have otherwise been unknown and lost in the boundless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of Grecian territory. The remote inhabitants, not only of European Greece, but of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, being assembled to the worship of common gods, were formed to the sense of a general <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and excited to the pursuit of national honour and prosperity. Strangers of similar dispositions might confirm in Elis the sacred and indissoluble ties of hospitality. If their communities were endangered by any barbarous power, they might here solicit assistance from their Grecian brethren. On other occasions they might explain the benefits which, in peace or war, their respective countries were best qualified to communicate. And the Olympic festival might thus serve the purpose of resident ambassadors, and other institutions alike unknown to antiquity.

OLYMPUS

Pages 143-143

the name of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.—One bounding Bithynia on the south.—Another in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, on whose top was a temple of Venus, which women were not permitted either to enter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to fee (Strabo).—A third, Olympus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a> (Livy).—A fourth, of Lycia, with a noble cognominal town, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> (Strabo, Cicero), extinct in Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, there remaining only a citadel: the town was destroyed by P. Servilius Isauricus (Florus), having been the retreat of pirates. From this mountain there was an extensive prospect of Lycia, Pamphylia, and Pisidia (Strabo).—A fifth, Olympus of Mytilene (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); thence furred Olympus, anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; one of the highest mountains, and furrowed Mytus (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>); situated on the Propontis, and thence extending more inland.—A sixth, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Thessaly, or on the confines of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the giants (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Horace, Seneca); reckoned the highest in the whole world, and to exceed the flight of birds (Apuleius), which is the reason of its being called heaven, than which nothing is higher: the ferocity and calmness which reign there are celebrated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Lucan, and Claudian.

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledons; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OMAR IBN AL KHATTAB

Pages 143-144

successor of Abu Bekr.—The Mohammedan imposture, like every other fallacy of its kind, copies after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> as far as was thought convenient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proper; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, it was to be expected that all pretences to that should assume at least the appearances of them. Few systems of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> are more absurd than Mohammed's; yet, though he disclaimed miracles, it was supported, as we are told by latter writers, by a variety of them, which, however, unfortunately for the creed they were contrived to support, are too trifling, absurd, and contradictory, to deserve the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. They tell us, but upon grounds too vague and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> to command <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, that Omar was miraculously converted to this faith: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> he is reported to have been, before this event, truly respectable, and in particular a violent opponent of the Arabian prophet. Mohammed, it seems, felt this opposition, and regretted it; he therefore, with the fervour, and as it happened, with the success of a true prophet, according to his followers' account, prayed for the conversion of this his dangerous antagonist. Omar, it is said, had no sooner read the 20th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Koran than he was convinced: upon which he instantly repaired to Mohammed and his followers, and declared his conversion. It is said, that at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he intended to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> the prophet; and various causes are assigned for the prevention of this shocking piece of sacrilege. After his wonderful conversion, the Mohammedan writers inform us that he was named Al Faruk, or the "divider;" because, say they, when a certain Moflem was condemned by Mohammed for his iniquitous treatment of a Jew, and appealed afterwards from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the prophet to Omar, he cut him in two with his scimitar, for not acquiescing in the decision of so upright a judge: which circumstance when Mohammed heard, he gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Al Faruk, or "the divider;" because, by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, he had shown himself capable of perfectly distinguishing between truth and falsehood. Al Kodai affirms, that 39 of Omar's adherents followed his example the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he professed himself a votary of Mohammed. The conversion of Hamza and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMAR_EBN_AL_KHATTAB">Omar Ebn Al Khattab</a> happened in the year preceding the first flight of the Moles into Ethiopia, or the fourth year of Mohammed's mission, according to Abulfeda. He was unquestionably a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> acquisition to the prophet, and enabled him to carry on his schemes to far more purpose than he could possibly have done without him, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his enemy. Omar at length found his services in the cause he had undertaken sufficiently honoured and amply rewarded; for on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Abu Beir, who had succeeded the impostor himself, he was promoted to the regal and pontifical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> first assigned him was the caliph of the caliph of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of God; or in other words the successor of the successor of Mohammed: but the Arabs considering that this title, by the addition to be annexed to it at the accession of every future caliph, would be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, they, by universal consent, saluted him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>; which illustrious title, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> conferred on Omar, descended afterwards to all the successors of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Our readers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not expect us to follow the caliph with minute exactness through the transactions of his reign. This would indeed swell our article beyond all proportion. We shall therefore confine ourselves to some of the leading facts. His arms appear to have been particularly successful; the Persians he conquered, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> submitted to his power; nor does he appear to have been checked in a single instance. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, however, of his success, an attempt was made to assassinate him. The fact is thus related: Wathak Ebn Mofafer, a resolute young Arab, was procured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ghafsan, and sent to Medina for this very purpose. Some time after his arrival, observing Omar to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> asleep under a tree on which he had placed himself, so as not to be discovered by any person, he drew his dagger, and was upon the point of stabbing him, when, lifting up his eyes, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a lion walking round about him, and licking his feet. Nor did the lion cease to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the caliph till he awoke; but then instantly went away. This phenomenon struck Wathak with a profound reverence for Omar, whom he now revered as the peculiar care of heaven. He therefore came <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the tree, on which the lion had forced him to remain, kissed the caliph's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, confessed his crime, and embraced the Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; being so strongly affected with the wonderful deliverance he had been an eye witness of. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, however, was at length ended by assassination; for about two years after the conclusion of the Nohawandian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in which the Arabs probably still farther extended their conquests, though no account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations during that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> has reached us, that is, in the 23rd year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, according to Abu Jaafar Al Tabari, the caliph Omar Ebn Al Khattab was assassinated by a Persian slave; of which horrid fact the Arab writers have handed down the following particulars: Abu Luluah, a Persian of the Magian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, whose name was Firuz, one of Al Mogheira Ebn Al Shabab's slaves, was obliged by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to pay daily two dirhems, in conformity to the Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, for the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of this religion. Firuz resenting this treatment, complained of it to the caliph, and desired that some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> at least of the tribute exacted of him might be remitted; but this favour being refused by Omar, the Persian threatened his destruction; which he soon after effected, by stabbing him thrice in the belly with a dagger, while he was in the mosque at Medina performing his morning devotions. The Arabs then present perceiving that the villain had imbrued his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the blood of their sovereign, immediately rushed upon him; but he made so desperate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, that he wounded 13 of the assailants, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of them mortally. At last one of the caliph's attendants threw his vest over him, and seized him; upon which he stabbed himself and soon after expired. According to Theophanes, this Firuz was an apostate or renegade, and consequently had before embraced the Mohammedan religion; but this assertion is by no means probable; because on his becoming a convert to Islamism, he must have been unmindful of his master, and on his relapsing into Magism, he would have been put to death by the caliph's order: neither of which particulars are consistent with what we find related by the Arab historians, and even by our Greek chronicographer himself. Omar languished three days and then died, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of Dhul'Hajja, and the 23rd year of the Hegira, which began in the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 643. Authors are not agreed with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of his caliphate. The Arab historians, whom we are inclined to follow, say that he reigned between 10 and 11 years. Theophanes affirms, that he was murdered in the 12th year of his caliphate, and Dionysius Telmarchus extends the length of his reign to 12 complete years. Only one of the wounds given him by Firuz was mortal, and that he received under his navel. At his death he was 63 years old; which, as we are told by an Arab author, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Mohammed himself, Abu Beir, and Ayesha, one of the prophet's wives, when they died. When Omar fell in the mosque, Abd'alrahman Ebn Awf, one of Mohammed's first converts, supplied his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> during the remainder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; and three days before his death, Sahib Ebn Tarif, at his command, officiated for him. His body was interred in Ayesha's apartment, near that of the prophet Mohammed. We are informed by Eutychius, that during his caliphate he performed the pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times. His extensive conquests made the Moles empire one of the most powerful and formidable monarchies in the world. His disposition is represented to us, with evident partiality indeed, as one of the best possible, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> has always been highly extolled.

OMB

Pages 144-145

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, afterwards called Arsinoe and Crocodilopolis, was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of one of the nomes into which that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was divided, and is remarkable, in the annals of idolatry, for the hatred of its inhabitants to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of their neighbours the citizens of Tentyra. The genius of paganism was so complying with respect to the objects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, that although each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, each city, and almost every family, had its own tutela—god, we know not a single instance, out of Egypt, of one tribe of Pagans persecuting another for worshipping gods different from theirs. The Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were indeed persecuted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, not however for worshipping the true God, but because, together with him, they would not worship <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, Juno, and all the rabble of heathen divinities. The reason of the almost universal tolerance of ideologues to one another, and of the intolerance of all to the Jews and Christians, is very obvious. Not a single Pagan, a very few philosophers perhaps excepted, ever thought of paying his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to the Supreme and self-existent Being, but to inferior divinities, to whom it was supposed that the care of particular persons, families, cities, and nations was configned by the God of the universe. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that, as no person denied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of his neighbour's object of worship, an intercommunity of gods was everywhere admitted, and all joined occasionally in adoring the gods of the various nations. By the Jews and Christians this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> was rejected as in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> impious; and it could not well be maintained between the citizens of Ombi and those of Tentyra. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> were worshipped in Egypt is universally known (See Polytheism); and Diodorus the Sicilian informs us, in a passage quoted by Eulæus*, that "the cities and nomes of Egypt being at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prone to rebellion, and to enter into conspiracies against monarchical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, one of their most politic kings contrived to introduce into the neighbouring nomes the worship of different animals; so that while each reverenced the deity which itself held sacred, and despised that which its neighbours had consecrated, they could hardly be brought to join cordially in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to the disturbance of the government." In this distribution of gods he conferred upon Ombi the crocodile, and upon Tentyra, the mortal enemy of that monster, the ichneumon. The consequence of which was, that while the Ombites worshipped the crocodile, the Tentyrites took every opportunity of slaughtering him, insomuch that, according to Strabo, the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of an inhabitant of Tentyra put the crocodile to flight. This, we confess, is a very improbable fact; but it is certain that the mutual hatred of those cities, on account of their hostile gods, rose to such a height, that whenever the inhabitants of the one were engaged in the more solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of their religion, those of the other were sure to embrace the opportunity of setting fire to their houses, and rendering them every injury in their power to inflict. And what may, to a superficial thinker, appear extraordinary, though it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> excite no wonder in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of him who has studied mankind, this animosity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> between the inhabitants of the two cities <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the crocodile and ichneumon had lost their divinity. The conduct of the Egyptian monarch was admirably calculated for preventing the nation from combining against the government; and it extended its influence over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Diodorus informs us, that he assigned to each nome an animal to worship, which was hated, killed, and sometimes fed upon by the inhabitants of the neighbouring nome; and we know upon higher authority than his, that the Israelites could not offer sacrifices in Egypt, because the bullock was deemed sacred over the whole country.

OMBRE

Pages 145-146

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, borrowed from the Spaniards, and played by two, by three, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by five persons, but generally by three. When three play at this game, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cards are dealt to each party; the whole ombre pack being only 40: because the eights, nines, and tens, are thrown out of the pack. There are two sorts of counters for stakes, the greater and the lesser; the last having the same proportion to the other as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> to a threepenny: of the greater counters each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> stakes one for the game; and one of the lesser for passing for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, when eldest, and for every card taken in. As to the order and value of the cards, the ace of spades, called *joadillo*, is always the highest trump, in whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the trump be; the manille, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> duce, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; and the bello, or ace of clubs, is always the third: the next in order is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, the six, the five, four, and three. Of the black there are 11 trumps; of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, 12. The least small cards of the red are always the belt, and the most of the black; except the duce and red seven, both of which are called the maniller, and are always second when the red is a trump. The red ace, when a trump, enters into the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is called *punto*; otherwise it is only called an ace. The three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cards are called *matadores*; which have this privilege, that they are not obliged to attend an inferior trump when it leads; but for want of a small trump, the person may renounce trumps, and play any other card; and when these are all in the same hand, the others pay three of the greater counters a-piece; and with these three for a foundation, he may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> as many matadores as he has cards in an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of trumps; for all which the others are to pay one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> a-piece. He who hath the first hand is called *ombre*, and has his choice of playing the game, of naming the trump, and of taking in as many and as few cards as he pleases; and after him the second, &c. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he does not name the trump before he looks on the cards he has taken in, any other may prevent him, by naming what trump he pleases. He that has the first hand should neither take in, nor play, unless he has at least three sure tricks in his hand; for, as he wins the game who wins most tricks, he that can win five of the nine has a sure game: which is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> if he wins four, and can so divide the tricks as that one person may win two, and the other three. If a person plays without discarding or changing any cards, this is called *playing sans prendre*; and if another win more tricks than he, he is said to *win codille*. The over-fights in the course of the game are called *beats*. And if the ombre wins all the nine tricks, it is called *winning the vote*. In ombre by five, which many, on account of its not requiring to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, prefer to that by three, only eight cards a-piece are dealt; and five tricks must be won, otherwise the ombre is beatified. Here the person who undertakes the game, after naming the trump, calls a king to his assistance; upon which the person in whose hand the king is, without discovering himself, is to assist him as a partner, and to share his fate. If, between both, they can make five tricks, the ombre wins two counters, and the auxiliary king only one; but when the counters are even, they divide them equally. If the ombre venture the game without calling in any king, this too is called *playing sans prendre*; in which case the other four are all against him, and he must win five tricks alone, or be beatified. The rest is much the same as by three. **OMBRE de soleil**, "Shadow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>," in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is when the sun is borne in armor, so as that the eyes, eyes, nose, and mouth, which at other times are represented, do not appear; and the colouring is thin, so that the field can appear through it.

OMBRIA

Pages 146-146

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of the pope, now called Spoleto and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>.

OMBRO

Pages 146-146
or LOMBRO, a town of Italy, in the duchy of Tuscany, and territory of the Sienoises, situated near the Tuscan sea, a little south of the lake of Caffignione, 45 miles south-west of Sienna.

OMBROMETER

Pages 146-146

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls. We have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of one in Phil. Trans. No. 473, p. 12. It consists of a tin funnel, whose surface is an inch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a flat board, and a glass tube set into the middle of it in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>. The rise of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the tube, whose capacity at different times must be measured and marked, shows the quantity of rain that has fallen.

OMELET

Pages 146-146
or AMLET, a kind of pancake or fricasse of eggs, with other ingredients, very usual in Spain and France. It may be made as follows: The eggs being beaten, are to be seasoned with salt and pepper, and then fried in butter made boiling hot; this done, gravy is to be poured on, and the whole stewed with chives and parsley shred small: when one side is fried enough, it is to be turned on the other.

OMEN

Pages 146-147

is a word which, in its proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a sign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indication of some future event, taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of a person speaking without any intent to prophecy. Hence Tully says, "Pythagorei non solum voces deorum observantur," sed etiam hominum, quae vocent omnia," "the Pythagoreans attend to the discourse not only of gods, but also of men, which they call omens." This sort of omen was supposed to depend much upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the person concerned in the event; whence the phrases accept omen, arripiat omen. Such were the original omens; but they were afterwards derived from things as well as from words. Thus Paternus, speaking of the head of Sulpicius on the rostrum, says it was velut omen imminentis proscriptio, "the omen of an impending proscription." Suetonius says of Augustus, that he believed implicitly in certain omens; and that, si mane fisci calcus perpetram, ac sinistris pro dextero induceretur, ut dirum, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his shoes were improperly put on in the morning, especially if the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> was put upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> foot, he held it for a bad omen." Omen was used in a still larger sense, to signify an augury; as in the following line of Tully: "Sic aquilae clarum fix- mavit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> omen?" "thus Jove confirmed the bright omen of the eagle?" It was lastly used, in the most generic sense of all, for a portent or prodigy; as in the third book of the Aeneid, where a myrtle torn up by Æneas dropped blood. Upon this appearance, says the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, Mihi frigidus horror Membra quatit, gelidique coit formidine sanguis. And the same thing being repeated upon his breaking a branch from another tree, he prayed to the gods to avert the omen. Multa movens animo Nymphas venerabat agrestes, Gradivumque patrem, Getici qui praedit feris, Iste fecundantem vitum, omneque levaret (A). The portentous or supernatural omens were either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> or internal. Of the former sort were those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of blood so frequently occurring in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which were much of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with this adventure of Æneas, which he calls monstra deum. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort were those sudden confusions, which, seizing upon men without any visible cause, were imputed to the agency of the god <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, and hence called panic fears. But indeed there was hardly anything, however trivial, from which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> did not draw omens. That it should have been thought a direful omen when any thing befell the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, altars, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the gods, need excite no wonder; but that the meeting of a eunuch, a negro, a bitch with whelps, or a snake lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, should have been looked upon as portending bad fortune, is a deplorable influence of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> weakness, and of the pernicious influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> on the mind. It is more than probable that this practice of making ordinary events ominous of good or bad fortune took its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of almost every superstition of paganism; but wherever it may have arisen, it spread itself over the whole inhabited globe, and at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> prevails in a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> among the vulgar of all nations. In England, it is reckoned a good omen, or a sign of future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> shines on a couple coming out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> after having been married. It is also esteemed a good sign if it rains whilst a corpse is burying: Happy is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> that the sun shines on; Happy is the corpse that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> rains on. To (A) Instead of translating these short quotations, we shall here give Dryden's version of the whole of this English reader, who alone can wish for a translation, together with its effects on the mind of the hero. It is as follows: Not far, a rising hillock stood in view; Sharp myrtles on the sides and corners grew. There, while I went to crop the Sylvan scenes, And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> our altar with their leafy greens, I pull'd a plant (with horror I relate) A prodigy so strange, and full of fate: The rooted fibres rose; and from the wound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> bloody drops distill'd upon the ground. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">Mute</a> and amaz'd, my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> with terror <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>; Fear shrunk my finews, and congeal'd my blood. Mann'd once again, another plant I try; That other gush'd with the same fanguine dye. Then, fearing guilt for some offence unknown, With prayers and vows the Dryads I atone, With all the fetters of the woods, and most The god of arms, who rules the Thracian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>: That they, or he, these omens would avert, Release our fears, and better signs impart. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a looking glass is extremely unlucky; the party to whom it belongs will lose his best friend. If, going a journey on business, a sow crosses the road, you will probably meet with a disappointment, if not a bodily accident, before you return home. To avert this, you must endeavour to prevent her crossing you; and if that cannot be done, you must ride round on fresh ground. If the sow is attended with her litter of pigs, it is lucky, and denotes a successful journey. It is unlucky to see first one magpie, and then more; but to see two, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> or merriment; three, a successful journey; four an unexpected piece of good news; five, you will shortly be in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. To kill a magpie, will certainly be punished with some terrible misfortune. If, in a family, the youngest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> should be married before her elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, they must all dance at her wedding without shoes: this will counteract their ill luck, and procure them husbands. If you meet a funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, or one passes by you, always take off your hat: this keeps all evil spirits attending the body in good humour. If, in eating, you miss your mouth, and the viands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, it is very unlucky, and denotes approaching sickness. It is lucky to put on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> the wrong side outwards: changing it alters the luck. When a person goes out to transact any important business, it is lucky to throw an old shoe after him. It is unlucky to present a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, scissors, razor, or any sharp or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, to one's mistress or friend, as they are apt to cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and friendship. To avoid the ill effects of this, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, a farthing, or some trifling recompense, must be taken. To find a knife or razor, denotes ill luck and disappointment to the party. In the Highlands of Scotland, it is thought unlucky if a person setting out upon a journey stumble over the threshold, or be obliged to return for anything forgotten. If a sportsman see any person stepping over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> rod, he expects but little success in that day's diversion. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SNEEZING">Sneezing</a> is also deemed ominous. If one sneeze when making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, a little of the straw or heath is taken out and thrown into the fire, that nothing may disturb the rest of the person who is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in the bed. Among the same people, success in any enterprise is believed to depend greatly upon the first creature that presents itself after the enterprise is undertaken. Thus, upon going to slumber, it is reckoned lucky to meet a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, but very unfortunate to see a hare, if the escape; and upon meeting any creature deemed unlucky, the best means of averting the omen is to roll a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> towards it. The Greeks attributed the same efficacy to the rolling of a stone, though they greatly preferred killing the ominous animal, that the evil portended might fall on its own head*. The motions and appearances of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago considered as certain signs by which the skilful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGHLANDER">Highlander</a> might attain to the knowledge of futurity. On the evening before new year's day, if a black cloud appeared in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the horizon, it was thought to prognosticate a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, a famine, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of some great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in that part of the country over which it should appear to set; and in order to ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> threatened by the omen, the motions of this cloud were often watched through the whole night, if it happened to continue so long visible above the horizon. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> in this superstition there are days, as well as words and events, which are deemed ominous of good or bad fortune. The first day of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, midsummer, and new year's day, are reckoned the most fortunate days in the year for accomplishing any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, ploughing, sowing, and reaping, are always begun on Tuesday, though the most favourable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> for these purposes be in this way frequently lost. That day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> on which the third of May falls, is deemed unlucky throughout the whole year. In Morven, none will upon any account dig <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">peat</a> or turf for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> on Friday; and it is reckoned unlucky to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> the people or cattle belonging to any family, and doubly so if the number be taken on Friday. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is also much attended to by the vulgar Highlanders. It is alleged, that during the increase things have a tendency to grow and stick together: and hence, in the isle of Sky, fences, which are there made of turf, are built only at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; whilst turf or peat for fuel are never, even in the most favourable weather, either made or stacked up but while the moon is in its wane. An <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> prevails in some places, that if a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> take fire during the increase of the moon, the family to which it belongs will prosper in the world; but that if the fire happen while the moon is in the decrease, the family will from that time decline in its circumstances, and sink into poverty. In attributing such influence to the moon, the superstitious Highlanders have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to agree with the philosophic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, who in his Georgics gives the following sage instructions to the husbandman: Ipsa dies alios alio dedit ordine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a> Felices, operum. Quintam fuge: * * * Septima <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> decimam felix et ponere viem, Et prensos domitare boves, et licta tela Addere: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONA">nona</a> fugae melior, contraria furtis. The lucky days in each revolving moon For labour choose: the fifth be sure to shun. * * * The seventh is next the tenth, the best to join Young oxen to the yoke, and plant the vine. Then weavers stretch your flays upon the weft: The ninth is good for travel, bad for theft.

OMENTUM

Pages 148-148
or **Epiloon**, the *Caul*, in Anatomy, a membranaceous part, usually furnished with a large quantity of fat; being placed under the peritoneum, and immediately above the intestines. See Anatomy, No 90.

OMOA

Pages 148-149

a Spanish town and fortification on the south side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a>, N. Lat. 15. 30. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 89. 50. from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> to the bay; and such is the depth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that ships of any burden may ride in the harbour with safety. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the utmost importance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, as the regal ships to and from Guatemala are sent to it in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The town was first established in 1751, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Antonio de Palma. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the inhabitants were about 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, 60 mulattoes and free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, and 200 slaves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> force consisted of about 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, besides officers. The fort was originally composed of sand confined in boarded coffers, and faced with half-burnt bricks. It was defended by 12 fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> 24 pounders mounted, four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> guns of different bores, and some field-pieces. The Spaniards sensible of the importance of the place, afterwards fortified it at an incredible expense, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of which the walls are built having been raised from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and brought from the distance of 20 leagues. The outworks were not completely finished in the year 1779, though 1000 men had then been employed upon them for 20 years. Towards the end of that year an expedition was undertaken against this fortress, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of one formed by the Spaniards against the British logwood cutters in the bay of Honduras and on the Moquito shore. The latter, finding themselves hard pressed by their enemies, applied to General Duilling, governor of Jamaica for assistance; who accordingly sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> to their relief under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Dalrymple, with necessary supplies of arms, ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. Before their arrival, however, the Spaniards had taken possession of St George's Key, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> settlement of the British in these parts, which they plundered, and took a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prisoners; but those who escaped, being joined by a body of their countrymen, retook it, and forced the enemy to retire. In the meantime Captain Dalrymple, who had been informed of the loss of the place, was hastening to the relief of the inhabitants, and in his way fell in with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Parker, who was in quest of some regal ships; but which, retreating into the harbour of Omoa, were too strongly protected by the fort there to be attacked by sea. As the Spaniards, however, had now been compelled to abandon St George's Key, it was proposed to unite the British forces by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and sea, and to attempt the conquest of this fortress. As the force under Captain Dalrymple was too inconsiderable to attempt the fort by land, it was augmented by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a> of the squadron and a strong party of the settlers; though, after all, it did not exceed the number of the garrison who opposed them. The troops were landed at about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles distance from the fort in the dusk of the evening, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> directly forward, in order to surprise and carry it by escalade in the night time. No <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, however, being found, they were obliged to explore their way through narrow foot-paths, morasses, and over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> so steep with precipices, that they were obliged, in order to avoid them, to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lights made of the cabbage tree. In consequence of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a> they were yet at a considerable distance from the fort, when the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> discovered them to the enemy. An engagement ensued, in which the Spaniards were quickly routed and driven into the town: from whence as they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to fire upon the British, it was found necessary to set fire to it, though very much against the inclination of the assailants. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the squadron took the opportunity, while the town was in flames, to come into the bay, and approach the fort with an intention to batter it; but the garrison returned the fire so briskly, that no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> could be made by that of the squadron, which was detained by want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from approaching sufficiently near. The troops then, being masters of the ground adjacent to the fort, erected several batteries in such situations as were most proper for annoying it; but though they carried on their operations with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> vigour, it was still found that heavier artillery than any they possessed would be requisite, the walls being no less than 18 feet in thickness; in consequence of which they resolved still to attempt the place by escalade. The attempt was made on the 21st of October, early in the morning. The troops entered the ditch, which fortunately for them happened to be dry, and fixed their scaling ladders against the walls, which were near 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Two seamen mounted first; and, with admirable courage and presence of mind, stood by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> which they had mounted, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> it till others ascended; ed; and boldly presented their pieces against a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> party drawn up to receive them, though they prudently retained their fire till their comrades came up. The squadron, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> near, kept up a heavy and continual fire upon the fort, while the Spaniards were struck with such surprize at the execellive celerity and boldness of the assailants, that they remained motionless and unable to oppose their enemies, notwithstanding the exhortation and example of their officers. From this panic they never recovered; and while the seamen and soldiers continued to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> the walls with amazing quickness, the Spaniards never made any effort to defend themselves. About 100 of them escaped over the walls on the opposite side of the fort; the remainder surrendered at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. The whole of this transaction reflected the highest lustre both on the conduct and courage of the British; and an instance of heroism is related in a British sailor to which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> affords nothing superior. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, having scaled the walls, had armed himself with a cutlass in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Thus armed, he met with a Spanish officer unarmed, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> roused from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. The generous tar scorned to take advantage of his condition, and therefore presented him with one of his own cutlasses saying, "You are now on a footing with me!" The officer, however, was too much struck with admiration at his conduct to accept the offer, and took care to make the circumstance sufficiently known. The value of the booty taken on this occasion amounted to three millions of dollars; but the loss most sensibly felt by the Spaniards was that of 250 quintals of quicksilver, a commodity indispensably necessary in extracting the precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> from their ores. They offered therefore to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> it at any price; but though the retention of it was far from affording a profit equal to that offered by the Spaniards, the British commanders absolutely refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with it, on account of the advantages the enemy would derive from having the metal in their possession. For the same reason they refused to accept of any ransom for the fort, though the governor offered to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> 300,000 dollars for it. The Spanish military and the inhabitants were treated with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; their personal effects remaining untouched; and this generosity must have appeared to greater advantage, when contrasted with the behaviour of their own countrymen at Honduras, where the British were treated with remarkable severity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> plate and ornaments were restored, on condition that the terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> should be faithfully kept. In a short time, however, it appeared that it would have been better to have accepted of a ransom for the fort, as from circumstances at that time it could not be retained in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. A garrison was indeed left for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> on the departure of the British squadron; but as it was very inconsiderable, on account of the small number of men that could be spared, the Spaniards quickly determined to make an attempt to regain the fort. For this purpose a body of 2000 men were collected, who invested it on the 25th of November. The British defended it with the utmost bravery; keeping up a constant fire on the enemy, and obliging them to retire for shelter, and take up their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> behind a hill. Here they made preparations for an assault, in which their numbers left the success, as they supposed, by no means dubious. The garrison was therefore summoned to surrender, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of the honours of war and a safe conveyance to Great Britain, denouncing at the same time the utmost vengeance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a refusal; which being refused, the necessary preparations were made for an escalade. The condition of the garrison was now such as could afford very little hope of being able to make any effectual resistance. They were but 85 in number, most of whom were become incapable of duty either from illness or excessive fatigue. They were now also obliged to make one sentinel answer for five, by shifting his place, and challenging as many times. There was no surgeon to attend the sick and wounded; nor had they even any water but what came from a floop of war that lay abreast of the fort. In this desperate situation, they resolved, notwithstanding the menaces of the Spanish commander to render the place as unserviceable as they could. For this purpose they spiked up all the guns; destroying the stores and ammunition that could not be carried off; they even locked the gates of the fort, after which they embarked without the loss of a single man. All this was performed in defiance of the large force that besieged them; and the exploit, when duly considered, must appear not less a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of astonishment than the extraordinary manner in which the fort had been taken. The officer who commanded in this remarkable retreat was Captain Hulke of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>.

OMOPHAGIA

Pages 149-149

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek festival, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, named Omophagos, i.e. eater of raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. This festival was observed in the same manner with the other festivals of Bacchus, in which they counterfeited madness. What was peculiar to it, was, that the worshippers used to eat the entrails of goats, raw and bloody, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the god, who was supposed to do the same thing.

OMPHACINE OIL

Pages 149-149

a viscous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> juice extracted from green olives. With this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> athletæ, when going to wrestle, anointed themselves; and when that gymnastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> was over, they rolled themselves in the sand, which, mixing with the oil and sweat on their bodies, constituted the frigmenta so highly esteemed in the cure of several diseases. This precious medicine was carefully scraped off the body of the athleta with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> something like a comb, which was called frigilis; and such was the demand for the scrapings, that they were a very lucrative article of trade.

OMPHALE

Pages 149-150

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Lydia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Jardanus. She married Tmolus, who at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> left her mistress of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Omphale had been informed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> exploits of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, and wished to see so illustrious a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. Her wish was soon gratified. After the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Eurytus, Hercules fell sick, and was ordered to be held as a slave, that he might recover his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his senses. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> was commissioned to sell him, and Omphale bought him, and restored him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. The hero became enamoured of his mistress, and the queen favoured his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and had a son by him, whom some call Agelaus, and others Lamon. From this son were descended Gyges and Croesus; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is different from the account which makes these Lydian monarchs. monarchs <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from Alcaeus, a son of Hercules, by one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> servants of Omphale. Hercules is represented by the poets as so desperately enamoured of the queen, that, to conciliate her esteem, he spins by her side among her women, while she covers herself with the lion's skin, and arms herself with the club of the hero, and often strikes him with her sandals, for the uncouth manner with which he holds the distaff, &c. Their fondness was mutual. As they once travelled together, they came to a grotto on Mount Timolus, where the queen drest herself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of her lover, and obliged him to appear in a female garment. After they had supped, they both retired to rest in different rooms, as a sacrifice on the morrow to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> required. In the night Faunus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, who was enamoured of Omphale, introduced himself into the cave. He went to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the queen, but the lion's skin persuaded him that it was the dress of Hercules; and therefore he repaired to the bed of Hercules, in hopes to find there the object of his affections. The female dress of Hercules deceived him, and he laid himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by his side. The hero was awakened, and kicked the intruder into the middle of the cave. The noise awoke Omphale, and Faunus was discovered lying on the ground, greatly disappointed and ashamed.

OMPHALEA

Pages 150-150

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledonous family; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

OMPHALO-MESENTERIC

Pages 150-150

in Anatomy. All foetuses are wrapped up in at least two coats <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> membranes; most of them have a third, called allantoides, or urinary. Some, as the dog, cat, hare, &c., have a fourth, which has two blood-vessels, viz. a vein and an artery, called omphalo-mesenteries, because passing along the string to the navel, and terminating in the mesentery.

OMRAH

Pages 150-150

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the Mogul empire; a nobleman. It is the plural of the Arabic ameer.

ON

Pages 150-150

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and by the Greeks, on that account, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>. (See Heliopolis.) It was remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and learning of its priesthood, and for the spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in which they cultivated the studies of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. The priests of On were esteemed more noble than all the other priests of Egypt. They were always privy counsellors and ministers of state; and therefore, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> resolved to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> prime minister, he very wisely gave him in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of On, thereby incorporating him into the most venerable caste in Egypt. Bishop Warburton thinks that the superior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of the priests of On was chiefly owing to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. That they were much given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of astronomy, we know from the testimony of Strabo; and indeed nothing is more probable than that they should be attached to the study of that system over which their god, the Sun, presided, not only in his exalted, but also in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> capacity. The learned prelate affirms, that "whether they received the doctrine from original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> invented it at hazard (which last supposition he thinks more probable, though we are of a very different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>), it is certain they taught that the Sun is in the centre of its system, and that all the other bodies move round it in perpetual revolutions. This noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> (he continues) came with the rest of the Egyptian learning into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> (being brought thither by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who received it from Oenuphis*; a* Plut.de priest of On); and after having given the most illustrious of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, it sunk into obscurity, and P. 632. suffered a total eclipse throughout a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> succession of learned and unlearned ages; till these times restored its ancient splendour, and immovably fixed it on the unerring principles of science." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it be true, as some philosophers allege, that Moses appears from the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> to have been acquainted with the true solar system, this account of the origin of that system is extremely probable. As it is of no importance to the civil or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of a state whether the system of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> or that of Copernicus be admitted by the people, we cannot reasonably suppose that the Jewish lawgiver was taught astronomy by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> from Heaven. But there can be no doubt of his knowing as much of that science as the priests of On; for we know that he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; and therefore, if he held the sun to be in the centre of the system, it is morally certain that the same thing was held by that priesthood.

ONALASHKA

Pages 153-153

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Northern Archipelago, visited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in his last voyage. The native inhabitants of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> are, to all appearances, a very peaceable people, having been much polished by the Russians, who now keep them in a state of subjection. As the island furnishes them with subsistence, so it does, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, with clothing, which is chiefly composed of skins. The upper garment, which is made like a waggoner's frock, reaches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Besides this, they wear a waistcoat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of breeches, a fur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, and a pair of boots, the legs of which are formed of some kind of strong gut; but the soles and upper-leathers are of Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Fish and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> animals, birds, roots, berries, and even sea weed, compose their food. They dry quantities of fish during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, which they lay up in small huts for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in winter. They did not appear to be very deficient of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, not to want any other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, except sewing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, their own being formed of bone. With these they sew their canoes, and make their clothes, and also <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> their curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. They use, instead of thread, the fibres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which they split to the thickness required. All sewing is performed by the females, who are shoemakers, tailors, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>-builders. They manufacture mats and baskets of grass, which are both strong and beautiful. There is indeed a neatness and perfection in most of their works, that shows they are deficient neither in ingenuity nor perseverance. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is sometimes severe, Captain Cook did not observe a fire-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in any of their habitations. They are lighted as well as heated by lamps; which, though simple, effectually answer the purpose for which they are intended. They consist of a flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, hollowed on one side like a plate; in the hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> they put the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, mixed with some dry grass, which serves for a wick. Both sexes often warm themselves over one of these lamps, by placing it between their legs, under their garments, and fitting thus over it for several minutes. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 139. 29. N. Lat. 53. 5.

ONANIA

Pages 150-151
or **ONANISM**, terms employed to denote the crime of self-pollution, mentioned in Scripture to have been committed by Onan, and punished in him with death. This practice, however common, hath among all nations been reckoned a very great crime. In Scripture, besides the instance of Onan above mentioned, we find self-polluters termed effeminate, unclean, filthy, and abominable. Even the heathens, who had not the advantage of revelation, were of the same opinion, as appears from the following lines of Martial. *Hoc nihil esse putes! scelus est, mihi crede; sed ingens Quantum vis animo concepis ipse tuo.* You think 'tis nothing! 'tis a crime, believe! A crime so great you scarcely can conceive. Dr Tissot has published a treatise on the pernicious effects of this shameful practice, which appears to be no less baneful to the mind than to the body. He begins with observing, that, by the continual waste of the human body, aliment are required for our support. These aliment, however, require certain preparations in the body itself; and when by any means we become altered that these preparations cannot be effected, the best aliment then prove insufficient for the support of the body. Of all the causes by which this morbid alteration is brought on, none is more common than too copious evacuations; and of all evacuations, that of the semen is the most pernicious when carried to excess. It is also to be observed, that though excess in natural venery is productive of very dangerous disorders, yet an equal evacuation by self-pollution, which is an unnatural way, is productive of others still more to be dreaded. The consequences enumerated by Dr Tissot are as follow: 1. All the intellectual faculties are weakened; the memory fails; the ideas are confused, and the patient sometimes... sometimes even falls into a flight degree of insanity. They are continually under a kind of inward restlessness, and feel a constant anguish. They are subject to giddiness; all the senses, especially those of seeing and hearing, grow weaker and weaker, and they are subject to frightful dreams. 2. The strength entirely fails, and the growth in young persons is considerably checked. Some are afflicted with almost continual watching, and others dole almost perpetually. Almost all of them become hypochondriac or hysterical, and are afflicted with all the evils which attend these disorders. Some have been known to spit calcareous matters; and others are afflicted with coughs, slow fevers, and consumptions. 3. The patients are affected with the most acute pains in different parts of the body, as the head, breast, stomach, and intestines; while some complain of an obtuse sensation of pain all over the body on the slightest impression. 4. There are not only to be seen pimples on the face, which are one of the most common symptoms; but even blotches, or suppurative pustules, appear on the face, nose, breast, and thighs; and sometimes fleshy excrescences arise on the forehead. 5.
