The organs of generation are also affected; and the semen is evacuated on the slightest irritation, even that of going to stool. Numbers are afflicted with an habitual gonorrhoea, which entirely destroys the vigour of the constitution, and the matter of it resembles a fetid fumes. Others are affected with painful priapisms, dysuries, stranguries, and heat of urine, with painful tumours in the testicles, penis, bladder, and spermatic cords; and impotence in a greater or less degree is the never-failing consequence of this detestable vice. 6. The functions of the intestines are sometimes totally destroyed; and some patients complain of coliciveness, others of diarrhoea, piles, and the running of a fetid matter from the fundament. With regard to the cure, the first step is to leave off those practices which have occasioned the disease; which our author affirms is no easy matter; as, according to him, the foul itself becomes polluted, and can dwell on no other idea; or if he does, the irritability of the parts of generation themselves quickly recall ideas of the same kind. This irritability is no doubt much more to be dreaded than any pollution the foul can have received; and by removing it, there will be no occasion for exhortations to discontinue the practice. The principal means for diminishing this irritability are, in the first place, to avoid all stimulating, acrid, and spiced meats. A low diet, however, is improper, because it would further reduce the body, already too much emaciated. The food should therefore be nutritive, but plain, and should consist of flesh rather roasted than boiled, rich broths, &c. ONCA and ONCE. See Felis Mammalia Index. ONEEHOURA and ONEEHOW, two small islands of that cluster which was discovered by Captain Cook, and by him called the Sandwich Islands. (See Sandwich Islands). Oneehoura is very small, and its chief produce is yams. Oneehow is considerably larger, being about ten miles over. It is remarkable for the great quantity of excellent yams which it produces, and for a sweet root called tee or tea, which is generally about the thickness of a man's wrist, though sometimes much larger. This root, which the natives commonly bake previous to their bringing it to market, is of a wet clammy nature, and with proper management makes excellent beer.

ONEGA

Pages 151-151

a river and lake of the Russian empire, between Mulcovite Carelia, the territory of Cargapol, and Swedish Carelia. It is 100 miles in length and 40 in breadth, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the lake <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADOGA">Ladoga</a>, and consequently with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. The river has its source in Cargapol, and gives its name to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> full of woods, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

ONEGLIA

Pages 151-151

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality; but it belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, which abounds in olive trees, fruit, and wine. It has often been taken and retaken in the wars of Italy, which is no wonder, as it is an open <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The French and Spaniards had possession of it in 1744, but were driven out by the Piedmontese; however, they retook it the following winter. It was last taken by the French in 1794. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 51. N. Lat. 43. 58.

ONEIROCRITICA

Pages 151-151

the art of interpreting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a method of foretelling future events by means of dreams. See Dream, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">Divination</a>, &c.—The word is formed from the Greek σνείος, "dream," and κρίνω, of κρίνειν, "judgment."—Some call it ονειροκρίτικα; and derive it from σνείος and κρίνω, "I profess, I command." It appears from several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, that there was, under the Jewish dispensation, such a thing as foretelling future events by dreams; but then there was a particular gift or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> required for that purpose. Hence it has been inferred, that dreams are really significative, and do forebode something to come; and all that is wanting among us is the oneirocritica, or the art of knowing what: yet it is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of many, that dreams are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> chimeras; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> indeed some relation to what has passed, but none to what is to come. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, it was possible for God, who knew all things, to discover to him what was in the womb of fate; and to introduce that, he might take the occasion of a dream.

ONEIROCRITICS

Pages 151-152

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to interpreters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those who judge of events from the circumstances of dreams. There is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> regard to be had to those Greek books called oneirocritics; nor do we know why the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Constantinople, and others, should amuse themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> on so pitiful a subject. Hugault has given us a collection of the Greek and Latin works of this kind; one attributed to Athramphius; another to Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople; to which are added the treatises of Artemidorus and Achmet. But the books themselves are little else than reveries; a kind of waking dreams, to explain and account for sleeping ones. The secret of oneirocriticism, according to them all consists in the relation supposed to be between the dream and the thing signified: but they are far from keeping to the relations of agreement and similitude; and frequently have recourse to others of dissimilitude and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a>. Concerning oneirocritics and oneirocritica, rocritics, the unlearned reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find much information in Warburton's Divine Legation of Moses, and the books to which he refers. ONESIAE THERMAE were, according to Strabo excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and salutary waters, at the foot of the Pyrenees in Aquitania. Near the river Aturus stands at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the town <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGNERES">Bagneres</a>, famous for its waters, which appear to be the Onese of Strabo; situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Bigorre in Gascony, near the river Adour. ONIÆ OPPIDUM and Templum (Josephus); so called from Onias, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Jews in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; who built a temple in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of that at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, by permission of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Egypt, on the spot where stood the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Ageritis in Leontopolis: it was encompassed with a brick wall, and had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tower like that at Jerusalem (Josephus); it was the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Nomos Heliopolites, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>;) because in Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> was fallen to decay.

ONGLEE

Pages 152-152

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an appellation given to the talons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> claws of beasts or birds, when borne of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from that of the body of the animal. ONION. See Allium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of its cultivation, see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> Index.

ONISCUS

Pages 152-152

a genus of insects belonging to the order of aptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ONKELOS

Pages 152-152

surnamed the Profylate, a famous rabbi of the first century, and the author of the Chaldee Targum on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>. He flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, according to the Jewish writers; who all agree that he was, at least in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Ben Uzziel, author of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Targum upon the prophets. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Prideaux thinks he was the elder of the two, for several reasons; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is the purity of the style in his Targum, therein coming nearest to that part of Daniel and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> which is in the Chaldee, and is the truest standard of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and consequently is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; since that language, as well as others, was in a constant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> deviating in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> from the original; nor does there seem to be any reason why Jonathan Ben Uzziel, when he undertook his Targum, should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and begin with the prophets, but that he found Onkelos had done this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> before him, and with a success which he could not exceed. Azarias, the author of a book entitled Meor Enaim, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the eyes, tells us, that Onkelos was a proselyte in the time of Hillel and Samai, and lived to see Jonathan Ben Uzziel one of the prime scholars of Hillel. These three doctors flourished 12 years before Christ, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Gauz; who adds, that Onkelos was contemporary with Gamaliel the elder, St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who was the grandson of Hillel, who lived 28 years after Christ, and did not die till 18 years before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. However, the same Gauz, by his calculation, places Onkelos 100 years after Christ; and to adjust his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with that of Azarias, extends the life of Onkelos to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length. The Talmudists tell us that he assisted at the funeral of Gamaliel, and was at a prodigious expense to make it most magnificent. Dean Prideaux observes, that the Targum of Onkelos is rather a version than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a>; since it renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text word for word, and for the most part accurately and exactly, and is by much the best of all this sort: and therefore it has always been held in esteem among the Jews much above all the other Targums: and being set to the same musical notes with the Hebrew text, is thereby made capable of being read in the same tone with it in their public assemblies.—From the excellency and accuracy of Onkelos' Targum, the dean also concludes him to have been a native Jew, since without being bred up from his birth in the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and learning, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> exercised in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and doctrines thereof, and being also thoroughly skilled in both the Hebrew and Chaldee languages, as far as a native Jew could be, he can scarce be thought thoroughly adequate to that work which he performed; and that the representing him as a proselyte seems to have proceeded from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of taking him to have been the same with Akilas, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">Aquila</a>, of Pontus, author of the Greek Targum or version of the prophets and Hagiography, who was indeed a Jewish proselyte.

ONOCLEA

Pages 152-152

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogamia class and order of Filicet. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ONOMANCIA

Pages 152-152
or rather ONOMANTIA, a branch of divination, which foretells the good or bad fortune of a man, from the letters in his name. See the article Divination and Name. From much the same principle the young Romans toasted their mistresses as often as there were letters in their names: Hence Martial says, Necia sex cyathis, septem Suffina bibatur.

ONOMATOPOEIA

Pages 152-152

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> where words are formed to resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> made by the things signified; as the buzz of bees, the cackling of hens, &c. Resemblances of this kind are often fancied when they are not real, though, no doubt, there are in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> some words of which the sound is very like to that which those words are employed to express. Yet, to the mortification of grammarians and rhetoricians, conjunctions, which have been justly pronounced no parts of speech, are the only sounds uttered by men that are wholly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and these are fewer than is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed. See Grammar and Language.

ONONIS

Pages 152-152

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the dandelion class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ONOPORDUM

Pages 152-152

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ONOSANDER

Pages 152-152

a Greek author and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who wrote Commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s Polities, which are lost; but his name is particularly famous for a treatise entitled Λόγος Ἐρευνητικός, "Of the duty and virtues of the general of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>?" which has been translated into Latin, Italian, Spanish, and French. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when he lived is not precisely known: but is imagined to be in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius.

ONOSMA

Pages 152-152

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 41st order, Apertifolae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ONTARIO

Pages 152-153

a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Iroquois, 180 miles in length and 65 in breadth. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that run into it: and from ONTOLOGY. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No. 3. ONYCOMANCY; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as some write it, ONYMANCY; a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> by means of the nails of the fingers.—The word is formed from the Greek ὄνυξ "nail," and μαντεία, "divination." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice was to rub the nails of a youth with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and root, or wax; and to hold up the nails thus smeared against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.—Upon them were supposed to appear figures or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which showed the thing required.

OONELLA

Pages 153-153

and OONEMAH, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the same archipelago with Onalashka; the former of which lies to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, being separated from it by a navigable strait; the other is more to the westward, being in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 192. 30. and N. Lat. 54. 30. The circumference of Oonella is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues, and the produce of both much the fame with that of Onalashka.

OPACITY

Pages 153-153

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of bodies which renders them imperious to the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

OPALIA

Pages 153-153

in Antiquity, feasts celebrated at Rome in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Ops. Varro says they were held on the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, which was one of the days of the Saturnalia: these two feasts were celebrated in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, because <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Ops were husband and wife: the vows offered to the goddess were made fitting on the ground.

OPARO

Pages 153-153
or OPARRO, a small island in S. Lat. 27° 36', and in E. Long. 215° 49', which was discovered by Vancouver. This island was supposed to be about 6½ miles long, and it was out of sight of any other land. It is composed of craggy mountains, forming in several places perpendicular cliffs from their summits to the sea, having narrow valleys or chasms interposed. On some of the highest hills were observed some kind of works, resembling fortified places; but as the discoverers did not land on the island, they could not learn their nature and use. In their language and appearance the natives resembled those of the Friendly islands; they seemed acquainted with the use of iron, preferring it to beads and other trinkets, and showed a hospitable disposition. There appeared to be anchoring ground near the north-west end of the island.

OPERA

Pages 153-153

a dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> set to music, and sung on the stage, accompanied with musical instruments, and enriched with magnificent dresses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and other decorations.—This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of drama is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. In its present state it was not known even in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> before the beginning of the last century; and at its introduction into England, a century afterwards, it divided the wits, literati, and musicians of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. By those who were esteemed the best judges of the art, the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was considered as too rough and inharmonious for the music of the opera; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, critics, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> was built on the basis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, looked upon a drama in a foreign and unknown tongue as the greatest of all absurdities. Many of them, however, pleaded for operas in the English language; and it is well known that Addison, who was one of the opposers of the Italian opera on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> stage, wrote in his native tongue the opera of Roland. This is confessedly a beautiful poem; but, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Dr Burney, it adds nothing to Addison's fame, as it shows his total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the first principles of music, and of course his unfitness for the task he had undertaken. In questions respecting the fine arts there is no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> from the general taste; and therefore, as the French opera, which is in the language of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where it is acted, has always been admired by persons of liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, it doubtless has merit conferred as a drama; but how the dramas of this kind which are composed in Italian should find admirers in England among persons who understand not a word of the language, it is to us a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of astonishment. The music of them may deserve and command the admiration of every one who...

OPHITES

Pages 184-184

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics, so called from both the veneration they had for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> that tempted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, and the worship they paid to a real serpent: they pretended that the serpent was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and that he taught men the knowledge of good and evil. They distinguished between Jesus and Chivay: Jesus, they said, was born of the Virgin, but Christ came <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven to be united with him; Jesus was crucified, but Christ had left him to return to heaven. They distinguished the God of the Jews, whom they termed Jaldabaoth, from the supreme God: to the former they ascribed the body, to the latter the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. They had a live serpent, which they kept in a kind of cage; at certain times they opened the cage door, and called the serpent: the animal came out, and mounting upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, twined itself about some loaves of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; this bread they broke and distributed it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, who all kissed the serpent: this they called their Eucharist.

OPIATES

Pages 184-184

medicines which are administered to procure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, whether in the form of electuaries, drops, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pills. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">OPINION</a> is that judgement which the mind forms of any proposition for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> or falsehood of which there is not sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> to produce science or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. That the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> triangle are equal to two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> angles, is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of opinion, nor can it with propriety be called an object of the mathematician's belief: he does more than believe it; he knows it to be true. When two or three men, under no temptation to deceive, declare that they were witnesses of an uncommon, though not preternatural event, their testimony is complete evidence, and produces absolute belief in the minds of those to whom it is given; but it does not produce science like rigid demonstration. The fact is not doubted, but those who have it on report do not know it to be true, as they know the truth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> intuitively or demonstrably certain. When one or two men relate a story including many circumstances to a third person, and another comes who positively contradicts it either in whole or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, he to whom those jarring testimonies are given, weighs all the circumstances in his own mind, balances the one against the other, and lends an assent, more or less wavering, to that side on which the evidence appears to preponderate. This assent is his opinion respecting the facts of which he has received such different accounts. Opinions are often formed of events not yet in being. Were an officer from the combined armies, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now besieging <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIENNES">Valenciennes</a>, to come into the room where we are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and tell us that those armies are in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirits; that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> which they fire upon the fortresses produces some effect; and that they have plenty of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, whilst the besieged are perishing by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>; we should absolutely believe every fact which he had told us upon the evidence of his testimony; but we could only be of opinion that the garrison must soon surrender. In forming opinions of this kind, upon which, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> depends our success in any pursuit, every circumstance should be carefully attended to, and our judgements guided by former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Truth is a thing of such importance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, that he should always pursue the best methods for attaining it; and when the object eludes all his researches, he should remedy the disappointment, by attaching himself to that which has the strongest resemblance to it; and that which most resembles truth is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, as the judgement which is formed of it is termed opinion. See Probability.

OPORTO

Pages 184-185
or Porto, a flourishing city and seaport of Portugal, in the province of Entre-Douro-e-Minho, with a bishop's see. Nature has rendered it almost impregnable; and it is justly celebrated for the strength of its wines, large quantities of which are exported. ported to Britain, and on this account all red wines either from Spain or Portugal are denominated port wines. After the earthquake at Lisbon in the year 1755, the trade of this city increased rapidly, before which memorable period its population did not exceed 20,000; but it is now computed at upwards of 40,000. Oporto is situated on the declivity of a mountain, near the river Douro, which forms an excellent and commodious harbour; and is about 147 miles north by east of Lisbon. W. Long. 8° 21'. N. Lat. 41° 10'.

OPOUN

Pages 185-185

one of the Navigators <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, of which there are ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, first discovered by Bougainville, and so called by him, because the inhabitants do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one village to another but in canoes. This and the other islands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in 14° south latitude, and from 171° to 173° <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> west from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, according to Peroufe. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> is to be met with growing spontaneously; but it is said to contain less of the saccharine substance than what is produced in the West Indies. The men are possessed of uncommon strength, and tattoo their bodies in such a manner that, although almost naked, they have the appearance at a little distance of being clothed. Ferocity and treachery are characteristic marks of this people, of which the unfortunate Peroufe had but too soon a melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, ii out of 60 of his crew having been murdered by them, although received at first with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of good humour. This ought to serve as a caution to future navigators, not to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> implicit confidence in the apparent kindness of these savages, which is frequently the opulent prelude of ruin and destruction. Among these fell the celebrated naturalist Lamanon; see LAMANON.

OPTICS

Pages 301-334
Apparatus by the combination of oxygen with any combustible sub- stance? Measuring Light. The ingenious author's experiments all conspired to show that the resistance of the air to light is too inconsiderable to be perceptible, and that the assumed law of the diminution of the intensity of light may be dependent upon with safety. He admits, however, that means may be found for rendering the air's resistance to light apparent; and he seems to have thought of the very means which occurred for this purpose to M. de Saufure. That eminent philosopher, wishing to ascertain the transparency of the atmosphere, by measuring the distances at which determined objects cease to be visible, perceived at once that his end would be attained, if he should find objects of which the disappearance might be accurately determined. Accordingly, after many trials, he found that the moment of disappearance can be observed with much greater accuracy when a black object is placed on a white ground, than when a white object is placed on a black ground; that the accuracy was still greater when the observation was made in the sun than in the shade; and that even a still greater degree of accuracy was obtained, when the white space surrounding a black circle, was itself surrounded by a circle or ground of a dark colour. This last circumstance was particularly remarkable, and an observation quite new. If a circle totally black, of about two lines in diameter, be fastened on the middle of a large sheet of paper or pasteboard, and if this paper or pasteboard be placed in such a manner as to be exposed fully to the light of the sun, if you then approach it at the distance of three or four feet, and afterwards gradually recede from it, keeping your eye constantly directed towards the black circle, it will appear always to decrease in size the farther you retire from it, and at the distance of 33 or 34 feet will have the appearance of a point. If you continue still to recede, you will see it again enlarge itself; and it will seem to form a kind of cloud, the darkness of which decreases more and more according as the circumference becomes enlarged. The cloud will appear still to increase in size the farther you remove from it; but at length it will totally disappear. The moment of the disappearance, however, cannot be accurately ascertained; and the more experiments were repeated the more were the results different. M. de Saufure, having reflected for a long time on the means of remedying this inconvenience, saw clearly, that, as long as this cloud took place, no accuracy could be obtained; and he discovered that it appeared consequence of the contrast formed by the white parts which were at the greatest distance from the black circle. He thence concluded, that if the ground was left white near this circle, and the parts of the pasteboard at the greatest distance from it were covered with a dark colour, the cloud would no longer be visible, or at least almost totally disappear. This conjecture was confirmed by experiment. M. de Saufure left a white space around the black circle equal in breadth to its diameter, by placing a circle of black paper a line in diameter on the middle of a white circle three lines in diameter, so that the black circle was only surrounded by a white ring a line in breadth. The whole was pasted upon a green ground. A green colour was chosen, because it was dark enough to make the cloud disappear, and the easiest to be procured. The black circle, surrounded in this manner with white on a green ground, disappeared at a much less distance than when it was on a white ground of a large size. If a perfectly black circle, a line in diameter, be pasted on the middle of a white ground exposed to the open light, it may be observed at the distance of from 44 to 45 feet; but if this circle be surrounded by a white ring a line in breadth, while the rest of the ground is green, all sight of it is lost at the distance of only 15 feet. According to these principles M. de Saufure delineated several black circles, the diameters of which increased in a geometrical progression; the exponent of which was 3. His smallest circle was \( \frac{1}{3} \) or 0.2 of a line in diameter; the second 0.3; the third, 0.45; and so on to the sixteenth, which was 87.527, or about 7 inches 3\(\frac{1}{2}\) lines. Each of these circles was surrounded by a white ring, the breadth of which was equal to the diameter of the circle, and the whole was pasted on a green ground. M. de Saufure, for his experiments, selected a straight road or plain of about 1200 or 1500 feet in circumference, which towards the north was bounded by trees or an ascent. Those who repeat them, however, must pay attention to the following remarks: When a person retires backwards, keeping his eye constantly fixed on the pasteboard, the eye becomes fatigued, and soon ceases to perceive the circle; as soon therefore as it ceases to be distinguishable, you must suffer your eyes to rest; not, however, by shutting them, for they would when again opened be dazzled by the light, but by turning them gradually to some less illuminated object in the horizon. When you have done this for about half a minute, and again directed your eyes to the pasteboard, the circle will be again visible, and you must continue to recede till it disappear once more. You must then let your eyes rest a second time in order to look at the circle again, and continue in this manner till the circle becomes actually invisible. If you wish to find an accurate expression for the want of transparency, you must employ a number of circles, the diameters of which increase according to a certain progression; and a comparison of the distances at which they disappear will give the law according to which the transparency of the atmosphere decreases at different distances. If you wish to compare the transparency of the atmosphere on two days, or in two different places, two circles will be sufficient for the experiment. According to these principles, M. de Saufure caused to be prepared a piece of white linen cloth eight feet square. In the middle of this square he sewed a perfect circle, two feet in diameter, of beautiful black wool; around this circle he left a white ring two feet in breadth, and the rest of the square was covered with pale green. In the like manner, and of the same materials, he prepared another square; which was, however, equal to only \( \frac{1}{3} \) of the size of the former, so that each side of it was 8 inches; the black circle in the middle was two inches in diameter, and the white space around the circle was 2 inches also. If two squares of this kind be suspended vertically Apparatus and parallel to each other, so that they may be both illuminated in an equal degree by the sun; and if the atmosphere, at the moment when the experiment is made, be perfectly transparent, the circle of the large square, which is twelve times the size of the other, must be seen at twelve times the distance. In M. de Saufure's experiments the small circle disappeared at the distance of 314 feet, and the large one at the distance of 3588 feet, whereas it should have disappeared at the distance of 3768. The atmosphere, therefore, was not perfectly transparent. This arose from the thin vapors which at that time were floating in it. M. de Saufure calls his instrument a daphanometer; but it serves one of the purposes of a photometer. From a number of experiments made with the photometer, Count Rumford found, that, by passing through a pane of fine, clear, well polished glass, such as is commonly made use of in the construction of looking-glasses, light loses \( \frac{1}{973} \) of its whole quantity, i.e., of the quantity which impinges on the glass; that when light is made to pass through two panes of such glass standing parallel, but not touching each other, the loss is \( \frac{1}{3184} \) of the whole; and that in passing through a very thin, clear, colourless pane of window-glass, the loss is only \( \frac{1}{1263} \). Hence he infers, that this apparatus might be very usefully employed by the optician, to determine the degree of transparency of glass, and direct his choice in the provision of that important article of his trade. The loss of light when reflected from the very best plain glass mirror, the author ascertained, by five experiments, to be \( \frac{1}{4} \) of the whole which fell upon the mirror. An ingenious photometer has also been invented by Professor Leslie, and fully described in his celebrated work on Heat, to which we must refer the reader for a complete description of this instrument. It measures the calorific effect of heat, and is founded upon this principle, "that if a body be exposed to the sun's rays, it will, in every possible case, be found to indicate a measure of heat exactly proportional to the quantity of light which it has absorbed." See Essay on Heat, p. 103. **CHAP. II. On the method of forming the Lens and Specula, of Refracting and Reflecting Telescopes.** **Sect. I. On the Method of grinding and polishing Lenses.** Having fixed upon the proper aperture and focal distance of the lens, take a piece of sheet copper, and strike a fine arch upon its surface, with a radius equal to half that distance, if it is to be plano-convex, and let the length of this arch be a little greater than the given aperture. Remove with a file that part of the copper which is without the circular arch, and a convex gage will be formed. Strike another arch with the same radius, and having removed that part of the copper which is within it, a concave gage will be obtained. Prepare of the two circular plates of brass, about \( \frac{1}{10} \) of an inch thick, and half an inch greater in diameter than the breadth of the lens, and folder them upon a cylinder of lead of the same diameter, and about an inch high. These formation tools are then to be fixed upon a turning lathe, and one of them turned into a portion of a concave sphere, so as to suit the convex gage; and the other into a portion of a convex sphere, so as to answer the concave gage. After the surfaces of the brass plates are turned as accurately as possible, they must be ground upon one another, alternately, with flour emery; and when the two surfaces exactly coincide, the grinding tools will be ready for use. Procure a piece of glass whose dispersive power is as small as possible, if the lens is not for achromatic instruments, and whose surfaces are parallel; and by means of a pair of large feelers or pincers, cut it into a circular shape, so that its diameter may be a little greater than the required aperture of the lens. When the roughness is removed from its edges by a common grindstone (A), it is to be fixed with black pitch to a wooden handle of a smaller diameter than the glass, and about an inch high, so that the centre of the handle may exactly coincide with the centre of the glass. The glass being thus prepared, it is then to be ground with fine emery upon the concave tool, if it is to be convex, and upon the convex tool, if it is to be concave. To avoid circumlocution, we shall suppose that the lens is to be convex. The concave tool, therefore, which is to be used, must be firmly fixed to a table or bench, and the glass wrought upon it with circular strokes, so that its centre may never go beyond the edges of the tool. For every 6 circular strokes, the glass should receive 2 or 3 cross ones along the diameter of the tool, and in different directions. When the glass has received its proper shape, and touches the tool in every point of its surface, which may be easily known by inspection, the emery is to be washed away, and finer kinds (B) successively substituted in its room, till by the same alternation of circular and transverse strokes, all the scratches and imperfections are removed from its surface. After the finest emery has been used, the roughness which remains may be taken away, and a slight polish superinduced by grinding the glass with pounded pumice-stone, in the same manner as before. While the operation of grinding is going on, the convex tool should, at the end of every five (A) When the focal distance of the lens is to be short, the surface of the piece of glass should be ground upon a common grindstone, so as to suit the gage as nearly as possible; and the plates of brass, before they are foldered on the lead, should be hammered as truly as they can be done into their proper form. By this means much labour will be saved both in turning and grinding. (B) Emery of different degrees of fineness may be made in the following manner. Take five or six clean vessels, and having filled one of them with water, put into it a considerable quantity of flour emery. Stir it well with a piece of wood, and after standing for 5 seconds pour the water into the second vessel. After it has stood about 12 seconds, pour it out of this into a third vessel, and so on with the rest; and at the bottom of each vessel will be found emery of different degrees of fineness, the coarsest being in the first vessel, and the finest in the last. Method of five minutes, be wrought upon the concave one for a few seconds, in order to preserve the same curvature to the polishing tools and the glass. When one side is finished off with the pumice-stone, the lens must be separated from its handle by inserting the point of a knife between it and the pitch, and giving it a gentle stroke. The pitch which remains upon the glass may be removed by rubbing it with a little oil, or spirits of wine; and after the ground side of the glass is fixed upon the handle, the other surface is to be wrought and finished in the very same manner. When the glass is thus brought into its proper form, the next and the most difficult part of the operation is to give it a fine polish. The best, though not the simplest way of doing this, is to cover the concave tool with a layer of pitch, hardened by the addition of a little rosin, to the thickness of one-fifteenth of an inch. Then having taken a piece of thin writing paper, press it upon the surface of the pitch with the convex tool, and pull the paper quickly from the pitch before it has adhered to it; and if the surface of the pitch is marked everywhere with the lines of the paper, it will be truly spherical, having coincided exactly with the surface of the convex tool. If any paper remains on the surface of the pitch, it may be removed by soap and water; and if the marks of the paper should not appear on every part of it, the operation must be repeated till the polisher, or bed of pitch, is accurately spherical. The glass is then to be brought on the polisher by circular and cross strokes, with the oxide of tin, called the flowers of putty in the shops, or with the red oxide of iron, otherwise called colcothar of vitriol, till it has received on both sides a complete polish (c). The polishing will advance slowly at first, but will proceed rapidly when the polisher becomes warm with the friction. When it is nearly finished, no more putty or water should be put upon the polisher, which should be kept warm by breathing upon it; and if the glass moves with difficulty from its adhesion to the tool, it should be quickly removed, lest it spoil the surface of the pitch. When any particles of dust or pitch infuse themselves between the glass and the polisher, which may be easily known from the very unpleasant manner of working, they should be carefully removed, by washing both the polisher and the glass, otherwise the lens will be scratched, and the bed of pitch materially injured. The operation of polishing may also be performed by covering the layer of pitch with a piece of cloth, and giving it a spherical form by pressing it with the convex tool when the pitch is warm. The glass is wrought as formerly, upon the surface of the cloth, with putty or colcothar of vitriol, till a sufficient polish is induced. By this mode the operation is slower, and the polish less perfect; though it is best fitted for those who have but little experience, and would therefore be apt to injure the figure of the lens by polishing it on a bed of pitch. (c) As colcothar of vitriol is obtained by the decomposition of martial vitriol, it sometimes retains a portion of this salt. When this portion of martial vitriol is decomposed by dissolution in water, the yellow ochre which results penetrates the glass, forms an incrustation upon its surface, and gives it a dull and yellowish tinge, which is communicated to the image which it forms. (d) The finest land which we have met with in this country, is to be found at Roxburgh castle, in the neighbourhood of Kelso. In this manner the small lenses of simple and compound microscopes, the eye-glasses and the object-glasses of telescopes, are to be ground. In grinding concave lenses, Mr Imison* employs leaden wheels with the same radius as the curvature of the lens, and with their circumferences as the convexity of the lens is to be concave. These spherical zones are fixed upon a turning lathe, and the lens, which is held steadily in Improperly the hand, is ground upon them with emery, while they are revolving on the spindle of the lathe. In the same way convex lenses may be ground and polished, by fixing the concave tool upon the lathe; but these methods, however simple and expeditious they may be, should never be adopted for forming the lenses of optical instruments, where an accurate spherical figure is indispensible. It is by the hand alone that we can perform with accuracy those circular and transverse strokes, the proper union of which is essential to the production of a spherical surface. Appendix to Ferguson's Lectures, vol. ii. p. 452. Sect. II. On the Method of Casting, Grinding, and Polishing the Specula of Reflecting Telescopes. The metals of reflecting telescopes are generally composed of 32 parts of copper, and 15 of grain tin, of the metal with the addition of two parts of arsenic, to render the composition more white and compact. The Reverend Mr Edwards found, from a variety of experiments, that if one part of brass, and one of silver, be added to the preceding composition, and only one part of arsenic used, a most excellent metal will be obtained, which is the whitest, hardest, and most reflective, that he ever met with. The superiority of this composition, indeed, has been completely evinced by the excellence of Mr Edwards' telescopes, which excel other reflectors in brightness and distinctness, and show objects in their natural colours. But as metals of this composition are extremely difficult to cast, as well as to grind and polish, it will be better for those who are inexperienced in the art, to employ the composition first mentioned. After the flasks of fund (d) are prepared, and a mould made for the metal by means of a wooden or metallic pattern, so that its face may be downwards, and a few small holes left in the sand at its back, for the free escape of the included air—melt the copper in a crucible by itself, and when it is reduced to a fluid state, fuse the tin in a separate crucible, and mix it with the melted copper, by stirring them together with a wooden spatula. The proper quantity of powdered arsenic, wrapped up in a piece of paper, is then to be added, the operator retaining his breath till its noxious fumes are completely dissipated; and when the scoria is removed from the fluid mass, it is to be poured out as quickly as possible into the flasks. As soon as the metal is become solid, remove it from the flask into some hot ashes or coals, for the purpose of annealing. Method of annealing it, and let it remain among them till they are completely cold. The ingate is then to be taken from the metal by means of a file; and the surface of the speculum must be ground upon a common grindstone, till all the imperfections and asperities are taken away. When Mr Edwards' composition is employed, the copper and tin should be melted according to the preceding directions, and, when mixed together, should be poured into cold water, which will separate the mals into a number of small particles. These small pieces of metal are then to be collected and put into the crucible, along with the silver and bras, after they have been melted together in a separate crucible; the proper quantity of arsenic is to be added, and a little powdered rosin thrown into the fluid metal before it is poured into the flasks. When the metal is cast, and prepared by the common grindstone for receiving its proper figure, the gages and grinding tools are to be formed in the same manner as for convex lenses, with this difference only, that the radius of the gages must always be double the focal length of the speculum. In addition to the convex and concave bras tools, which should be only a little broader than the metal itself, a convex elliptical tool of lead and tin should also be formed with the same radius, so that its transverse may be to its conjugate diameter as 10 to 9, the latter being exactly equal to the diameter of the metal. On this tool the speculum is to be ground with flour emery, in the same manner as lenses, with circular and cross strokes alternately, till its surface is freed from every imperfection, and ground to a spherical figure. It is then to be wrought with great circumspection, on the convex bras' tool, with emery of different degrees of fineness, the concave tool being sometimes ground upon the convex one, to keep them all of the same radius; and when every scratch and appearance of roughness is removed from its surface, it will be fit for receiving the final polish. Before the speculum is brought to the polisher, it has been the practice to smooth it on a bed of stones, or a convex tool made of common blue stones. This additional tool, indeed, is absolutely necessary, when silver and bras enter into the composition of the metal, in order to remove that roughness which will always remain after the finest emery has been used; but when these metals are not ingredients in the speculum, there is no occasion for the bed of stones. Without the intervention of this tool I have finished several specula, and given them as exquisite a lustre as they could possibly have received. Mr Edwards does not use any bras tools in his process, but transfers the metal from the elliptical leaden tool to the bed of stones. By this means the operation is simplified, but we doubt much if it is, in the least degree, improved. As a bed of stones is more apt to change its form than a tool of brass, it is certainly of great consequence that the speculum should have as true a figure as possible before it is brought to the stones; and we are persuaded, from experience, that this figure may be better communicated on a bras' tool, which can always be kept at the same curvature by its corresponding tool, than on an elliptical block of lead. We are certain, however, that when the speculum is required to be of a determinate focal length, this length will be obtained more precisely with the bras tools than without them. But Mr Edwards has observed, that these tools are not only unnecessary, but 'really detrimental.' That Mr Edwards found them unnecessary, we cannot doubt, from the excellence of the specula which he formed without their affluence; but it seems inconceivable how the bras tools can be in the least degree detrimental. If the mirror is ground upon 20 different tools before it is brought to the bed of stones, it will receive from the last of these tools a certain figure, which it would have received even if it had not been ground on any of the rest; and it cannot be questioned, that a metal wrought upon a pair of bras tools, is equally, if not more, fit for the bed of stones, than if it had been ground merely on a tool of lead. When the metal is ready for polishing, the elliptical leaden tool is to be covered with black pitch, about polishing one-twentieth of an inch thick, and the polisher formed the metal in the same way as in the case of lenses, either with the concave bras tool, or with the metal itself. The colochar of vitriol should then be triturated between two surfaces of glass, and a considerable quantity of it applied at first to the surface of the polisher. The speculum is then to be wrought in the usual way upon the polishing tool till it has received a brilliant lustre, taking care to use no more of the colochar, if it can be avoided, and only a small quantity of it, if it should be found necessary. When the metal moves fluidly on the polisher, and the colochar assumes a dark muddy hue, the polish advances with great rapidity. The tool will then grow warm, and would probably stick to the speculum, if its motion were discontinued for a moment. At this stage of the process, therefore, we must proceed with great caution, breathing continually on the polisher, till the friction is so great as to retard the motion of the speculum. When this happens, the metal is to be flipped off the tool at one side, cleaned with soft leather, and placed in a tube for the purpose of trying its performance; and if the polishing has been conducted with care, it will be found to have a true parabolic figure. Appendix to Ferguson's Lectures, vol. ii. p. 457.

OPTIO

Pages 339-339

an officer in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, being an assistant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a>. The optio was so called because he was the choice or option of the centurion in later times; at first, however, he had been chosen by the tribune, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commander of the legion. These optiones are also sometimes called succenturiates and tergitudinarii; the last name was given them because their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> was in the rear of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Some authors make mention of sub-optiones or sub-lieutenants. It is proper, however, to add, that optiones were not peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, but were also used in a variety of other offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

OPTION

Pages 339-340

the power <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of wishing, or choosing; or the choice a person makes of any thing. When a new suffragan bishop is consecrated, the archbishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, by a customary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, claims the collation of the first vacant benefice, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, in that see, according as he shall choose; which choice is called the archbishop's option. But in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the bishop dies, or is translated, before the the present incumbent of the promotion chosen by the archbishop shall die or be removed, it is generally supposed that the option is void; inasmuch as the grantor, singly and by himself, could not convey any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of his continuance in that see. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the archbishop dies before the avoidance shall happen, the right of filling up the vacancy shall go to his executors or administrators.

OR

Pages 340-340

the French word for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, by which this metal is expressed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>. In engraving it is denoted by small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> all over the field or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>. It may be supposed to signify itself, generosity, splendour, or fidelity; according to G. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is compounded with Gul. \[ \begin{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>}{l} \text{Courage.} \\ \text{Truft.} \end{array} \] Azu. \[ \begin{array}{l} \text{Joy.} \\ \text{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a>.} \end{array} \] Vor. \[ \begin{array}{l} \text{Confiancy.} \\ \text{Confiancy.} \end{array} \] Pur. \[ \begin{array}{l} \text{Confiancy.} \\ \text{Confiancy.} \end{array} \] Sab. \[ \begin{array}{l} \text{Confiancy.} \\ \text{Confiancy.} \end{array} \]

ORA

Pages 340-340

in antiquity, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to an ounce; but it has been much debated among our antiquaries, whether the ora, the mention of which so often occurs, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account. Dr Hiekes observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of reckoning money by marks and oras was never known in England till after the Danish settlements; and by examining the old nummulary climates among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Gothic states upon the Baltic, it appears, that the ora and solidus were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms, and that the ora was the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mark. From several of the Danish laws, it likewise appears, that the Danish ora, derived by corruption from aureus, was the same as the Frank solidus of twelve pence. As a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the ora was regarded as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINA">mina</a> or unit, by which the Danish mark was divided; and in Doomsday book the ora is used for the ounce, or the twelfth part of the nummulary Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, and the fifteenth of the commercial: as a coin, it was an aureus, or the Frank solidus of twelve pence. And from the accidental coincidence of the Frank aureus with the eighth part of their mark, the Danes probably took occasion to give it the new name of ora. There was another ora mentioned in the rolls of the 27th of Henry III. the value of which was sixteen pence; and this was probably derived from the half mancus of the Saxons. Such, in all appearance, was the original of these two oras; as there were no aurei of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, to which these two denominations of money of sixteen and twelve pence can possibly be ascribed. It is observed farther, that the name ora distinguishes the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> coins in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The Portuguese moideira is nothing else but moeda d'oro, from the Latin moneta de auro; the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> d'ors come from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word, and owe their appellation to the ora. See Clarke on Coins. ORACH. See ATRIPLEX, Wild ORACH. See CHENOPODIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ORACLE

Pages 340-343

among the heathens, was the answer which the gods were supposed to give to those who consulted them upon any affair of importance. It is also used for the god who was thought to give the answer, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it was given. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> was so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that in all doubts and disputes their determinations were held sacred and inviolable: whence vast numbers flocked to them for advice about the management of their affairs; and no business of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was undertaken, scarce any peace concluded, any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> waged, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any new form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> instituted, without the advice and approbation of some oracle. The answers were usually given by the intervention of the priests or priestesses of the god who was consulted; and generally expressed in such dark and unintelligible phrases, as might be easily wrested to prove the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the oracle whatever was the event. It is not, therefore, to be wondered at, that the priests who delivered them were in the highest credit and esteem, and that they managed this reputation so greatly to promote their own particular advantage. They accordingly allowed no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to consult the gods, before he had offered costly sacrifices, and made rich presents to them. And to keep up the veneration for their oracles, and to prevent their being taken unprepared, they admitted persons to consult the gods only at certain stated times; and sometimes they were so cautious, that the greatest performances could obtain no answer at all. Thus Alexander himself was peremptorily denied by the Pythia, or priestess of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, till she was by downright force obliged to ascend the tripod; when, being unable to resist any longer, she cried out, Thou art invincible: and these words were accepted instead of a farther oracle. Of the ambiguity of oracles, the following, out of a great many examples, may be mentioned. Croesus having received from the Pythianess this answer, That by palling the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>, he would destroy a great empire; he understood it to be the empire of his enemy, whereas he destroyed his own.—The oracle consulted by Pyrrhus gave him an answer, which might be equally understood of the victory of Pyrrhus, and the victory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> his enemies: Aio te, Æacida, Romanos vincere posse. The equivocation lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the Latin tongue, which cannot be rendered in English.—The Pythones advised Croesus to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Lydia understood nothing of the oracle, which denoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> descended from two different nations; from the Medes, by Mandana his mother, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a>; and from the Persians, by his father Cambyses, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> was by far less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and illustrious.—Nero had for answer, from the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a>, that seventy-three might prove fatal to him. He believed he was safe from all danger till that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but, finding himself deserted by every one, and hearing Galba proclaimed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, who was 73 years of age, he was sensible of the deceit of the oracle. When men began to be better instructed by the lights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> had introduced into the world, the false oracles infinibly lost their credit. Chrysippus filled an entire volume with false or doubtful oracles. Oenomaus, to be revenged of some oracle that had deceived him, made a compilation of oracles, to show their ridiculous vanity. Eusebius has preserved some fragments of this criticism on oracles by Oenomaus. "I might (says <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>) have recourse to the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>, to make the Pythones much suspected; I might extract from the writings..." writings of Epicurus and his sectors an abundance of things to discredit oracles; and I might shew that the Greeks themselves made no great account of them." The reputation of oracles was greatly lessened when they became an artifice of politics. Themistocles, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of engaging the Athenians to quit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and to embark, in order to be in a better condition to resist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, made the Pythones d'Ever an oracle, commanding them to take refuge in wooden walls. Demoithenes said, that the Pythones <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>-pized; to signify that he was gained over by Philip's pretexts. The cessation of oracles is attested by several profane authors; as Strabo, Juvenal, Lucan, and others. Plutarch accounts for it, by saying, that the benefits of the gods are not eternal as themselves are; or that the genii, who presided over oracles, are subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; or that the exhalations of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> had been exhausted. It appears that the last reason had been alleged in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Cicero, who ridicules it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">Divination</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the spirit of prophecy, supposed to be excited by subterraneous effluvia, had evaporated by length of time, as wine or pickle by being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> kept. Suidas, Nicephorus, and Cedrenus, relate, that Augustus, having consulted the oracle of Delphos, could obtain no other answer but this: "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> child whom all the gods obey, drives me hence, and sends me back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>: get out of this temple without speaking one word." Suidas adds, that Augustus dedicated an altar in the Capitol, with this inscription, "To the eldest Son of God." Notwithstanding these testimonies, the answer of the oracle of Delphos to Augustus seems very suspicious. Cedrenus cites Eusebius for this oracle, which is not now found in his works; and Augustus's peregrination into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> was 18 years before the birth of Christ. Suidas and Cedrenus give an account also of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> oracle delivered to Thulis, a king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, which they say is well authenticated. The king having consulted the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAPIS">Serapis</a>, to know if there ever was, or would be, one so great as himself, received this answer: First, God, next the Word, and the Spirit with them. They are equally eternal, and make but one, whose power <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never end. But thou, mortal, go hence, and think that the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of man is uncertain." Van Dale, in his treatise of oracles, does not believe that they ceased at the coming of Christ. He relates several examples of oracles consulted till the death of Theodosius the Great. He quotes the laws of the emperors Theodosius, Gratian, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, against those who consulted oracles, as a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of oracles still subsisted in the time of those emperors. According to others, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of those who believe that demons had no share in the oracles, and that the coming of the Messiah made no change in them, and the contrary opinion of those who pretend that the incarnation of the Word imposed a general silence on all oracles, should be equally rejected. They allege, that two sorts of oracles ought to be distinguished: the one dictated by the spirits of darkness, who deceived men by their obscure and doubtful answers; the other, the pure artifice and cheat of the priests of false divinities. As to the oracles given out by demons, the reign of Satan was destroyed by the coming of the Saviour; truth that the mouth of lies; but Satan <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his old craft among idolaters. All the devils were not forced to silence at the same time by the coming of the Messiah; it was on particular occasions that the truth of Christianity, and the virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, imposed silence on the devils. St. Athanasius tells the Pagans, that they have been witnesses themselves that the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> puts the devils to flight, silences oracles, and dissipates enchantments. This power of silencing oracles, and putting the devils to flight, is also attested by Arnobius, Lactantius, Prudentius, Minutius Felix, and several others. Their testimony is a certain proof that the coming of the Messiah had not imposed a general silence on oracles. Plutarch relates, that the pilot Thamus heard a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, crying out, "The great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> is dead;" whereupon Eusebius observes, that the accounts of the death of the demons were frequent in the reign of Tiberius, when Christ drove out the wicked spirits. The same judgment, it is said, may be passed on oracles as on predictions. It was on particular occasions, by the divine permission, that the Christians <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out devils, or silenced oracles, in the presence, and even by the confession, of the Pagans themselves. And thus it is we should, it seems, understand the palliages of St Jerome, Eusebius, Cyril, Theodore, Prudentius, and other authors, who said that the coming of Christ had imposed silence on the oracles. As to the second sort of oracles, which were pure artifices and cheats of the priests of false divinities, and which probably exceeded the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those that immediately proceeded from demons, they did not cease till idolatry was abolished, though they had lost their credit for a considerable time before the coming of Christ. It was concerning this more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and general sort of oracles that Minutius Felix said, they began to discontinue their responses, according as men began to be more polite. But, however oracles were decreed, impostors always found dupes, the greatest cheats having never failed. Daniel discovered the imposture of the priests of Bel, who had a private way of getting into the temple to take away the offered meats, and who made the king believe that the idol confirmed them.—Mundus, being in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with Paulina, the eldest of the priestesses of Isis, went and told her, that the god Amibus, being passionately fond of her, commanded her to give him a meeting. She was afterwards shut up in a dark room, where her lover Mundus, whom she believed to be the god Amibus, was concealed. This imposture having been discovered, Tiberius ordered those detestable priests and priestesses to be crucified, and with them Idea, Mundus's free woman, who had conducted the whole intrigue. He also commanded the temple of Isis to be levelled with the ground, and her statue to be thrown into the Tiber; and, as to Mundus, he contented himself with sending him into banishment. Theophilus, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, not only destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the false gods, but discovered the cheats of the priests, by showing that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, some of which were of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and others of wood, were hollow within, and led into dark palliages made in the wall. Lucian, in discovering the impostures of the false prophet Alexander, says, that the oracles were chiefly afraid of the subtleties of the Epicureans and Chritians. The false prophet Alexander sometimes feigned himself seized with a divine fury, and by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> popowort, which he chewed, frothed at the mouth in an extraordinary manner, that the ignorant people attributed it to the strength of the god he was possessed by. He had long before prepared a head of a dragon made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, which opened and shut its mouth by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. He went by night to a place where the foundations of a temple were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>; and having found <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, either of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that had settled there, he hid in it a goose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, in which he had enclosed a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> that had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> hatched.
